title: fix(capability-client,ts-capability-client,go-capabilityclient,dart-capability-client): bind a capability reply to the request it answers
body:
The four capability clients (Rust `trust-tasks-capability-client`, TS `@openvtc/trust-tasks-capability-client`, Go `trust-tasks-go/capabilityclient`, Dart `trust_tasks_capability_client`) matched a reply to its request by `threadId` and slug alone. The HTTPS clients apply four equalities to a response; these applied one. As a result:

- a `trust-task-error` under any authority, for example `https://elsewhere.example/spec/trust-task-error/9.9`, carrying `git-trust/grant:already_granted` on the right thread was reported as an idempotent success of a write;
- a `git-trust/revoke#response` on a grant's thread was reported as a successful grant;
- an enable/disable acknowledgement without `enabled` was reported as "disabled", and a listing without `capabilities` as "no capabilities";
- in TypeScript, a body whose `payload` was missing or not an object threw a `TypeError` from the classifiers.

## What changed (the same in all four ports)

**New, request-bound classifiers.** Each takes the document you sent instead of its thread id:

| | Rust | TypeScript | Go | Dart |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| binding check | `answers_request` | `answersRequest` | `AnswersRequest` | `answersRequest` |
| git-trust writes | `classify_git_trust_reply_to(reply, request, policy)` | `classifyGitTrustReplyTo(reply, request, policy?)` | `ClassifyGitTrustReplyTo(reply, request, policy)` | `classifyGitTrustReplyTo(reply, request, {policy})` |
| governance replies | `parse_capability_reply_to(reply, request)` | `parseCapabilityReplyTo` | `ParseCapabilityReplyTo` | `parseCapabilityReplyTo` |

A reply answers a request when all of the following hold:

- its `threadId` is the request's correlation thread;
- its `issuer` is the request's `recipient`, and its `recipient` is the request's `issuer` (each checked where the request named one, and absence is a mismatch);
- its `type` is the request's `type` with `#response`, or the framework's `trust-task-error` under `https://trusttasks.org/spec/`, in which case a payload `inResponseTo.id`, where present, must be the request's `id`.

The git-trust form only accepts a `git-trust/grant` or `git-trust/revoke` request. The governance form only accepts a `governance/capability/*` request.

**Existing thread-only classifiers, tightened.** `classify_git_trust_reply[_with_policy]`, `parse_capability_reply`, `parse_envelope_reply` and their ports:

- read `trust-task-error` as a refusal only under the registry's authority, and a family `#response` only under the registry's authority;
- return "not an answer" (`None` / `undefined` / `ok=false` / `null`) for a toggle acknowledgement without a string `capability` and boolean `enabled`. The same applies to a listing without a `capabilities` array, or with any entry lacking `manifest.capability` or a boolean `enabled`. These replies used to be read as defaults.

They still cannot tell a grant's response from a revoke's, or check who answered. The module docs point to the `…_to` forms for that.

**TypeScript**: `parseEnvelopeDocument` (and so every envelope entry point) accepts a body only when `payload` is a JSON object. `errorCodeAndMessage` no longer assumes one.

**Rust**: `try_build_document` returns `CapabilityClientError::Document` for a Type URI that does not parse. `build_document` keeps its signature. It still panics on such input, now with a message naming `try_build_document`, and documents this under `# Panics`. Before, it panicked through `unreachable!`.

## Behaviour changes (R3.6)

- A `trust-task-error` or family `#response` typed under an authority other than `https://trusttasks.org/spec/` is no longer classified. Callers keep waiting, as for any non-answer.
- A listing with any malformed entry is no longer returned with that entry dropped. The whole reply is "not an answer". This changes an existing test in TS, Go and Dart (Rust dropped such entries too).
- A toggle acknowledgement missing `capability` or `enabled` is "not an answer" instead of `{capability: "", enabled: false}`.
- TypeScript: a body without an object `payload` is not parsed as a document. Before, it was parsed and could make a classifier throw.
- No signature changes. Everything else is additive, so this is not marked `!`. A caller that relied on a malformed or foreign-authority reply being classified will now see "not an answer". If reviewers judge that a break for the release, the title can take `!` on the four scopes.

Callers holding the request should move to the `…_to` forms. The thread-only forms are kept, not deprecated, so that callers that only keep a thread id continue to compile without warnings.

## Tests

Each port gains the same three tests:

- **a reply answers only the request it was made for**: another issuer, another recipient, an absent issuer, a revoke's response on a grant's thread, and an error naming another request are each "not an answer". A conforming success, an idempotent refusal, and one naming this request are classified. Families do not mix.
- **only the registry authority is read as this family or an error**.
- **a malformed governance reply reports nothing**: four toggle payloads and four listing payloads.

Each port also has its own tests:

- TypeScript: a body whose payload is `undefined`, `null`, a string, a number or an array is not a document.
- Rust: `try_build_document` returns an error, not a panic.

Only `cargo fmt`, `gofmt` and `dart format` were run locally (and `go vet` on the Go module, by mistake). CI runs the tests.

## Checklist

- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2): pure wire logic, no I/O
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3): n/a
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1): n/a. These functions decide whether a write is reported done; a reply that does not answer the request no longer does.
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4): n/a
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5): a malformed reply is "not an answer", never a throw (TS)
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6): n/a
- [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, deny_unknown_fields where security-relevant, schema registered, all consumers (incl. JS) updated (R3.*): no wire types changed; all four ports changed together
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive; fail-closed if enforcement can't start (R5.*): an unverifiable reply is "not an answer"
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified; background-job failures are surfaced (R6.*): a write is reported done only on a reply bound to its request (`…_to` forms)
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1): no mutations
- [x] Deviations from this guide flagged explicitly with rule numbers: none
author: stormer78
significance_reasons: Normative requirement language changed
Authority, delegation, approval, or revocation semantics
Interoperability, canonicalisation, conformance, or protocol behaviour
Security, privacy, threat, or vulnerability relevance

title: fix(rs,ts,go,dart): issue an error response as the consumer, not as the rejected document's recipient
body:
SPEC §8.1: "The *error response*'s `issuer` is the *consumer* that emitted it." All four runtimes built the error with `issuer: request.recipient`. That is the rejected document's in-band `recipient`, which is wrong in two cases:

- **Refusals raised before §7.2 item 5.** An expired, malformed, unsupported-type or similar document has not had its `recipient` checked, so the error claimed whatever issuer the sender wrote.
- **`wrongRecipient`.** The in-band `recipient` is by definition a party this consumer is not, yet the refusal claimed to be issued by that party.

Example: an authenticated HTTPS caller posting `"recipient": "did:web:bank.example"` to a server whose `localVid` is `did:web:svc.example` got back a `wrongRecipient` error with `"issuer": "did:web:bank.example"`.

## Was it intended?

No. §8.1 states the rule without qualification, and none of the runtimes' docs describe another intent. Success responses are unaffected: `respond_with` also uses `request.recipient`, but only after item 5 has established that it is this consumer or absent. The spec gives no rule for a consumer that does not know its own identity. That case is handled below by leaving the issuer out, which §4.8.1 allows, since a transport-derived identity supplies it.

## What changed (all four runtimes, the transport-level `reject` only)

`TransportHandler::reject` (Rust), `reject` (TS), `Reject` (Go) and `reject` (Dart) now set the error's `issuer` as follows:

- to the transport's own identity (`derive_parties().recipient` / `deriveParties().recipient` / `DeriveParties().Recipient`) where the transport has one. This is the HTTPS server's `localVid`, the TSP/DIDComm recipient, and so on;
- with no transport identity, to the in-band `recipient` as before, **except** under `wrongRecipient`, where the `issuer` is left out.

`reject_with`, `reject_with_recipient`, `rejectWith`, `rejectWithRecipient`, `RejectWithRecipient` and `rejectWithRecipient` are unchanged. These are the builders a handler uses when it refuses after the pipeline has validated the recipient. Every pipeline refusal (`consume_inbound` / `consumeInbound`, the HTTPS servers, the TSP and DIDComm consumers) goes through the transport-level `reject`. The Rust `GuardedConsumer`'s refusal of an unparsable body already issued as the transport's identity.

## Behaviour changes (R3.6)

- Error responses built by the pipelines carry the transport's own identity as `issuer`. For a document whose `recipient` named this consumer, which is every case a conforming producer sends, the value is unchanged.
- `wrongRecipient` and pre-item-5 refusals no longer echo the sender-chosen `recipient` as `issuer`.
- With a transport that has no identity of its own (`UnauthenticatedTransport`, `InMemoryHandler::new()`), a `wrongRecipient` error has no `issuer`.
- A client that checks an error response's `issuer` against the VID it addressed (for example `HttpsClient` with `server_vid` set) now sees the server's real identity on a misaddressed request. Before, it saw the identity it had addressed.
- No signature changes, so this is not marked `!`.

## Tests

Each runtime gains the same case:

- with a transport identity, both `wrongRecipient` and `proofRequired` on a misaddressed document are issued as that identity;
- without one, `wrongRecipient` carries no `issuer`, and `proofRequired` on a correctly addressed document keeps the in-band recipient.

The tests are `trust-tasks-rs/tests/error_flow.rs` `handler_reject_issues_the_error_as_the_consumer`, the TS `consume.test.ts` block "§8.1 — the error response is issued by the consumer", Go `TestRejectIssuesTheErrorAsTheConsumer`, and the Dart `consume_test.dart` group of the same name.

Only `cargo fmt`, `gofmt` and `dart format` were run locally. CI runs the tests.

## Checklist

- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2): n/a
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3): n/a
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1): n/a
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4): n/a
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5): n/a
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6): n/a
- [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, deny_unknown_fields where security-relevant, schema registered, all consumers (incl. JS) updated (R3.*): no type changed; the value of `issuer` on pipeline error responses changes as listed (R3.6); all four runtimes changed together
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive; fail-closed if enforcement can't start (R5.*): with no transport identity, nothing unverified is claimed under `wrongRecipient`
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified; background-job failures are surfaced (R6.*): an error no longer names an issuer the consumer has not established
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1): no mutations
- [x] Deviations from this guide flagged explicitly with rule numbers: none

title: feat(rs,https)!: build the HTTPS server on consume_dispatched; async handlers and auth
body:
The Rust HTTPS server ran its own copy of the §7.2 pipeline, and that copy had drifted from `consume_core` on routing, item 2 and check order (#1089). Its handlers and `Auth::resolve` were synchronous and ran on the async executor (#1090). This PR rebuilds `HttpsServer` on the shared pipeline and adds async handlers and async authentication.

## What changes

**One pipeline.** The server now keeps only what is HTTP: the body limit, the content type, the bearer token and the mapping of an outcome onto a status line. Every framework check runs in `trust_tasks_rs::consume_dispatched_answer` over an `AsyncDispatcher`. Proofs are verified over the body as received (`ProofPolicy::VerifyReceived`, or `RejectIfPresentReceived` with no verifier). The item-11 digest is taken over the received body too, as before.

**trust-tasks-rs additions:**
- `consume_dispatched_answer` and `AnswerOutcome<A>`. This is `consume_dispatched` for a dispatcher whose handlers answer with any `Serialize`. The server's handlers answer `Option<Value>`, where `None` is a fire-and-forget acknowledgement. An answer that serialises to `null` is recorded as "no response", so a duplicate of an acknowledged document is still absorbed in silence (204). `consume_dispatched` is now a thin wrapper over it, and `consume_inbound` is unchanged in shape.
- The checks only the server had are now `ConsumeChecks` options, so every binding can use them:
  - `require_attribution`
  - `proof_did_methods`: the DID-method pre-screen, which runs before the proof policy.
  - `received_bytes` and `default_max_document_bytes`: the per-type `maxDocumentBytes` bound. `consume_inbound` and `consume_dispatched` apply it as soon as the type is known.
- The "identity first when no sender is authenticated" order (§8.1 suppression) is now part of `consume_core` itself. It only differs when the transport reports a recipient but no sender, which is the HTTPS case. The message bindings always authenticate a sender, so they are unaffected.
- `impl ProofVerifier for dyn DynProofVerifier`, so an erased verifier can be handed to `ProofPolicy`.
- `RouteFacts` now carries `MAX_DOCUMENT_BYTES`.

**trust-tasks-https additions:**
- `on_async` and `on_ack_async`. Handlers take the typed request and a `RequestContext` by value and return a future.
- `AsyncAuth` (`resolve_async`, boxed future). A blanket `impl<A: Auth> AsyncAuth for A` means every existing `Auth` keeps working, and `with_auth` now takes `impl AsyncAuth`.
- `with_payload_validator`, for the item-2 schema residue (#1089).
- `max_body_bytes` and `HttpsServer::body_limit()`.

**Includes #1117 (the Rust HTTPS half) and #1121 (the Rust HTTPS half).** Both fell out of the rebuild:
- A registered slug at an unregistered version is now `unsupportedVersion`. A later version whose `extends` chain reaches a registered one is routed to it, with the payload pruned, and answered as the received version's `#response`.
- The router's body limit is the larger of 256 KiB and the largest `maxDocumentBytes` among the registered request types, unless `max_body_bytes` sets it outright.
- After routing, a document over its own type's bound is `malformedRequest`. A type that declares no bound is held to 256 KiB, or to the explicit `max_body_bytes`.

## Wire behaviour that changes (declared break)

Each item names the document affected and the answer it now gets.

1. A known slug at an unregistered `MAJOR.MINOR` is now `unsupportedVersion` (422) instead of `unsupportedType` (422).
2. A later version declaring `extends` to a registered version is now accepted and served (it was `unsupportedType`).
3. **The payload is parsed before validation.** Before, the payload was deserialized after the claim. Now it is deserialized right after routing, before expiry, freshness, identity, the attribution gate and the proof. A document that fails both a payload parse and one of those checks is now `malformedRequest` instead of that check's code. Two cases matter:
   - An unauthenticated, proofless document with a bad payload gets `malformedRequest`, not `proofRequired`.
   - A conflicting resend under a reused `id` with a bad payload gets `malformedRequest`, not `idConflict`.

   `end_to_end.rs` `different_document_under_a_reused_id_is_an_id_conflict` used a member `acl/list/0.3` does not define (`pageSize`) as its "different content". I changed it to a valid `role` filter. The test's intent is unchanged.
4. **Per-spec policy now runs before the claim.** The policy covers `recipient` REQUIRED, `proof` REQUIRED, audience binding and `issuedAt` REQUIRED. It used to run after the claim, inside the dispatch closure, with the claim released on refusal. It now runs before the claim, as `consume_core` does. So a policy-violating document under an `id` that is already recorded is now refused on policy grounds instead of being answered as a duplicate or `idConflict`.
5. **A handler's non-retryable refusal is now recorded.** Before, the server released the claim on every handler refusal. Now it follows `consume_core`:
   - A **retryable** refusal (`unavailable`, …) releases the claim.
   - A **non-retryable** one (`permissionDenied`, …) is recorded. A bit-for-bit resend is answered with the same error document and its own status (403 again), without running the handler.

   A recorded `trust-task-error` replayed as a duplicate keeps its error status rather than 200. `end_to_end.rs` `a_refused_dispatch_releases_the_claim` asserted the old behaviour. It is replaced by `a_retryable_refusal_releases_the_claim` and `a_non_retryable_refusal_is_recorded_and_replayed`. The maintainer confirmed this ("record and replay"). It is `consume_inbound`'s documented semantics (§7.2 "previously determined result"; a new attempt is a new `id`, §8.4), and keeping the old HTTPS behaviour would need a further `ConsumeChecks` option.
6. **Payload-parse messages no longer carry serde detail.** A payload that does not deserialize is `malformedRequest` with `RejectReason::malformed_from_serde`'s category message. This applies to the server and to every `Dispatcher` / `AsyncDispatcher` / `consume_dispatched` caller. The old message was `payload does not match <type>: <serde detail>`, which named the member, the offending value and the offset (§10.4).
7. **Size bounds.** Documents over their type's declared bound, or over 256 KiB for undeclared types under a raised router limit, are `malformedRequest` (400). Documents under a declared bound larger than 256 KiB, previously 413, are accepted.
8. **The claim is keyed per issuer.** The item-11 claim is made with `claim_for(resolved issuer, …)` instead of `claim(…)`. The default implementation delegates. `InMemoryReplayGuard` shares capacity per issuer.

Order relative to `docs/runtime-parity.md` and the Dart server:
- The parity doc's `maxDocumentBytes` row is updated, and a row is added for HTTPS `extends` routing.
- `trust-tasks-dart-https` is documented as mirroring this server step for step, and now differs on items 1–5 and 7. CLAUDE.md says so, and that bringing it into line is the Dart half of #1117/#1121 (decision brief group D).

## API changes (why `!`)

- `rs`: `ConsumeChecks` gains public fields, so a struct literal outside the crate now needs `..ConsumeChecks::not_consequential()`. The three binding crates' `checks()` are updated. #1241's `GuardedConsumer` will need the same one-line change when it merges.
- `https`:
  - `with_auth` takes `impl AsyncAuth`. Source-compatible for every `Auth`.
  - `on` and `on_ack` require `P: Send`, which every generated payload is.
  - `MAX_BODY_BYTES` is unchanged in value. It is now documented as the floor and default bound.

## Handlers and blocking: `block_in_place`, not `spawn_blocking`

The brief suggested `spawn_blocking` for sync handlers. I used `tokio::task::block_in_place` on a multi-threaded runtime (inline on a current-thread one) instead, and documented why. With `spawn_blocking`, a request abandoned by `TimeoutLayer` or by a disconnect releases its item-11 claim while the closure keeps running on the blocking pool. A resend could then execute the effect a second time concurrently with the first. `block_in_place` frees the worker's other tasks without making the handler outlive its request.

The documented consequence: `request_timeout` bounds async handlers, not sync ones. Async handlers are cancelled at an await point, and their claim is released, as `consume_core` already documents. `tokio` gains its `rt-multi-thread` feature in this crate.

## Security review

- **Auth before handler.** The bearer token is resolved before the pipeline. The attribution gate (`require_attribution`, still on by default) runs after identity and before the proof and the handler, in the same place as before.
- **Error routing to the authenticated party.** Pipeline refusals go through `HttpsHandler::reject` (§8.1). Handler refusals are routed the same way, from a header copy of the request. A suppressed answer is still the generic `malformedRequest`/400.
- **Body limit before buffering.** `DefaultBodyLimit` still applies before the body is read. It only grows as far as a registered task's own declaration, so a server that registers no large task never buffers more than 256 KiB.
- **DID-method pre-screen.** The screen and its default (`did:key` only with a verifier) are unchanged and still run before the verifier. The proof is still the last step that can egress before the claim.
- **New exposure.** Payload deserialization now precedes the attribution gate, so an unauthenticated stranger learns "payload malformed" for a supported type. The message is category-only now (item 6), and routing already revealed that the type is supported.
- **Replayed refusals.** A replayed non-retryable refusal is returned to whoever resends the identical document. That is the same exposure the server already had for recorded success responses: identity and attribution still run before the record is consulted.

## Cancellation mid-handler (security review follow-up)

Before, cancelling a request while its async handler ran (timeout, disconnect, RST_STREAM) released the item-11 claim through `HeldClaim::drop` → `release_abandoned`. An effect that had already committed could then execute again on a resend.

Now, once the handler has started, cancellation leaves the claim **in flight**:
- A resend is answered as an in-flight duplicate (`202` over HTTPS) until the record expires with the acceptance window. It is never re-executed.
- Cancellation before the handler first runs still releases the claim, as does cancellation after it returns (during a retryable refusal's release). A handler panic still releases it too.

This is a `consume_core` change, so it applies to every Rust binding. `trust-tasks-rs/tests/replay_guard.rs` `a_cancelled_handler_releases_the_claim_so_a_resend_runs` asserted the old behaviour; it is now `a_handler_cancelled_after_committing_is_not_executed_again`. A new HTTPS test, `an_async_handler_cancelled_after_committing_is_not_executed_again`, covers a 408 followed by a resend that gets 202 with no second execution.

`block_in_place` stays for sync handlers. `spawn_blocking` would no longer double-execute, but it would run on with nobody left to record its result.

## Tests

- New `trust-tasks-https/tests/pipeline.rs` (13 tests) uses hand-written `example.test` payload types. It covers async handlers, async refusal routing, async ack plus a silent duplicate, `AsyncAuth`, a blocking sync handler on a multi-thread runtime, `extends` routing, `unsupportedVersion` vs `unsupportedType`, the derived and overridden body limit, declared and default per-type bounds, 413, and the payload validator.
- New `consume.rs` unit tests cover `require_attribution`, `proof_did_methods`, `received_bytes`, and an acknowledgement recorded as no response.
- The `end_to_end.rs` adaptations are described in items 3 and 5. The server-local `release_tests` unit test is removed with the code it tested; `consume_core`'s `HeldClaim` covers cancellation.

Results:
- `cargo test -p trust-tasks-https`: 66 + 13 + 3 pass.
- `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --features acl`: passes.
- `cargo test -p trust-tasks-tsp -p trust-tasks-didcomm-v1`: passes.
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`: clean.
- `cargo fmt --all --check`: clean.

Part of #1117. Part of #1121.

Closes #1089. Closes #1090.

title: feat(rs,build,ts,ts-gen,go,dart): emit only the $defs each schema constant reaches
body:
Every generated request and response schema constant now carries only the root `$defs` its own root reaches. Before this change, the request schema kept `$defs.Response` and everything only the response uses, and the response document carried a full copy of the request's definitions. Now the request drops those, the response document drops what only the request uses, and `$defs` is left out entirely when nothing is reached. This applies to the Rust `PAYLOAD_SCHEMA` constants, the TypeScript `PAYLOAD_SCHEMA` / `RESPONSE_PAYLOAD_SCHEMA`, the Go `PayloadSchemaJSON` / `ResponsePayloadSchemaJSON` and the Dart `payloadSchemaJson` / `responsePayloadSchemaJson`, in both the prebuilt libraries and the consumer-side generators.

The pruning happens in the generators, not in the registry bundles. A bundle's `schema` and `responseSchema` are unchanged, so `bundleVersion` and every digest pinned in a `trust-tasks.lock` stay the same. Types are still generated from the whole schema, so no generated type is added or removed. Only the text of the schema constants changes.

The rule is the same everywhere: start from the root object without its `$defs` (including the root's own `$ref`, which is all a response document has), follow every `#/$defs/<name>[/...]` reference, and walk each reached definition whole. A local `$ref` of any other form, such as `#` or an anchor, keeps every definition. No current specification has one. Following CLAUDE.md, each generator implements the rule independently: `prune_unreachable_defs` in `trust-tasks-build` (which also covers the prebuilt Rust tree), `pruneUnreachableDefs` in each of the three `build-*-bindings.mjs` scripts and in `trust-tasks-ts-gen`, and its own copies in the Go `trust-tasks-gen` and the Dart generator.

## Measurements

`cargo package -p trust-tasks-rs --no-verify`:

- before: 10,349,753 bytes (9.87 MiB), 89.0 MiB uncompressed
- after: 10,037,990 bytes (9.57 MiB), 81.9 MiB uncompressed

That saves 304 KiB (3.0%) of the compressed crate and gives roughly 335 KiB of headroom below the 9.9 MiB failure line in the `package` job. The crate is still above the 9.5 MiB warning line. The compressed saving is much smaller than the uncompressed one because gzip already removed most of the duplication between the two adjacent literals.

Generated source size (uncompressed, in-tree):

| tree | before | after | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| `trust-tasks-rs/src/specs` | 91.3 MB | 83.8 MB | -8% |
| `trust-tasks-ts/src` | 32.9 MB | 23.7 MB | -28% |
| `trust-tasks-go/specs` | 34.8 MB | 27.4 MB | -21% |
| `trust-tasks-dart/lib/specs` | 40.7 MB | 33.7 MB | -17% |

The uncompressed figures are what a consumer's binary carries as rodata, and what the npm and pub packages unpack to.

## Checks

- `check-bindings` still compares the four shipped schemas with each other. It now also fails when any shipped schema has a `#/$defs/` reference to a definition it does not carry. Comparing the four with each other cannot catch the case where all four make the same pruning mistake. That is not hypothetical: the first draft of this change ignored the root's own `$ref`, emptied every response document's `$defs`, and all four languages agreed. The new check flagged it immediately.
- `check-bundles` now re-derives the pruning itself and compares each pruned bundle schema with the TypeScript module. It checks that `defsOrder` names exactly the bundle's `$defs`, and that, restricted to the pruned set, it matches the TypeScript module's order.
- `trust-tasks-codegen`'s `bundle_agrees_with_generated_module` now asserts the following from the outside, without calling the generator's pruning: the module's schema equals the bundle's apart from `$defs`, each kept definition is identical, no local reference dangles, the request has no `Response`, and the response has one.
- New unit tests for `prune_unreachable_defs` in `trust-tasks-build`.

Ran locally: `npm run regen`, `npm run check-bindings`, `npm run check`, `npm run test:checks`, `npm run build && npm run build-bundles && npm run check-bundles`, `cargo test -p trust-tasks-build --all-features`, `cargo test -p trust-tasks-codegen`, `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --no-default-features --features acl`, `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --features all-specs,validate --test conformance --test validate`, `cargo test -p trust-tasks-example-consumer-app`, the TypeScript core `npm test` and `npm run smoke`, `trust-tasks-ts-gen` `npm test` and `scripts/equivalence.mjs` over the whole registry, the Go `trust-tasks-gen` equivalence test over the whole registry and `go test ./...`, `scripts/check-dart-consumer-generation.mjs`, `dart test`, and `dart format` at the 3.3 floor.

## Why there is no `!`

No public signature changes in any language. Rust's constants are still `Option<&'static str>`. Since #1236 the TypeScript constants are typed `{ readonly [key: string]: unknown }`, so changing the schema text is no longer a type change. Go's `check-go-api-compat.sh` already exempts `PayloadSchemaJSON` / `ResponsePayloadSchemaJSON` value changes, and Dart's constants are strings. Validation results are unchanged because a definition nothing reaches cannot affect them. The one observable difference is for code that reads `$defs.Response` out of the request schema constant to validate responses. That was never documented, and `Response`'s own constant is the supported path.

Closes #1098.

title: fix(tsp,ts-tsp,go-tsp): open a TSP message only when it names this consumer's VID
body:
In a TSP envelope, the receiver VID is written by the sender. The HPKE seal binds it, but it only shows that the message was encrypted to the recipient's **key**, not that the sender addressed it to the recipient's **VID**. The Rust and TypeScript bindings used that VID as the transport recipient (`TspHandler::new(Some(unpacked.receiver), …)`, `new TspTransport(message.receiver || recipientVid, …)`).

A sender holding our X25519 public key could therefore seal a message to it, label both the envelope and the document `recipient` as another VID, and pass the recipient check (§7.2 item 5). The consumer then answered with `issuer` set to that other VID.

## What changed, per port

| Port | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Rust `trust-tasks-tsp` (`pack.rs` `open`, used by `unpack_trust_task`, `TspConsumer::receive` and `receive_dispatched`) | no receiver check (`affinidi-tsp` 0.3 `direct::unpack` takes no receiver VID); transport recipient = wire receiver | a non-empty receiver other than `recipient.id` is refused as `TspError::Upstream(InvalidMessage("the message is not addressed to this receiver"))`; transport recipient = `recipient.id` |
| TypeScript `@openvtc/trust-tasks-tsp` (`unpackTrustTask`, used by `TspConsumer`) | no receiver check (`vti-tsp-js` `unpack` takes no receiver VID); transport recipient = wire receiver | refused as `TspEnvelopeError("notForThisReceiver")`, carrying the authenticated sender; transport recipient = `recipientVid` |
| Go `trust-tasks-go/tsp` | `affinidi-tsp-go`'s `Open` already refuses a receiver other than the opening identity (`KindReceiver`) | same refusal, plus a local check (`FailNotForThisReceiver`) and transport recipient = `recipient.VID` (no change in what is accepted) |
| Dart `trust_tasks_tsp` | `affinidi_tsp`'s `Tsp.open` already refuses it (`TspReceiverException` → `notForThisReceiver`) | unchanged |

In every port, an empty receiver (the NULL-VID form, which none of these bindings sends) is still opened as the configured VID, as before.

The Rust refusal reuses the existing `Upstream` variant, so it maps to `malformedRequest` through `into_reject_reason` like other open failures, and `TspError` gains no variant. This keeps the change non-breaking for an exhaustive `match`.

## Behaviour changes (R3.6)

- Rust and TypeScript: a message sealed to this consumer's key whose receiver VID names another VID is now refused at unpack. Before, it was opened and treated as addressed to that VID.
- Rust, TypeScript and Go: the transport recipient handed to the pipeline is always the configured VID. For a message that passes the new check, this is the same value as before.
- No public signature changes.

## Tests

- Rust `tests/end_to_end.rs`: `a_message_naming_another_receiver_is_refused` packs with `direct::pack` to bob's encryption key under another receiver VID.
- TypeScript `test/tsp.test.ts`: the same message is refused as `notForThisReceiver` and names the sender. A round trip's transport recipient is the configured VID.
- Go `tsp_test.go`: the same message is refused as `FailNotForThisReceiver`. A round trip's `Transport.Local` is the opening identity.

Only `cargo fmt` / `gofmt` were run locally. CI runs the tests.

## Checklist

- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2): n/a
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3): n/a
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1): the refusal is at unpack, before the item-11 record
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4): n/a
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5): n/a
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6): n/a
- [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, deny_unknown_fields where security-relevant, schema registered, all consumers (incl. JS) updated (R3.*): no wire types changed; all four ports now behave the same
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive; fail-closed if enforcement can't start (R5.*): a mismatch fails closed
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified; background-job failures are surfaced (R6.*): the transport recipient is now the identity that opened the message, not a value nobody verified
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1): no mutations
- [x] Deviations from this guide flagged explicitly with rule numbers: none

title: fix(https,dart-https): run the attribution gate before the route lookup
body:
Both HTTPS servers, `trust-tasks-https` (Rust) and `trust_tasks_https` (Dart), looked the route up before the attribution gate. A sender with neither a bearer token nor a proof therefore got `unsupportedType` for an unregistered type and `proofRequired` for a registered one. That made the route table readable without attribution, even though discovery keeps it unreadable without authentication. The Dart server also decoded the payload (`malformedRequest`) before the gate, which gave a second way to tell the two apart.

## What changed

The checks that depend on nothing a route holds now run before the route lookup, in both servers:

1. expiry and recipient, freshness, and identity, in §7.2 order (identity first when there is no authenticated sender, so a misaddressed document is still suppressed per §8.1)
2. the attribution gate
3. the route lookup

The DID-method pre-screen and proof verification still come after the route lookup. So an unregistered `type` still never reaches a resolver, and the existing `unknown_type_is_rejected_before_the_verifier_is_called` test is unchanged.

- Rust (`trust-tasks-https/src/server.rs`): the route lookup moves from before step 4 to after the attribution gate. The module docs and the step comments are renumbered.
- Dart (`trust-tasks-dart-https/lib/src/server.dart`): the envelope checks and the attribution gate move into `_envelopeChecks`, which runs over the parsed envelope before `_lookup`. `_dispatch` keeps the identity resolution it needs for `RequestContext`. It also keeps the DID-method pre-screen after the payload decode, where it was. `consumeInbound` repeats the pure §7.2 checks as before.

## Behaviour changes (R3.6)

- A request with no authenticated sender and no proof is refused `proofRequired` (with `requireAttribution` on, the default) whatever its `type`. Before, an unregistered type got `unsupportedType`, another version of a registered specification got `unsupportedVersion`, and in Dart an oversized or undecodable payload got `malformedRequest`.
- An unattributed misaddressed document is suppressed, as a registered-type one already was. Before, the route lookup answered first for an unregistered type.
- Dart only: a document that fails both a route-level check (size bound, payload decode, version read) and an envelope check (expired, stale, wrong recipient, identity) is now refused for the envelope check. This is the order the Rust server already used.
- Authenticated senders, proof-bearing documents and `requireAttribution: false` see the same answers as before. A sender attributed only by a proof can still tell registered from unregistered types. Such a sender can already invoke any registered handler, so this PR does not change that.

No public API changes.

## Tests

- Rust `end_to_end.rs`: `unattributed_sender_gets_one_answer_for_registered_and_unregistered_types`. An anonymous sender gets `proofRequired` for both a registered and an unregistered type, and an authenticated sender still gets `unsupportedType`.
- Dart `server_test.dart`: a registered type, its `#response`, an unregistered type, an unregistered version, and an undecodable payload all give `proofRequired` without a token. An authenticated sender still gets `unsupportedType`.

Only `cargo fmt` / `dart format` were run locally. CI runs the tests.

## Checklist

- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2): no client code
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3): n/a
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1): the item-11 claim is still after every refusal
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4): n/a
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5): n/a
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6): n/a
- [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, deny_unknown_fields where security-relevant, schema registered, all consumers (incl. JS) updated (R3.*): no wire types changed. The refusal order changed as listed above (R3.6).
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive; fail-closed if enforcement can't start (R5.*): the default (`requireAttribution` on) is the configuration that hides the route table
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified; background-job failures are surfaced (R6.*): unchanged; refusals emit the same events
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1): no mutations moved
- [x] Deviations from this guide flagged explicitly with rule numbers: none

title: fix(build,cli): require a spec slug and version for every locked task, and the canonical path for every index entry
body:
`trust-tasks-build` turns each lockfile entry's slug and version into path segments of the vendored bundle's location (`<bundle_dir>/<slug>/<M.N>.bundle.json`). For a task from a `[sources.*]` table both were already checked, through `type_uri_parts`. For an official task they were only compared with `official_type_uri(slug, version)`, which is built from the same two strings, so any slug and version passed that comparison, including ones with `..` or empty segments. The digest check and the bundle's own slug check still stopped generation, but the file was read first, and its SHA-256 was printed on a mismatch.

## What changed

- `trust-tasks-build`: `LockedTask::check_identity`, which `Lockfile::parse` runs for every entry, now requires `is_spec_slug(slug)` (SPEC §6.1) and `is_spec_version(version)` (SPEC §5.1) first, for official and sourced entries alike.
- `trust-tasks-cli`: `Index::parse` requires each entry's `path` to be `<slug>/<version>/bundle.json`. That is the only form the registry publishes: `check-bundles.mjs` already fails a deploy on any other path, and all 1390 entries in the live index use it. The path was safe before only because `check_slug` runs first and the `path` read is relative to `specs/`. The rule now holds on its own.

## Behaviour changes (R3.6)

- A lockfile with an entry whose slug or version does not have its SPEC form is refused by `Lockfile::parse`, with a message naming the entry. The CLI never writes such an entry: its own lock parser already goes through `TaskId::parse` and `Version::parse`.
- An index (registry or source) with an entry whose `path` is not `<slug>/<version>/bundle.json` is refused by the CLI. Before, the CLI read whatever the path named.

No public signature changes.

## Tests

- `trust-tasks-build`: `an_official_entry_names_a_spec_slug_and_version`, covering `..`, empty, absolute and upper-case slugs, and malformed versions.
- `trust-tasks-cli`: `index_entry_path_names_its_own_bundle`, covering traversal, absolute, other-version, other-slug and absolute-URL paths.

Only `cargo fmt` was run locally. CI runs the tests.

## Checklist

- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2): no client code touched
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3): n/a
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1): n/a, parse-time validation only
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4): n/a
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5): n/a
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6): n/a
- [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, deny_unknown_fields where security-relevant, schema registered, all consumers (incl. JS) updated (R3.*): no wire type changed. The index rule matches what `check-bundles.mjs` already enforces on publish.
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive; fail-closed if enforcement can't start (R5.*): an entry that fails the new checks fails the whole parse
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified; background-job failures are surfaced (R6.*): n/a
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1): no mutations
- [x] Deviations from this guide flagged explicitly with rule numbers: none

title: fix(vta/vtc/voting-service): follow-ups to #2676, #2677 and #2678
body:
Follow-ups from review of #2677, #2678 and #2676 (all merged). There are three commits, one per change.

## 1. Redelivery record: more bearer-carrying responses (follow-up to #2677)

**vta-service**
- The backup initiators `vta/backup/initiate-export/1.1` and `initiate-import/1.1` are classed `[ Mutating None false ]`. Their `descriptor.transportToken` was therefore kept in the duplicate-execution record and handed back on a redelivery.
- A new `BEARER_RESPONSES` list keeps them out of the record, together with:
  - `credential-exchange/pending/approve/0.1` (`vp_token`)
  - `vta/pcs/prove/0.1` and `vta/pcs/attest/0.1` (a spent attestation `token`)
- `records_response` is now one function: secret class, bearer list, or personal state.
- The PR description of #2677 said vta-service never kept these tokens. That was wrong for the backup initiators; it held only for the pre-session `auth/*` family.

**vtc-service**
- `git-ns/account/link/0.1` (a forge device-flow `userCode`) is no longer recorded.
- `vtc/badges/claims/create/0.1` (a claim code the community otherwise keeps only as a digest) is no longer recorded.
- `git-ns/bridge/job/0.7` is a task the VTC sends, not one it serves, so it is outside this record.

**Censuses** (`trust_tasks::response_record_census`, in vtc-service and, new, in vta-service)
- Both now flag every reachable response member whose name contains `token` or `secret` or ends in `code`.
- A flagged member passes only if an allow-list entry names the Type URI prefix, the member and the reason. Allow-listed so far: refusal and error codes, public PCS labels and counts, a consent sync cursor, a device's Play Integrity attestation, a vault entry's `secretKind`, an external account's secret *state* and token endpoint/scope.
- A new token-bearing response now fails the census until someone decides about it.

**Correction to #2677's R3.6 note on refresh.** A redelivered `auth/refresh/0.2` is answered `204`. What happens to a fresh refresh request carrying the old token depends on timing (`vti-common/src/auth/handlers/refresh.rs`, `is_innocent_retry`):
- Inside `refresh_reuse_grace` (30 s), with the successor token still unused, it is treated as an innocent retry and re-serves the rotation.
- Only outside that window is it treated as reuse.

## 2. Badge group: an owner who manages only that group (follow-up to #2678)

New test `a_badge_owner_who_manages_only_its_group_is_refused_update_and_delete`. It covers a member made the badge's owner, and so the badge group's only manager under a grant qualified to that group. That member is refused `vtc/groups/update` and `vtc/groups/delete`. The refusal comes from the badge-group check, not from the manager check, and the group is left unchanged.

## 3. HTTPS door on an open box (follow-up to #2676)

- **The problem.** On an open box (`allow_any`), anyone could mint a `did:key`, register an election over HTTPS as its community, and list any `did:web`/`did:webvh` as an auditor or trustee. A request signed as one of those DIDs then passed `names_party` and was resolved on every request.
- **The fix.** A party an election lists is now resolved on the HTTPS door only when that election's community either:
  - is named in `[communities] allowed`, or
  - is itself a DID that had to be resolved to register. On this door an unlisted community's DID is not resolved, so such a registration came over TSP or DIDComm.

  This needs no new journal state.
- The proof's verification method is now checked with `vti_common::auth::check_issuer_binding`: it must be a DID URL under the issuer, with a non-empty fragment.
- Proof verification, including resolution, is wrapped in a 15 s `tokio::time::timeout`. Past it the request is refused `unavailable`.
- Docs:
  - The operator guide's refusal list is updated.
  - The threat-model table (row 21) is corrected.
  - A new "Still open" note: on an open box, a community that proves its own DID over TSP or DIDComm can still list any DID as a party. Naming communities in `allowed` closes that.

## Behaviour changes (R3.6)

- Within the acceptance window, a redelivery of `vta/backup/initiate-{export,import}/1.1`, `credential-exchange/pending/approve/0.1`, `vta/pcs/{prove,attest}/0.1`, `git-ns/account/link/0.1` or `vtc/badges/claims/create/0.1` gets no body: `204` in vtc-service, absorbed in vta-service. The first execution is unchanged.
- On an open box, an auditor or trustee of an election whose community is a `did:key`/`did:peer` must either sign with a `did:key`/`did:peer` on the HTTPS door or reach the box over TSP or DIDComm. Boxes that list their communities in `allowed`, and elections whose community is a resolved DID, are unaffected.
- A verification method with no fragment is now `proofInvalid`.
- A proof verification that takes more than 15 s is now `unavailable`.

Wire shapes are unchanged. No version or CHANGELOG edits.

## Tests

- `cargo test -p vtc-service -p vti-trust-task-server -p vta-service --no-fail-fast`: 6158 passed, 1 failed. The failure was the new badge test's own assertion: it read owners from `payload.owners`, but the response reports them as `payload.group.managers`. After fixing the assertion, `cargo test -p vtc-service --test it -- badges::a_badge` gave 4 passed, exit 0. The full suite was not rerun after that one-line test fix.
- `cargo test -p vti-voting-service -p vti-voting`: 97 passed, exit 0. New tests:
  - `an_open_box_never_resolves_the_parties_a_did_key_community_names`
  - `a_verification_method_without_a_fragment_is_refused`
  - the existing door test now registers under an allowed community
- `cargo clippy -p vtc-service -p vti-trust-task-server -p vta-service --all-targets -- -D warnings`: exit 0
- `cargo clippy -p vti-voting-service -p vti-voting --all-targets -- -D warnings`: exit 0
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`: exit 0

## Pre-merge checklist

- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2). There are no new clients, and proof verification on the ballot box now has a 15 s bound.
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3). The ballot-box mutex is taken only for the synchronous `names_party` lookup.
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1). Claims still complete after success, now without a body for the listed tasks.
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4). n/a
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5). n/a
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6). n/a
- [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, deny_unknown_fields where security-relevant, schema registered, all consumers (incl. JS) updated (R3.*). No wire types change. Behaviour changes are listed above.
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive; fail-closed if enforcement can't start (R5.*). Without `allowed`, parties of a `did:key` community are not resolved on HTTPS. A verification timeout refuses the request.
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified; background-job failures are surfaced (R6.*). n/a
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1). No mutation paths added.
- [x] Deviations from this guide flagged explicitly with rule numbers. None.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(voting-service): the parties a did:key community names vouch for nobody on the HTTPS door

Follow-up to #2676.

On an open box (`allow_any`), anyone can mint a `did:key`, register an
election over HTTPS as its community, and name any DID as an auditor or a
trustee. `names_party` then let a request signed as one of those DIDs reach
the resolver. Now a party an election lists is resolved on the HTTPS door
only when that election's community is named in `[communities] allowed`, or
is itself a DID that had to be resolved to register: on this door an
unlisted community's DID is not resolved, so that registration came over TSP
or DIDComm. This needs no new journal state.

Also:
- the proof's verification method is checked with
  `vti_common::auth::check_issuer_binding`: a DID URL under the issuer with
  a non-empty fragment;
- verification, resolution included, is bounded at 15 s and refused
  `unavailable` past it.

Docs: the operator guide's refusal list and the threat model (row 21, and an
open-box residual under "Still open").

Behaviour change: on an open box, an auditor or trustee of an election whose
community is a `did:key`/`did:peer` signs with a `did:key`/`did:peer` on the
HTTPS door, or reaches the box over TSP or DIDComm; a bare-DID verification
method is refused; a verification over 15 s is `unavailable`.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(vta-sdk): satisfy clippy needless_bool in is_network

title: feat(understanding): add the proof-of-understanding trust task family and ceremony
body:
Hello, and thank you for taking a look. This is a **draft** and is very open to comment and revision: the shape, the wording and the open questions listed below are all up for discussion, and I would be glad to change anything that does not fit the group's direction.

**Draft.** Opened for review in context rather than for merge; four judgement items are listed under "What is open". Two commits, 1571 added lines across eleven files, no deletions, all under `specs/understanding/*` and `ceremonies/understanding/*`.

## What this adds

**Three draft tasks and a shared schema under `understanding/*`, category `consent` (commit 1).** A joining party and a host reach a bilateral, machine-readable agreement whose shape is IEEE Std 7012-2025 clause 5:

- `understanding/offer`: the joining party asks to begin an engagement; the host answers with a resolvable, versioned, hash-pinned `termsRef` (`uri`, `version`, `digestMultibase`). Where the host's DID document carries a `GovernanceFramework` service (VTI-KEY-052 in the companion PR), the offer MUST name the same document. `proposedIdentifier` must be a `did:`.
- `understanding/exchange`: the joining party answers comprehension questions drawn from the offered terms and the host records whether the answers show understanding. This gate is this framework's own; it is not required or addressed by 7012, whose own approach is a small roster (clause 4.1).
- `understanding/seal`: the joining party proposes an agreement grounded in a passed exchange; the host accepts, counters with a single alternative from the same roster, or refuses (7012 5.3.1 a to c), with no negotiation beyond that single choice (5.2.2). Acceptance is bound to the accepted request by `id` and task digest (SPEC 4.9.3) so a relationship credential or a VAC can cite it; the accepted request's `id` serves as 5.2.3's contract identifier.

Both `exchange` and `seal` bind the request's `issuer` to the party the cited offer or exchange response was addressed to (`issuerMismatch`): thread and document ids are correlation handles, not secrets, so without the binding a third party could answer or seal against someone else's offer and the host's record would name that party.

Departures from 7012 are stated in `seal`'s Relationship section rather than left implicit: the handshake is extended to any two parties (7012 fixes an individual as first party and an entity as second, 5.4.3); a host may point at a roster it authored rather than the neutral registrar clause 4.2 assumes; recording is a SHOULD rather than 7012's shall (5.2.4, 5.3.1, 5.4.4); and no location member is carried (5.4.4).

**The `proof-of-understanding` ceremony definition (commit 2).** `understanding/proof-of-understanding/0.1`: offer, then exchange, then seal between a `joining-party` and a `host`, chained evidence, a one-day window, `enactmentPrivacy: shared` because all three steps reach the same two parties and a single correlatable record of the engagement is what makes the seal citable. The seal step's accept, single-alternative and refuse outcomes follow 7012 5.3.1 under 5.2.2's rule; the exchange step's comprehension check is this framework's own addition. Completion checks only that the seal exchange is present, since this evidence layer cannot express a check over response content, so a relying party must confirm from the step's own documents that the terminal document is the `#response` and not a counter or a refusal carried as `trust-task-error`.

## What is open

1. **A purpose description on the agreement.** IEEE 7012 clause 4.3 wants a "high-level description of the purposes" beside the agreement's name and version. `Agreement` (in `_shared/0.1/agreement.schema.json`) has no description member. Either add one, or record the omission as a further stated departure in `seal`'s Relationship section.
2. **Clause 5.4.5's IP-address requirement.** 7012 says the parties' identifiers must include an IP address. A seal bound to DIDs carries none, and would not want to. This is a further divergence candidate that the Relationship section does not yet record.
3. **`exchange` declares no `outcomeEvidence`.** A VAC that cites the seal inherits an unverifiable grounding for the comprehension step: the seal's grounding in a passed exchange can be checked by id and digest, but the exchange's own result is not declared as outcome evidence under SPEC 7.3 item 20. The gap is disclosed in the specification; whether to declare the exchange response as evidence, or to leave comprehension as a fact the host alone attests, is a judgement call.
4. **Category `consent`.** The `category` enumeration is closed (and append-only, per the repository's check), and `consent` is the nearest existing value for an agreement ceremony. An `agreement` category would be a better name; adding one is a separate change to the enumeration and is not made here.

## How it was checked

`npm run validate` at the branch tip: 1023 specifications validate, 0 non-conforming. `npm run validate-ceremonies`: 4 of 4 ceremony definitions validate, 0 warnings. The three specifications and the ceremony declare `targetFrameworkVersion: "0.6.0"`. Each specification carries `payload.invalid-examples.json` exercising its refusals. Every IEEE Std 7012-2025 clause quoted or cited (4.1, 4.2, 4.3, 5.2.2, 5.2.3, 5.2.4, 5.3.1, 5.4.3, 5.4.4, 5.4.5) was checked against the standard's text; the one-round limit is the standard's own rule, the comprehension step is ours.

## Relation to the discussions

This is the "sealed bilateral agreement as a Trust Task family: offer, exchange, seal" row of the "What exists, and what is missing" table in dtgwg-general discussion 36 (https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-general/discussions/36), listed there as "a draft is ready and will be linked here", and the sealed-agreement section and divergence rows V2 to V4 of that discussion. It sits at the Operations layer of discussion 35 (https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-general/discussions/35), and the five result states there are what a seal's accept, counter and refuse map onto. The decision-point vocabulary and the composition rules of discussion 36 are not in this PR; the seal records a `termsRef`, not values.

**Read together with the companion VTI specification PR** (https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-vti-spec/pull/78): the governance-framework reference shape (`GovernanceFramework` service: `serviceEndpoint`, `version`, `digestMultibase`) is defined there as VTI-KEY-052, and `offer`'s `termsRef` is the same `{ uri, version, digestMultibase }` triple, required to match the host's published service where one exists. A change to the shape in either PR changes the other.

title: Ask a VTC to publish which VRC subjects it admits
body:
Closes #25. **Stacked on #74** (base is #74's branch) so it builds on the reworked correlation-scope text; it retargets to `main` when #74 merges. It doesn't touch the lines #90 changes, and the two merge cleanly together.

Based on geoffturk's proposed text on #25 (7 Sep), with his three open questions answered as follows. Reviewers can push back on any of them:

1. **SHOULD, not MUST, on publication.** A failed cross-community edge is a policy outcome, not a conformance failure. The disclosure-practice requirement is a MUST because without it a member's `pairwise` declaration becomes false; nothing equivalent breaks here.
2. **Subject side only.** The failure case in #25 is about the subject. The issuer's own scope is already declared in `issuerScope` on the credential.
3. **The ordering sentence stays, briefly.** It states the intended ordering and leaves the exchange to the planned DTG Core Trust Task Protocols spec, with no mechanism defined here.

### Changes (`spec/body.md`)
- **New `#### Relationship Admissibility`** at the end of Edge Verifiability (the alternative location geoffturk suggested, which keeps it clear of #90's edits). A VTC whose members issue VRCs SHOULD publish the correlation scopes it accepts for VRC subjects and whether it admits non-member subjects. A VTA SHOULD show a counterparty community's answer before a member issues their half. It states the intended ordering, and that a policy-hiding (ZK) form of mutual admissibility is out of scope (mitchuski's note on #25).
- **Governance Considerations item 10:** these are governance determinations, and publishing them is what makes the pre-flight check possible.

title: Bind a VTC to the disclosure practice it publishes
body:
Closes #81. **Stacked on #74**: the base is #74's branch, because the text lives in the subsection #74 renames ("A scope the controller cannot declare alone"). Once #74 merges, GitHub retargets this to `main`.

Implements the three suggested changes from #81, all in that subsection:

- **A. Pre-join notice is a MUST.** The VTC publishes its *disclosure practice* (whether member identifiers go beyond the VTA, to whom, and whether that depends on declared scope), and the VTA MUST show it before a prospective member chooses a scope.
- **B. The VTC is held to it.** A VTC MUST NOT disclose a member's identifier beyond the practice published when that member joined. A changed practice applies only to members who join or re-acknowledge after the change, and the VTA MUST tell a member before they re-acknowledge.
- **C. A third option.** A VTC MAY publish that it *respects declared scope*: it then MUST NOT disclose a `pairwise` or `directed` member identifier beyond the VTA (directory, presenting the acknowledgement, or otherwise), and MAY disclose a `public` one.

The verifier rule ("MUST NOT infer from a `pairwise` declaration…") is kept, since none of this is checkable from the credentials.

Follow-on edits:
- **Membership lifecycle editor's note:** "withdrawal of consent is self-sovereign" now says it is in the member's hands but all-or-nothing, and does not by itself stop the community disclosing an identifier it already holds (the Exit Rights point in #81).
- **Privacy Considerations item 8:** presenting the acknowledgement to a third party is bounded by the published practice, and a scope-respecting VTC doesn't do it for `pairwise`/`directed` members.
- **Governance Considerations item 3:** updated to match.

Not in scope here (#81's "food for thought"): consent before a VTC presents an acknowledgement, a member-controlled status mechanism, and a ZK acknowledgement form. Those belong to the Trust Task protocols and ZKP specs.

title: Salt every DTG credential so digest references cannot be enumerated
body:
Closes #38.

Implements the placement agreed on #38 (stormer78's 25 Sep proposal, +1 from bmiller59, matching ZKP record 022): one top-level `salt` inside every credential's hashed block, so every digest that references the credential is blinded at once.

### Changes (`spec/body.md`)
- **Base Structure:** new `salt` member: REQUIRED under context `v3` and later, absent under `v1`/`v2`; exactly 32 bytes from a CSPRNG, fresh per credential, never reused or derived, base-58-btc multibase. Kept on re-proof, redrawn on re-issue. Mandatory-disclosure under selective-disclosure suites. Verifiers reject a `v3` credential with a missing or malformed salt. The `@context` bullet now admits later context versions (it already had to, for `v2`).
- **Context Versions:** `v3` = `v2` + `salt`; once its digest is recorded, every credential lists `v3` or later. Editor's note (same pattern as #84): `v3` isn't published yet, so issuers MUST NOT emit `salt` until it is, and examples move to `v3` when the digest is recorded.
- **Digest Encoding:** the "none of these is salted" editor's note becomes a **Salting** subsection: why, a salted grant + acknowledgement example whose `digestMultibase` reproduces from the grant as printed (and the unsalted digest for contrast), and what a salt does *not* do: presentation linkability, `taskDigestMultibase` (going away under #58), and VSC `predicate` blinding stay with ZKP work. Profile-defined digests: SHOULD reference something salted or say why enumeration isn't a concern.
- **Vetting profile** and the **ZK editor's note** updated to point at the new subsection.
- **`CONTEXT.md`:** Salt entry.

### Follow-ups
- **Registry:** `dtgwg-vsc-registry` needs a `v3` context (= `v2` + a plain-string `salt` term) per GOVERNANCE §3.1; then a small PR records the digest, drops the editor's note and moves the examples to `v3` with salts (several example digests will change then).
- **`nodeType` (#53)** could join `v3` if its value list is settled first.
- No Document Status bump here; leaving that for the release that records `v3`.

title: Admit the draft quantum-resistant suites and hybrid proof sets
body:
Addresses parts 1 and 2 of #80. Part 3 (issuers signing a commitment so a ZK presentation never verifies a signature in-circuit) is ZKP task force work and is left open on #80.

### Changes (`spec/body.md`)
- **New "Cryptosuites" subsection** (after Context Versions):
  - `eddsa-jcs-2022` stays RECOMMENDED, with a short explanation of why the issuer signature is the part that must be quantum-safe and why it matters for long-lived credentials (memberships, VAC chain roots).
  - **Quantum-resistant suites (draft):** an issuer MAY sign with `mldsa44-jcs-2024` or `slhdsa128-jcs-2024`, using the identifiers and key encodings the [Trust Tasks framework pins](https://trustoverip.github.io/dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec/#cryptosuites), so a credential and the task document carrying it can share a suite set. Same rule as Trust Tasks: if the W3C draft changes an identifier, that's a new suite. Notes that neither suite is selective-disclosure/unlinkable. FN-DSA isn't mentioned (FIPS 206 not final).
  - **Proof sets:** permitted (e.g. Ed25519 + ML-DSA-44), all by the `issuer`'s controller, evaluated per [VTI-KEY-102 – 105](https://trustoverip.github.io/dtgwg-vti-spec/#selecting-and-verifying-by-role) by reference, summarized as three bullets. Digests are unaffected because Digest Encoding already excludes the whole `proof` member.
- **Base Structure:** `proof` may be an object or a proof set; a governing VTC/VTN may require a quantum-resistant suite.
- **Security Considerations item 1:** added a sentence on proof sets and suite downgrade, folded into the existing item so the list doesn't need renumbering.
- **Informative References:** W3C Quantum-Resistant Cryptosuites v1.0 (experimental draft).

No context change: `proof` and `cryptosuite` come from the VC v2 context.

What merging does, per registry (all in `publish.yml`, each keyed on "this
version is not published yet"):

- **crates.io** — `release-plz-release` tags `<crate>-v<version>`, publishes in
  dependency order and creates a GitHub Release per crate. Bump levels come from
  the commit subjects.
- **npm** — `publish-npm` publishes with OIDC provenance and tags
  `<prefix>-v<version>`.
- **Go** — `verify-go` builds, vets and tests, then `publish-go` pushes the
  tag, which *is* the publication. **Irreversible**: proxy.golang.org never forgets a tag.
- **pub.dev** — `verify-dart` checks each package against the *published* core,
  `tag-dart` pushes the tag, and `publish-dart.yml` publishes from it.

Every bump follows the commit subjects; an undeclared API break is refused on its
pull request by that language's API compatibility check (`rs`, `ts`, `go` and
`Dart API compatibility`).

This branch is regenerated from `main` on every push, so do not commit to it —
edits are force-pushed away. See RELEASING.md.

title: feat(rs,tsp,didcomm,didcomm-v1)!: one guarded consumer for the binding crates; answer an authenticated unparsable body
body:
The TSP, DIDComm v2.1 and DIDComm v1 crates each carried a near-identical consumer wrapper: where the item-11 record lives, the freshness policy, and the calls into `consume_inbound` and `consume_dispatched`. A fix to any of it had to be made three times. That wrapper now lives once in `trust-tasks-rs` as `GuardedConsumer`. `DidcommConsumer`, `TspConsumer` and `DidcommV1Consumer` are thin wrappers that dereference to it and keep the same constructor names. Each binding now keeps only its unpack (an internal `open` that stops before parsing the body) and its envelope check (the DIDComm and DIDComm v1 thread-header cross-check), passed in as a closure. Behaviour change: when the transport has authenticated the sender, `receive` and `receive_dispatched` now answer a body that fails to deserialise, or that fails the thread cross-check. The answer is `Ok(ConsumeOutcome::Rejected(malformedRequest))` instead of an `Err`. That is what each binding's §4 requires, and what the Go bindings (DIDComm, and TSP since #1226) and Dart DIDComm already do. The error response is addressed from the transport-authenticated recipient to the transport-authenticated sender, never to the in-band `issuer`, which nothing has checked yet. It names the document by the `id`, `type` and thread members read one by one from the received JSON. The reason is the category-only `malformed_from_serde` text, so no deserializer detail goes on the wire. Two cases still return an error, reported as the binding's existing error (`InvalidBody` / `InvalidDocument`), through a new `UnanswerableBody` type: a body with no string `id` or no parseable Trust Task `type`, which leaves nothing to name in `inResponseTo`, and a transport that authenticated no sender. Envelope-level refusals are unchanged and still return `Err`: authentication, the allowlist, envelope type, carriage, and a missing v1 attachment. The typed `receive` path now reads the parsed document through `extension::read_as::

`. A `type` that `P` cannot read is therefore answered `unsupportedType` or `unsupportedVersion`, again to the authenticated sender. A later version declaring `extends` to `P`'s version is pruned the same way the dispatched path prunes it. Security review: - Sender authentication, the `skid` and expected-sender enforcement, the TSP cleartext-sender check, and v1's unknown-verkey case are untouched. They run in `open` before any body is parsed. - The DIDComm allowlist is still checked against the advertised `skid` before decryption (`open_from`). - Every new refusal happens before `consume_inbound` / `consume_dispatched`, so it never touches the replay guard and never uses up the document `id`. Each binding has a test showing that a corrected document under the same `id` then executes rather than getting `idConflict`. - The proof is still verified over the body exactly as received (`ProofPolicy::with_received(&body)`), and the item-11 digest is taken over it too. - `consume_core` and `consume_dispatched` are unchanged and do not gain a second copy of any check. This is breaking for `trust-tasks-rs` and the three binding crates, which release together. Existing consumer tests pass unchanged. New tests: a `guarded` unit-test module in `trust-tasks-rs`, and `tests/malformed.rs` in each binding. Those cover a payload that does not parse, a framework member that does not parse, the thread disagreement (DIDComm and v1), a body with no `id`, and the dispatched path. Ran `cargo test` on the three binding crates and on `trust-tasks-rs` with only the `acl` family, `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`, `cargo fmt --all --check`, and rustdoc for the binding crates. CLAUDE.md gains a short section so the wrapper is not duplicated again. Closes #1096.

title: feat(dart,dart-https,dart-didcomm)!: JSON priorResponse, observability hook, forward routing and per-type size bounds
body:
This is the Dart breaking batch. It covers #1118, #1116, and the Dart halves of #1117 and #1121, in one Dart core minor.

## JSON replay record (#1118)

consumeInbound now always records the response as JSON. responseToJson is required. ReplayGuard.recordResponse and Duplicate.priorResponse take a Map<String, dynamic>?. DuplicateOutcome.priorResponse is a Map<String, dynamic>? and has an isError getter (also available as isErrorDocument). The three bindings no longer each carry a switch over "typed document or map". newUrnUuid() now lives in the core and is the default for newErrorId. The HTTPS, DIDComm and TSP packages re-export it, so callers keep compiling and importing both packages is not ambiguous. The capability client and the DIDComm message id use it as well, so the four copies of the generator are gone.

## Observability hook (#1116)

The core gains a sealed ServerEvent hierarchy: DocumentMalformed, AuthenticatorFailed, PayloadDecodeFailed, ProofRejected, HandlerFailed, DocumentSuppressed (which carries the ConsistencyError), DocumentRejected and InternalFailure. It also gains emitServerEvent. HttpsServer, DidcommConsumer and TspConsumer each take an optional onEvent. The hook is called after the decision and is not awaited. Anything it throws, or a future it returns failing, is caught and dropped, so a hook cannot change an answer. With no hook, behaviour is unchanged. io.dart reports its bare-500 path through the same hook.

ProofRejected carries whatever the verifier threw. The ProofVerifier interface returns a bool, so trust_tasks_proof's verifyDetailed text only appears if the application wraps the verifier and throws the result. That is documented on the event.

## Forward routing along extends (Dart part of #1117)

HttpsServer looks up the exact type first. On a miss, it walks the received type's extends chain and routes to the highest registered version of the same specification (same authority, form, slug and variant) that the chain reaches. The document is read through readForVersion, so its payload is pruned to that version's schema. The proof and the item-11 digest stay over the document as received, and the reply is `<received type>#response`. Any other version of a registered specification is answered unsupportedVersion; a specification with no registered version is still unsupportedType. Both consumers now read through readForVersion. All three take an optional extendsIndex for third-party specifications.

## Per-type size bounds (Dart part of #1121)

Both Dart generators, written independently, emit `maxDocumentBytes: N` on `spec` and `responseSpec`, only for a variant that declares a bound (the same rule as Rust's MAX_DOCUMENT_BYTES): scripts/build-dart-bindings.mjs from the front matter, and lib/src/generator/emit.dart from the bundle's policy.maxDocumentBytes. check-bindings-conformance.mjs re-derives the expected value and compares it for Dart as it does for Rust: 70 of 70 bounds match. Forcing a wrong value fails the check. The regeneration adds a line in 48 libraries.

HttpsServer.bodyLimitBytes is the largest bound among the registered specifications, never below defaultMaxDocumentBytes (256 KiB by default, configurable, and it must be greater than 0). The 413 check and io.dart's streaming read both use it. Once the route is known, a document over its route's bound, or over defaultMaxDocumentBytes when the specification declares none, is refused malformedRequest with a constant message. A document read forward along `extends` is held only to bodyLimitBytes, not to the bound of the earlier version it is read as: Dart has no index of other versions' bounds, and holding it to the earlier one could refuse a document within its own version's bound, which SPEC §12.4 forbids.

CLAUDE.md and CONTRIBUTING-SPECS.md now say that maxDocumentBytes is generated for Rust and Dart only, and enforced by the Dart HTTPS server. TypeScript and Go do not emit it yet, and the Rust server keeps its flat cap until #1089.

## Breaking changes and release

- trust_tasks (`dart`) breaks its API: responseToJson is now required, and priorResponse and recordResponse are typed as JSON maps.
- trust_tasks_https and trust_tasks_didcomm (`dart-https`, `dart-didcomm`) change behaviour. A document over its type's bound is now refused, including a declared bound below 256 KiB. A later version is now accepted instead of refused, and an unregistered version gets unsupportedVersion instead of unsupportedType.
- trust_tasks_tsp is unreleased, and `dart-tsp` is not a commit-lint scope, so the TSP changes are not in the title. The capability client change is internal, so it is a patch, not a `!`.

The siblings use core API that is not published yet. Their downgrade legs will warn, as RELEASING.md describes, and the sibling floors are deliberately not raised. The Release PR raises them when the core crosses the minor.

## Security review notes

- The pre-parse limit grows only with what the server registers. A server registering messaging/mux/attach (4 MiB) reads and parses up to 4 MiB before authentication, for any type. That is the trade-off #1121 asks for. The per-type check runs right after parsing, before authentication, decoding or verification.
- On a route miss the lookup walks the registered routes and a bounded extends chain, which is cheap. Pruning has a step budget, and it runs before the proof is checked.
- unsupportedVersion versus unsupportedType tells an unauthenticated prober that a slug is implemented. An exact-version probe already revealed that, and the Rust dispatcher does the same.
- Events carry exactly what SPEC §12.4 keeps off the wire: exception text, in-band identities, and anything a verifier threw. They are documented as log-only. Values that come from a peer, such as ConsistencyError.inBand, are attacker-controlled strings.

## Verification

- `dart analyze --fatal-infos` and `dart test` pass for the core, https, didcomm, tsp, proof and capability client packages.
- `dart format` at each package's floor language version is clean.
- examples/consumer-app-dart generates, analyzes and runs.
- `npm run check-bindings`, `npm run check-sibling-core-ranges` and `npm run check-dart-packages` pass.
- scripts/check-dart-consumer-generation.mjs passes over freshly built bundles.
- Re-running the TS, Go and Rust generators with pinned dependencies gives no diff.

Closes #1118. Closes #1116.

Part of #1117. Part of #1121.

title: feat(dart,dart-https,dart-didcomm)!: JSON priorResponse, observability hook, forward routing and per-type size bounds (#1242)

feat(dart,dart-https,dart-didcomm)!: JSON priorResponse, observability hook, forward routing and per-type size bounds (#1242)

* feat(dart,dart-https,dart-didcomm)!: JSON priorResponse, observability hook, forward routing and per-type size bounds

trust_tasks: DuplicateOutcome.priorResponse is now Map<String, dynamic>?
(with an isError getter), because consumeInbound always records the
response as JSON: responseToJson is required, and ReplayGuard.recordResponse
and Duplicate.priorResponse take the JSON map. newUrnUuid() moves into the
core and is newErrorId's default. A sealed ServerEvent hierarchy and
emitServerEvent, which drops anything a hook throws. SpecPolicy gains
maxDocumentBytes, generated per variant by both Dart generators from the
front matter and compared by check-bindings.

trust_tasks_https: an optional onEvent hook. A later version whose declared
extends chain reaches a registered version is routed to the highest such
version and read as it; any other version of a registered specification is
unsupportedVersion. The body limit is the largest registered maxDocumentBytes
with a 256 KiB floor (defaultMaxDocumentBytes), and each document is then held
to its type's bound (malformedRequest above it).

trust_tasks_didcomm, trust_tasks_tsp: onEvent and extendsIndex; documents are
read through readForVersion. The capability client uses the core newUrnUuid.

* fix(dart-https): hold a forward-routed document only to the body limit

A later version may declare a larger maxDocumentBytes than the version it is
read as, and SPEC §12.4 forbids refusing a document within its own bound.
