    recognised while full.
  - The default capacity is 100 000 live records (was 10 000), documented as
    a ceiling on distinct documents per retention window, and exported as
    DEFAULT_REPLAY_CAPACITY / DefaultReplayCapacity / defaultReplayCapacity.
  - TypeScript, Go and Dart gain the expiry horizon Rust already had
    (`expiryHorizonMs` / `ExpiryHorizon` / `expiryHorizon`, 30 days in the
    consequential policy): a stated expiresAt bounds the acceptance window in
    place of the maximum age, up to issuedAt + horizon, and the retained
    record's expiry is clamped to the same instant, so a producer can no
    longer pin a record indefinitely with a distant expiresAt.

- **runtime**: Digest item 11 over the received document, and check envelope types and nesting depth ([#1171](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1171))

* fix(runtime)!: digest item 11 over the received document, and check envelope types and nesting depth

  Item 11's duplicate-execution digest is now taken over the document as
  received wherever a pipeline holds it, so two documents under one id that
  differ only in a member the payload type does not model, or in the spelling
  of a timestamp, are an idConflict rather than a duplicate:

  - Go ConsumeInbound digests ConsumeOptions.Received when set.
  - Dart consumeInbound digests `received` whenever it is passed (it did only
    for a forward read), and the HTTPS server, DIDComm and TSP consumers pass it.
  - Rust consume_inbound / consume_dispatched digest the received JSON under
    ProofPolicy::VerifyReceived, with or without a proof; the HTTPS server
    digests the body. New received_document_digest.

  TypeScript consumeInbound now checks the envelope before anything reads it:
  member types (string id/type and string-valued optional members, object
  payload/proof/ceremony, @context string/array/object) and a nesting bound of
  128 levels, refused malformedRequest and addressed only from string members.
  validateEnvelope and MAX_NESTING_DEPTH are exported.

  Dart consumeInbound refuses a document nested beyond maxNestingDepth (128)
  with malformedRequest instead of overflowing the stack, and the new
  parseTrustTaskDocument decodes a received value without throwing, returning
  a malformedRequest reason for a mistyped member.

  Shared vectors in fixtures/consume/item11-digest.json run in all four
  runtimes.

title: trust-tasks-ceremony-v0.2.1
body:
### Documentation

- Fix drifted counts, release runbook, licences and stale examples across the four libraries ([#1224](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1224))

* docs(getting-started): move the worked example to acl/grant/0.3 and stamp issuedAt with issued_at_now()

  The example pinned acl/grant/0.2, superseded by 0.3, and stamped issuedAt
  with chrono::Utc::now(), the full-precision form #970 removed from the
  libraries. The TS consumer example wrote toISOString() milliseconds into
  document fields the same way. The dependency snippet now uses cargo add,
  so it cannot name a stale version, and §4.4 describes the shared version
  group instead of versions from 0.14.



### Fixed

- **ceremony**: Decode the salt as multibase in every build, and compare digests by their decoded bytes ([#1232](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1232))

A default-features = false build hashed the salt's string bytes, so its digests changed whenever anything else in the graph enabled affinidi. trust-ceremony-receipt/0.1 defines the salt as decoded from multibase; multibase is now an unconditional dependency and the salt is decoded under every feature set.

  Step, prev and definition digests are compared as decoded multihash bytes (length-bounded, constant-time over equal lengths), so the same digest in another multibase base matches, and a malformed digest never matches a well-formed one. The fixture suite now runs without the affinidi backend, and CI runs it that way.

- **proof, ts-proof, dart-proof, dart-didcomm, ceremony**: Bound multibase decoding of unauthenticated values ([#1167](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1167))

* fix(proof, ts-proof, dart-proof): bound base58 decoding of proofValue and did:key

  The Rust, TypeScript and Dart proof verifiers decode a proof's proofValue
  and its did:key multikey with base58btc decoders whose cost grows with
  the square of the input length, and they do so before any signature is
  checked. A 1 MiB value took about 50 s per field in trust-tasks-proof
  (release build), and would take minutes in the Dart package and in the
  TypeScript package on @scure/base 2.0-2.3 (2.4 refuses over 4096
  characters itself).

  Each verifier now refuses a base58btc value longer than 175 characters
  before decoding it, or one that decodes to more than 128 bytes - the
  bounds the Go module adopts in #1166. The largest value any of them reads
  is a 96-byte P-384 signature; a did:key multikey is at most 51 bytes;
  175 = ceil(128 * log 256 / log 58).

  Nothing that could verify before is refused: a value over the bounds
  always decoded to more bytes than any supported key or signature.

title: trust-tasks-rs-v0.38.0
body:
### Added

- **messaging/mux/ack**: Acknowledge frames on the mux connection they were delivered on (0.1) ([#1174](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1174))

* feat(messaging/mux/ack): acknowledge frames on the mux connection they were delivered on (0.1)

- **vta/dids**: Key assurance levels — create/1.1 and upgrade/1.0, recovery only at level 3, threshold custodians ([#993](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/993))

* feat(vta/dids): key assurance levels — create/1.1 and upgrade/1.0, recovery only at level 3, threshold custodians

  Key roles were all-or-nothing: every key-role identity needed an external
  recovery key, and an identity without roles was not served at all. The VTI
  specification now gives every service DID a key assurance level its operator
  chooses (VTI-KEY-194): 1 single key, 2 role-separated, 3 recoverable.

  - vta/dids/create/1.1: `assuranceLevel` (2 or 3) is required;
    `recoveryCommitment` is required at level 3 and refused at level 2; a level-3
    identity under a method with witnesses needs one (witnessRequired); a
    template MAY set a level floor (assuranceLevelBelowTemplate). create/1.0 is
    released, so the changed shape is a new version rather than an in-place edit.
  - vta/dids/upgrade/1.0 (new): raise an identity's level in place, from 1 to
    2 or 3 or from 2 to 3, with fresh keys for every tightened role; never lower.
    `previousKeys` is retire (RECOMMENDED), revoke, or, from level 1, keep.
  - _shared/0.1 (additive): KeyAssuranceLevel, RecoveryCustodian and its kind,
    ThresholdRecoveryCommitment (a condition over whole keys, VTI-KEY-210–221),
    the declareAssuranceLevel change, the roleKeysInBackups warning; CONVENTIONS
    §3.4 (levels and the `keyAssurance` member), §3.5 (raising), §5.6–§5.7
    (recovery custodians, threshold custodians), §19, two family error codes
    (assuranceLevelMismatch, witnessRequired), and level-scoped custody, witness
    and approval rules.
  - 1.0 tasks, additively: keys/rotate gains `useRecoveryKey` and
    `recoveryProof`; keys/list reports `assuranceLevel`; keys/revoke
    `scope: boundary` and recover are level 3 only; update refuses
    `keyAssurance` and the removal of a level-3 identity's last witness.
  - Method profiles: did:webvh names the recovery commitment in
    `state.keyAssurance`; did:webs maps the levels onto its next-key threshold,
    every rotation exposes K and commits a fresh K′.
  - vta/webs/dids/create/0.2 now links vta/dids/create/1.1.

  Rebased onto main as one commit (was five, including a merge of main).
  Bindings regenerated (Rust, TS, Go, Dart).

- **vta/webs/dids/create**: DID classes, service DIDs and DID templates (0.2) ([#1159](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1159))

create 0.2 takes a required didClass (relationship, persona or service,
  VTI-KEY-190 - 193) and records it. A service did:webs - the durable identity
  of the VTA, a VTC, a VTN, a host service or an integration - is allowed at
  level 1 as an optional, alpha method (VTI-KEY-001 / VTI-KEY-003 as being
  amended, dtgwg-vti-spec#120), enabled separately in the VTA's configuration
  (serviceDidNotPermitted when it is off); didClassConflict holds VTI-KEY-193.

  A DID may be shaped by a DID template (template, templateContext,
  templateVars), exclusive of the explicit service and alias members. The VTA
  renders it and maps its document onto the did:webs derivation: one Ed25519
  signing key in authentication and assertionMethod, one designated X25519 key
  agreement key, designated services and aliases; anything else is refused
  with templateNotRepresentable (details.reason, details.members), and
  templateNotFound / templateVarsInvalid as for the other template consumers.

  Family conventions move to vta/webs/_shared/0.2 (CONVENTIONS.md section 1
  rewritten for classes and service DIDs, section 9 the template mapping;
  webs-records adds WebsDidClass and an optional didClass on the record).
  0.1 is unchanged and now superseded.

  Bindings regenerated for Rust, TS, Go and Dart.

- **rooms/watch**: A live watch for an open conversation (0.2), and rooms/keys/watch 0.2 ([#1087](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1087))

* feat(rooms/signal-delay/set): a room may turn off the watch signal's randomised delay (0.1), served by rooms/info 0.4

  A host waits a randomised few seconds before sending a rooms/changed
  signal (producer item 4), so that a signal's time does not mark one
  write. In a room used as a conversation that is a few seconds between
  one member writing and another seeing it, on every message.

  rooms/signal-delay/set/0.1 lets a holder of `admin` set the room's
  signal delay to `randomised` (the default) or `none`. It is the room's
  setting, not a watcher's: an undelayed signal lets a party who sees both
  the write reach the host and the signal leave it match the two, which
  gives away every writer, so one watcher cannot opt out for itself. The
  request carries a reason and a proof; the host audits each change and
  may refuse a setting its governance will not apply
  (`signalDelayNotPermitted`). A room can choose only whether there is a
  delay, never its interval.

  rooms/info/0.4 serves `signalDelay` to every member, always present.
  rooms/changed/0.1 producer item 4 applies the setting the host serves
  and never a watcher's preference, and its Correlation section says what
  `none` gives up. `SignalDelay` is a new definition in
  rooms/_shared/0.2. Links to rooms/info/0.3 move to 0.4.

- **rooms/signal-delay/set**: A room may turn off the watch signal's randomised delay (0.1), set at rooms/create 0.3 and served by rooms/info 0.4 ([#1084](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1084))

* feat(rooms/signal-delay/set): a room may turn off the watch signal's randomised delay (0.1), served by rooms/info 0.4

  A host waits a randomised few seconds before sending a rooms/changed
  signal (producer item 4), so that a signal's time does not mark one
  write. In a room used as a conversation that is a few seconds between
  one member writing and another seeing it, on every message.

  rooms/signal-delay/set/0.1 lets a holder of `admin` set the room's
  signal delay to `randomised` (the default) or `none`. It is the room's
  setting, not a watcher's: an undelayed signal lets a party who sees both
  the write reach the host and the signal leave it match the two, which
  gives away every writer, so one watcher cannot opt out for itself. The
  request carries a reason and a proof; the host audits each change and
  may refuse a setting its governance will not apply
  (`signalDelayNotPermitted`). A room can choose only whether there is a
  delay, never its interval.

  rooms/info/0.4 serves `signalDelay` to every member, always present.
  rooms/changed/0.1 producer item 4 applies the setting the host serves
  and never a watcher's preference, and its Correlation section says what
  `none` gives up. `SignalDelay` is a new definition in
  rooms/_shared/0.2. Links to rooms/info/0.3 move to 0.4.

- **rooms/records/list**: Newest-first listing for a conversation's head (0.7), and rooms/keys/browse 0.5 ([#1088](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1088))

Chat clients open a conversation at its newest messages, but a room
  listing only paged forward from sinceVersion, so a client opening a room
  with tens of thousands of records had to page from the start.

  rooms/records/list 0.7 adds an optional `order` (`oldestFirst`, the
  default, or `newestFirst`), defined once as `ListOrder` in
  rooms/_shared/0.2. Newest first returns rows in descending version;
  sinceVersion still bounds from below; tombstones and lastPrune are
  unchanged; a cursor is valid only under the order it was issued for
  (invalidCursor otherwise). The spec states what makes it correct for chat
  although edits move a record's version: a newest-first listing whose
  lowest version is V holds every record whose current version is above V,
  so every message created since V; a reader orders by createdAt, not by
  row order. A record changed mid-listing moves above the listing's first
  row, so a catching-up reader takes the first page's highest version as
  its watermark, and only after reading to the end.

  rooms/keys/browse 0.5 passes `order` through, and adds `maxPages`,
  `cursor` and response `nextCursor`: a 0.4 recipient always reads the
  host's listing to its end, so order alone would still read the whole
  room before answering. The MemberProfile "Near the room's head" rule
  now says how a newest-first reader finds names (500 rows below the
  earliest record it shows reach at least 500 versions).

- **rooms/keys/read-marker**: A member's read marker kept by their key holder, so every device agrees on unread (0.1), and rooms/keys/list 0.3 ([#1086](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1086))

rooms/changed 0.1 counts unread messages against a read marker that was each
  client's own, so a member's phone and laptop disagreed about what is unread and
  a notification read on one device stayed on the other.

  - rooms/keys/read-marker/set 0.1: a member's client tells their key holder
    where the member has seen a room up to (room version + host createdAt of the
    newest message seen). The marker only moves forward (greater version; at equal
    version, later createdAt) unless `rewind: true` ("mark as unread"); the answer
    is the marker in force and `moved`, so racing devices converge without a
    precondition. Acting as the member, delegates refused, notHeld as for
    rooms/keys/label. Idempotent; retry class two.
  - rooms/keys/read-marker/moved 0.1: one-way, key holder to the member's other
    clients holding a rooms/keys/watch on the room as that member (never the
    setter), so a device can clear a notification.
  - rooms/keys/list 0.3: each entry may carry `readMarker`, returned under
    includePersonal beside the personal label.
  - ReadMarker in rooms/_shared/0.1/read-marker.schema.json.
  - rooms/changed 0.1 (draft, prose): a reader MAY keep its marker with its key
    holder; it is still never sent to the host, the room or another member.

- **messaging/mux**: Connections, an administrator's view of live mux connections ([#1083](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1083))

Adds messaging/mux/connections/0.1: an administrator lists a mediator's live mux connections — principal, wire (didcomm | tsp), openedAt, exact memberCount, and members with source, grantId, scope, expiresAt and deliveryActive — paged by cursor/limit with a per-page member budget that splits a large connection across pages, and a required coverage (allInstances | thisInstance) so a horizontally scaled mediator never implies completeness it lacks. Regenerates the Rust, TypeScript, Go and Dart bindings.



### Build & CI

- Guard version edits, release lists, crate size and released spec policy; one-pass registry dates ([#1213](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1213))

* ci: guard version edits, release lists, crate size and released spec policy; one-pass registry dates

  Pipeline fixes from the 2026-11-11 repository review.

  - Crate size ([#1097](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1097)): the `package` job fails when the trust-tasks-rs .crate
    exceeds 9.9 MiB and warns above 9.5 MiB; CHANGELOG.md is excluded from the
    package. Measured here at 10,308,682 bytes (9.83 MiB) after the exclusion.
  - deploy.yml ([#1133](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1133)): the deploy job joins one `deploy-production`
    concurrency group (never cancelled) and skips a queued deploy whose commit
    main has moved past, so an older run cannot roll the site back.
  - check-published-schemas ([#1134](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1134)): front matter parsed as YAML; the full
    derived per-variant policy (proof and issuedAt request/response,
    parties[].requirement, bearer) is compared; a deleted or renamed released
    file fails. Regression fixtures and tests in scripts/test-checks/.
  - rust.yml ([#1135](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1135)): the path filter covers fixtures/, ceremonies/,
    check-rs-api-compat.sh and release-plz.toml; published-schemas moved to the
    unfiltered checks.yml.
  - build-registry.mjs ([#1136](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1136)): created/updated dates and git authors come from
    one `git log` over specs/, skipped under --validate-only. Build 1m43s -> 6s
    with identical output; validate 2.6s.
  - Release rules ([#1137](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1137)): checks.yml refuses a version-declaration change in
    any PR but the Release PR; commit-lint refuses a BREAKING CHANGE line in the
    commits or description and accepts only an explicit list of `!` scopes.
  - check-release-lists.mjs ([#1139](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1139)): the npm, Go and crate release lists, and
    commit-lint's scopes against the release scripts', held in agreement.
  - timeout-minutes on every job that had none; rust-cache in ts.yml
    gen-equivalence ([#1141](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1141)).
  - `npm run check`, `npm run regen`, .nvmrc, new-spec's closing message, and a
    readable reserved-slug failure ([#1142](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1142)).
  - Drift checks use `git status --porcelain`; release-plz-release has a
    concurrency group; a withdraw re-run updates its existing PR ([#1143](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1143)).



### Documentation

- Fix drifted counts, release runbook, licences and stale examples across the four libraries ([#1224](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1224))

* docs(getting-started): move the worked example to acl/grant/0.3 and stamp issuedAt with issued_at_now()

  The example pinned acl/grant/0.2, superseded by 0.3, and stamped issuedAt
  with chrono::Utc::now(), the full-precision form #970 removed from the
  libraries. The TS consumer example wrote toISOString() milliseconds into
  document fields the same way. The dependency snippet now uses cargo add,
  so it cannot name a stale version, and §4.4 describes the shared version
  group instead of versions from 0.14.



### Fixed

- **runtime**: Bound the work of pruning a payload read forward along extends ([#1209](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1209))

* fix(runtime): bound the work of pruning a payload read forward along extends

  Pruning a later version's payload to the implemented version's schema runs
  before any proof is checked. Its cost could grow exponentially with the
  payload's nesting depth: in TypeScript, choosing a oneOf/anyOf branch pruned
  the whole subtree once per branch, at every level; in all four runtimes, a
  recursive member named from more than one place (properties and an allOf
  branch) was pruned once per place, at every level.

  Each runtime now gives a prune at most 100,000 steps plus 64 per value in
  the payload. readForSpec (TS), ReadForSpec (Go), readForVersion (Dart), and
  read_as, the dispatchers and consume_dispatched (Rust) refuse a payload
  that needs more as malformedRequest, saying why. prunePayload /
  prune_payload on their own return the payload untouched instead.

  TypeScript also remembers, for the rest of a walk, the branch chosen for
  each value and the structural matcher's answers, so a value under nested
  oneOfs is decided once rather than once per enclosing branch, and compiles
  each patternProperties pattern once per walk.

- **rs,build,cli,codegen**: Review fixes — declared guard code, SchemaValidator, keyword slugs, generate --lang rs, registry hints, docs.rs ([#1215](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1215))

* fix(rs): declared acl/revoke code in the guard, a caching SchemaValidator, docs.rs metadata

  - guards::acl::reject_last_authority returns acl/revoke:lastAuthorityProtected,
    the code every acl/revoke version declares (was snake_case); new
    LAST_AUTHORITY_PROTECTED constant, pinned to the generated declarations ([#1093](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1093)).
  - validate::SchemaValidator: a PayloadValidator compiling each schema once,
    cached by the schema text's address and confirmed against its content;
    validate_value and check_details use a shared one; prune_payload reuses a
    parsed-schema cache; PayloadPolicy::accept_unvalidated() ([#1091](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1091)).
  - docs.rs builds trust-tasks-rs with validate + acl and the facade with its
    non-spec features, and trust-tasks-rs / trust-tasks-https enable doc_cfg
    under docsrs, without which the docs.rs build cannot compile ([#1106](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1106)).

- **ts,go,dart,rs**: Whole-second capability-client issuedAt, tested Dart core floors, TS default export condition, Go schema caching ([#1214](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1214))

* fix(dart-capability-client,go-capabilityclient,go-didcomm): stamp issuedAt in whole seconds and fail on entropy failure

  The Dart capability client stamped issuedAt with toIso8601String (full
  precision); it now uses the core's systemClock. The Go port now stamps
  through trusttasks.SystemClock. The TS port already stamped whole seconds.

  The Go capabilityclient and didcomm UUIDv4 generators ignored crypto/rand
  errors and would mint an all-zero id; they now panic, as tsp's does.

- **dart-https**: Advertise the expiry horizon, and pin all four runtimes' freshness to shared vectors ([#1212](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1212))

* test(runtime): shared freshness vectors run by all four runtimes

  fixtures/consume/freshness.json pins SPEC §7.2's acceptance window (items 4
  and 13, *Bounding the record*): now / policy / issuedAt / expiresAt to a
  verdict and, for an accepted document, the replay record's expiry. It covers
  a stated expiresAt replacing the maximum age, the 30-day expiry horizon and
  its clamp on the record, a zero horizon, the half-open edges to the
  millisecond, skew on both sides, a missing issuedAt with and without
  requireIssuedAt, offsets, fractions and calendar-invalid timestamps, and
  holds each runtime's default and consequential policies to the same values.

  Run by trust-tasks-rs (tests/freshness_vectors.rs), @openvtc/trust-tasks
  (test/freshness-vectors.test.ts), trust-tasks-go
  (trusttasks/freshness_vectors_test.go) and trust_tasks
  (test/freshness_vectors_test.dart). The Rust workflow now runs on a change
  under fixtures/, which its integration tests read.

- **rs,ts,go,dart,proof,ts-proof,go-proof,dart-proof**: Refuse out-of-range timestamp fields instead of rolling them over ([#1210](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1210))

issuedAt and expiresAt, and a proof's created, are now read with every
  field range-checked after the shared pattern: month 1-12, a day the month
  has, hour 0-23, minute and second 0-59 (no leap second), and an offset of
  at most 23:59 (14:00 for a proof's dateTimeStamp, as for expires).

  Before, the four runtimes disagreed on the same bytes. TypeScript's
  Date.parse read 2026-02-30 as 2 March and 24:00 as the next day; Dart's
  DateTime.tryParse rolled 2026-13-45T25:61:61Z over into 2027 and took any
  offset; Rust's chrono read :60 as a leap second and accepted a space for
  the T; Go's time.Parse accepted +24:00 and +23:60. In the TypeScript proof
  verifier a regex-valid but unparseable created (month 13) gave NaN, which
  never compares later than the clock-skew horizon, so it was accepted.

  New shared vectors: fixtures/consume/timestamps.json, run by all four
  runtimes, and five correctly signed created-* proof vectors.

- **messaging/mux/ack**: NotPermitted only for a member whose mail the connection reads (0.1) ([#1179](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1179))
- **rs,ts,go,dart**: The in-memory replay guard refuses when full instead of dropping live records ([#1163](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1163))

* fix(runtime): the in-memory replay guard refuses when full instead of dropping live records

  InMemoryReplayGuard (Rust, TypeScript, Go, Dart) made room for a new id by
  dropping the least-recently-used record, whether or not that record was
  still inside its retention window. A document whose record was dropped that
  way was then accepted again inside its window, with nothing logged.

  - When every slot holds a live record, a claim for a new id now fails
    (Rust ReplayGuardError, TS ReplayGuardFullError, Go ErrReplayGuardFull,
    Dart ReplayGuardFullException), which the pipeline answers `unavailable`
    (retryable). Records whose window has closed are reclaimed first; a
    record is never dropped to make room. Duplicates and conflicts are still
    recognised while full.
  - The default capacity is 100 000 live records (was 10 000), documented as
    a ceiling on distinct documents per retention window, and exported as
    DEFAULT_REPLAY_CAPACITY / DefaultReplayCapacity / defaultReplayCapacity.
  - TypeScript, Go and Dart gain the expiry horizon Rust already had
    (`expiryHorizonMs` / `ExpiryHorizon` / `expiryHorizon`, 30 days in the
    consequential policy): a stated expiresAt bounds the acceptance window in
    place of the maximum age, up to issuedAt + horizon, and the retained
    record's expiry is clamped to the same instant, so a producer can no
    longer pin a record indefinitely with a distant expiresAt.

- **runtime**: Settle or release the item-11 claim on every remaining path ([#1177](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1177))

- Rust: the claim stays armed across a retryable refusal's awaited
    release and is disarmed on the next statement, so a pipeline dropped
    mid-release still releases it. A response or refusal whose `Serialize`
    panics is recorded with no response before the panic continues.
  - HTTPS server: `release_claim` holds a drop guard across its awaited
    release, on both the refusal and the panic branch.
  - `ReplayGuard::release_abandoned` documents that it must not block,
    require a runtime context or panic, and the default's degradation for a
    `release` that suspends, which a test now pins.
  - Go: a `MarshalJSON` panic in `settle` records the claim with no
    response, then the panic continues.
  - Dart: a final refusal that cannot be encoded releases the claim, so a
    resend is evaluated again, before the error is rethrown.

- **messaging/mux/ack**: An id held for a DID off the connection is notFound (0.1) ([#1176](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1176))
- **rs,ts,go,dart**: Refuse a document whose type is not the spec it is consumed under ([#1162](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1162))

* fix(runtime): refuse a document whose type is not the spec it is consumed under

  The typed consume functions took the document's payload type, or a spec
  policy, as given and never compared the document's `type` with it. A
  document of another specification whose payload happened to fit was run
  under the consumed spec's policy and handler, and answered as its own type.
  SPEC §7.2 item 3 assigns that check to the consumer.

  Each runtime's typed path now checks it before any other step, so a refused
  document never reaches the item-11 record:

  - accepted: the spec's own Type URI (`#request` and no fragment alike), or a
    later version of the same specification and variant whose declared
    `extends` chain reaches it (SPEC §5.2);
  - `unsupportedVersion`: the same specification and variant at any other
    version;
  - `unsupportedType`: anything else — another slug, the same slug under
    another authority or form, the `#response` variant, or a `type` that is not
    a Type URI.

- **runtime**: Release the item-11 claim when a handler does not return, and end the acceptance window where the record does ([#1175](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1175))

* fix(runtime): release the item-11 claim when a handler does not return, and close the window where the record expires

  A handler that panicked (Rust, Go) or whose future was dropped mid-await
  (Rust: a request timeout, a client disconnect) left its item-11 claim in
  flight until the record expired, so every resend of the document was
  absorbed as an in-flight duplicate and never ran. The claim is now
  released on those paths exactly once:

  - Rust: `consume_core` holds the claim in a drop guard across the handler
    await. A panic or cancellation releases it through the new defaulted
    `ReplayGuard::release_abandoned` (synchronous, as it runs from a
    destructor); a returned handler settles it as before. The default polls
    `release` once; `InMemoryReplayGuard` releases directly.
  - Go: a deferred release covers a panicking handler without recovering, so
    the panic continues unchanged. Release and settle run on a context
    detached from the request's cancellation (bounded at five seconds), so a
    store-backed guard is not handed an already-cancelled context.
  - Dart: when the response encoder throws after the handler returned, the
    claim is settled with no cached response before the error is rethrown,
    rather than left in flight. The effect happened, so a resend is absorbed.
  - TypeScript already released the claim on a throwing handler.

  The acceptance window over `issuedAt` (and the expiry horizon in Rust) now
  ends exclusively, at the instant `recordExpiry` returns, in all four
  runtimes. A guard drops a record once `retainUntil <= now`, while a
  document was still accepted at exactly `retainUntil`, so at that instant
  it could be accepted with no record and executed again. The window is now
  half-open, as `expiresAt` already was.

  The shared `fixtures/consume/item11-digest.json` vectors gain an optional
  per-case `secondAt` and two boundary cases, run by all four runtimes.

- **runtime**: Digest item 11 over the received document, and check envelope types and nesting depth ([#1171](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1171))

* fix(runtime)!: digest item 11 over the received document, and check envelope types and nesting depth

  Item 11's duplicate-execution digest is now taken over the document as
  received wherever a pipeline holds it, so two documents under one id that
  differ only in a member the payload type does not model, or in the spelling
  of a timestamp, are an idConflict rather than a duplicate:

  - Go ConsumeInbound digests ConsumeOptions.Received when set.
  - Dart consumeInbound digests `received` whenever it is passed (it did only
    for a forward read), and the HTTPS server, DIDComm and TSP consumers pass it.
  - Rust consume_inbound / consume_dispatched digest the received JSON under
    ProofPolicy::VerifyReceived, with or without a proof; the HTTPS server
    digests the body. New received_document_digest.

  TypeScript consumeInbound now checks the envelope before anything reads it:
  member types (string id/type and string-valued optional members, object
  payload/proof/ceremony, @context string/array/object) and a nesting bound of
  128 levels, refused malformedRequest and addressed only from string members.
  validateEnvelope and MAX_NESTING_DEPTH are exported.

  Dart consumeInbound refuses a document nested beyond maxNestingDepth (128)
  with malformedRequest instead of overflowing the stack, and the new
  parseTrustTaskDocument decodes a received value without throwing, returning
  a malformedRequest reason for a mistyped member.

  Shared vectors in fixtures/consume/item11-digest.json run in all four
  runtimes.

- **messaging/mux**: Revoke-all ends session attaches; accountBlocked covers ACLs narrowed below scope ([#1165](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1165))

messaging/mux/revoke-all 0.1 (draft) now ends the member DID's session
  attaches admitted before it, on every connection, before answering, with
  reason epochBumped; a principal that carried the DID only through an
  attach gets the live detached event and no notice. The attach spec lists
  revoke-all and a blocked or removed account among the ways an attach
  ends. DetachReason's description says accountBlocked also covers ACLs
  that no longer cover the member's scope. Bindings regenerated
  (descriptions only).

title: fix(runtime): bound the work of pruning a payload read forward along extends
body:
## Summary

When a consumer reads a later version's document as the version it implements (SPEC §5.2 declared extension), the runtime prunes the payload to the implemented version's schema. That walk runs before any proof is checked, and in some schema shapes its cost grew exponentially with the payload's nesting depth. This PR bounds it in all four runtimes.

### Where the walk could grow

- **TypeScript, `oneOf`/`anyOf`.** `chooseBranch` pruned the whole subtree against every branch to decide which one fits, and then pruned it again against the chosen one, at every level. With a recursive three-branch expression schema, a payload of about 200 bytes and 20 levels took seconds. Rust, Go and Dart choose a branch with a shallow test (type, `const`/`enum`, `required`, discriminator members) and prune once, so they do not have this shape.
- **All four runtimes, repeated applicators.** A recursive member named from more than one place at the same level (`properties` and an `allOf` branch, or a `$ref` target and `properties`) is pruned once per place. Each level then doubles the work.

No schema in the registry has either shape today. Schemas generated from third-party specifications are not constrained.

### What changes

- **Step budget (all four).** One prune may take at most 100,000 steps plus 64 per value in the payload. A step is a value visited against a subschema, or a branch test. Ordinary payloads use a small fraction of that. A payload that needs more is refused `malformedRequest`, with a message that says the payload is too complex to re-read as the implemented version:
  - TS `readForSpec`
  - Go `ReadForSpec` / `ReadForSpecWith` (new exported `PruneLimitWireMessage`)
  - Dart `readForVersion`
  - Rust `read_as`, `Dispatcher::dispatch`, `AsyncDispatcher::dispatch` and `consume_dispatched` (all through a new crate-private `prune_forward`)

  The standalone `prunePayload` (TS, Dart) and `prune_payload` (Rust) return the payload untouched instead, as they already do for an undecidable branch. Rust prunes a copy so that a partial prune is never kept.
- **TypeScript memoisation.** For the rest of one walk, the runtime remembers the branch chosen for each value (keyed by value and `oneOf`/`anyOf` list) and the structural matcher's answer (keyed by value and subschema). A value under nested `oneOf`s is then decided once, not once per enclosing branch, so the expression case above is now polynomial and well inside the budget. `patternProperties` patterns are compiled once per walk instead of once per member per call.

### Why pruning still runs before authentication

SPEC §7.2 validates the payload against the implemented schema at item 2, and checks the proof at item 7. Validation needs the pruned payload, so pruning has to happen before item 2. In TS, Go and Dart, `readForSpec`/`ReadForSpec`/`readForVersion` is also called by the application before `consumeInbound`, and the proof is then verified over the received document. Moving pruning after the proof would mean changing the §7.2 order or the public read-then-consume API. So this PR bounds the work and leaves the order alone.

## Behaviour changes (R3.6)

- A forward-read payload whose pruning needs more than the budget is refused `malformedRequest`. Before, it was pruned, however long that took. The budget scales with payload size, so this only affects schemas whose work per value is far above the norm. No registry schema comes near it.
- `prunePayload` / `prune_payload` return such a payload unchanged.
- TS: branch choices are made once per value per walk. The result is the same. The only possible difference would be at the 64-level depth cutoff, where the same value could appear at two depths.
- No exported signature changes. Go gains the `PruneLimitWireMessage` constant. No `!`: nothing that completed in reasonable time before is refused.

## Tests

Not run locally. Remote CI runs them.

- **TS** `test/extends.test.ts`, "prunePayload work limit": a 60-level recursive three-branch `oneOf` prunes correctly and quickly; the doubling schema still prunes a 3-level payload; at 40 levels it is returned untouched; `readForSpec` refuses it `malformedRequest`.
- **Go** `extends_test.go`: `TestReadForSpecPrunesWithinTheWorkLimit`, `TestReadForSpecRefusesAPayloadBeyondTheWorkLimit`.
- **Dart** `test/extension_test.dart`, "prunePayload work limit": shallow prune, untouched beyond the limit, `readForVersion` refusal.
- **Rust** `extension.rs` unit tests: shallow prune, unchanged beyond the limit, and `forward` refusing `MalformedRequest`.

## Overlap with open PRs

`git merge-tree` against #1204, #1066, #1206 and #1208 merges cleanly.

## Checklist (dev guide §9)

- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2): n/a, no clients
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3): n/a
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1): n/a. The refusal comes before any item-11 record.
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4): n/a
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5): n/a. The refusal is an ordinary `malformedRequest` reject, not an exception.
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6): n/a
- [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, deny_unknown_fields where security-relevant, schema registered, all consumers (incl. JS) updated (R3.*): no wire type changes. The behaviour change is listed above (R3.6).
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive; fail-closed if enforcement can't start (R5.*): no config. Running out of budget refuses.
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified; background-job failures are surfaced (R6.*): the refusal message says the payload exceeded the work limit.
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1): no mutations
- [x] Deviations from this guide flagged explicitly with rule numbers: none

title: fix(ceremony): decode the salt as multibase in every build, and compare digests by their decoded bytes
body:
trust-tasks-ceremony read the enactment salt differently depending on a Cargo feature. With affinidi (the default) it was multibase-decoded; with default-features = false it was hashed as the string's bytes. trust-ceremony-receipt/0.1 says the salt is "decoded from its multibase form", so the no-backend build did not conform, and because features unify across a dependency graph, a build that implemented its own Digester saw every digest change as soon as any other crate enabled affinidi.

multibase is now an unconditional dependency (it was already in the lockfile) and decode_salt decodes under every feature set.

Digests are now compared as decoded multihash bytes rather than as strings, in all four places verify compares them: the recomputed step digest against the receipt, a signed prev entry against the receipt, and the definition digest (supplied vs. receipt, and step document vs. receipt). The same digest written in another base (u…, f…) now matches. A value that does not decode only equals itself byte for byte, so a malformed digest can never match a well-formed one; a receipt step digest that does not decode is Invalid. A Digester whose output is not multibase is Error::DigestEncoding, since that is a broken backend rather than a bad receipt.

Security notes from reviewing the diff. Decoding receipt-supplied digests means running multibase decoders, some quadratic in input length, on attacker-controlled strings, which string equality never did; decode_digest therefore refuses anything over 256 characters (a SHA-512 multihash is 91 base58btc or 133 base16 characters) before decoding, mirroring the existing MAX_SALT_CHARS bound, with a timing test. Byte comparison uses a small length-then-XOR-fold helper with black_box rather than a new dependency; the spec says the salt is not secret from receipt holders, so this is defence in depth rather than a load-bearing property. The comparison is over multihash bytes, so the multibase prefix itself carries no meaning, which is what a multibase value means.

The fixture suite previously did not compile without affinidi. It now runs under both configurations, using a stand-in test digester when the backend is absent, and gains tests for the salt decoding, other-base digests at each comparison site, malformed and over-long digests, and a non-multibase digester. The test-single-family job in rust.yml now also runs cargo test and clippy for trust-tasks-ceremony with --no-default-features, since every other job builds it with the backend on.

No public signature changes, so no !. It is a behavioural fix for default-features = false builds only. TS, Go and Dart carry the ceremony.prev type but implement no receipt verification, so there is nothing to change there.

Closes #1094.

title: fix(proof,ts-proof,go-proof,dart-proof): follow the JCS cryptosuites' @context rule in all four proof backends
body:
A Trust Task document MAY carry `@context` (SPEC §4.6). Before this change, the four proof backends disagreed about what a proof over such a document covers. The Dart verifier, through ssi, copied the document's `@context` into the proof configuration before hashing it. The Rust, TypeScript and Go signers and verifiers did not. As a result, the Dart signer's own output failed the Dart verifier, and the other three signers' output failed it too. This PR applies the W3C cryptosuite rule in all four.

## What the cryptosuite specifications say

Data Integrity EdDSA Cryptosuites v1.0 (https://www.w3.org/TR/vc-di-eddsa/) has §3.3.1 Create Proof (eddsa-jcs-2022). ECDSA (https://www.w3.org/TR/vc-di-ecdsa/) has the same step in its §3.3.1 Create Proof (ecdsa-jcs-2019). Step 2:

> If unsecuredDocument.@context is present, set proof.@context to unsecuredDocument.@context.

The EdDSA text adds a note: "Not implementing step 2 can lead to interoperability failures".

§3.3.2 Verify Proof, identical in both specifications, step 4:

> If proofOptions.@context exists:
>   1. Check that the securedDocument.@context starts with all values contained in the proofOptions.@context in the same order. Otherwise, set verified to false and skip to the last step.
>   2. Set unsecuredDocument.@context equal to proofOptions.@context.

The JCS Proof Configuration algorithm (§3.3.5) has no `@context` step: the proof configuration is the proof options as given, canonicalized. The JCS suites therefore never inject a context at verification time. Only the RDFC suites do.

## What changed

Signers: Rust `sign_trust_task`, TypeScript `signTrustTask`, Go `Signer.Sign` and Dart `signTrustTask` now copy the document's `@context` into the proof (step 2). It is hashed as part of the proof configuration. A document without `@context`, the normal case, gets a byte-identical proof. The existing fixture tests pass unchanged, and a new Rust test reproduces the shared baseline vector byte for byte.

Rust has one limit here. `affinidi-data-integrity` 0.8's proof type holds `@context` only as `Vec<String>`. So the Rust signer copies an array of strings and emits no proof `@context` for any other form. That form still verifies everywhere, because step 4 applies only when the proof carries `@context`. A context passed through `SignOptions::with_context` is now replaced by the document's, because any other value would make the stock verifier refuse the proof.

Verifiers: all four apply step 4 the same way. A proof that carries `@context` must have one exactly equal to the document's (canonical JSON equality), or it is refused as `malformedProof`. A proof without `@context` is hashed as received.

Dart: the verifier now uses subclasses of ssi's `DataIntegrityEddsaJcsVerifier` and `DataIntegrityEcdsaJcsVerifier`. They override `prepareProofForVerification` to hash the proof as received, instead of injecting the document's `@context`. They also override `validateCryptosuite`, because ssi's prefix check compares inline contexts by identity and our own check has already run. This was tested against ssi 4.3.0 and against ssi 3.9.6 pinned, as the `dart.yml` matrix does.

Rust: the verifier refuses a proof `@context` that is not an array of strings, as unsupported, with a clear message instead of a serde parse error. The new shared vector records this as a Rust exception in the manifest, the same way the `expires` gap is recorded.

The "a Trust Task document carries no JSON-LD `@context`" statements are corrected in the Dart and TypeScript READMEs and source docs. Each README now describes the `@context` rule.

## Deliberate deviation: equality, not prefix

Step 4 accepts a document whose `@context` extends the proof's, for proof sets and chains. It hashes the proof's `@context` in place of the document's (step 4.2) and returns that rewritten document as the verified one. Our `ProofVerifier` interfaces return only valid or invalid, never a document. The consumer then acts on the document as received, including `@context` entries no signature covers. All four verifiers therefore require equality. This refuses nothing that any of them accepted before: the extended form already failed everywhere, because each hashed the received document. `eddsa-jcs-2022-context-extended.json` pins it as invalid, and the manifest says why. If the framework later wants proof sets, a verifier API that returns the verified document can relax this.

## Shared vectors (fixtures/proof)

All signed with the seed-7 Ed25519 key. Every library's existing shared-vector test runs them.

- `eddsa-jcs-2022-context.json` (valid): an `@context` array, copied into the proof. The Rust, TypeScript, Go and Dart signers each reproduce it byte for byte in a new test.
- `eddsa-jcs-2022-context-proof-omits.json` (valid): the same document with no proof `@context`, which is what every signer emitted before. Dart refused it before this change.
- `eddsa-jcs-2022-context-string.json` (valid): a single-string `@context`. Rust exception: refused as unsupported (upstream type).
- `eddsa-jcs-2022-context-extended.json` (invalid): see the deviation above.
- `eddsa-jcs-2022-context-mismatch.json` (invalid): the proof's `@context` is not a prefix of the document's (step 4.1).
- `eddsa-jcs-2022-context-proof-only.json` (invalid): the proof carries `@context` and the document has none (step 4.1).

Each library also gains tests that removing, reordering or changing the `@context` after signing gives `malformedProof`. TypeScript, Go and Dart also round-trip an inline-object context.

## Security review

The verification-side changes, and whether any of them accepts a proof that was refused before:

- Rust, TypeScript and Go verifiers: the only change is a new refusal. A proof whose `@context` differs from the document's, or that carries one when the document has none, is now refused, even when the signature over the two as they stand is correct. Step 4.1 requires this. Nothing is newly accepted.
- Rust also newly refuses a proof `@context` that is null, a string or an object. A string or object already failed to parse. A null used to parse as absent.
- Dart now accepts two things it refused before, both of which the specification requires:
  1. A proof without `@context` over a document with one, hashed as received. ssi used to hash a configuration the signer never signed.
  2. An equal inline-object `@context`. ssi's prefix check compared maps by identity.
- Dart now refuses one thing it accepted before. If a proof without `@context` was signed over a configuration that included the document's `@context`, ssi's injection used to make it verify. The configuration is now hashed as received, as in the other three libraries.
- Skipping ssi's `validateCryptosuite` removes only its `@context` prefix check. In ssi 3.9.6 and 4.3.0, `BaseJcsVerifier.validateCryptosuite` does nothing else, and neither suite subclass overrides it. Our equality check runs first and is stricter. Proof-structure, expiry, issuer-binding and signature checks in ssi's `verify` are unchanged.
- Canonicalizing the two `@context` values is bounded by the document's size, which is already canonicalized for the signature. A canonicalization failure is a refusal, not a throw (TypeScript and Dart catch it; Go returns it).
- Signers: the copied `@context` is part of the signed proof configuration, so it is covered by the signature. A proof signed here also verifies with the previous releases of all four verifiers. Old TypeScript, Go and Rust hash the proof as received, and old Dart injected the same value the proof now carries. The exception is Rust, old or new, when the proof `@context` is not an array of strings.

Library API: no public signature changes. Rust's new message constant is private. Behaviour tightens only where a proof's `@context` disagrees with its document, which no signer in this repository produced. So this is not marked `!`.

Closes #1113.

title: fix(ts-gen): generate locks that pin acl/grant/0.3, and move the consumer apps to it
body:
The four consumer-side example apps (examples/consumer-app in Rust, and its TypeScript, Go and Dart siblings) pinned the superseded acl/grant/0.2. They now pin acl/grant/0.3 together, so the cross-language fixtures stay in lockstep. Each was repinned with the CLI (`trust-tasks remove acl/grant` then `trust-tasks add acl/grant/0.3`), which vendored the same bundle digest that examples/getting-started already uses (sha256:0b99efcb…). `trust-tasks check` passes offline for every app and for index-equivalence. 0.3 makes the entry's `purposes` scope required, so each app's grant entry now carries `{"scope": "any"}`. The Go app's request also gained the `keys` scope it had always left out. The Rust index-equivalence test now names the 0.3 Type URI.

Moving the TypeScript app turned up a generator bug. trust-tasks-gen-ts could not generate any lock that pins acl/grant/0.3. acl/_shared/0.3's `Purpose` has a `type` beside an `anyOf`, and json-schema-to-typescript compiles that to `Purpose = Purpose1 & Purpose2`. A lock that reaches only one shape of `Purpose` names it bare, and the check for counter-suffixed duplicates then refused the component's own numbered parts. The prebuilt package never hit this because it qualifies the name over the whole registry (`Purpose_AclV0_3`). The check now skips a component's own intersection parts. scripts/build-ts-bindings.mjs gets the same exclusion so the two checks stay diffable, and its output does not change: `npm run build-ts-bindings` leaves trust-tasks-ts untouched. The trust-tasks-gen-ts equivalence run over the whole registry still passes.

The trust-tasks-ts-gen and Dart generator tests read these example locks, so they follow the change. The ts-gen test now uses the vendored 0.3 bundle's real defOrigins instead of synthesising them, and asserts the bare `Purpose` intersection. The Dart test's "the example's bundles predate defsOrder" check now names the bundles that do.

Verified locally:
- Rust: `cargo run`/`cargo test -p trust-tasks-example-consumer-app` and both `trust-tasks check` runs.
- TypeScript: `npm run all` in consumer-app-ts, `npm test` and the equivalence run in trust-tasks-ts-gen.
- Go: `go generate` reproduces the committed tree; `go vet` and `go run` pass; `go test ./cmd/...` passes.
- Dart: generate, `dart analyze --fatal-infos` and `dart run`; the generator tests pass.

These ran on current toolchains only, not the Go 1.22 or Dart 3.3 floors.

Part of #1129.

title: fix(go): rename schema definitions that collide with the generated file's own declarations
body:
#1230 raised this as a follow-up. It said, from reading the code, that the Go generators might not guard a `$defs` name against the identifiers the generated file declares itself. I tested it, and it is a real defect in both Go generators: `scripts/build-go-bindings.mjs` (prebuilt) and `trust-tasks-go/cmd/trust-tasks-gen` (consumer-side).

## How it was checked

I added a temporary spec (not committed) whose `$defs` were named `Spec`, `TypeURI`, `Extends`, `Deprecation`, `PayloadSchemaJSON`, `ResponseSpec`, `ResponseTypeURI` and `ResponsePayloadSchemaJSON`. Those are the eight identifiers the package tail declares. The spec also had two enum cases: `$defs.Type` with the value `URI`, and `$defs.Kind` with the value `spec` next to a `$defs.KindSpec` object. I generated it with the prebuilt generator, built its registry bundle, and generated it again with `trust-tasks-gen`.

Neither output compiled. `go build -gcflags=-e` reported `TypeURI`, `Extends`, `Deprecation`, `ResponseTypeURI`, `PayloadSchemaJSON`, `ResponsePayloadSchemaJSON`, `Spec` and `ResponseSpec` redeclared, and `Spec` initialised from `TypeURI (type)`. The consumer-side output also had `KindSpec redeclared` and `KindSpec (constant) is not a type`.

So there are three ways to hit it:

1. A `$defs` name that matches a tail identifier.
2. A name derived from a path that matches one. An inline object at `Response.spec` becomes `ResponseSpec`, and one at `Payload.schemaJson` becomes `PayloadSchemaJSON`.
3. An enum constant (`<Type><Value>`). It was only de-duplicated within its own enum, so it could match a type (`KindSpec`) or the tail (`TypeURI`).

## The fix

I fixed each generator separately, as CLAUDE.md requires, and used the same approach as the Dart fix in #1230: rename, don't refuse.

- Before any name comes from the schema, the eight tail identifiers are taken in the emitter's name table. `reserve()` then adds the numeric suffix it already uses for other collisions (`Spec2`). All eight are reserved even when the package doesn't emit `ResponseTypeURI`/`ResponseSpec`, so a type's name doesn't depend on whether the spec declares a response. The prebuilt generator does this only for request packages. Shared-schema packages have no tail.
- Enum constants are now checked against, and added to, the same table. A constant that collides gets the `_` suffix already used for duplicate constants within an enum, and a type declared later avoids it.

## No generated output changes

Every name these rules change would have been a compile error before. `npm run build-go-bindings` gives no diff in `trust-tasks-go/specs`. `npm run check-bindings` passes. The equivalence test (`TRUST_TASKS_BUNDLES=… go test ./cmd/trust-tasks-gen -run Equivalence`) passed against a full registry that included the probe spec, so the two generators pick the same suffixed names. No published API changes, so the title has no `!`.

## Tests

- `trust-tasks-go/cmd/trust-tasks-gen`: `TestReservedNames` generates a package for the probe schema, parses it, and checks that every top-level identifier is declared once, along with the expected suffixed names. With the reservation removed it fails with 25 errors.
- Prebuilt: `scripts/test-checks/go-bindings-names.test.mjs` (run by `npm run test:checks`) checks the same rules against the `.mjs` emitter. To make that possible, `build-go-bindings.mjs` now runs `main()` only when invoked as a script, and exports the emitter functions it tests.

title: fix(dart,dart-bindings): escape names the generated Dart cannot declare
body:
#1215 fixed Rust codegen for schema member names that are Rust keywords (#1100) and asked whether the TS, Go and Dart generators have the same problem. This PR checks all six generators: the in-repo `scripts/build-{ts,go,dart}-bindings.mjs` and the consumer-side `trust-tasks-ts-gen`, `trust-tasks-go/cmd/trust-tasks-gen` and `trust-tasks-dart/lib/src/generator/`.

## How it was checked

I added a temporary spec (not committed). Its member names, enum values and `$defs` names were reserved or meaningful words in each language: `default`, `class`, `func`, `go`, `type`, `interface`, `new`, `in`, `is`, `var`, `const`, `package`, `import`, `return`, `switch`, `function`, `late`, `required`, `dynamic`, `await`, `yield`, `int`, `num`, `double`, `bool`, `toJson`, `fromJson`, `hashCode`, `toString`, `runtimeType`, `noSuchMethod`, `value`, `values`, `1st`, and `$defs` named `class`, `function`, `default`, `interface`, `String`, `Map`, `MapEntry`, `List`, `Object`, `Type`, `Error`, `DateTime`, `SpecPolicy` and `Deprecated`. I generated it with all six generators (the consumer-side ones from its registry bundle) and compiled the output.

| Generator | Result |
|---|---|
| Go (both) | **No defect.** Every identifier is exported PascalCase, so no Go keyword (all lowercase) can come out. The runtime is imported qualified (`trusttasks.SpecPolicy`). `go vet` is clean. The consumer-side output matches the prebuilt output apart from the header and schema text. |
| TypeScript (both) | **No defect.** Property names may be any IdentifierName, enum values are string literals, and json-schema-to-typescript PascalCases type names. An interface named `Object`/`String`/`Function` exists only in type space, and the module tail uses none of those names as types. `tsc --strict` is clean. |
| Dart (both) | **Defect: 243 analyzer errors.** Details below. |

## The Dart defect

`_dartReserved` only covered the reserved words. These cases still produced invalid code:

1. **Type names.** `$defs.Function` became `class Function`. `Function` is a built-in identifier and can't be used as a type name. `$defs.String` / `Map` / `List` / `Object` / `MapEntry` shadowed the `dart:core` types that every generated `fromJson`/`toJson` is written in. `$defs.SpecPolicy` / `Deprecated` shadowed the names the tail uses (the runtime import is unprefixed). These names are now pre-reserved in the emitter, so `reserve()` adds a suffix as it does for any other collision (`String2`).
2. **Class fields.** A field named `dynamic`, `int`, `double`, `num` or `bool` shadows that type throughout the class body (`Map<String, dynamic>`). A field named `toJson` conflicts with the class's own method. Fields named `hashCode`, `toString`, `runtimeType` or `noSuchMethod` are invalid overrides of the `Object` members. These now get the existing `Value` suffix, as keywords already do. A field named `fromJson` is legal and is left alone.
3. **Extension-type constants.** Enum values `value` and `values` collided with the extension type's representation field and its `values` list, so they now get the `Value` suffix too. This set is kept narrow on purpose: `GroupKind.dynamic` (vtc/groups) is a legal, published constant and does not change.

Both Dart generators are fixed separately, as CLAUDE.md requires.

## No published output changes

`npm run regen` gives no diff in any of the four libraries. No current spec uses any of the newly escaped names in a position where the escape applies, so no published API moves and the title has no `!`. `npm run check-bindings` passes, and `dart test test/generator_test.dart` gains a `names` group that pins the three rules.

Follow-up (not fixed here, not keyword-related): from reading the code (not tested), the Go generators don't appear to guard a `$defs` name against the tail's own identifiers (`Spec`, `TypeURI`, `Extends`, `Deprecation`, `PayloadSchemaJSON`, …). TypeScript refuses the equivalent collision.

title: fix(ts): stop shipping src and source maps in the npm package
body:
This is the non-breaking part of the package-size work. `@openvtc/trust-tasks` shipped `src/` (the generated TypeScript sources) next to `dist/`, along with a `.js.map` and a `.d.ts.map` for every module that pointed back into it. This PR stops shipping all three.

Changes:

- `trust-tasks-ts/package.json`: `src` is removed from `files`.
- `trust-tasks-ts/tsconfig.json`: `sourceMap` and `declarationMap` are turned off for the published build.
- `trust-tasks-ts/tsconfig.test.json`: `sourceMap` is turned back on for the test build only, so test stack traces still map to the `.ts` sources.

Measured with `npm pack --dry-run` on a fresh `npm run build` of this checkout:

- Before: 161.2 MB unpacked (161,161,279 bytes), 7,879 files, 12.3 MB packed.
- After: 101.4 MB unpacked (101,419,071 bytes), 3,154 files, 8.2 MB packed.

That is 59.7 MB and 4,725 files less. The 0.28.28 release on npm reports 143.7 MB and 7,778 files; main has grown since then.

Nothing relied on the removed files:

- `npm run smoke` imports `dist/` and passes.
- `npm test` passes (248 tests).
- `api-compat` builds its PR-side declarations with `--declarationMap false --sourceMap false` and only reads `.d.ts` files from the published tarball, so it is unaffected. `npm run api-compat` reports ok, and the incompatibilities it lists come from #1210, which already declares the break. `scripts/api-compat.test.mjs` passes.
- `check-bundles` and the trust-tasks-ts-gen equivalence check read `trust-tasks-ts/src` from the repository, not from the package.
- The sibling packages use the core through `dist` and its `exports` map.

The sibling TS packages already publish only `dist`. They still emit maps that point at sources they don't ship, but those packages are small, so I left them alone.

Not done here: the generated schema constants still use `as const`. Each declaration file therefore repeats its whole schema as a readonly literal type, which is the larger part of the remaining `.d.ts` weight. Widening that annotation changes declared types, which is a public-API change, so it waits for the maintainer to decide. Splitting the runtime into its own package is also left for later.

Part of #1107.

CI and release-pipeline fixes from the 2026-11-11 repository review. Each item below lists the issue and what changed.

### #1097: trust-tasks-rs crate size
- `rust.yml` `package`: after `cargo package`, a step reads `target/package/trust-tasks-rs-<version>.crate`. It **fails above 9.9 MiB** and **warns above 9.5 MiB**, and prints the headroom left and a rough count of how many more spec versions fit.
- `trust-tasks-rs/Cargo.toml`: `exclude` now also lists `CHANGELOG.md`.
- Measured locally after the exclusion with `cargo package -p trust-tasks-rs --no-verify`: **10,308,682 bytes (9.83 MiB)**. The new warning fires today. The crate is ~72 KB below the fail line, roughly 10 more spec versions. Scheduling the milestone-5 removal, or asking crates.io for a raised limit, is still open.

### #1133: deploy.yml
- The `deploy` job alone joins `concurrency: { group: deploy-production, cancel-in-progress: false }`. Builds still run in parallel; deploys queue.
- The first step of `deploy` skips the rest when `main` has already moved past `github.sha`. A queued older run therefore cannot `sync --delete` over a newer deploy, and the newer commit's own run deploys it. Both jobs already had `timeout-minutes`.

### #1134: check-published-schemas
- Front matter is parsed with `yaml` (`parseFrontMatter` in `schema-compat.mjs`).
- `frontMatterIncompatibilities` compares the full derived per-variant policy: proof request/response, issuedAt request/response (both forms, with an omitted `response` taking the request's value), `parties[].requirement` (the response's recipient is the request's issuer), and `bearer`. The derivation is independent of the one in `check-bindings-conformance.mjs`. The build's `extends` check uses the same function and still passes all 30 declarations.
- The diff uses `--no-renames --diff-filter=MD`, so deleting or renaming a released schema or `spec.md` now fails. Deleting `payload.invalid-examples.json` does not.
- Regression fixtures for the per-variant form are in `scripts/test-checks/fixtures/published-schemas/`. Unit and end-to-end tests run against throwaway git repos.
- The CLAUDE.md check-table row is updated.

### #1135: rust.yml path filter
- Added `fixtures/**`, `ceremonies/**`, `scripts/check-rs-api-compat.sh` and `release-plz.toml`.
- `published-schemas` moved to a new **unfiltered** `checks.yml`, keeping the same job name, so it can be a required check. It now runs `npm ci` because it needs `yaml`.

### #1136: build-registry.mjs git dates
- A single `git log --format=… --name-only -- specs` pass, run on first use, replaces the 2–3 `git log` processes per spec version. Every ancestor directory of a changed path is credited. Git-derived authors use the same pass.
- Under `--validate-only` the dates are not computed.
- `npm run build`: **1m43s → 5.7s**. `website/assets/tasks.generated.js` is byte-identical apart from the `Generated at` line. `npm run validate`: 2.6s.

### #1137: release rules
- `checks.yml` `versions change only in the Release PR` runs `scripts/check-version-edits.mjs`. It compares parsed values for each workspace member's `[package] version`, `trust-tasks-ts*/package.json` `"version"`, Go `const Version`, pubspec `version:` and Dart `packageVersion` against the merge base. The job is skipped when the head branch is `release` **from this repository**; a fork's `release` branch is not exempt. Files the PR adds, dependency requirements and reformatting are not changes, so Dependabot and the withdrawal batch pass.
- `commit-lint.yml`: a new `breaking-trailer` job fails when any PR commit message, or the description, has a line matching `^BREAKING[ -]CHANGE`, the pattern the bump scripts read. The repository squash setting is `COMMIT_MESSAGES`, so the commit messages become the squash body.
- `commit-lint.yml`: the `!` scope regex is replaced by the explicit union the release tooling recognises. `runtime`, `bindings` and the `ts-…`/`go-…`/`dart-…` wildcards are gone. `check-release-lists` fails if this list and the scripts' lists disagree.

### #1139: release lists
- New `scripts/check-release-lists.mjs` (`npm run check-release-lists`). It runs as an extra step of the existing `Dart package lists agree` job, so no check names change. `check-dart-packages` is unchanged.
  - **npm:** the `build-npm` and `publish-npm` matrices are identical. Each entry agrees with its `package.json` name, with `TS_PACKAGES` (core first) and with its `release-bump-ts.sh` arm (dir and tag prefix). Every sibling is built by some `ts.yml` job.
  - **Go:** the `verify-go` and `publish-go` matrices are identical. Entries agree with `go.mod` module paths, version files, `GO_MODULES` and the `release-bump-go.sh` arms (dir, version file, tag prefix, module). Every nested `go.mod` (including the unreleased `tsp`) is in both core `:(exclude)` lists and has a `go.yml` job.
  - **Crates:** published library crates match `check-rs-api-compat.sh` `CRATES`. Every crate with a published `trust-tasks-rs` dependency is in release-plz's `core` group. Core crates are in `CORE_SCOPES`, crates versioned on their own have a `scopes_for` arm, and every workspace member is in `rust.yml`'s path filter.
- Mutation tests cover each kind of drift in `scripts/test-checks/release-lists.test.mjs`.

### #1141 (partial)
- Every job without `timeout-minutes` now has a generous one: 90–120 min for the heavy Rust compiles, 5–45 min elsewhere. `publish-dart.yml` `publish` is the exception: it calls a reusable workflow, which cannot take one.
- `ts.yml` `gen-equivalence` now uses `Swatinem/rust-cache`, saving from main only.

### #1142 (partial)
- `npm run check` runs validate, check-bindings, check-published-schemas, check-version-edits, check-sibling-core-ranges, check-dart-packages, check-release-lists, check-withdrawal-readiness and the ceremony checks. Locally it takes ~22s.
- `npm run regen` runs all four generators and then `cargo fmt --all`.
- Added `.nvmrc` (24).
- `new-spec.mjs`'s closing message prints both commands. It no longer says to "bump both libraries" (the old release flow).
- A reserved slug missing from the allowlist now fails with one message naming the enum to edit, instead of `/slug must NOT be valid`. The CLAUDE.md paragraph that quoted the old output is updated.

### #1143
- The TS, Go and Dart drift checks use `git status --porcelain`, so untracked generated files are caught. On failure they `git add -N` before diffing so new files show in the log.
- `release-plz-release` has `concurrency: release-plz-release-${{ github.ref }}`, never cancelled.
- When `withdraw.yml` is re-run, an open `withdraw/<as-of>` PR is updated through REST, as `release-pr.sh` does, instead of failing at `gh pr create`.

### Verified locally
- `npm run validate` and `npm run build` pass.
- `npm run check` passes.
- Test suites pass: `npm run test:checks` (24), `test:release-scripts` (33) and `test:website` (17).
- `npm run extends-candidates` runs.
- `actionlint` is clean on every workflow.
- `cargo package -p trust-tasks-rs --no-verify --list` no longer lists `CHANGELOG.md`.

### Not run locally
- The workflows themselves.
- `npm run regen`, which runs the Rust codegen.
- The full verify build in `cargo package`.

Closes #1133

Closes #1139
Closes #1143

title: fix(rs,build,cli,codegen): review fixes — declared guard code, SchemaValidator, keyword slugs, generate --lang rs, registry hints, docs.rs
body:
Rust-side fixes from the 2026-11-11 repo review.

## Per issue

**#1093 — `reject_last_authority` emitted an undeclared code.** It now returns `acl/revoke:lastAuthorityProtected`, the code every `acl/revoke` version declares, through a new `guards::acl::LAST_AUTHORITY_PROTECTED` constant. An `acl`-feature unit test pins that constant to the generated `error_codes::LAST_AUTHORITY_PROTECTED` of 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3. The doc no longer says to put the code into `RejectReason::TaskFailed`, which has no code member. It now shows building the payload with `ErrorPayload::new(code.parse()?)`, or with the `acl` feature, `ErrorPayload::from(<generated DeclaredErrorCode>)`. The signature is unchanged (`Option<&'static str>`), so the runtime gains no new dependency on a non-framework family. TS, Go and Dart ship no equivalent helper: I checked, and nothing there needed changing. Closes #1093

**#1091 — no shipped `PayloadValidator`.**
- New `validate::SchemaValidator` (feature `validate`) implements `PayloadValidator`. It compiles each schema once and caches the compiled validator, keyed by the schema text's `(address, length)`.
- `PayloadValidator` takes `&str`, not `&'static str`. So a cache hit is confirmed by comparing the text, and the cache is bounded. A schema that is freed and then reallocated at the same address can make the validator recompile, but it can never get the wrong validator.
- `new()` is `const`, so `static V: SchemaValidator = SchemaValidator::new()` works.
- `ValidatedPayload::validate_value` and `DeclaredErrorCode::check_details` now share one process-wide instance.
- `extension::prune_payload` reuses a parsed-schema cache built the same way (not feature-gated).
- New `PayloadPolicy::accept_unvalidated()` removes the need for the turbofish.
- All of this is additive. Closes #1091

**#1099 — doc-block stripping edited the printed source.** The `<details><summary>JSON schema</summary>` blocks are now removed from `#[doc]` attributes on the `syn` tree, before unparsing. Only a run of doc attributes whose whole text is the opening line, through one whose whole text is the closing line, is removed; a run that is interrupted or never closes is left alone. New tests:
- unit tests on the pass itself
- an end-to-end `generate_module` test with a schema `description` that contains the marker. `PAYLOAD_SCHEMA`, the impls, `EXTENDS` and `ERROR_CODES` all survive.

Closes #1099

**#1100 — a slug segment that is a Rust keyword could not be generated.** The new `trust_tasks_build::module_name` / `module_file_name` (both `#[doc(hidden)]`) handle it:
- `move` → `r#move`, stored in `move.rs`
- `self`, `super`, `crate` and `Self` take a `_` suffix

Both `generate_locked` (slug segments and source names) and `trust-tasks-codegen`'s tree writer use them: `mod.rs` tree, file paths, conformance tree, index paths. Tests cover every keyword, a locked `keys/move` + `self/type` with the index on, a source named `type`, and the codegen `mod.rs` tree.

**Follow-up, not done here:** the TS, Go and Dart generators have the same question for their own keywords (`go`, `func`, `class`, `default`, …). Closes #1100

**#1103 — `generate --lang rs` did nothing.** It now runs `trust_tasks_build::Config::generate` in-process and writes `<out>/trust_tasks_generated.rs`, the file `build.rs` would write. Like the other languages, it requires `--out`. After `--` it accepts `--index` and `--runtime-path <path>`, and refuses any other option rather than ignoring it. The CLI README and `--help` are updated, and the `generate` integration test covers it. Closes #1103

**#1104 — CLI registry messages.**
- `check`'s lock/registry mismatch hint now says how to keep the lock's registry (``set `registry = "<url>"` in trust-tasks.toml``, or `--registry` / `TRUST_TASKS_REGISTRY`) as well as how to move off it (`update`).
- `add` and `update` print a note when `--registry` / `TRUST_TASKS_REGISTRY` differs from what `trust-tasks.toml` names. The manifest is left unchanged, since the env var sets the same flag and writing the manifest from it would be surprising.
- HTTP 401 is now an error ("authentication required"). A 403 on the index, or on a bundle path, is reported as a refusal (mentioning S3's 403-for-missing-key), not as "no registry index". A 403 from the by-digest store still falls back to the version path.
- `registry build` now uses the shared `http_agent`, so it honours `TRUST_TASKS_CA_FILE`.
- `check_slug` and `Version::parse` now use `trust_tasks_build::is_spec_slug` / `is_spec_version`: `vault/get/00.3` and `1abc/x` are refused as invalid slugs.

Tests: an https mock that returns 401, 403 and 404, plus the 403 fallback on by-digest; the hint and note in `cli.rs`, including a bare `check` passing once the manifest names the registry; and the stricter grammar. Closes #1104

**#1105 — codegen hygiene.**
- Dropped the unused `typify`, `schemars`, `heck` and `serde` dependencies, and `syn`'s `visit-mut`. Clippy is clean with them gone.
- Rewrote the module header.
- `GeneratedSpec` keeps the parsed `Bundle`. `write_schema_index` and `write_extends_index` now read the policy, `extends` and response side from it; `Spec::policy()` and the schema re-reads are gone.
- `cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen && cargo fmt --all` leaves every generated file byte-identical.
- Hard-coded size and count figures are reworded so they cannot drift: `Cargo.toml`, `trust-tasks-rs/Cargo.toml`, `rust.yml`, `release-plz.toml`, `CLAUDE.md`, and the codegen comment. `trust-tasks-rs/README.md`'s "941 modules / ~66 MB" was left as is.

Closes #1105

**#1106 — docs.rs.** The docs.rs builds page confirms that every build of `trust-tasks-rs` 0.37.15 failed. Beyond the size problem, simulating the docs.rs build locally (nightly, `--cfg docsrs`) fails with E0658: `trust-tasks-rs` (and `trust-tasks-https`) use `doc(cfg)` without `#![cfg_attr(docsrs, feature(doc_cfg))]`. This PR adds that attribute to both crates and sets docs.rs metadata:
- `trust-tasks-rs`: `no-default-features` + `validate`, `acl`
- the facade: every non-spec feature

Both now document cleanly under the simulated docs.rs build; the facade peaked at about 430 MB RSS. Closes #1106

## Not breaking
No `!`: every API change is additive (`SchemaValidator`, `accept_unvalidated`, `LAST_AUTHORITY_PROTECTED`, the hidden `module_name` helpers). One behavioural change to note: `reject_last_authority` now returns the lowerCamelCase code. The old snake_case value matched no declared code, so this is treated as a bug fix.

## Checks run
- `cargo test`:
  - `trust-tasks-rs` (`--no-default-features --features acl --all-targets`, and `--features validate,acl --lib` + doctests, with `-D warnings` on the lib tests)
  - `trust-tasks-build`, `trust-tasks-codegen`, `trust-tasks-cli`, `trust-tasks-example-consumer-app`
- clippy `-D warnings` on the touched crates
- codegen no-drift
- `cargo fmt --all --check`

Not run: the whole-workspace `cargo build --workspace --all-targets`, and the default (all-specs) `trust-tasks-rs` test build.

A documentation pass over the issues from the 2026-11-11 review. Every claim was rechecked against current `main` first, and some items were already fixed there. Library behaviour is unchanged: the only code edits are to examples (the `issuedAt` stamp, and the `acl/grant/0.3` move with the `purposes` field it requires) and to comments.

Where a number had drifted, the text now gives a command or a table, or uses `cargo add`, so there is no version or count left to go stale.

## Status per issue

**Closes #1140**
- RELEASING.md now describes the single Release PR in "Merge it". It lists all five version declarations contributors must not edit and adds the `trust_tasks_capability_client` row.
- It also drops the stale "tested-but-unreleased" paragraph, and the npm first-publish note no longer splits the package table.

- Extending `stale-references` to `*.md` outside `specs/` is not done. The docs mention old versions on purpose in many places (CHANGELOGs, SPEC examples, infra tests), so it needs its own allowlist design.

## Checks run
- `npm run validate`, `npm run check-bindings`
- `cargo test -p trust-tasks --test getting_started_snippets`; `cargo run -p trust-tasks-example-getting-started` (output pasted into GETTING-STARTED)
- `cargo fmt --all --check`
- `cargo doc` for `trust-tasks-rs` (`--no-default-features --features validate,acl`), `-https`, `-tsp`, `-didcomm-v1`, `-capability-client` and `trust-tasks`: no warnings
- `cargo check` of the edited examples
- `cargo package --list` for the new README/LICENSE files
- `trust-tasks-ts`: `npm test` (212 pass)
- Go: `gofmt -l`; `go vet` and `go test` for the core `trusttasks`, `proof` and `didcomm`
- Dart: `dart analyze --fatal-infos` and `dart format` on the touched files; `dart run example/main.dart`

docs: fix drifted counts, release runbook, licences and stale examples across the four libraries (#1224)
