title: ci: read-only workflow tokens by default, and keep release tokens out of jobs that run package code
body:
Narrows what each workflow job can do with its token, and keeps the release token and OIDC tokens out of the jobs that run third-party package code.

## Read-only by default

Every workflow now declares `permissions: contents: read` at the top (`codegen`, `dart`, `deploy`, `go`, `publish-dart`, `rust` and `ts` had no block and inherited the repository default). A job that needs more asks for it:

| Workflow | Job | Permissions |
|---|---|---|
| `go.yml`, `rust.yml` | `api-compat` | + `pull-requests: read` (reads the PR title through the API) |
| `deploy.yml` | `deploy` | + `id-token: write` |
| `publish.yml` | `publish-npm` | `contents: write`, `id-token: write` (unchanged) |
| `publish.yml` | `publish-go`, `tag-dart` | `contents: write` (unchanged) |
| `publish.yml` | `release-pr-open` | `contents: write`, `pull-requests: write` |
| `withdraw.yml` | `open-pr` | `contents: write`, `pull-requests: write` (was workflow-wide) |

Every `actions/checkout` now sets `persist-credentials: false`. The jobs that push no longer pass a token to checkout; `scripts/git-push-with-token.sh` gives `$PUSH_TOKEN` to the one `git push` that needs it, through `GIT_CONFIG_*` environment variables (not `.git/config` or argv).

## Release jobs split into an unprivileged job and a privileged job

| Before | Now: runs package code, read-only | Now: publishes or pushes, runs no package code |
|---|---|---|
| `publish-npm` (`npm ci && npm run build` beside `id-token: write`) | `build-npm`: `npm ci`, build, `npm pack`, upload the tarball | `publish-npm`: `npm publish <tarball>` (OIDC, provenance), tag |
| `publish-go` (`go test` beside `contents: write`) | `verify-go`: build, vet, test | `publish-go`: tag, warm the proxy |
| `tag-dart` (`dart pub get` / `dart test` beside the PAT) | `verify-dart`: pub get, analyze, test, dry run | `tag-dart`: push the tag with the PAT |
| `release-pr` (release-plz and git-cliff beside the PAT) | `release-pr`: `release-pr.sh prepare` → patch artifact | `release-pr-open`: `release-pr.sh open` → apply, commit, push, PR |
| `withdraw.yml` `batch` (`npm ci`, cargo, generators beside the PAT) | `batch`: flip and regenerate → patch artifact | `open-pr`: apply, commit, push, PR |

Each pair shares one matrix through a YAML anchor (`&npm-packages` / `*npm-packages`, and likewise for Go and Dart), so the legs line up by construction and `check-dart-packages` still reads the `tag-dart` matrix. The decide step is shared the same way, and the privileged job re-reads the decision from its own checkout. A leg of the privileged job runs only if its own leg of the first job passed: it downloads that leg's artifact, which is uploaded only on success.

`scripts/release-pr.sh` gains `prepare DIR` and `open DIR` subcommands. With no arguments it runs both, as before. `open` checks that the patch was computed against the commit it is applying to.

### What a token job accepts from the job before it

- **Patches** (`release-pr-open`, and `open-pr` in `withdraw.yml`). Before applying, each job checks the patch from its own checkout with `scripts/check-patch-paths.sh` (`git apply --numstat -z` and `--summary`).
  - Allowed for `release`: the files a real `prepare` run changed, which were 40 files from main at 774ccaea6. That means the root `Cargo.toml`/`Cargo.lock`, `<pkg>/Cargo.toml`, `<pkg>[/<module>]/CHANGELOG.md`, `<pkg>/package.json`/`package-lock.json`, `<pkg>/pubspec.yaml`, `trust-tasks-go/<module>/version.go` and `trust-tasks-dart/lib/src/runtime/version.dart`.
  - Allowed for `withdraw`: `specs/` plus the four generators' output trees (the same trees the drift checks compare).
  - Always refused: `.github/`, `scripts/`, `.gitattributes`, `.gitmodules`, mode 120000/160000, renames and copies.
  - After `git apply`, nothing from the working tree runs. The push is a function in `release-pr.sh` and inline in `withdraw.yml`, with tracing off.
- **npm tarball.** `publish-npm` extracts `package/package.json` from the tarball. It requires `name` to equal the matrix package and `version` to equal the version the job decided from its own checkout, and it refuses any `publishConfig`.
- **Verify markers.** `publish-go` and `tag-dart` require the marker's recorded commit to equal `$GITHUB_SHA`. I kept the artifact names stable rather than adding `run_attempt`: re-running only a failed publish leg must still find the marker from the earlier verify attempt.
- `git-push-with-token.sh`, now used only on unpatched checkouts, turns tracing off before it reads the token.

`release-plz-release` is unchanged apart from a comment. The libdbus step's comment no longer says that job compiles what it publishes; the step stays for now. It runs the release-plz action beside the crates.io token and `contents: write`, but it compiles nothing (`publish_no_verify = true`), so no dependency build script runs there. Its checkout already persisted no credentials.

## Deploy: GitHub OIDC for AWS

`deploy.yml` uses `aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials` (same pin, v6.3.0) with `role-to-assume: ${{ vars.AWS_DEPLOY_ROLE_ARN }}` when that repository variable is set. Until it is set, the existing `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` / `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` secrets are used as before, so merging this changes nothing until the role exists. The deploy job now runs in a `website` environment, so the role's trust policy can name it. GitHub creates that environment on the first run. Both jobs have timeouts: build 30 minutes, deploy 15 (recent runs take about 3).

To finish, in this order (also in RELEASING.md, "Setup this depends on"):
1. **In GitHub first:** create the `website` environment (Settings → Environments) and restrict its deployment branches to `main`. The role trusts the environment, not the branch, so this rule is what limits it to `main`, and it must be in place before the role exists.
2. Confirm the repository uses the default OIDC subject template. I checked this today: `gh api repos/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/actions/oidc/customization/sub` returns `{"use_default":true,...}`.
3. In AWS, add the IAM OIDC provider `token.actions.githubusercontent.com` (audience `sts.amazonaws.com`) if the account has none.
4. Create the role.
   - **Trust policy:** allow `sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` from that provider with `StringEquals` on `token.actions.githubusercontent.com:aud` = `sts.amazonaws.com` and `token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub` = `repo:trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf:environment:website`.
   - **Permissions:**
     - `s3:ListBucket` on `arn:aws:s3:::<bucket>`, with `StringLike` `s3:prefix` = `website/*`
     - `s3:PutObject` and `s3:DeleteObject` on `arn:aws:s3:::<bucket>/website/*`
     - an explicit **Deny** of `s3:DeleteObject` on `arn:aws:s3:::<bucket>/website/specs/by-digest/*`, because the by-digest store is append-only
     - `cloudfront:CreateInvalidation` on the distribution
   - No `s3:GetObject` is needed: `aws s3 sync` compares by listing.
5. Set the repository variable `AWS_DEPLOY_ROLE_ARN` to the role's ARN and let a deploy run.
6. Once a deploy succeeds through the role, delete the `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` / `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` secrets and the IAM user's key, and remove the access-key step from `deploy.yml`.

## Behaviour changes

- A release now runs as two jobs per registry, so the Actions UI shows `Build … for npm`, `Verify … before tagging`, and `Open or update the Release PR` alongside the existing job names. The idempotency of a re-run is unchanged. A re-run now means "Re-run failed jobs", which reruns the failed verify leg and the publish leg that depends on it.
- Dart: all packages are verified before any is tagged. Before, the dependents were verified one at a time after the core's tag. In both cases a dependent that needs core API released in the same merge fails verification, and the remedy is still to re-run once the core is on pub.dev. Now the core is still tagged when a dependent fails.
- The `withdraw.yml` job is now `prepare the withdrawal batch` followed by `open the withdrawal pull request`.
- RELEASING.md now says the release token must be a user PAT, since the scripts already refuse an App token, and recommends a fine-grained one limited to this repository. A fine-grained PAT on a `trustoverip` repository works only if the organization allows fine-grained PATs and an owner approves this one.
- A Release PR or withdrawal batch that touches a file outside its allowlist is now refused. The `open` job fails and names the file, and nothing is pushed. Adding a new kind of file to a release means adding it to `check-patch-paths.sh`.
- New workflow `Release scripts`, which runs `npm run test:release-scripts` on every PR and push to main.
- Nothing in any published package changes.

## Checks

- `actionlint` 1.7.12 on every workflow: clean.
- `shellcheck` on `git-push-with-token.sh` and `check-patch-paths.sh`: clean.
- `npm run test:release-scripts`: 8 of 8 pass, exit 0.
  - `open` is refused, with nothing applied, pushed or sent to `gh`, for a patch that touches `scripts/other.sh`, `scripts/release-pr.sh`, a new `.github/workflows/*.yml`, a `.gitattributes`, a symlink, or a file off the release list.
  - An ordinary release patch is applied, committed with sign-off and pushed.
  - The `withdraw` allowlist takes spec and generated paths and refuses others.
  - With the check commented out, 6 of the 8 fail. On `release-pr.sh`: only the three SC2016 infos already on `main`.
- `node scripts/check-dart-packages.mjs`: lists agree (it reads the `tag-dart` matrix through the alias).
- `release-pr.sh prepare` then `open`, re-run after these changes on a local clone of `main` (774ccaea6), with a stub `gh`, a local bare remote and `PUSH_TOKEN` set.
  - `prepare` exited 0, produced the 18-package, 40-file patch, and left the tree clean.
  - `open` exited 0: all 40 files were on the release allowlist, and it applied the patch, committed as the token owner with sign-off, and pushed.
- The publish, deploy and withdraw jobs cannot be exercised from a PR. Their first real run is the next merge (deploy, and the publish no-op legs), the next Release PR merge, and the next quarterly withdrawal.

## Checklist (development guide §9)

- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2) — no client code; deploy jobs gained timeouts
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3) — n/a
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1) — each privileged job re-checks registry/tag state before acting, as before
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4) — existing bounded loops unchanged
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5) — n/a
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6) — n/a
- [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, deny_unknown_fields where security-relevant, schema registered, all consumers (incl. JS) updated (R3.*) — no wire types. The `release-pr.sh` interface is extended (no-argument behaviour kept), and its only caller is `publish.yml` (R3.6)
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive; fail-closed if enforcement can't start (R5.*) — no `permissions` means read-only. Without the role variable, deploy keeps today's access-key path, which is a deliberate transition and is listed above.
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified; background-job failures are surfaced (R6.*) — a publish leg fails visibly when its verify leg did not pass
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1) — the publish, tag and push steps are the same idempotent steps as before. A failed `open` leaves the branch as it was, and a re-run recomputes it.
- [x] Deviations from this guide flagged explicitly with rule numbers — none

body:
ci: read-only workflow tokens by default, and keep release tokens out of jobs that run package code (#1181)

* ci: read-only workflow tokens by default, and keep release tokens out of jobs that run package code

Every workflow now declares `permissions: contents: read` at the top, and
a job that needs more asks for it by name: the API compatibility jobs in
go.yml and rust.yml read the PR title (`pull-requests: read`), and the
deploy job requests `id-token: write`. No checkout persists credentials.

The publish and tag jobs in publish.yml are each split in two. The first
(`build-npm`, `verify-go`, `verify-dart`) installs, builds and tests with
read-only permissions and no OIDC token; the second (`publish-npm`,
`publish-go`, `tag-dart`) publishes the packed tarball or pushes the tag
and runs no package code. The two share one matrix through a YAML anchor,
and a leg of the second runs only if its own leg of the first passed.

The Release PR job is split the same way: `release-pr` runs
`release-pr.sh prepare` (release-plz, git-cliff, the bump scripts) and
uploads the change as a patch; `release-pr-open` runs `release-pr.sh open`,
which applies it, commits and pushes with RELEASE_PLZ_TOKEN. withdraw.yml
follows the same shape. scripts/git-push-with-token.sh hands the token to
the single `git push` that needs it through the environment.

deploy.yml takes AWS credentials from GitHub OIDC (`role-to-assume`) when
the AWS_DEPLOY_ROLE_ARN repository variable is set, and from the existing
access-key secrets until then. The deploy job runs in a `website`
environment, and both deploy jobs have timeouts.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* docs(releasing): release-plz-release builds nothing, so say what it does hold

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* ci: check what a token job takes from the job before it

release-pr-open and withdraw.yml's open-pr apply a patch computed in a
read-only job. They now check it first, from their own checkout, with
scripts/check-patch-paths.sh. The patch may touch only the files a release
(or a withdrawal batch) changes, and never .github/, scripts/,
.gitattributes, .gitmodules, a symlink, a submodule, a rename or a copy.
After applying it, they run nothing from the working tree: the push is a
function in release-pr.sh and inline in withdraw.yml, not the helper script.

publish-npm checks that the tarball's package.json names the package and
version it decided to publish, and carries no publishConfig. publish-go and
tag-dart require the verify marker to name the commit being tagged. The
push helper turns tracing off before it reads the token.

scripts/test-release/ runs `release-pr.sh open` against patches touching
scripts, a workflow, .gitattributes, a symlink and a spec. Each is refused
with nothing applied, pushed or sent to gh, and an ordinary release patch
still goes through. A new `Release scripts` workflow runs it on every PR.

The libdbus comment in release-plz-release no longer says that job
compiles what it publishes.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* docs(releasing): the deploy role setup, and the patch and tarball checks

Website deploy role: create and restrict the environment first, check the OIDC subject template, then the role. The role gets no s3:GetObject, ListBucket is limited to the website/ prefix, and an explicit deny stops it deleting from the by-digest store. Also notes that a fine-grained PAT on an organization repository needs the organization to allow and approve it.

title: fix(messaging/mux/ack): notPermitted only for a member whose mail the connection reads (0.1)
body:
Follow-up to #1174 and #1176. `messaging/mux/ack` 0.1 (draft) no longer lets a principal confirm mail it was never shown.

**The problem:** after #1176, rule 3 answers `notPermitted` for any message held for a member the connection carries without `delete`. A member may be carried with only `send` (or another scope that never shows its mail). An id is a hash of the message, so a principal that knows one (it sent the message, say) could ask for it and learn from `notPermitted` vs `notFound` whether that member still holds it.

**Change:**
- **Rule 3:** `notPermitted` only for a member carried with `receive` or `pickup`, whose mail the connection already sees. A member carried with neither is answered `notFound`, the same as a DID the connection does not carry.
- **Security & Privacy → Data carried:** names the sent-message case.
- **`AckRefusal.reason` description** updated to match. Same enum, no schema change beyond the description.

Bindings regenerated (doc comments only). `npm run validate`, `check-bindings` and `check-published-schemas` pass. The reference mediator implements this in a follow-up to affinidi/affinidi-messaging-mediator#231.

title: fix(rs,ts,go,dart)!: the in-memory replay guard refuses when full instead of dropping live records
body:
`InMemoryReplayGuard` — the batteries-included SPEC §7.2 item 11 record in all four runtimes, and the default in the Rust HTTPS/DIDComm/TSP consumers — made room for a new `id` by dropping the least-recently-used record, whether or not that record was still inside its retention window. A document whose record was dropped that way was accepted again inside its window, silently. The default capacity (10 000) was sized for the five-minute window, while a document with `expiresAt` must be remembered for up to 30 days. Separately, TypeScript, Go and Dart retained a record until the producer's `expiresAt` with no upper bound, so a distant `expiresAt` kept a record indefinitely.

## What changes

**Full guard: refuse, don't forget (all four runtimes)**
- When every slot holds a record still inside its window, a claim for a new `id` fails — Rust `ReplayGuardError`, TS `ReplayGuardFullError`, Go `ErrReplayGuardFull`, Dart `ReplayGuardFullException` — which `consume_inbound` / `consumeInbound` / `ConsumeInbound` already answer `unavailable` (retryable, no detail on the wire). Expired records are reclaimed first; a live record is never dropped to make room. Duplicates and conflicts are still answered while full.
- Rust indexes records by retention deadline, so reclaiming is `O(expired · log n)`; TS/Go/Dart track the earliest deadline and only scan when something can have expired.
- Default capacity is now **100 000** live records (≈ five-minute window at ~330 distinct documents/s), exported as `DEFAULT_REPLAY_CAPACITY` (Rust, TS) / `DefaultReplayCapacity` (Go) / `defaultReplayCapacity` (Dart), and documented as a ceiling per retention window, with the sizing guidance for consumers that admit long-lived documents (raise it, lower the horizon, or use a shared store).

**One party's share (all four runtimes)**
- No issuer may hold more than a share of the guard: a tenth of the capacity by default, rounded up; configurable (Rust `InMemoryReplayGuard::with_per_issuer_limit`, TS/Dart second constructor argument, Go `WithPerIssuerLimit`). An issuer at its share is refused `unavailable` (retryable) for its *own* new documents only; every other party is unaffected. Without this, one signer sending documents with `expiresAt` = `issuedAt` + 30 days could hold every slot for a month.
- The pipeline passes the issuer it resolved (SPEC §4.8.1) through a new issuer-aware claim, added without breaking existing guards: Rust `ReplayGuard::claim_for` (default method → `claim`), TS optional `ReplayGuard.claimFor`, Go `IssuerScopedReplayGuard` (optional interface, type-asserted), Dart `IssuerScopedReplayGuard` (separate interface, `is`-checked). Documents with no resolved issuer, and direct `claim` calls, share one allowance.
- Limitation, documented on each guard: the share is per identifier. Where anyone can mint identifiers (an unauthenticated transport with `did:key`), one party using many is bounded only by the overall capacity.

**Expiry horizon in TypeScript, Go and Dart (port of Rust's `expiry_horizon`)**
- `FreshnessPolicy` gains `expiryHorizonMs` / `ExpiryHorizon` / `expiryHorizon` (optional; the consequential policy sets 30 days, `DEFAULT_EXPIRY_HORIZON_MS` / `DefaultExpiryHorizon` / `defaultExpiryHorizon`).
- `recordExpiry` clamps a retained record's expiry to `issuedAt + horizon + skew`, as Rust's `record_expiry` does.
- `validateFreshness` follows Rust: a stated `expiresAt` bounds the window in place of the maximum age, up to the horizon; past `issuedAt + horizon + skew` the document is `expired`, so it is never accepted after its record could be dropped.
- Zero horizon means the same in all four: no horizon only when absent (`None` / `undefined` / `nil` / `null`); a zero horizon clamps at `issuedAt`. Go's `ExpiryHorizon` is therefore a `*time.Duration` (unlike `MaxAge`, where zero is "unbounded").

**Documentation**
- Each guard documents its worst-case memory (≈ capacity × (largest `id` + largest cached response)) and that a document with `expiresAt` but no `issuedAt` is not bounded by the horizon under a policy that does not require `issuedAt` (the consequential policy does). I did not cap the stored response size: dropping it would turn a duplicate's answer into silence, so I left that to a decision about the transport's own body limit.
- `GETTING-STARTED.md`: a consumer may keep its record for less than a stated `expiresAt`, provided it stops accepting the document at the same point (SPEC §7.2, *Bounding the record*); the in-memory guard's full and per-issuer behaviour. (`SPEC.md` is generated from the canonical repo, so it is not edited here.)

Refs #1120 — this ports the "`expiresAt` replaces maxAge" rule and the horizon with its record clamp. The issue's shared cross-runtime freshness vector file (including calendar-invalid timestamps) is not in this PR.

## Behaviour changes (R3.6)
**Breaking (`!`):** a consumer now refuses documents it used to accept (a full guard, an issuer at its share), and the Go/TS/Dart freshness verdicts change. The `go API compatibility` job also needs the `!` for the new exported names.
- An issuer holding a tenth of the guard is refused for its own new documents until its records expire.
- A full in-memory guard now answers new documents `unavailable` instead of accepting them after dropping an older record. With the larger default this needs ~10× the previous concurrent load; deployments with sustained high rates or long-lived documents should size explicitly or use a shared guard.
- Default capacity 10 000 → 100 000: the memory bound rises accordingly (≈ 100 000 × typical cached response size).
- TS/Go/Dart, consequential policy: a document with `issuedAt` older than five minutes but an `expiresAt` still ahead is now **accepted** (as Rust already does); a document stated to expire more than 30 days after `issuedAt` is treated as expiring at the horizon.
- Additive API: the new error types, constants and the optional horizon field/parameter. Nothing removed.

## Tests
- Rust `replay.rs`: full guard refuses (mapped to `unavailable`) and keeps both records; expired records are reclaimed first; one issuer at its share is refused while another issuer and the no-issuer allowance are not, the share frees on expiry, and the limit is configurable. The LRU test is replaced.
- TS `replay.test.ts`, Go `replay_test.go`, Dart `replay_test.dart`: the same two guard cases, a pipeline case (second `id` → retryable `unavailable`, first `id` still a duplicate, one execution), `expiresAt` replacing the maximum age, the horizon clamp for acceptance and for the record, the per-issuer share (same cases as Rust), and (Go, Dart) a zero horizon clamping at `issuedAt`.

Run locally (exit codes):
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check` 0; `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --no-default-features --features acl --all-targets` 0; `cargo test -p trust-tasks-https -p trust-tasks-didcomm -p trust-tasks-tsp -p trust-tasks-didcomm-v1 -p trust-tasks-capability-client --all-targets` 0; `cargo clippy … -D warnings` (trust-tasks-rs acl; the binding crates and capability-client) 0
- `trust-tasks-ts`: `npm test` 0 (131/131), `npx tsc -p tsconfig.json --noEmit` 0, `npm run smoke` 0
- `trust-tasks-go`: `go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, `gofmt -l .` (empty), `go test -race ./...` 0
- `trust-tasks-dart`: `dart analyze --fatal-infos` 0, `dart format` clean, `dart test` 0; `trust-tasks-dart-{didcomm,https,tsp}`: `dart test` 0

Full-workspace `cargo test`/`clippy` were left to CI (memory).

## Not in this PR
- Capping `id` length / storing a digest of oversized ids, capping the cached response size, and keeping records of refused documents from competing with executed ones for capacity.
- An eviction/full counter or callback for metrics.

## Pre-merge checklist (vti-stack development guide §9)
- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2) — n/a
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3) — the guards hold their mutex only for in-memory work
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1) — a refused claim writes nothing; the producer's retry is absorbed or executed once capacity frees
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4) — `unavailable` is retryable by the producer; nothing retries here
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5) — a full guard is a per-document refusal, not a loop failure
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6) — n/a
- [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, deny_unknown_fields where security-relevant, schema registered, all consumers (incl. JS) updated (R3.*) — no wire type changed; all four runtimes changed together
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive; fail-closed if enforcement can't start (R5.*) — a full record fails closed; the consequential policy carries the horizon by default
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified; background-job failures are surfaced (R6.*) — the guard error carries the record count for logs; the wire message stays generic
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1) — in-memory record only; restart loses it as before (documented)
- [x] Deviations from this guide flagged explicitly with rule numbers — R3.6 behaviour changes above

title: fix(rs,ts,go,dart)!: the in-memory replay guard refuses when full instead of dropping live records (#1163)
body:
fix(rs,ts,go,dart)!: the in-memory replay guard refuses when full instead of dropping live records (#1163)

* fix(runtime): the in-memory replay guard refuses when full instead of dropping live records

InMemoryReplayGuard (Rust, TypeScript, Go, Dart) made room for a new id by
dropping the least-recently-used record, whether or not that record was
still inside its retention window. A document whose record was dropped that
way was then accepted again inside its window, with nothing logged.

- When every slot holds a live record, a claim for a new id now fails
  (Rust ReplayGuardError, TS ReplayGuardFullError, Go ErrReplayGuardFull,
  Dart ReplayGuardFullException), which the pipeline answers `unavailable`
  (retryable). Records whose window has closed are reclaimed first; a
  record is never dropped to make room. Duplicates and conflicts are still
  recognised while full.
- The default capacity is 100 000 live records (was 10 000), documented as
  a ceiling on distinct documents per retention window, and exported as
  DEFAULT_REPLAY_CAPACITY / DefaultReplayCapacity / defaultReplayCapacity.
- TypeScript, Go and Dart gain the expiry horizon Rust already had
  (`expiryHorizonMs` / `ExpiryHorizon` / `expiryHorizon`, 30 days in the
  consequential policy): a stated expiresAt bounds the acceptance window in
  place of the maximum age, up to issuedAt + horizon, and the retained
  record's expiry is clamped to the same instant, so a producer can no
  longer pin a record indefinitely with a distant expiresAt.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(runtime): give each issuer a share of the in-memory replay guard

One signer could fill the in-memory guard with documents whose records
live to the expiry horizon (issuedAt now, expiresAt 30 days on) at a few
documents an hour per slot, after which every party was refused.

- No issuer may hold more than a share of the guard's capacity: a tenth by
  default, rounded up, configurable (Rust `with_per_issuer_limit`, TS and
  Dart second constructor argument, Go `WithPerIssuerLimit`). An issuer at
  its share is refused `unavailable` for its own new documents only.
- The pipeline passes the issuer it resolved (SPEC §4.8.1) through a new
  issuer-aware claim: Rust `ReplayGuard::claim_for` (default method calling
  `claim`), TS optional `claimFor`, Go `IssuerScopedReplayGuard`, Dart
  `IssuerScopedReplayGuard`. Existing guards are unaffected; documents with
  no resolved issuer, and direct `claim` calls, share one allowance.
- Zero expiry horizon means the same everywhere: none only when absent
  (None / undefined / nil / null); zero clamps at issuedAt. Go's
  `ExpiryHorizon` is now a `*time.Duration` to say so.
- Documented: the share is per identifier; a document with expiresAt and no
  issuedAt is not bounded by the horizon; the guard's worst-case memory; and
  in GETTING-STARTED that a consumer may retain below a stated expiresAt
  (SPEC §7.2, Bounding the record).

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* docs: place the record-retention note where it does not overlap the item 3 note

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(runtime): end the clamped expiry window where its record does

With the acceptance window over `issuedAt` now half-open (refused once
`issuedAt + maxAge + skew <= now`), the expiry-horizon clamp in the
TypeScript, Go and Dart runtimes follows suit: a document whose
`expiresAt` lies beyond the horizon is refused from
`issuedAt + expiryHorizon + skew`, the instant `recordExpiry` returns
and a guard may drop the record, rather than one instant later. Rust's
clamp already did.

The horizon tests now accept one millisecond before that instant and
expect `expired` at it, and the shared `fixtures/consume` vectors gain
the clamped-horizon boundary, run by all four runtimes. The
`recordExpiry` docs say "refuses from", as Rust's do, and a redundant
rustdoc link target is dropped.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

---------

title: feat(keys)!: every node resolves did:webs; withdraw the resolvedMethods gate (VTI-KEY-003, VTI-KEY-008)
body:
Each party chooses its own identifier method, and the stack works whichever it chooses. For example, a did:webs client talks to a did:webvh service, and the reverse.

#121 admitted did:webs as an *optional* method that no peer had to resolve. A did:webs node could then act only toward peers that declared `resolvedMethods` (VTI-KEY-008). That made a party's choice of method limit who it could talk to. This PR reverses the choice:

- **VTI-KEY-003:** did:webs is a required method; every node resolves it, with the key-role designation extension (VTI-KEY-173).
- **VTI-KEY-001:** which durable method a node uses is its operator's choice, and a node must not require a peer to use any one of them.
- **VTI-KEY-008:** withdrawn. There is nothing to declare.
- **VTI-KEY-009:** keeps the receiver's `unsupportedDidMethod` refusal (now for genuinely unsupported methods) and the no-downgrade rule. `methodNotDeclared` is gone.
- **Follow-on edits:** the alpha note, the rationale (rewritten), the level 2/3 open issue under VTI-KEY-173, the DID-class table, the [DID-WEBS] reference and the Appendix F row. The Appendix F row records what implementations still lack: the push gateway and the browser client library don't resolve did:webs yet, and the gate is still in the VTI code.

did:webs stays at alpha maturity.

This touches the same chapter as #122 (the VTI-KEY-184/199/129 narrowing) but different requirements, so either can merge first.

title: fix(keys): narrow VTI-KEY-184 to dependent keys; a next-key threshold stands in for a witness in VTI-KEY-199
body:
Two changes, both prompted by trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#993 (key assurance levels, and the `webs` method profile).

**VTI-KEY-184: narrowed, with the rest as best practice.**
- *Was:* at level 2 and 3, a node MUST NOT publish any X25519 key computed from an Ed25519 key.
- *Now:* it MUST NOT publish a key computed from a key it publishes, or from a key of another role. An X25519 key computed from a *published* Ed25519 key is one such key.
- *New SHOULD:* derive each key agreement key independently of every signing key.
- *Not prohibited:* an X25519 key that is the image of an Ed25519 key derived for it alone, and published and used nowhere else. This is what a key hierarchy that derives on one curve produces; VTI's derives on Ed25519 only.
- The rationale gains a sentence on why: VTI-KEY-071 targets a dependence between published keys or between roles, and this form creates neither.

**VTI-KEY-199 item 3: the VTI-KEY-129 stand-in.**
- *Was:* item 3 capped every unwitnessed level-3 version at level 2, although VTI-KEY-129 lets a next-key threshold stand in for the witness. That stand-in is what a level-3 did:webs (KERI) identity relies on: `nt` over `[R′, K]`, which cannot be met without the recovery key K.
- *Now:* item 3 accepts the stand-in when two things hold: the threshold makes the recovery custodian's signature necessary for every change of the change authority, and the history is published at the one location the identifier names.
- VTI-KEY-129 adds that such an identity SHOULD still be witnessed. A witness also detects a duplicitous history (two histories published for one identifier), which no threshold can.

title: fix(runtime): settle or release the item-11 claim on every remaining path
body:
Follow-up to #1175. It closes the remaining paths on which an item-11 claim could be left neither released nor settled, or settled the wrong way.

## Changes

**Rust core (`trust-tasks-rs/src/consume.rs`)**
- **Cancellation during a retryable-refusal release.** `HeldClaim` now stays armed across `guard.release(..).await` and is disarmed on the very next statement, with no await in between. If the pipeline is dropped while that release is pending, the destructor releases through `release_abandoned`. Before, the claim was disarmed as soon as the handler returned, so a pipeline dropped mid-release left it in flight.
- **A panicking `Serialize`.** The handler returned, so the effect happened. If its response or a final refusal panics while being serialised for the record, the claim is now recorded with no response before the panic continues unchanged, so a resend is absorbed. Before, the claim stayed in flight.

**Rust HTTPS server (`trust-tasks-https/src/server.rs`)**
- `release_claim` is used on the refusal branch and the panic branch. It now holds a small drop guard across its `release().await`, so a request dropped mid-release (a timeout layer, a client disconnect) still releases the claim through `release_abandoned`.

**`ReplayGuard::release_abandoned` docs (`trust-tasks-rs/src/replay.rs`)**
- The method **MUST NOT** block, **MUST NOT** require a runtime context, and **MUST NOT** panic.
- The docs now state the default's degradation: a `release` that suspends is polled once and abandoned, so the record stays until `retain_until`.
- Overriding guidance no longer suggests `tokio::spawn`, which needs a current runtime.

**Go (`trust-tasks-go/trusttasks/consume.go`)**
- A `MarshalJSON` that panics inside `settle` (after the handler returned) now records the claim with a nil response in a deferred block, and the panic continues unchanged.

**Dart (`trust-tasks-dart/lib/src/runtime/consume.dart`)**
- On the non-retryable refusal branch, a refusal that cannot be encoded for the record now **releases** the claim before the error is rethrown. A refusal executed nothing, so the resend is evaluated again rather than answered as a completed duplicate with no body.
- The success branch is unchanged from #1175: there the handler ran, so the claim is settled with no response.

## Tests
- **Rust:**
  - `tests/replay_guard.rs`:
    - a response whose `Serialize` panics → panic propagates, and the resend is a completed duplicate with no response;
    - a pipeline dropped while a retryable refusal's release is pending → the claim is released and the resend runs.
  - `src/replay.rs`: the default `release_abandoned` on a guard whose `release` returns `Pending` → polled exactly once, returns without a runtime, and the record stays.
  - `trust-tasks-https` (new `release_tests` module): a release cancelled mid-await still releases the claim.
- **Go** (`claim_release_test.go`): a response whose `MarshalJSON` panics → panic propagates, and the resend is a settled duplicate.
- **Dart** (`replay_test.dart`): a final refusal whose payload cannot be encoded → the error propagates, the claim is released, and the resend is handled.

Each new test fails on `main` and passes here.

## Behaviour changes
- **Rust:** after a response or refusal `Serialize` panic, a resend is absorbed as a completed duplicate with no response. Before, it was answered "in flight" until the record expired. The panic still reaches the caller.
- **Rust and HTTPS:** a pipeline or request dropped while a claim's release is pending now releases the claim. Before, it was left in flight.
- **Go:** after a response `MarshalJSON` panic, a resend is absorbed as a settled duplicate instead of "in flight". The panic still reaches the caller.
- **Dart:** after a final refusal fails to encode, a resend is evaluated again instead of being answered as a completed duplicate with no body. The encoder error still reaches the caller.
- **No public API change:** documentation only on `release_abandoned`.

## Checklist

- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2): no clients touched.
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3): unchanged.
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1): the item-11 record is the idempotency record. It is now settled or released on every path the handler's outcome leaves.
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4): no retries added. A claim whose handler returned is never released for a re-run, except a refusal, which executed nothing.
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5): n/a.
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6): n/a.
- [x] New/changed wire types (R3.*): none.
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive; fail-closed if enforcement can't start (R5.*): unchanged.
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified (R6.*): no logging changes.
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1): in-process cancellation and panics now settle or release; a process death still leaves a persistent record until `retain_until`, as before.
- [x] Deviations from this guide flagged explicitly with rule numbers: none.

title: fix(messaging/mux/ack): an id held for a DID off the connection is notFound (0.1)
body:
Follow-up to #1174. `messaging/mux/ack` 0.1 (draft) no longer lets an ack confirm another DID's mail.

**The problem:** consumer rule 3 said to answer `notPermitted` when "the message is a member's and the member is not on the connection". A message id is the SHA-256 of the message, so a principal could name an id it guessed. A `notPermitted` for a DID the connection doesn't carry would then confirm that someone holds that message, where `notFound` would not.

**Change:**
- **Rule 3:** `notPermitted` only for a message held for a member *this connection carries*, which lacks `delete` (or whose account no longer stands). Everything else is `notFound`, and a message held for a DID the connection does not carry **MUST** be answered as if it did not exist.
- **Security & Privacy → Data carried:** says why.

title: feat(vta): a TEE VTA can take a key-role did:webs as its own DID at first boot
body:
A TEE (Nitro) VTA can take a key-role did:webs as its own DID at first boot (design note did-webs-in-the-vta, S8).

- **Config:** new `[tee.kms.vta_did_webs]` (`server_did`, `domain`, optional `path`, `server_id`). It needs `[dids] webs_enabled` and the new, off-by-default `webs` feature on vta-enclave (`VTA_ENABLE_WEBS=true` in `build-vta.sh`). Existing images, PCR0 and attested config digests are unchanged. Setting it together with `vta_did_template` is refused. It is not in the fleet tenant overlay.
- **First boot:** `vta_service::tee_webs::maybe_generate_webs_vta_did` mints through `operations::did_webs::create_own_identity`, the same path setup's `create_webs` now uses. That function refuses if the VTA already has an identity and is reachable only from first boot and setup, never from a transport. A refused mint is fatal on Nitro, never a fallback to another identifier (VTI-KEY-009). `server::run` publishes the DID as before.
- **Interrupted boot:** the next boot adopts the identity already minted instead of minting a second one (R2.1).
- **Egress proxy:** allowlists the host and domain. `extract_host_from_did` handles did:webs and now keeps the `%3A` port for did:web and did:webvh (it used to drop it).
- **Restore fix:** `detach_hosted_dids` now also detaches did:webs slots on a cross-identity restore.
- **Refactor:** `build_vta_additional_services` moves into the library (`operations::protocol::document::vta_additional_services`) so the TEE and setup designate the same services.
- **CI:** a `tee_` test step and an enclave `…,webs` check.

Local: nextest workspace all passed (the two known flaky tests pass when rerun alone), vtc 3702/3702, doctests, clippy `-D warnings` (workspace, `tee,rest,didcomm[,webs]`), fmt, and the narrow no-webs check. Not run locally: the Linux `vsock-store` enclave builds; CI covers them.

Open questions for review:
1. Should the fleet tenant overlay be able to set `vta_did_webs`, as it can `vta_did_template`?
2. The proxy assumes the host's endpoint is on the host DID's own domain; if it isn't, the operator adds it to `ALLOWLIST_HOSTS`.
3. A detached did:webs has no command to re-attach it to a server.

title: fix(runtime): release the item-11 claim when a handler does not return, and end the acceptance window where the record does
body:
Two robustness fixes to the SPEC §7.2 item-11 duplicate-execution record, across the runtimes.

## 1. A handler that does not return releases its claim

When a handler panicked, or the future running the pipeline was dropped while the handler was awaited, the item-11 claim stayed "in flight" until the record expired (five minutes by default, up to the expiry horizon with `expiresAt`). Every resend in that time came back as an in-flight duplicate and never ran. The claim is now released on those paths, exactly once, and a resend runs again.

| Runtime | Before | Now |
|---|---|---|
| Rust (`consume_core`, so `consume_inbound` and `consume_dispatched`) | released only on the two normal returns | the claim is held in a drop guard across the handler await. A panic or a dropped future releases it through the new **defaulted** `ReplayGuard::release_abandoned` (synchronous, because it runs from a destructor). A returned handler settles it as before. |
| Go (`ConsumeInbound`) | a panicking handler skipped the release; release/settle reused the request `ctx`, which was already cancelled when the handler failed for that reason | a `defer` releases the claim if the handler did not return. It does not `recover`, so the panic reaches the caller unchanged with its original stack, and `runtime.Goexit` is covered too. Release and settle run on `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` bounded at 5 s, so a store-backed guard is not handed a cancelled context. |
| Dart (`consumeInbound`) | a throwing response encoder (`responseToJson`, or encoding a non-retryable refusal) after the handler returned left the claim in flight | the claim is settled with no cached response before the error is rethrown. The handler did run, so a resend is absorbed rather than executed a second time. This is what Rust and Go already do when encoding a response fails. |
| TypeScript | already released the claim when the handler throws (and a promise cannot be cancelled) | unchanged; the existing test covers it |

`release_abandoned`'s default polls `release` once with a no-op waker and drops it. That completes for any guard whose `release` does not suspend; `InMemoryReplayGuard` overrides it to release directly and to tolerate a poisoned lock during unwinding. A guard backed by a network store should override it to hand the release to its own runtime (documented on the method). Otherwise its record stays until `retain_until`, which is no worse than before.

`trust-tasks-https`'s server is unchanged here. Its dispatch is synchronous and already releases on panic. *Correction:* cancellation can also interrupt the awaited `release_claim` on its refusal and panic branches, leaving the claim in flight; that, and the same window around the core pipeline's retryable-refusal release, are fixed in the follow-up PR.

## 2. The acceptance window ends where the record does

All four runtimes accepted a document whose `issuedAt + maxAge + skew` equalled `now` (stale only when `< now`), while `InMemoryReplayGuard` treats a record as absent once `retainUntil <= now`, and `recordExpiry` returns exactly that sum. At that one instant a resend passed freshness, found no record, and ran again. The window is now half-open (refused when `bound <= now`), as `expiresAt` already was (`expiresAt <= now` is expired). The same applies to Rust's expiry-horizon clamp. Moving the boundary on the freshness side, rather than in the guard, also fixes custom `ReplayGuard` implementations that drop at `retainUntil <= now`, as the trait contract allows.

## Tests

- Rust (`tests/replay_guard.rs`): panicking handler → resend handled, then absorbed; dropped future → resend handled; a resend while the handler is still running is still an in-flight duplicate; window boundary. `src/replay.rs`: `release_abandoned` through the override and through the default. `src/freshness.rs`: window and horizon boundaries.
- Go (`trusttasks/claim_release_test.go`): panicking handler, with the panic value propagating unchanged; handler failing because its context was cancelled, against a guard that refuses a cancelled context; window boundary.
- Dart (`test/replay_test.dart`): throwing response encoder → claim settled, resend absorbed; window boundary.
- TypeScript (`test/replay.test.ts`): window boundary.
- Shared vectors: `fixtures/consume/item11-digest.json` gains an optional per-case `secondAt` and two cases (one millisecond before the window closes → `duplicate`; at the instant it closes → `expired`). The Rust, TypeScript, Go and Dart harnesses all run them, and now report a refusal by its code.

The new claim-release and boundary tests fail on `main` and pass here (checked in Rust, Go and Dart).

## Behaviour changes

- A document arriving at exactly `issuedAt + maxAge + skew` (or, in Rust, at exactly `issuedAt + expiryHorizon + skew` for a clamped `expiresAt`) is now refused `expired`; it was accepted. One instant earlier than before, and consistent with `expiresAt`.
- Rust and Go: a resend after a handler panic, or (Rust) after the pipeline future was dropped mid-handler, now runs the handler again instead of being answered as an in-flight duplicate.
- Dart: after a response-encoder failure, a resend is absorbed as a settled duplicate with no prior response, instead of an in-flight duplicate. The encoder's error still reaches the caller as before.
- Rust public API: one new trait method with a default body (`ReplayGuard::release_abandoned`). Additive; no existing implementation needs to change.

## Checklist

- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2): no clients touched. Go's detached settle/release context is bounded at 5 s.
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3): `InMemoryReplayGuard` takes its lock synchronously, as before.
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1): the item-11 record *is* the idempotency record; this makes an abandoned claim releasable, so the producer's bit-for-bit resend proceeds.
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4): no retries added. A claim is released only when the handler did not return; a handler that returned is settled, never released for a re-run (Dart encoder path).
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5): n/a.
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6): n/a.
- [x] New/changed wire types (R3.*): none. The shared fixture format gains an optional `secondAt`, and all four harnesses read it.
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive; fail-closed if enforcement can't start (R5.*): unchanged; the window boundary moves toward refusing.
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified (R6.*): no logging changes.
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1): a process death mid-handler leaves an in-memory record nowhere to go (it dies with it); a persistent guard keeps the claim until `retain_until`, as before. The drop guard addresses the in-process cases: panic and cancellation.
- [x] Deviations from this guide flagged explicitly with rule numbers: none.

- **Fix:** `build_did_secrets_bundle` (room-host export) included the KERI pre-rotated successor key for a did:webs. It now holds only the keys the document lists.

title: fix(rs,ts,go,dart)!: refuse a document whose type is not the spec it is consumed under
body:
SPEC §7.2 item 3 (an unrecognised `type`) was documented in every runtime as "the caller's parse and dispatch — already succeeded by the time you hold a typed document". On the typed paths that is not true: deserialising into `TrustTask

` / `Document[P]` / `TrustTaskDocument

` (or, in TypeScript, nothing at all) never compares `type` with the spec being consumed, and the binding consumers (Rust DIDComm/TSP/DIDComm v1 `receive`, the TS TSP consumer, the Go DIDComm/TSP consumers, the Dart DIDComm/TSP consumers) take one spec and go straight to `consumeInbound`. A document of another specification whose payload happened to fit was therefore run under the consumed spec's policy and handler, and answered as its own type. The Rust dispatched path and the HTTPS servers (exact route lookup) were already correct. ## What changes Each runtime's typed consume function checks the document's `type` first, before the item-11 claim, so a refused document never burns its `id`: | Document `type` | Outcome | |---|---| | the spec's Type URI, `#request` or no fragment | accepted | | a later version of the same spec and variant whose declared `extends` chain reaches it (SPEC §5.2) | accepted (as `read_as` / `readForSpec` / `ReadForSpec` / `readForVersion` already accept it) | | the same spec and variant, any other version | `unsupportedVersion` | | anything else — another slug, the same slug under another authority or form, the `#response` variant, not a Type URI | `unsupportedType` | These are the codes SPEC §8.3 defines for item 3 and the ones each runtime's existing reader (`read_as`, `readForSpec`, `ReadForSpec`, `readForVersion`) already returns. - **Rust** — `consume_inbound` uses the decision factored out of `extension::read_as`. Every binding crate's typed receive goes through it. - **TypeScript** — `consumeInbound`. A `readForSpec` re-reading (recognised through `receivedDocumentOf`) has already been routed with whatever index the caller gave, and is not re-checked. - **Go** — `ConsumeInbound`. New optional `ConsumeOptions.Extends` names the extension lookup for a forward reading (nil: `RegistryExtends`); pass the one given to `ReadForSpecWith`. - **Dart** — `consumeInbound`. New optional `extendsIndex` argument, same purpose. - Module docs, `trust-tasks-ts/README.md` and `GETTING-STARTED.md` no longer say item 3 has already succeeded. ## Review follow-ups (second commit) - **Extension links:** Go `chainReaches` and Dart `extensionChain` now follow a declared link only to a strictly earlier MINOR of the same MAJOR, as Rust (`extension.rs`) and TypeScript (`extendsChain`) already did. A caller-supplied lookup declaring an upward, same-version or cross-MAJOR link no longer routes. Tests in `extends_test.go` and `extension_test.dart`. - **TS re-readings are tied to their spec:** `readForSpec` records the `spec.typeUri` it read for; `consumeInbound` skips its own check only when consuming under that same spec. `readForSpec(raw, A)` then `consumeInbound({ spec: B, doc })` is now checked (test in `extends.test.ts`). - **Custom indexes documented:** Go `ConsumeOptions.Extends` and Dart `extendsIndex` say a caller re-reading with its own lookup/index MUST pass it (otherwise a chain only that index declares is refused `unsupportedVersion`); the TS README says `consumeInbound` reads the generated index plus `declareExtends` tables and takes no index of its own. ## Behaviour changes (R3.6) **Breaking (`!`):** a consumer now refuses documents it used to accept, which CLAUDE.md counts as a breaking library change. All four libraries move together. - A typed consumer now refuses documents of a type other than the spec it consumes under. Callers that consumed a document under a *different* spec on purpose (none in this repo outside tests) must route on `type` first. - Rust `extension::read_as` now answers a `#response` document read as a request type `unsupportedType` (was `unsupportedVersion`), matching TypeScript and Go. - Go `didcomm` / `tsp` require the published core (`v0.9.3`); they pick the check up when that requirement moves to the release containing it. The Rust binding crates and the Dart siblings (path / `pubspec_overrides` deps) get it now. - Additive API only: Go `ConsumeOptions.Extends`, Dart `consumeInbound(extendsIndex:)`. ## Tests Each runtime gets the same negative set — another slug, the same slug under another authority, the `#response` variant, (TS/Go/Dart) a non-Type-URI, and two versions that do not reach the implemented one — plus `#request` ≡ bare, and a refusal-before-claim case (the right document under the same `id` is still handled). Existing tests that consumed a document typed for one spec under another were aligned to consume it under its own. Run locally (exit codes): - `cargo fmt --all -- --check` 0; `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --no-default-features --features acl --all-targets` 0; `cargo test -p trust-tasks-https -p trust-tasks-didcomm -p trust-tasks-tsp -p trust-tasks-didcomm-v1 --all-targets` 0; `cargo clippy -p trust-tasks-rs --no-default-features --features acl --all-targets -- -D warnings` 0; `cargo clippy -p trust-tasks-didcomm -p trust-tasks-tsp -p trust-tasks-didcomm-v1 -p trust-tasks-https --all-targets -- -D warnings` 0 - `trust-tasks-ts`: `npm test` 0 (135/135 after the follow-ups), `npx tsc -p tsconfig.json --noEmit` 0, `npm run smoke` 0 - `trust-tasks-go`: `go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, `gofmt -l .` (empty), `go test -race ./...` 0 - `trust-tasks-dart`: `dart analyze --fatal-infos` 0, `dart format` clean, `dart test` 0 (161 after the follow-ups); `trust-tasks-dart-{didcomm,https,tsp,proof,capability-client}`: `dart test` 0 The full-workspace `cargo test --workspace` / `cargo clippy --workspace` were not run locally (memory); CI runs them. ## Pre-merge checklist (vti-stack development guide §9) - [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2) — no network code touched - [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3) — n/a - [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1) — the check runs before the item-11 claim; nothing is written for a refused document - [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4) — n/a - [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5) — n/a - [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6) — n/a - [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, deny_unknown_fields where security-relevant, schema registered, all consumers (incl. JS) updated (R3.*) — no wire type changed; all four runtimes changed together - [x] Config absence = most restrictive; fail-closed if enforcement can't start (R5.*) — the check is unconditional; the optional extension lookups default to the registry's - [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified; background-job failures are surfaced (R6.*) — n/a - [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1) — no mutation precedes the check - [x] Deviations from this guide flagged explicitly with rule numbers — R3.6 behaviour changes above

title: fix(rs,ts,go,dart)!: refuse a document whose type is not the spec it is consumed under (#1162)
body:
fix(rs,ts,go,dart)!: refuse a document whose type is not the spec it is consumed under (#1162)

* fix(runtime): refuse a document whose type is not the spec it is consumed under

The typed consume functions took the document's payload type, or a spec
policy, as given and never compared the document's `type` with it. A
document of another specification whose payload happened to fit was run
under the consumed spec's policy and handler, and answered as its own type.
SPEC §7.2 item 3 assigns that check to the consumer.

Each runtime's typed path now checks it before any other step, so a refused
document never reaches the item-11 record:

- accepted: the spec's own Type URI (`#request` and no fragment alike), or a
  later version of the same specification and variant whose declared
  `extends` chain reaches it (SPEC §5.2);
- `unsupportedVersion`: the same specification and variant at any other
  version;
- `unsupportedType`: anything else — another slug, the same slug under
  another authority or form, the `#response` variant, or a `type` that is not
  a Type URI.

Rust: `consume_inbound` (and so every binding's typed receive) uses the
same decision as `extension::read_as`. `read_as` now answers a variant
mismatch `unsupportedType` rather than `unsupportedVersion`, as the
TypeScript and Go readers already did.
TypeScript: `consumeInbound`; a `readForSpec` re-reading is already routed
and is not checked again.
Go: `ConsumeInbound`, with a new optional `ConsumeOptions.Extends` naming the
extension lookup for a forward reading (nil: the registry's).
Dart: `consumeInbound`, with a new optional `extendsIndex` argument.

The module docs and READMEs that said item 3 had "already succeeded" by the
time a typed document is held are corrected.

- Go `chainReaches` and Dart `extensionChain` follow a declared extension
  link only to a strictly earlier MINOR of the same MAJOR, as Rust and
  TypeScript already do. A caller-supplied lookup declaring an upward,
  same-version or cross-MAJOR link no longer routes.

  `readForSpec` re-reading made for the spec it is consuming under; one made
  for another spec is checked like any other document.
- Documented that Go and Dart callers re-reading with their own extension
  lookup must pass it to `ConsumeOptions.Extends` / `extendsIndex`, and that
  TypeScript's `consumeInbound` reads the generated index plus
  `declareExtends` tables only.

title: fix(runtime): release the item-11 claim when a handler does not return, and end the acceptance window where the record does (#1175)
body:
fix(runtime): release the item-11 claim when a handler does not return, and end the acceptance window where the record does (#1175)

* fix(runtime): release the item-11 claim when a handler does not return, and close the window where the record expires

A handler that panicked (Rust, Go) or whose future was dropped mid-await
(Rust: a request timeout, a client disconnect) left its item-11 claim in
flight until the record expired, so every resend of the document was
absorbed as an in-flight duplicate and never ran. The claim is now
released on those paths exactly once:

- Rust: `consume_core` holds the claim in a drop guard across the handler
  await. A panic or cancellation releases it through the new defaulted
  `ReplayGuard::release_abandoned` (synchronous, as it runs from a
  destructor); a returned handler settles it as before. The default polls
  `release` once; `InMemoryReplayGuard` releases directly.
- Go: a deferred release covers a panicking handler without recovering, so
  the panic continues unchanged. Release and settle run on a context
  detached from the request's cancellation (bounded at five seconds), so a
  store-backed guard is not handed an already-cancelled context.
- Dart: when the response encoder throws after the handler returned, the
  claim is settled with no cached response before the error is rethrown,
  rather than left in flight. The effect happened, so a resend is absorbed.
- TypeScript already released the claim on a throwing handler.

The acceptance window over `issuedAt` (and the expiry horizon in Rust) now
ends exclusively, at the instant `recordExpiry` returns, in all four
runtimes. A guard drops a record once `retainUntil <= now`, while a
document was still accepted at exactly `retainUntil`, so at that instant
it could be accepted with no record and executed again. The window is now
half-open, as `expiresAt` already was.

The shared `fixtures/consume/item11-digest.json` vectors gain an optional
per-case `secondAt` and two boundary cases, run by all four runtimes.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* refactor(runtime): keep the claim-release change clear of neighbouring edits

Wrap the claim in its drop guard just before the handler runs, keep the
record-expiry doc wording, and move the Go claim-release tests into their
own file.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* docs(runtime): keep the TypeScript record-expiry wording

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: fix(vtc-service)!: keyed list cursors for badges, boards and elections; application and suspended entries read as members do not
body:
Two fixes on vtc-service's read paths: list cursors are keyed, and `application` and suspended entries no longer pass gates meant for members and administrators.

## 1. Keyed list cursors (badges, boards, elections)

The three families paged with `"{offset}.{mac}"` cursors. The "mac" was `SHA-256("vtc/<family>/cursor/v1" ‖ binding ‖ offset)`, truncated and unkeyed, so any caller could compute a valid cursor for any binding and offset. It was compared with `==`. On the five badge lists (`list`, `claims/list`, `awards/list`, `holders/list`, `kudos/list`), `page()` then computed `offset + limit` unchecked, so an offset near `usize::MAX` overflowed. In release it wrapped and sliced `items[len..small]`, which panics. Boards clamped `start` first and did not panic. Elections added the offset to a schema-capped limit with no check.

- New `trust_tasks::offset_cursor`, used by all three families:
  - `mint`: `"{offset}.{hex(HMAC-SHA256(key, family ‖ binding ‖ offset)[..16])}"`.
  - `read`: refuses anything but the canonical decimal offset, then verifies the tag with `verify_truncated_left` (constant time).
  - `key`: the audit writer's active key, as `directory_tasks` / `group_tasks` cursors use. With no audit writer, a random per-process key, so cursors stop verifying at a restart and the client starts the list again. Rotating the audit key does the same.
  - `window(offset, limit, len)`: a page that is always inside the result.
- `badge_tasks`, `board_tasks` and `election_tasks` drop their own MAC functions. The bindings (caller and filters) are unchanged.

## 2. `application` and suspended entries read as members do not

An `application` entry is not a membership (VTI-ACL-037), and a suspended entry may read the action list and nothing else (`vtc-action-list.md` §8.2, VTI-APV-019). Several gates let both through:

| gate | before | now |
|---|---|---|
| `vtc/relationships/list` (`acting_party`) | any live row | an active member, or an administrator not suspended (`Actor::may_read_as_member`) |
| `member_signer` fallback (badge, board, directory, group, community and session reads) | any live row | a live row that is neither suspended nor `application` |
| `groups::Standing::read` `administrator` | `is_administrator()` | `is_administrator() && !is_suspended()` |
| capability-module list | refused `application` only | also refuses a suspended entry |
| `vtc/join-requests/query` | `as_admin` (any administrative role) | `as_capable(.., vtc.join.decide)`. It is a write: it queues a community-signed credential query to a DID the caller names. |

Checked and already correct: the other `as_admin` reads (vetting show, revocations list, policy list/get) go through `admin_signer` → `resolve_admin_claims`. That path refuses a non-administrator (so an `application` entry) and a suspended entry outside the action-list tasks. Those reads stay open to any administrative role, as designed.

## Behaviour changes (R3.6)

- **Cursors:** every badge, board and election cursor issued before this change is refused as `cursorInvalid` (badges, boards) or `malformedRequest` (elections), so a client mid-list starts again. That also happens after a restart when the community has no audit writer, and after an audit-key rotation. The cursor stays an opaque string, now 32 hex characters after the dot instead of 24. The admin console and portal only echo `nextCursor`.
- **Newly refused** with `permissionDenied`:
  - an `application` entry on `relationships/list` and on every `member_signer` read;
  - a suspended entry (administrator or member) on those reads, on group reads and on the capability-module list. That includes `auth/sessions/list` and `auth/revoke-session` for the suspended entry's own sessions, consistent with "the action list and nothing else";
  - an administrator without `vtc.join.decide` (Auditor, Approver, a custom role without it) on `vtc/join-requests/query`.
- A live `member` row with no member record (or a removed one) no longer reads `relationships/list`. Such an entry is not an active member.
- No wire types change. No JS client sends these as an `application` entry. Git bridges, the `application` holders, use the `git/*` tasks, which are capability-gated and unchanged.

## Tests

- `offset_cursor` unit tests:
  - a cursor reads back for its own binding only (not another caller, family or key);
  - edited cursors are refused: offset, `usize::MAX`, `+50`, `050`, missing, short or long tag, non-hex;
  - the old unkeyed construction is refused;
  - `window` stays in bounds for any input.
- `it::badges::a_list_cursor_is_honoured_only_as_the_community_minted_it`:
  - a real `nextCursor` pages;
  - the old unkeyed cursor at 1 and at `usize::MAX` is refused (before, the second reached the slice);
  - an edited offset is refused;
  - another caller's cursor is refused.
- `it::board_tasks::vti_brd_003_a_list_cursor_is_honoured_only_as_the_community_minted_it` (feature `voting`).
- New `it::standing_gates`:
  - `vti_acl_037_an_application_entry_reads_nothing_members_read`;
  - `a_suspended_administrator_reads_no_relationships_groups_or_badges`, each answered before the suspension;
  - `a_suspended_member_reads_no_badges`;
  - `a_join_query_takes_the_join_decide_capability_not_any_administrative_role`.

Local results:
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`: exit 0
- `cargo clippy -p vtc-service --all-targets -- -D warnings`: exit 0
- `cargo clippy -p vtc-service --features vetting-pcs,voting --all-targets -- -D warnings`: exit 0
- `cargo nextest run -p vtc-service -p vtc-client --features vtc-service/vetting-pcs,vtc-service/voting --no-fail-fast` with `VTC_SKIP_ADMIN_UI_BUILD=1`: 3800 passed, 13 failed, exit 100. 12 of the 13 are the embedded-console tests (`admin_ui::tests::*`, `routing_modes::*`, the member-portal page tests), which need the console bundle that variable skips; they pass with the bundle built (verified on the same base in #2693). The 13th was a test edit of mine that broke an assertion in `arranging_the_wall_pins_within_the_limit_and_never_a_hidden_badge`; it is fixed, and `badges::` now passes 32/32 (exit 0).
- `cargo test -p vtc-service --features vetting-pcs,voting --doc`: exit 0

## Pre-merge checklist

- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2). n/a
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3). n/a
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1). n/a, read paths only.
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4). n/a
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5). n/a
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6). n/a
- [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, deny_unknown_fields where security-relevant, schema registered, all consumers (incl. JS) updated (R3.*). No wire types change. Refusals use the codes each task already declares.
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive; fail-closed if enforcement can't start (R5.*). With no audit writer the cursors are still keyed (per-process key). Every gate changed here fails closed.
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified; background-job failures are surfaced (R6.*). n/a
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1). n/a. `join-requests/query` changes only its gate.
- [x] Deviations from this guide flagged explicitly with rule numbers. None.

title: fix(vtc-service)!: keyed list cursors for badges, boards and elections; application and suspended entries read as members do not (#2694)
body:
fix(vtc-service)!: keyed list cursors for badges, boards and elections; application and suspended entries read as members do not (#2694)

List cursors

The badge, board and election lists bound their offset cursors to the
caller and the question with an unkeyed SHA-256, which any caller could
compute for any offset. On the badge lists, `offset + limit` was then
unchecked, so an offset near `usize::MAX` overflowed and indexed past the
slice.

`trust_tasks::offset_cursor` is now shared by all three:
- `"{offset}.{tag}"`, the tag being 128 bits of HMAC-SHA256 over the task
  family, the binding and the offset. The key is the audit writer's
  active key, as the directory and group cursors use, or a random key
  made once per process when there is no audit writer.
- The tag is verified in constant time. Only the canonical decimal form
  of the offset is read.
- `window` clamps every page to the result whatever the offset and limit,
  and the election list's next offset uses a saturating add.

Who reads as a member

- `vtc/relationships/list` admitted any live ACL row. It now requires an
  active member or an administrator who is not suspended, so an
  `application` entry (never a membership, VTI-ACL-037) and a suspended
  entry (which may read the action list and nothing else, VTI-APV-019)
  are refused.
- `member_signer`'s fallback for a signer that is not an administrator
  admitted any live row. It now refuses suspended and `application`
  entries. That covers the badge, board, directory, group, community and
  session reads that use it.
- `groups::Standing` counted a suspended administrator as an
  administrator. It no longer does.
- The capability-module list refuses a suspended entry as well as an
  `application` one.
- `vtc/join-requests/query`, which queues a credential query the
  community signs to a DID the caller names, was gated on holding any
  administrative role. It now requires `vtc.join.decide`.
