title: feat(vta-service): memory reads are audited per item, and the trail names items by commitment, never by key (#2116)
body:
Closes #2116.

## What #2116 asked for, and what was already there

- **Hash-chaining:** already implemented since the issue was filed (VTI-AUD-004).
- **Item-level reads:** added here.
- **"Who read or changed my memory":** added here as `pnm memory history`.

## The problem it turned up (VTI-AUD-005)

The chained sink commits a DID-shaped resource, but keeps any other resource in the clear inside the hashed event, on the rule that only a DID is personal data. A memory key isn't a DID, but it is personal: it names what was remembered, often a person. So every `memory.put` and `memory.delete` wrote one where no erasure can reach it without breaking verification. Logging the keys a read returned, as the issue suggested, would have made that worse.

## Change

- **`AuditSink::commit`**, plus `vti_common::audit::commit_reference`: a domain-separated HMAC under the active audit key, `hmac-sha256:<key id>:<hex>`.
  - It's a provided trait method defaulting to `None`, so it's additive.
  - A sink with no key returns `None`, and the caller records no reference rather than an unkeyed digest, which a dictionary lookup would reverse.
- **Memory audit records** name each item by its commitment over `(contextId, key)`:
  - `put` / `delete`: the commitment as the resource;
  - `get`: `items=N refs=…`, one per item returned (never a deferred or missing key);
  - `list`: `items=N keySet=…`.
- **`pnm memory history --context … [--actor] [--from] [--to] [--limit]`:** who read or changed a context's memory, newest first, from `audit/list`. It runs one query per memory action, since the action filter is exact.
- **`MockVta` now writes the chained trail production writes**, not the flat keyless one. Three persona tests that decoded raw rows as flat entries now read both forms.
- **Docs:** `docs/02-vta/personal-ai-agents.md`.

## Not covered

- **Rows written before this change** keep their keys until the retention sweep. That's recorded in the divergence register: trustoverip/dtgwg-vti-spec#113.
- **Looking up "was item X read?" by key** needs an `audit/list` filter that recomputes the commitment, which is a spec change. Today, rows about one item can be matched by their shared commitment.
- **VTI-AUD-006** (reading the trail is itself audited) is still open. `memory history` reads the trail the same way `pnm audit list` does.

## Tests

- New: the commitment is deterministic, differs per context and never contains the value, and a flat sink commits nothing.
- New handler test: four memory rows, and no key anywhere in the trail.
- New end-to-end test (`memory_audit.rs`): over the wire, the `get` row names the item the `put` wrote, attributed to the agent.
- `cargo nextest run --workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client`: 7189 passed.
- `cargo nextest run -p vtc-service -p vtc-client`: 3674 passed.
- Doctests, `clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings` and `fmt --check`: all clean.

title: docs(audit): record agent-memory keys held in the clear by earlier audit records (VTI-AUD-005)
body:
Adds an *observed* VTI-AUD-005 entry to Appendix F.4.

At one agent node, the chained audit trail committed actor and DID-shaped target identifiers, but kept any other resource in the clear inside the hashed event. Agent-memory writes recorded the item's key as that resource. A key names what was remembered (often a person), so those records embed personal data that no erasure can reach without breaking verification.

OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#2116 changes what new records hold: each item is named by a keyed commitment under the audit key, and reads record which items they returned the same way. The records already written can't be rewritten. They leave only at the retention sweep, and the entry says so.

The entry also records that the node's "a non-DID resource is not personal data" rule hasn't been checked for its other actions.

title: feat(pnm): memory commands use vta/memory 0.2; the 0.1 client methods are deprecated
body:
Follow-up to #2520 (#2115). The registry marked memory 0.1 superseded when 0.2 was published and will withdraw it, so `pnm memory` moves to 0.2:

- **`plant`:** an unconditional 0.2 put. It prints the version it took.
- **`recall <key>`:** `vta/memory/get/0.1`.
- **`recall`:** pages through `vta/memory/list/0.2`. `--json` keeps the 0.1 `{ items: [{ key, value }] }` shape.
- **`delete` / `forget`:** a 0.2 delete. It still fails on a key holding nothing, as before.
- **`wipe`:** each delete is conditional on the version the list showed. An item another writer changed after you confirmed stops the wipe with a `versionConflict` instead of being deleted.

`VtaClient::{memory_put, memory_list, memory_delete}` are now `#[deprecated]`, pointing at the 0.2 methods. Nothing in the workspace calls them any more.

- New `mock_vta::versioned_memory_round_trips_through_the_client` drives the four 0.2 client methods against a running VTA, including the typed `versionConflict`.
- New unit tests: page decoding (tombstones skipped, cursor read), and a malformed page errors instead of shortening the list.
- `cargo nextest run --workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client`: 7184 passed.
- Workspace doctests, `clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings` and `fmt --check`: all clean.

The registry marked vta/memory/{put,list,delete}/0.1 superseded when 0.2

  item another writer changed after the operator confirmed stops the wipe
  with a `versionConflict` instead of being deleted with the rest.

favour of `memory_put_versioned`, `memory_list_page`,
`memory_delete_versioned` and `memory_get`. A new mock-VTA test drives

feat: send vta/memory 0.2 — prefix-narrowed recall, a real get, tombstoned forget

The registry marked vta/memory/{put,list,delete}/0.1 superseded when 0.2
was published (OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#2115) and will
withdraw them. The store moves to the 0.2 client methods:

- save: `memory_put_versioned`, unconditional, still under
  `VtaClient::idempotent`. put/0.2 is classified Keyed, so the stable
  idempotency key now also stops a retried save taking a second version.
- list_of_type: `list/0.2` asks the VTA for `<type>/` only and pages by
  cursor, instead of fetching the whole context and filtering here.
- get: one `vta/memory/get/0.1` instead of a full list plus a lookup.
- forget: `delete/0.2` leaves a tombstone, so the user's other devices
  learn of the deletion. An absent key is still an error.
- Responses decode into the generated 0.2 types. A live item that comes
  back without its value is an error, not a skipped entry.

Needs vta-sdk 0.86 (with vti-secrets 0.35). That release carries the 0.2
client methods and `CreateAclRequest::handoff`, set to false here.
Cargo.lock is not updated in this commit because 0.86 is not published

title: feat(keys): did:webs meets VTI-KEY-170 with the key-role designation extension (VTI-KEY-173)
body:
## Why

VTI-KEY-173 refused did:webs for key-role identities, for two reasons. Its document is derived from the KEL with every key-state key in `authentication` and `assertionMethod`, and it has no member for `keyRoles` or `revoked`. Its open issue preferred a did:webs extension that anchors role keys in the KEL and renders the key-state keys into no relationship, over amending VTI-KEY-093.

That extension now exists as a proof of concept:
- **Reference implementation:** the *key-role designation* in `affinidi-did-webs` 0.9.1 (affinidi/affinidi-tdk-rs#991).
- **Method profile:** `vta/dids/_shared/0.1/method-profiles/webs.md`, updated in the companion trust-tasks PR.
- **Proposal:** it is being proposed to the did:webs specification (ToIP KSWG).

## What

- **VTI-KEY-173:** did:webs meets VTI-KEY-170 only with the key-role designation extension its method profile states. A node MUST NOT create a key-role identity under did:webs without it.
- **Open issue:**
  - **Interop caveat:** until the did:webs specification adopts the extension, a did:webs resolver without it refuses the published document. So such an identity is verifiable only by resolvers that implement it.
  - **Why the VTI-KEY-093 amendment isn't taken:** it would keep the change authority in two relationships.
  - **VTI-KEY-001 is unchanged:** it doesn't yet name did:webs for a node's durable identity. Naming it would oblige every peer to resolve did:webs (VTI-KEY-003), so that waits on adoption.

No divergence-register entry is needed. No VTI implementation creates did:webs key-role identities, which this text still forbids without the extension.

title: feat(vta-service)!: versioned agent memory — vta/memory/{put,delete,list}/0.2 and get/0.1 (#2115)
body:
Implements trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#1067 for #2115. 0.1 keeps working against the same store.

## How

- **Store:** memory items are now application-state records under a fixed namespace in the existing `MEMORY` keyspace. Versions, tombstones, the change feed, cursors and reaping come from `operations::app_state`, not a second copy. The keyspace stays memory's own, so backup, purge-on-context-delete and the capability gates are unchanged.
- **Size measure:** memory measures a value's UTF-8 text, as `put/0.2` specifies, not its JSON encoding. This uses `put_measured` with `ValueMeasure`.
- **Migration:** at boot, `migrate_legacy` moves 0.1 `mem:<ctx>:<key>` rows into the new layout. It's idempotent and never drops data: an over-cap value (0.1 had no cap) moves uncapped, and a row it can't place stays put.
- **Write-only callers:** a `versionConflict` hides `currentValue` from a caller holding `memoryWrite` without `memoryRead`, since a conflict amounts to a read.
- **Access refusals:** 0.2 tasks and `get` refuse with the declared `contextForbidden`. 0.1 still answers `permissionDenied`.
- **0.1 on the new store:** `put` is an unconditional put; `delete` leaves a tombstone and still answers `notFound`; `list` drains every page.

## Also

- **App-state cursor errors:** `vta/app-state/list` now sends its declared `cursorInvalid`, not `malformedRequest`. This comes from the new `AppStateError::CursorInvalid`; the enum is `non_exhaustive`, so the variant is additive.
- **SDK:** new constants and retry classes (`put/0.2` is Keyed), plus four `VtaClient` methods.
- **Census:** conformance witnesses for all four tasks, and a test for every declared code. The error-code baseline shrinks by four.

## Things to know

- **Breaking (hence `!`):** `operations::memory`'s public functions changed signature.
- **0.1 is now superseded.** The registry marks it so automatically once 0.2 exists, and withdraws superseded versions about 90 days later. vta-agent-memory, `pnm memory` and vta-mcp still send 0.1 and need moving to the new client methods.
- **Not fixed here:** app-state has the same unchecked-context-id gap that memory now guards against.

## Tests

- `cargo nextest run --workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client`: 7181 passed.
- `cargo nextest run -p vtc-service -p vtc-client`: 3672 passed.
- Workspace doctests, `clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings` and `fmt --check`: all clean.
- I re-ran the SDK and memory tests after adding the client methods: 1455 passed.

Closes #2115

title: feat(vta-service)!: versioned agent memory — vta/memory/{put,delete,list}/0.2 and get/0.1 (#2115) (#2520)
body:
feat(vta-service)!: versioned agent memory — vta/memory/{put,delete,list}/0.2 and get/0.1 (#2115) (#2520)

Serves the memory versions specified in trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#1067.
0.1 keeps working against the same store.

The store. Memory 0.2 has application state's semantics with one
namespace: a per-context counter that is both the `expectedVersion` token
and the `sinceVersion` watermark, conflicts that carry the winner's view,
tombstones reaped behind a watermark, and a version index that makes the
change feed paginatable. `operations::memory` therefore stores items as
application-state records, under a fixed namespace in the MEMORY
keyspace, instead of keeping a second copy of that machinery. The
keyspace stays memory's own, so backup, purge-on-context-delete and the
memory capabilities are unchanged.
- `app_state::put_measured` with `ValueMeasure`: memory measures the
  UTF-8 text of a value (as `put/0.2` says), not its JSON encoding, so a
  note full of quotes or newlines does not hit the 64 KiB cap early.
- 0.1 rows (`mem:<ctx>:<key>`) move into the versioned layout at boot
  (`memory::migrate_legacy`). The migration is idempotent and never
  drops data: an over-cap value (0.1 had no cap) moves uncapped, and a row
  it cannot place stays where it is. Context-delete purges both layouts.
- Memory tombstones are reaped on app-state's retention window.
- A memory call naming a context id that is not a valid context path is
  refused, keeping the layout's prefixes unambiguous.

The tasks.
- put/0.2: `expectedVersion`; `versionConflict` carries `currentVersion`
  and `currentValue`, but the value is withheld from a caller holding
  `memoryWrite` without `memoryRead` (a conflict is a read).
- delete/0.2: tombstone; optional positive `expectedVersion`; deleting
  nothing succeeds with `existed: false`.
- list/0.2: a snapshot (prefix, cursor/limit, values by default) or the
  change feed with tombstones; `highWatermark`, `watermarkTooOld`,
  `cursorInvalid`, `filterConflict`.
- get/0.1: up to 256 named items, answered in `items` / `missing` /
  `deferred`.
- An access refusal is the declared `contextForbidden` on 0.2 and `get`.
  0.1 still answers `permissionDenied`.
- 0.1 on the new store: put is an unconditional put, delete leaves a
  tombstone and still answers `notFound` when nothing was live, and list
  drains every page.

Also:
- `AppStateError::CursorInvalid`: `vta/app-state/list` now answers its
  declared `cursorInvalid` instead of `malformedRequest`.
- vta-sdk adds `TASK_VTA_MEMORY_{PUT,DELETE,LIST}_0_2` and `_GET_0_1`
  with their retry classes (put/0.2 is Keyed, like app-state put), and
  `VtaClient::{memory_put_versioned, memory_delete_versioned,
  memory_list_page, memory_get}`.
- Conformance witnesses for all four tasks, and handler tests for every
  declared code. The error-code baseline shrinks by four.
- vti-specs-vta pins `vta/memory/{put,delete,list}` at 0.1 and 0.2, plus
  get 0.1. The registry now marks the 0.1 versions superseded, so the
  memory clients (vta-agent-memory, pnm memory, vta-mcp) should move to
  0.2 before the registry withdraws 0.1.

BREAKING CHANGE: `vta_service::operations::memory::{put, delete, list}`
take the `NamespaceLocks` and the new versioned parameters and return the
application-state outcomes; `list_all_live` replaces 0.1's `list`.

Closes #2115

title: fix: JWK-published DIDs (did:webs) in approver distinctness, re-rotation and SIOP login
body:
An audit of every place VTI decides which DID methods it accepts, or how it finds a DID's key, now that did:webs resolution (#2505) and rotation onto did:webs (#2517) are in. Most code is already method-agnostic, because it reads keys through `TrustTaskVmResolver`. Three places were not.

## Fixed

**1. Step-up approver distinctness failed open (security).**
- `acl::approver::subject_keys` read the subject's keys with `get_public_key_bytes`, which only handles `Multikey`.
- A subject that publishes its keys as JWKs had every key dropped: did:webs always does, and so can did:jwk or a JWK did:web. The subject then appeared to hold no keys, so `check_distinct` accepted any approver, including the subject's own key. That defeats the separate-approver requirement (attest/0.1 consumer item 6, `redeem/finish/0.1` item 4).
- Keys are now read with `decode_public_key` (Multikey or JWK).
- A method that carries no key, such as a `ConditionalProof2022`, is skipped. One whose key can't be read fails closed.

**2. A member who had rotated off did:key could never rotate again.**
- The old DID's signature was verified as a did:key only.
- Both signatures now go through one per-method verifier: did:key, did:webvh/did:scid, did:webs (VTI-MEM-041).

**3. SIOP id_token login read only `publicKeyMultibase`.** It now reads a JWK too. The Ed25519 codec check stays, so an X25519 JWK is refused.

## Left alone, by design

- **Spec restrictions:**
  - node identities stay did:webvh/did:scid (VTI-KEY-001);
  - client bootstrap, ephemeral, delegated and approver keys stay did:key (VTI-KEY-002 and the flow specs);
  - no key-role identity under did:webs (VTI-KEY-173).
- **Foreign protocols:** swiyu issuers are did:webvh; BBS needs BLS12-381.
- **`display_name::shorten_did`:** does not special-case did:webs. Its vectors are shared with a TypeScript copy, so that change needs both sides.
- **Signatures made before a rotation:** VTI does not resolve a DID at a past version for any method, did:webvh included (see `routes/audit.rs`). did:webs supports `versionId`, but the resolver SDK does not expose version-addressed resolution yet. That's a separate piece of work.

## Tests

Each new test fails on the old code:
- `a_subjects_jwk_key_is_not_a_distinct_approver`: a did:webs subject's own JWK key is refused as its approver, and a different key is accepted.
- `a_member_on_a_did_webs_can_rotate_again`: rotate onto a did:webs, then rotate again signing as it. The test signing helper now signs as a non-did:key party through `HolderKey::new`.
- `an_ed25519_jwk_issuer_verifies` and `an_x25519_jwk_is_not_a_signing_key` (SIOP).

Full suite:
- `cargo nextest run --workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client`: 7164 passed
- `cargo nextest run -p vtc-service -p vtc-client`: 3674 passed
- doc tests pass; clippy `-D warnings` and fmt are clean

title: feat(messaging/mux): DID multiplexing at a mediator (messaging/mux/*/0.1)
body:
Adds the `messaging/mux/*/0.1` family: **DID multiplexing at a mediator**. One authenticated connection (the *principal*, typically a device DID) carries live delivery and pickup for many *member* DIDs, instead of one WebSocket per DID. That matters most on mobile, where each extra connection costs a TLS handshake, an auth round trip, keepalives and its own reconnects.

A member proves it allows this in one of two ways. Both are JSON statements with an embedded Data Integrity proof (`eddsa-jcs-2022`, `proofPurpose: authentication`), verified with the verifier Trust Tasks already use:
- **`muxAttach`**: bound to one connection (`sessionId` + `muxNonce`), gone when it closes.
- **`muxGrant`**: stored; survives reconnects until it expires or is revoked.

## Specs

| Task | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `messaging/mux/attach` | Attach member DIDs to this connection (per-item outcomes) |
| `messaging/mux/detach` | Remove session attaches |
| `messaging/mux/grant` | Store or replace grants (per-item outcomes) |
| `messaging/mux/list` | List grants as principal or as member, paged |
| `messaging/mux/update` | Narrow a grant; widening needs a new grant |
| `messaging/mux/revoke` | Revoke as principal or as member |
| `messaging/mux/revoke-all` | Member bumps its epoch, voiding every grant (the hand-over switch) |
| `messaging/mux/event` | Mediator → principal, live only: `ready`, `attached`, `detached`, `refused` |
| `messaging/mux/notice` | Mediator → principal/member, durable: `grantsSuspended`, `grantsRevoked`, `grantsExpiring`, `grantsPresent` |

Shared definitions are in `messaging/mux/_shared/0.1/mux.schema.json`.

## Security model, as specified
- **Key binding.** A grant is valid only while its signing key is in the member's *current* authentication relationship. Once rotated out, the grant is stale and stays stale.
- **Epoch.** `revoke-all` bumps a per-DID epoch, voiding every grant issued under the old one.
- **Unknown-key suspension.** If a member proves control with a key that signed none of its active grants, those grants are suspended, and the principal is told durably to re-create them.
- **Replay protection.** A per-principal replay floor means a revoked or replaced grant can't be replayed.
- **Scope.** Scope is explicit and never exceeds the member's own ACLs. Expiry is required.
- **Disclosure.** The `exposure` front matter records the correlation this reveals: the mediator learns that the member DIDs share a device.

## Implementation
The Affinidi messaging mediator implements these on a feature branch, validated against these exact bundles. Every handler's response is deserialised into the generated `Response` types in tests, and an end-to-end test shows one socket receiving live delivery for two granted DIDs and nothing for a third.

## Open points for review
1. `iat`/`exp` in statements are integer NumericDate. Elsewhere this repo uses RFC 3339 instants (`<event>At`). Happy to switch if reviewers prefer.
2. How a *DIDComm* WebSocket becomes a mux connection is left to the transport binding. The implementation uses a provisional `affinidi-mux` subprotocol.
3. Whether a member may list, update or revoke through a session attach, rather than only by direct authentication, is still open; the specs allow both.
4. To keep `emptyScope` reportable per item, the signed `StatementScope` has no `minItems`. A statement with the wrong shape or `type` rejects the whole payload (`malformedRequest`).

## Checks run locally
- `npm run build` and `npm run validate`: 1349 specs validated.
- Generators for Rust, TS, Go and Dart produce no diff on top of `main`. `npm run check-bindings` reports all agree.
- `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --no-default-features --features messaging` passes. TS, Go and Dart tests passed before the rebase.
- Not run locally: the CI-only API-compatibility jobs. This change is additive: new spec modules only.

title: feat(vta/memory): versioned writes, tombstones, a change feed and named reads (put/delete/list 0.2, get 0.1)
body:
## Why

`vta/memory/*` 0.1 is an unconditional key/value upsert store. Requested in OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#2115:

- **`put` overwrites with no version.** Two agents, or one agent on two devices, clobber each other, and neither can tell.
- **`delete` is a hard delete.** Another device's cached copy never learns the item is gone.
- **`list` returns the whole context.** There is no prefix, no paging and no change feed.

`vta/app-state/*` already solved each of these. These versions apply its semantics to memory. They are restated in each spec, not referenced, so each can be implemented on its own.

## What

| Task | Change |
|---|---|
| `vta/_shared/0.1/memory-record` | New shared `MemoryRecord`, plus `MemoryKey`, `MemoryValue`, `MemoryVersion` and `MemoryExpectedVersion`. Versions come from a per-context counter, which is both the concurrency token and the sync watermark. |
| `vta/memory/put/0.2` | Optional `expectedVersion` (0 = create only). `versionConflict` carries the current version and value. The response returns `version`, `wasCreated`, `updatedAt` and `valueBytes`. |
| `vta/memory/delete/0.2` | Leaves a tombstone. Optional positive `expectedVersion`. Deleting nothing is a success (`existed: false`). |
| `vta/memory/list/0.2` | Snapshot (`prefix`, `cursor`/`limit`, values by default as in 0.1) or change feed (`sinceVersion`, tombstones included). Returns `highWatermark`; new errors `watermarkTooOld` and `cursorInvalid`. |
| `vta/memory/get/0.1` | **New.** Up to 256 named keys, each answered exactly once in `items`, `missing` or `deferred`. Its audit can name exactly which items were read; OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#2116 builds on this. |

Points for review:
- **No separate `query` task.** #2115 proposed `vta/memory/query/0.1` for prefix and cursor paging. `list/0.2` already does both, as `app-state/list/1.1` does, so a second task would duplicate it. `get/0.1` provides the named-item read instead.
- **Write-only callers.** A conflict's `currentValue` is a read. It is withheld from a caller that may write the context but not read it.
- **Values by default.** `list/0.2`'s `includeValues` defaults to **true**, unlike app-state. Recall is why an agent lists memory, and 0.1 always returned values.
- **0.1 stays published, not superseded.** A VTA serving both versions writes one store, and the 0.2 prose says how 0.1 writes get versions and tombstones there.
- **`delete/0.2` is `destructive`.** The value can't be recovered.

## Checks run locally

- `npm run build`: 1344 specs validated, no warnings on these.
- All four libraries regenerated. `npm run check-bindings`: all four languages agree.
- `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --features vta --test conformance memory`: 16 passed, including the new `payload.invalid-examples.json` fixtures.
- `npm run check-published-schemas`: no released schema changed.

title: feat(vtc): a member can rotate onto a did:webs (VTI-MEM-041, VTI-KEY-003)
body:
## What

Member DID rotation (`vtc/members/rotate/0.1`) accepted did:key, did:webvh and did:scid. It now also accepts **did:webs**.

## How the new DID's signature is checked

A did:webs document has no `#key-0`. Its keys are the KERI identifier's current keys, identified by their CESR encoding and all listed in `authentication`. The document only resolves when the key event log verifies (VTI-LNK-052), so a signature by one of those keys proves control of the identifier (VTI-MEM-041).

- The new-DID signature is accepted from any key the document authorises for `authentication`, at most 16, tried in order.
- Each candidate goes through the same purpose and controller check as the did:webvh path (`TrustTaskVmResolver`, Authentication).
- A multi-key identifier's `ConditionalProof2022` entry is skipped, because it isn't a key.
- No wire change. The spec says only "signature over the challenge by the NEW key"; `#key-0` is VTI's own did:webvh convention.

A did:webs member's Trust Task proofs already verified through the shared proof resolver, so nothing else needed to change for a member to act once rotated.

## Spec pin, plus a did:scid fix

`rotate/0.1`'s response `method` allowed only `did:key` and `did:webvh`. trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#1064 appended `did:scid` and `did:webs` in place (an additive change), and this PR re-pins the bundle.

That also fixes rotation onto a **did:scid**. Its successful reply (`method: "did:scid"`) failed the published schema, so the member got an internal error back.

## Tests

- `rotation_onto_a_did_webs_with_any_current_key`: the document, shaped as the resolver hands it over, has two keys and a `ConditionalProof2022`. The member signs with the second key, and the membership, ACL row and credentials move to the did:webs.
- `rotation_onto_a_did_webs_refuses_a_key_outside_its_document`: a signature by an unlisted key gets `signatureInvalid`, and the membership stays put.
- `method_of_recognises_did_webs`.
- Full suite:
  - `cargo nextest run --workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client`: 7142 passed
  - `cargo nextest run -p vtc-service -p vtc-client`: 3667 passed
  - doc tests pass; clippy `-D warnings` and fmt are clean
  - `trust-tasks -C vti-specs-vtc check` matches the lock

title: fix(vtc): name members by name and short DID in pickers, and stop the icon browser repeating Book
body:
Two console bugs found on first.openvtc.net.

**Icon browser: a run of "Book" tiles.** The offered "Book" icon is lucide's `BookOpen`, and lucide's own `Book` icon is also labelled "Book". Both icon grids key each tile by its name, so the two icons got the same React key. On each re-render React left orphaned "Book" tiles behind, even under a search that matched 5 icons.
- The offered icon is now "Open book".
- The catalogue keeps every name unique: an icon whose label an offered icon already uses gets lucide's own key appended.
- A test checks that all 1,544 names are distinct.

**Member lists: "(no name)" and directory ids.** Members who have set no display name showed as "(no name)" in *Give* and the new-badge *Owners* picker. In the *Appoint an owner* dropdown they showed as raw `dir_…` entry ids. Group managers, group members and board facilitators had the same problems.
- Every one of those lists now reads "Name · did:…short".
  - With no name, a member shows as the shortened DID alone.
  - The full DID is in the title.
  - A directory entry id is never shown.
- The DID comes from the derived `did` directory field that list items already carry.
- Named members come first by name, then unnamed members by DID. `"~"` was meant to sort unnamed members last, but `localeCompare` puts punctuation before letters, so they came first.
- The pickers' search matches a DID as well as a name.
- `EntryName` (holders, owners, managers) falls back to the short DID instead of "(no name)".
- The portal's member select (giving kudos, appointing) shows the short DID when the name is withheld, instead of "A member".

One helper set in `components/EntryName.tsx` (`faceLabel`, `byFace`, `faceMatches`) serves all the console lists.

**Also:** the browse-dialog test now has a 30 s timeout. It renders all 1,544 tiles, which took more than 5 s in jsdom when the rest of the suite ran alongside it. It passed when run alone. This is likely the one-off failure noted on #2499.

**Checks:**
- `npm run lint` passes.
- `vitest` passes 1595 of 1595.
- The console and portal bundles both build.

What merging does, per registry (all in `publish.yml`, each keyed on "this
version is not published yet"):

- **Go** — `publish-go` builds, vets and tests, then pushes the tag, which *is*

pull request by that language's API compatibility check (`rs`, `ts`, `go` and
`Dart API compatibility`).

edits are force-pushed away. See RELEASING.md.

title: feat(contexts)!: context-create capability so an agent gateway can provision sub-contexts
body:
## What and why

An Agent Gateway provisions a trust context for each agent it manages. It faces the internet, so it must never hold super-admin rights, and it should not be an administrator of the contexts it provisions: an administrator can rewrite ACL entries and re-point keys.

**`Capability::ContextCreate` (`context-create`)** is an additive capability, registered in the VTI spec's Appendix C.2 (trustoverip/dtgwg-vti-spec#111). No role derives it, and only a super-admin can grant it (VTI-ACL-033). It lets a non-admin entry:

- **create sub-contexts** under a context it can already act in (VTI-CTX-020). Top-level creation still requires super-admin. The check runs inside `operations::contexts::create_context`, so every transport goes through it.
- **set the first DID of a context it created**, only while that DID is unset and only to the `did:key` of an active Ed25519 key that the context holds. Changing or clearing an established DID, or setting the DID of any other context (its own root, a context an admin created, or one another provisioner created), stays an administrator's act. When a provisioner creates a context, the same atomic write records who created it. The DID write is a compare-and-swap against the record that was checked, so a concurrent change is never overwritten.

Provisioning refusals are logged with `security_alert = true`. The ACL break-glass CLI gains `--capabilities` on `vta acl create/update`, which enforces the role ceiling (VTI-ACL-031). `--capabilities ''` clears the list.

### Breaking change

These `vta-service` functions take the ACL keyspace: `create_context`, `update_context_did`, `ensure_target_context_or_create` and `resolve_target_context`. `ensure_may_create_context` returns `CreateAuthority`. `Capability` is `#[non_exhaustive]`, so the new variant is not breaking; it is appended last.

One unrelated chore is included: `.gitignore` entries for operator-local `local-dev/` configs and `.vscode/`.

## Requirements

- **VTI-CTX-020**: creation requires act authority over the parent; a root requires unrestricted authority.
- **VTI-ACL-031**: the CLI refuses capabilities outside the role's ceiling.
- **VTI-ACL-033**: an additive capability needs unrestricted authority to grant.
- Spec registry: Appendix C.2 `context-create` (trustoverip/dtgwg-vti-spec#111, merged).

## Backport

None. This is feature work, and it is breaking.

## Checklist

- [x] Targets `main`
- [x] No `version =` edits
- [x] Tests cover the change; workspace nextest, doctests, vtc-service, `cargo fmt` and `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` are clean

title: feat(contexts)!: context-create capability so an agent gateway can provision sub-contexts (#2302)
body:
feat(contexts)!: context-create capability so an agent gateway can provision sub-contexts (#2302)

* feat(keys): keys/sign-jws/0.1 — a VTA-built compact JWS walled off to JWT types

Add a `keys/sign-jws/0.1` Trust Task that produces a compact JWS (a JWT) over
a caller-supplied JOSE header and claims set, signed by a stored key. Unlike
`keys/sign/0.1` it is not a general signing oracle: the VTA assembles the
`b64url(header).b64url(payload)` signing input itself and signs it under
`SigningDomain::ProtocolDefined`, so the result verifies as a JWS rather than
as a VTA opaque-signing payload.

The task is walled off so it can never be pointed at producing a credential or
issuer artifact:

- the finalized protected header's `typ` must be on a small allow-list of JWT
  profiles (`JWT`, `at+jwt`, `oauth-id-jag+jwt`, `dpop+jwt`, `logout+jwt`);
  anything else — e.g. a Verifiable Credential media type — is refused before
  the key is touched;
- the VTA, not the caller, sets `alg` from the key, so a caller cannot request
  a signature under an algorithm the key does not implement or mislabel one;
- the payload must be a JSON object (a JWT claims set); raw bytes still go
  through the opaque oracle, not here.

Authorized exactly as `keys/sign` is — per the key's context — so the same
context separation that walls off a signer's identities applies. Added to the
dispatch table with the spec's (none / none / actsAsSubject) class, and
acknowledged in `UNSPECCED_DISPATCHED_URIS` pending an upstream spec in
trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf (dispatched unvalidated like any
unknown-schema task until then).

Enables the Agent Gateway to delegate JWT signing (STS access tokens, ID-JAG)
to the VTA while keeping the JWT-signing path structurally separate from
credential signing.

Tests: six `sign_jws` unit tests over the header wall-off in vta-sdk, and three
conformance tests in vta-service (a real compact JWT is built with the VTA-set
`alg`; a non-JWT `typ` is refused; a non-object payload is refused).

* feat(VTA-28): context-scoped credential issuance below super-admin

`credentials/issue/0.2` signs as the VTA itself with its own `#key-0`, so it
is instance-super-admin gated by construction. An agent delegating its own
credential signing to a VTA cannot use it without being handed authority over
the whole instance — a far larger grant than the operation warrants.

Adds `vta/credentials/issue-in-context/0.1`, which issues as a *context's* own
DID with that context's own key. The authority it needs is over the context,
so a caller holding only that context can issue. `credentials/issue/0.2` is
unchanged and still instance-gated.

The caller supplies no key id. A credential's `issuer` must be the DID whose
verification method produced the proof, so for a given context exactly one key
is valid: the caller would have no choice to make, and offering one would let
it name a key the context does not own. The VTA resolves the key from a new
`ContextRecord::issuer_key_id` designation instead, and a caller may *assert*
the verification method it expects — a mismatch is refused rather than signed
with the other key. Rotating a context's issuer key is therefore invisible to
callers.

Three refusals, all audited: a caller outside the context; a designation
pointing at a key that does not live in the context (which is what puts the
VTA's own context-less `#key-0` out of reach); and a context with no
designation at all, which fails closed rather than falling back to the VTA's
key and minting a credential attributed to the wrong issuer.

Private key material is never held. The proof's signing input is built with
`prepare_sign_input` and handed to the existing signing oracle under
`SigningDomain::ProtocolDefined`, so an internal non-exportable key — the
right custody for an issuer key — works like any other.

The designation gets its own task, `vta/contexts/set-issuer-key/0.1`, rather
than a member on `contexts/update/1.0`: that task has a published schema which
forbids additional properties, so a designation sent there is refused on the
wire before a handler sees it. It validates key residency at designation time
as well, to fail an operator's mistake where they make it.

Also classifies `keys/sign-jws/0.1` in `RETRY_SAFETY`, which had been left
unclassified.

Tests: a context-scoped caller issues and the proof verifies against the
context's issuer key; cross-context refusal; key-separation refusal;
undesignated-context fail-closed; expected-verification-method mismatch
refused and match issuing normally; no caller-supplied `keyId`; designation
residency; `credentials/issue` still instance-gated; plus a conformance test
driving the whole flow over the dispatch spine.

* feat(VTA-29): server-built Data-Integrity proof task for context keys

An agent's VP holder proof today requires whoever builds it to hold the agent's
private key. No existing task can replace that: `keys/derive-and-sign-document`
signs with an **ephemeral** derived key, so its verification method resolves to
nothing and there is no key to publish, rotate or revoke; `keys/sign` is
domain-separated and cannot produce a proof a verifier accepts; `keys/sign-jws`
produces JWTs, and for a VP the problem is *who holds the key*, not the
artifact's shape.

Adds `vta/proofs/attach/0.1`: attach an `eddsa-jcs-2022` Data-Integrity proof
to a document, signed with a **persisted key in a context**, authorized by that
context. The VTA frames the signed bytes itself — canonicalize, build the proof
configuration, hash — so this is a proof *producer*, not a signing oracle: a
caller obtains a proof it is authorized to obtain and cannot obtain a signature
over anything else.

The key is a function of (context, `proofPurpose`), never supplied. A DID
document declares a different verification method per purpose, which a
caller-supplied key id could not express correctly anyway, and letting the
caller choose would undercut the server-built property the task exists for.
`proofPurpose` is constrained to an allow-list — a proof purpose is a claim
about what a signature *means*, so an unrecognised one would mint a signature
whose meaning the VTA never agreed to.

`challenge`/`domain` are accepted on the wire and **refused**: the cryptosuite
in use carries neither member, so a proof claiming to be bound to one could not
be. Returning a proof the caller believes is replay-bound when it is not is
worse than refusing the request.

An inbound `proof` member is dropped before the signing input is built. JCS
canonicalization is presence-sensitive, so hashing a document that still
carried one would produce a proof that verifies against nothing.

Designation extends VTA-28's: `ContextRecord::proof_key_ids` maps purpose to
key, and `contexts/set-issuer-key/0.1` gained an optional `proofPurpose`.
`assertionMethod` falls back to the context's issuer key when no explicit proof
key is set — that *is* the context's assertion key, and requiring it to be
named twice would let the two disagree.

Refactors VTA-28's resolution and signing into `operations::context_signing`,
now shared by both tasks: one place decides which key a context signs with, one
place enforces that it lives in the context (which is what keeps the VTA's
context-less `#key-0` unreachable), and one place audits refusals.

Tests (11 unit + a conformance test over the dispatch spine): a context-scoped
caller gets a proof that verifies with a standard DI verifier; purpose
allow-list; cross-context refusal; key-separation refusal; undesignated-purpose
fail-closed; `assertionMethod` fallback; expected-verification-method
mismatch/match; neither a `keyId` nor raw bytes accepted; inbound proof
replaced and the replacement still verifies; `challenge`/`domain` refused.

* feat(VTA-28): carry caller-supplied JSON-LD contexts on issue-in-context

A credential whose type defines its own terms needs the context that declares
them, and the issuer — not the VTA — is what knows which one. Without this the
task could only mint credentials using the VC Data Model 2.0 base vocabulary,
which excludes every typed credential an agent actually issues.

The VTA does not resolve or interpret them; they travel with the credential for
its verifier. The base context stays first and is not duplicated if a caller
repeats it, since that would make the credential non-conformant rather than
more correct.

* feat(VTA-16): narrow context-create capability, so provisioning needs no super-admin

Creating a sub-context required `Role::Admin` of the parent. An automated
provisioner — an agent gateway minting a context per managed agent — cannot be
an admin of the context it provisions into: it is internet-facing, and the
point of its least-privilege grant is that a compromise cannot rewrite the
agent. The gateway's own `assert_scoped` refuses an `admin` grant for exactly
that reason.

The answer on the table was a separate always-on control service holding the
shared VTA super-admin, which the gateway would call to have contexts made for
it. That is a new deployment unit whose only purpose is to hold the most
dangerous credential in the system, and a new target with it.

`Capability::ContextCreate` is the smaller answer to the same need. It is
additive (no role derives it, so it reaches a non-admin, which is the whole
point) and super-admin-only to grant, which is the one-time consent step
pairing already is.

What it confers is bounded by the rules already there, not by new ones:
`create_context` still requires super-admin for a **top-level** context, and
still requires the caller to reach the parent. So the power is "branch under
what I already reach", never "create anywhere" — both pinned by tests. An admin
keeps passing through the role exactly as before; this adds a path rather than
replacing one.

The gate lives in the operations layer, not the handler, because the create
surface is reachable over more than one transport and a gate written per
transport is one that eventually differs between them. A failed ACL read
refuses rather than falling through to the role check: not being able to
confirm a capability is not the same as not having one.

Tests: a capability holder creates a sub-context without being an admin; it
cannot create a top-level context; it cannot reach another context's subtree; a
non-admin without it is still refused; an admin still passes without it.

* feat(VTA-16): grant capabilities from the CLI, so context-create can be conferred

The capability was enforced but ungrantable: neither `vta acl create` nor
`vta acl update` could set one, so the feature could not be turned on by any
operator. Found by driving the end-to-end flow against a running VTA.

`--capabilities` on both, by wire name. Replaces rather than merges, so an
operator can narrow as well as widen; an unknown name is an error rather than
something to skip, because silently dropping one stores an entry holding less
than was asked for and reports success.

`update` matters as much as `create`: an existing gateway enabling
provisioning has to gain the capability without being deleted and recreated.

* feat(contexts): let a provisioner configure a context it created, once

VTA-16. A caller holding `context-create` could create a sub-context but
not make it usable: naming its DID and designating its signing key were
admin-only, so every provisioned context needed an administrator to
finish it by hand. That defeats self-provisioning.

Both operations now admit a second path. The ordinary admin gate is
checked first and is unchanged; only when it refuses does a caller that
(a) reaches the context and (b) holds `context-create` get considered.
Such a caller may fill a field that is **unset** and nothing else:
re-pointing an established DID, clearing one, or re-designating a key
stays an administrator's act and is refused by name.

Write-once is what keeps this from being a privilege grant. No ACL entry
is written, so authority never accumulates; a provisioner can bring a
blank context to life but can never reconfigure one, including one it
created itself. Reach is unchanged — a context outside the granted
subtree stays out of reach whether its fields are blank or not.

* fix(contexts): let the provisioning path reach update-did and set-issuer-key

The write-once provisioning path was unreachable over the Trust Task
surface: both handlers pre-gated on admin / super-admin before calling
the operation, so a provisioner was refused with "admin role required"
having never reached the code that would have allowed it.

The gate now lives in one place — the operation — which already checks
the ordinary admin gate first and only then considers a provisioner with
an unset field. Caught by the live end-to-end, not by a unit test: the
operations were tested directly, which is exactly the seam that skips
the handler.

* feat(sign-jws): permit the gateway issuer-attestation JWT type

An Agent Gateway tells a peer gateway which issuer DID stands behind a
connection with a `gateway-issuer-attestation+jwt`. The peer verifies it
by resolving the claimed `iss` and checking the signing key is declared
in that document — so the signature has to come from the same party the
DID names, which means signing it here rather than with a key the
gateway holds locally.

`JWS_ALLOWED_TYPS` refused it, so that artifact was the one thing still
signed with a locally held key.

Unlike the other entries this one is not IANA-registered; it is an
application type. It is listed on the same basis the registered ones
are: it names a JWT profile, so permitting it widens nothing
structurally — the task still cannot be pointed at producing a
credential proof or a task envelope. The doc comment records that
boundary, because "it was convenient" is how an allow-list like this
stops meaning anything.

* chore: ignore operator-local VTA configs under local-dev/

The setup files tracked in `local-dev/` are portable by construction. A
*running* local instance needs absolute paths — `config_path`, `data_dir`
— which name one machine and one checkout, so such a file can only ever
be local and must never reach the history.

`vta-local-persistent.toml` was sitting untracked and unignored, which is
exactly the state #888's CI log was in before a `git add -A` committed a
home directory's worth of path into the repository.

Anchored to the directory and prefixed `vta-local-`, so the tracked
`vta-root-webvh-setup.toml` and `vta-pathful-webvh-setup.toml` are
unaffected and the convention extends to further local configs.

* fix: add vscode to ignore

* test(vtc): count the three gateway URIs bound ahead of their specs

`every_bound_canonical_task_exists_in_the_registry` pins, per authority,
how many bound `trusttasks.org/spec/` URIs the registry does not serve.
The Agent Gateway work binds three under `spec/vta/` and never updated
the count, so the assertion read 7 against an expected 4.

It went unnoticed because `vtc-service` does not build without Node
>= 20.19 for its admin UI, so the crate was excluded from local runs.

Raised to 7 with the three named. The test says raising the number is
the wrong fix, and that is the right default — but the same note records
`vta/webvh/servers/reconcile/0.1` going up and back down inside a day,
and calls the round trip "the whole mechanism working, not an exception
to it". This is that case: all three are already tracked as the same
debt in the VTA's `UNSPECCED_DISPATCHED_URIS`, with the route back to 4
being an upstream spec in dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf and a trust-tasks-rs bump
— not an edit here.

The note spells out why each cannot use a published task: `issue/0.2`
signs as the VTA and is instance-gated by construction; `contexts/update/1.0`
forbids additional properties, so the designation cannot ride on it; and
`keys/derive-and-sign-document` signs with an ephemeral key whose
verification method resolves to nothing.

* Revert "feat(VTA-29): server-built Data-Integrity proof task for context keys"

This reverts commit cb50c2a3ec5fee62789fe1b9278998ebb02dc0f9.

* Revert "feat(VTA-28): carry caller-supplied JSON-LD contexts on issue-in-context"

This reverts commit b34f2bca9fc7e804ba4d350bc04e54f818003e73.

* Revert "feat(VTA-28): context-scoped credential issuance below super-admin"

This reverts commit dd1b0c4aed0979be2c78a847d74b622a8b2cbc2c.

* fix: clean up

* fix(sdk): list context-create among the additive capabilities

vti-common registers context-create as additive but the SDK's copy did not,
so the test that pins the two lists equal failed once it landed on main. An
SDK client sending a grant of context-create beside a role now treats it as
additive, as the VTA does.

* fix(contexts): bind context-create provisioning to the context its holder created

Review fixes for the context-create capability (VTI-CTX-020, VTI-ACL-033;
registered in the VTI specification's Appendix C.2, trustoverip/dtgwg-vti-spec#111).

- A provisioner's DID write is a compare-and-swap on the record its write-once
  check read, so a DID set in between (by an administrator or another
  provisioner) is no longer overwritten.
- A context created under the capability records its provisioner in the same
  atomic write, and only that provisioner, still holding the capability, may
  fill its unset DID. Reaching a context is no longer enough: a provisioner
  scoped to `gw` cannot set the DID of `gw` itself or of a context an
  administrator created beneath it. Deleting the context removes the record.
- The create gate (admin role or context-create) moves into
  `operations::contexts::create_context`, so every transport and in-process
  caller meets it, not only the Trust Task handler.
- `vta acl create/update --capabilities` refuses a capability outside the
  role's ceiling (VTI-ACL-031), reuses the shared parser, and accepts
  `--capabilities ''` to clear the list.
- One operations-level `caller_has_capability`, used by the create gate and
  the Trust Task `require_capability`; the DID-key check reuses
  `find_key_by_public_multibase_in_context`.
- Provisioning refusals are logged with `security_alert = true`.
- Fixes the misplaced rustdoc on `create_context` and restores the
  `UNSPECCED_DISPATCHED_URIS` census comment.

Breaking for vta-service: `create_context`, `update_context_did`,
`ensure_target_context_or_create` and `resolve_target_context` take the ACL
keyspace, and `ensure_may_create_context` returns `CreateAuthority`.

title: fix(vtc)!: room documents over DIDComm and TSP are charged the room budgets, so file chunks are no longer held to five a minute (#2294)
body:
## Why

Reported in #2294 (Keyring wallet, follow-up comment). Over DIDComm, an upload chunk above 64 KiB was held to the large-document budget of 5 per minute per sender, which works out to about 1.25 MiB a minute. Only the HTTPS door charged room traffic to the room budgets, and that charge is what lets a chunk skip the large-document budget. Off HTTPS, `admit_room` admitted everything, so room operations over DIDComm and TSP had no rate limit at all.

## Change

`dispatch_trust_task_core` is the entry point for every messaging transport. It now gives room documents the same admission the HTTPS door does (`MessagingRoomAdmission`):

| Step | HTTPS (unchanged) | DIDComm / TSP (new) |
|---|---|---|
| before verification | the address's room ceiling | the authenticated sender's room ceiling: a hashed VID, or one shared key if the sender is unauthenticated |
| never authorized by its room | ×25 failure cost | same |
| once authorized | the (room, presenter) or transfer budget | **the same budget maps**, now in `AppState::room_limiters` |
| upload chunk > 64 KiB | admitted at its own size | same (`room_precharged`) |
| refusal | `429` + `Retry-After` | signed `trust-task-error` `unavailable` + `retryAfter` |

Because the presenter and transfer budgets are shared, switching transport doesn't give a second budget. `docs/02-vta/data-rooms.md` §8.2 and the refusal table are updated.

**Breaking:** `AppState` gains a public field, `room_limiters`. That's why the title has `!`. The only consumer is the `vtc` binary.

## Tests

- New integration tests in `tests/it/room_rate_limits.rs`, all three over DIDComm:
  - an 8-chunk upload of more than 64 KiB per chunk lands;
  - the presenter budget is shared with HTTPS: 2 reads over HTTPS + 1 over DIDComm, then both transports refuse;
  - an unauthorized flood stops at the sender's ceiling, and another sender is unaffected.
- I disabled the fix and all three new tests failed, so they test the change.
- New unit tests: sender keys are per-VID and per-process; the shared settlement logic.
- `cargo nextest run -p vtc-service -p vtc-client`: 3669 passed. `clippy --all-targets -D warnings` and `fmt --check` are clean.

Refs #2294. That issue covers more, so this PR doesn't close it.

title: fix(vtc)!: room documents over DIDComm and TSP are charged the room budgets, so file chunks are no longer held to five a minute (#2294) (#2515)
body:
fix(vtc)!: room documents over DIDComm and TSP are charged the room budgets, so file chunks are no longer held to five a minute (#2294) (#2515)

Only the HTTPS door charged room traffic to the room budgets
(`[rooms.rate_limits]`). Off it, `admit_room` admitted everything, so room
operations over DIDComm and TSP were uncharged, and an upload chunk over
64 KiB fell to the large-document budget: five a minute per sender, about
1.25 MiB a minute for a file at the default chunk size. The Keyring wallet
integration reported it and capped its chunks at 32 KiB to work around it.

`dispatch_trust_task_core`, the one entry point of every messaging
transport, now gives a room document the HTTPS door's admission
(`MessagingRoomAdmission`):

- before anything is verified, the transport-authenticated sender's room
  ceiling (a hash of its VID under the per-process secret, so the map
  names nobody; one shared key for a sender the transport did not
  authenticate), with the same failure cost for a document its room never
  authorizes;
- once the room authorizes it, the (room, presenter) or transfer budget.
  These are the same maps the HTTPS door charges, now held in
  `AppState::room_limiters`, so switching transport buys no second budget;
- `room_precharged`, so an upload chunk from the holder of the open upload
  is admitted at its own size, as over HTTPS.

A refusal on a messaging transport is a signed `trust-task-error`
`unavailable` with `retryAfter` (the HTTPS door's `429` is unchanged).

BREAKING CHANGE: `AppState` gains the public field `room_limiters`
(`SharedRoomLimiters`, `Default` is unbuilt). Code constructing `AppState`
with a struct literal adds `room_limiters: Default::default()`.

Refs #2294

title: fix(vtc/members/rotate): a rotation onto did:scid or did:webs can be reported
body:
## Why

The `vtc/members/rotate/0.1` response's `method` allowed only `did:key` and `did:webvh`. A community verifies rotations onto other methods too:

- **`did:scid:vh:1`** (VTI-KEY-161). VTI already rotates members onto these, but reports `method: "did:scid"`, which the published response schema refuses. A rotation that succeeds therefore comes back to the member as an internal error.
- **`did:webs`** (VTI-KEY-003, verified by its KERI key event log per VTI-LNK-052). VTI is adding rotation onto did:webs and hits the same wall.

## What

- Appends `did:scid` and `did:webs` to the response `method` enum, in place. An appended enum value is an additive change to a released version (CONTRIBUTING-SPECS), and `check-published-schemas` agrees.
- Adds a description of `method`, and one sentence in Conformance: `method` is the DID method of `newDid`, with `did:scid` for a `did:scid:vh:1` identifier.
- Regenerated the Rust, TypeScript, Go and Dart bindings (`cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen && cargo fmt --all`, `npm run build-{ts,go,dart}-bindings`). The Rust `ResponseMethod` gains two appended variants, which is compatible by policy.

## Checks

`npm run validate`, `npm run check-bindings` (all four bindings agree), `npm run check-published-schemas` (additive only) and `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --features vtc --test conformance members` all pass.

title: fix(vta-service): a webvh update that cannot reach its host keeps the typed NoMatchingProtocol refusal (#2279)
body:
## What

Publishing a webvh update to its host wrapped the typed `AppError::NoMatchingProtocol` refusal in `UpdateDidWebvhError::Publish(String)`, which became a 500 `internalError`. Online callers never got `VtaError::NoMatchingProtocol`, and the offline CLI matched on rendered text (`NO_TRANSPORT_MARKER`).

## Change

- New `UpdateDidWebvhError::NoMatchingProtocol { step, refusal }`. It's additive because the enum is `#[non_exhaustive]`. It maps to `AppError::NoMatchingProtocol` (502) at the boundary, the same way `register_server::Publish(AppError)` already passes its host error through.
- `UpdateDidWebvhError::publish_failed(step, AppError)` is used at every host call: the reconcile re-publish, `publish_did`, `agent_name`, `list_agent_names` and `check_agent_name`. Other failures are still `Publish`, with the same text as before.
- `webvh_cli::offline_publish_failure` matches on the type. `NO_TRANSPORT_MARKER` and its wording test are removed. #2275's before/after-commit distinction is unchanged.

## Tests

- New: the refusal keeps its type through the boundary (502, same payload), and other host failures stay `Publish` (500).
- The offline CLI tests now build the typed error. A string error that happens to contain "no transport in common" no longer gets the transport hint.
- `cargo nextest run -p vta-service`: 2383 passed. `cargo clippy -p vta-service --all-targets -D warnings` and `cargo fmt --check` are clean.

Closes #2279

fix(vta-service): a webvh update that cannot reach its host keeps the typed NoMatchingProtocol refusal (#2279) (#2514)

Publishing a webvh update to its hosting server wrapped every failure in
`UpdateDidWebvhError::Publish(String)`, which maps to `AppError::Internal`.
When the outbound seam shared no transport with the host, the typed
`AppError::NoMatchingProtocol` was rendered to text: an online edit
answered a retryable internal error instead of the refusal, so the SDK's
`VtaError::NoMatchingProtocol` never reached the CLI, and the offline
`vta webvh update-did` path detected the case by matching the rendered
"no transport in common" text.

`UpdateDidWebvhError` gains a `NoMatchingProtocol { step, refusal }`
variant (additive; the enum is `#[non_exhaustive]`), built by
`publish_failed` at every call that reaches the host: the reconcile
re-publish, the publish of the new entry, agent-name operations, and the
agent-name list and availability lookups. It maps to
`AppError::NoMatchingProtocol` (502) at the boundary. Every other host
failure is still `Publish` with the same text as before.

The offline CLI now matches on the variant. `NO_TRANSPORT_MARKER` and the
test pinning its wording are gone. The before/after-commit distinction
from #2275 is unchanged.

Closes #2279

title: fix(vtc): the console builds from its own directory, without type-checking tests (#2430)
body:
## Summary

`npm run build` in `vtc-service/admin-ui` type-checked the tests (one `tsconfig.json`, `include: ["src"]`, no exclude), and `election-manifest.test.ts` imports the vendored `vtc/elections/create/0.5` bundle by a path that leaves the package — so the console could not be built from a `git archive` of that directory.

- `tsconfig.json` is what ships: excludes `src/**/*.test.ts`, `src/**/*.test.tsx`, `src/**/*.test-data.ts` and `src/test/` (the only test-only files in the tree; nothing shipping imports them).
- New `tsconfig.test.json` extends it with everything included. New `npm run typecheck` = `tsc -b tsconfig.json tsconfig.test.json --noEmit`; `npm run lint` and CI's Typecheck step (`Test (VTC admin UI)` job, was `npx tsc -b --noEmit`) run it, so tests are still type-checked in CI.
- New `src/vite-env.d.ts` carries `/// <reference types="vite/client" />` (removed from `list-limits.test.ts`), which `community-theme.ts`'s `*.css?raw` imports need.
- The bundle import is now `@vti-specs-vtc/trust-tasks/vtc/elections/create/0.5.bundle.json`, a **vitest-only** alias (`vitest.config.ts`) with a matching `paths` entry in `tsconfig.test.json`. The pinned vendored bundle stays the single source of truth; `vite.config.ts` and `tsconfig.json` reference nothing outside the package.
- `rule-ir.test.ts` still reads `../policies/default/*.rego` at run time — vitest-only, so the suite needs a checkout but the build does not. Documented in the README.
- `vtc-service/build.rs` and `scripts/build-vtc-web-bundles.sh` only run `npm run build`; no change needed.

## Test evidence (local, macOS)

- `npm ci` ✓, `npm run build` ✓, `npm run lint` (wire:check + typecheck) ✓
- `npx vitest run`: 126 files, 1590 tests passed
- `tsc -p tsconfig.json --listFilesOnly`: 0 test files; `tsc -p tsconfig.test.json --listFilesOnly`: 126 test files plus the `vti-specs-vtc` bundle
- Isolation: `git archive HEAD vtc-service/admin-ui | tar -x` into an empty directory, then `npm ci && npm run build` there ✓

## Answers to the issue's questions

- **Was type-checking tests in the build deliberate?** No — it was the default single `tsconfig.json` never having been split. CI's own Typecheck step is what should catch a broken test, not `cargo build`.
- **Is the split welcome?** Yes; this PR is that split (tsconfig exclude + `tsconfig.test.json` + `src/vite-env.d.ts`).
- **The cross-crate fixture?** It now resolves through a vitest alias, keeping the vendored pinned bundle as the one source rather than a copy under `admin-ui/`.

Closes #2430

title: feat(vta-mcp): --listen, on a listener vti-mcp-common now shares with vtc-mcp
body:
> **Stacked on #2506**, which is stacked on #2504. Merge order: #2504 → #2506 → this. Each PR's base is a feature branch, and CI only runs on PRs into `main`/`release/**`, so **CI starts when GitHub retargets each PR to `main`**. That needs a new push afterwards, because a retarget alone doesn't trigger the workflow.

## Why

`vta-mcp` has both problems that #2504 fixed for `vtc-mcp`:

1. **One socket per DID.** It holds a mediator session as its identity, so two stdio bridges on one identity (two assistant sessions) evict each other's socket, and a reply flushed onto the other process's socket is lost.
2. **Confirmations at MCP `2026-07-28`.** `--confirm` uses server-to-client elicitation, which `2026-07-28` forbids, and `vta-mcp` had no protocol cap. Claude Code's v2 runtime probes **stdio** servers for `2026-07-28` too, so `vta-mcp`'s confirmations can already fail without `--listen`.

## Change

- **`vti_mcp_common::listen`** (new), moved out of `vtc-mcp` as design note D7 said it would be once a second bridge took it:
  - `check_loopback`, `load_token`, `require_bearer`, `router`, `serve`, `write_owner_only`, the `Serving` stdio/HTTP choice, and `supported_protocol_versions` (the `2025-11-25` cap)
  - Each bridge names itself with a `Bridge { name, token_env, state_dir_env }`.
- **`vtc-mcp`:** `src/listen.rs` is now its `Bridge` plus the two tests that need `VtcMcp` itself. Its `main.rs` and `key_reuse.rs` use the shared code. No behaviour change.
- **`vta-mcp`:**
  - `--listen <loopback addr>` (`VTA_MCP_LISTEN`), with the token from `VTA_MCP_LISTEN_TOKEN` or `listen-token` in `VTA_MCP_STATE_DIR` / `$XDG_STATE_HOME/vta-mcp` / `~/.local/state/vta-mcp`
  - `ServerHandler::supported_protocol_versions` returns the shared cap.
  - `listen` added to the hand-written `Debug` of `Args`.
- **Docs:**
  - `docs/02-vta/vta-mcp.md`: §2.1, new §6.1, troubleshooting rows
  - design note D7
  - `CLAUDE.md` for `vti-mcp-common` (a new rule), `vta-mcp` and `vtc-mcp`, plus the crate map

## Tests

- `vti-mcp-common` (9 new), against a minimal `ServerHandler`:
  - loopback-only bind
  - token generated with mode 0600, then reused
  - group-readable token file refused
  - environment wins over the file; short token refused, with the error naming both variables
  - the cap stops before `2026-07-28`
  - over HTTP: missing, wrong and Basic credentials → `401` (body names the bridge); `Origin` → `403`; two sessions; a `2026-07-28` request refused with the supported list
- `vta-mcp`: `hosts_are_held_to_a_version_that_can_be_asked`. It fails when the cap is swapped for `KNOWN_VERSIONS`.
- `cargo nextest run -p vta-mcp -p vtc-mcp -p vti-mcp-common`: **90 passed**. Clippy (`-D warnings`, all targets) and `cargo fmt --check` are clean.
- **Smoke test, `vta-mcp` release binary:** `--listen 0.0.0.0` refused; token file created 0600; `401` without the token, `200` with it, at protocol `2025-11-25`; exit on SIGTERM.
- **Live, `vtc-mcp` on the shared listener:** the launchd `--listen` bridge against first-vtc was reinstalled from this build and served a `vtc_call` to Claude Code over TSP.

## Not in this PR

Moving confirmation to `InputRequiredResult` (MRTR) so the cap can lift. Claude Code documents `input_required` only for the MCP tasks extension, not for a plain `tools/call` result, so building it now could ship a path no host in use completes. The cap's doc comment says when to lift it.

## Pre-merge checklist

- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch() (R1.2): `reqwest` is a dev-dependency only.
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3): none added.
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect (R2.1): only the token file, written atomically before serving.
- [x] Retries (R1.4): none.
- [x] Accept loops survive transient errors (R1.5): `axum::serve`.
- [x] Acks (R1.6): n/a.
- [x] Wire types (R3.*): none; MCP over HTTP is rmcp's.
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive (R5.*): no `--listen` means stdio. With it, a non-loopback address, no token source, or an unreadable or too-open token file is fatal at startup.
- [x] Logs/status (R6.*): the startup log names the serving mode and the token's source, never the token.
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" (R2.1): atomic token write.
- [x] Deviations flagged: none.

title: feat(vta-mcp): --listen, on a listener vti-mcp-common now shares with vtc-mcp (#2508)
body:
feat(vta-mcp): --listen, on a listener vti-mcp-common now shares with vtc-mcp (#2508)

* fix(vta-sdk): reconnect a TspSession whose websocket the mediator closed

The mediator closes every websocket when the access token it was opened
with expires (close 1008, "authentication token expired"; 900 s by
default). `TspSession::request` reconnected only after a reply timeout, so
a long-lived session kept the dead socket and every later request failed
at once with "TSP websocket closed by the mediator". vtc-mcp, which holds
one session for the life of the MCP server, stopped working after a
quarter of an hour.

A request that finds the socket closed or broken now reconnects once (a
fresh authentication, so a fresh token) and keeps waiting on the same
waiter until its own deadline, or STRANDED_REPLY_GRACE if that is later.
The request went out over the TSP transport's HTTP post, so its reply is
in the inbox and the new socket's flush-on-connect delivers it; nothing
is resent.

Concurrent requests failing on the same close share one reconnect: the
session numbers its sockets, and a waiter reconnects only if the socket
it saw die is still the current one. Each opening its own would evict the
one before, losing any reply already flushed onto an evicted socket
(raw-TSP mode deletes a frame once written).

tests/e2e/tests/tsp_reconnect_on_close.rs drives both cases against a
TestMediator with a 5 s access token; both fail on the previous code with
the production error.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* feat(vtc-mcp): --listen serves every MCP host on the machine from one bridge

The mediator holds one websocket per DID. A stdio bridge is one process per
MCP host, so two assistant sessions on one agent key are two sockets for one
DID: each reconnect evicts the other, and in raw-TSP mode (flush-on-connect,
delete-on-send) a reply flushed onto the other process's socket is gone, so
the request it answers fails although the community acted on it.

`--listen <loopback addr>` serves MCP's streamable HTTP transport at /mcp
from one process holding the one community session. Each MCP session is a
clone of the bridge over the same client, guard, recorder and sign-in state;
TspSession already routes concurrent replies to their waiters, and an
elicitation goes back on the calling session's own peer. stdio stays the
default.

The endpoint speaks with the bridge's standing, so it takes the place of the
boundary stdio got from process spawn:

- loopback only, checked before binding, with no flag to widen it;
- a bearer token on every request, compared in constant time, from
  VTC_MCP_LISTEN_TOKEN or an owner-only `listen-token` file in the state
  directory, generated on first use and refused when others can read it;
- no `Origin` and a loopback `Host` (rmcp's checks, both enforced), so a
  browser page cannot reach it by DNS rebinding.

Stops on SIGINT/SIGTERM, closing every MCP session and then the community
session. Design note D7 and phase 8; operator page section 7.1.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(vtc-mcp): serve MCP up to 2025-11-25 so confirmations can ask the human

Over --listen, Claude Code speaks MCP 2026-07-28: no `initialize`, the
version and capabilities in each request's _meta. rmcp serves that
statelessly with no client capabilities, and 2026-07-28 forbids
server-to-client requests, so every confirmation (--confirm,
vtc_actions_decide) was refused as "this MCP host cannot ask you" — seen
live on auth/signing-key/enroll.

VtcMcp now supports protocol versions up to 2025-11-25. A host offering
2026-07-28 is refused with the versions the bridge serves and falls back to
`initialize`, keeping a session and its elicitation capability. Verified
against Claude Code: it probed with 2026-07-28, was refused, initialized at
2025-11-25 with form elicitation, and the enroll and revoke confirmations
both reached the human.

The cap lifts once confirmation is answered with an InputRequiredResult.
a_host_speaking_2026_07_28_is_sent_back_to_a_version_that_can_ask fails
without the cap.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(vtc-mcp): vtc_status reports reachability from calls, not a flag latched at connect

`connected` was `self.client.is_some()`: true for the life of the process
once a session had been opened, so a bridge whose mediator socket had been
closed for hours reported itself connected while every call failed (R6.2:
a health flag must be driven by a signal that can go false again).

Every community call now reports its result to a shared TransportHealth:
a session or HTTPS transport failure turns `connected` false; the next
answer from the community (a success, a refusal, a parked action) turns it
true; a local refusal (unpinned URI, schema failure) says nothing.
`vtc_status` adds `transportHealth` (lastReachedAt, lastFailureAt,
lastFailure) and `serving` (`stdio` or the --listen URL).

every_community_call_is_observed is a census over the sources: an awaited
`client.<method>(…)` that is not the argument of `health.observe(` fails it
(checked by unwrapping one call). Operator page section 6 and the skill
say what `connected: false` means.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* feat(vta-mcp): --listen, on a listener vti-mcp-common now shares with vtc-mcp

vta-mcp holds a mediator session as its identity, so it has vtc-mcp's
problem: two stdio bridges on one identity are two sockets for one DID,
evicting each other, and a reply flushed onto the other process's socket
is lost. It also confirms by server-to-client elicitation, which MCP
2026-07-28 forbids, and had no protocol cap, so a host that negotiates
2026-07-28 (Claude Code probes stdio servers too) could never be asked.

The listener moves from vtc-mcp into vti_mcp_common::listen, as design
note D7 said it would once a second bridge took it: check_loopback,

title: docs: the memory minimum no longer carries fjall's journal-replay floor (#1777)
body:
fjall 3.1.13 (in `Cargo.lock` since #2392) includes fjall-rs/fjall#332: on open, journal replay skips items at or below each keyspace's persisted seqno. The 256 MiB minimum in both non-interactive-setup docs (#2091) existed only because the whole active journal (up to ~64 MiB, flushed writes included) was replayed whatever the `[fjall]` settings said. This PR re-measures on 3.1.13 and updates the docs.

## Method

A throwaway standalone cargo project (not committed) depending on `fjall = "=3.1.13"` (lsm-tree 3.1.10, as in our lockfile), opened with the small `[fjall]` settings from #1803: `cache_size(8 MiB)`, `max_journaling_size(64 MiB)`, `max_write_buffer_size(16 MiB)`. 4 keyspaces, ~1 KB pseudo-random values. Each phase runs as its own process under `/usr/bin/time -l` (macOS) for peak RSS; `Database::write_buffer_size()` is read straight after reopen.

- **A**: write N MB, `rotate_memtable_and_wait` on every keyspace, `persist(SyncAll)`, clean close, reopen.
- **B**: write N MB, sealing all memtables whenever `write_buffer_size() > 16 MiB` (the rule `vti-common`'s flusher applies), `persist(SyncAll)`, then `SIGKILL` itself (an OOM kill), reopen twice with no flush in between.
- **C**: write N MB with no flushing at all, `persist`, `SIGKILL`, reopen (no-flusher worst case).

## Results

| Case | N | Write buffer after reopen | Reopen peak RSS |
|---|---|---|---|
| empty DB baseline | – | 0 | 2.7 MB |
| A (flushed, clean close) | 20 MB | **0** | 3.2 MB |
| A | 60 MB (2 journals at close) | **0** | 3.4 MB |
| A | 100 MB (2 journals at close) | **0** | 4.1 MB |
| B (flusher rule, SIGKILL) | 20 MB | 5.25 MB (same on 2nd reopen) | 8.7 MB |
| B | 60 MB | 15.76 MB (same on 2nd reopen) | 19.7 MB |
| B | 100 MB | 9.40 MB (same on 2nd reopen) | 13.1 MB |
| C (no flushing, SIGKILL) | 20 MB | 22.1 MB | 26.1 MB |
| C | 60 MB | 66.4 MB | 72.1 MB |

On 3.1.12 case A put the full 21.5 MB back (issue comment). On 3.1.13 a restart replays exactly the unflushed writes. Since the flusher keeps those near `write_buffer`, a kill costs about `write_buffer` on restart, and repeated kills don't make it worse.

## Doc changes

- `docs/02-vta/non-interactive-setup.md`: the "floor none of these settings lower" paragraph is replaced with "What a restart costs" (the 3.1.13 behaviour plus the numbers above). The sizing advice is now `block_cache + write_buffer` plus headroom, not `+ max_journal`, since the journal lives on disk. The `fjall.write_buffer` row is corrected: the store's flusher enforces it, with a default of 8 MiB, not "unbounded". The minimum is now **128 MiB** with small settings, with a note to check the service's own RSS before going lower.
- `docs/03-vtc/non-interactive-setup.md`: the 256 MiB / replay-floor sentence now points to the VTA doc.

I found no other mentions of 256 MiB or the replay floor in docs/, the CLAUDE.md files, or deploy manifests. The repo has no helm, k8s or compose memory limits; the Nitro `--memory 512` is enclave sizing and is left as it is.

Note: the 128 MiB figure is a conservative recommendation. The store's share was measured (≤ ~20 MB on reopen with these settings), but a full VTA/VTC process was not.

Closes #1777
author: stormer78

title: feat(vtc): the badge picture builder finds icons by meaning, and browses them all
body:
It was hard to find an icon in the badge picture builder without knowing lucide's name for it. This adds two ways to find one.

**Search by meaning.** *Find an icon* now matches each word against the icon's name or the words lucide files the icon under: "insect" finds Bug, "prize" finds Trophy, "issue" finds Bug and others.
- Icons whose name holds every word come first, then icons found only through their tags.
- Hyphens read as word breaks, so lucide's own spelling (`bug-off`) works.
- Each icon's title lists its tags, for example "Bug: issue, report, debug, code, insect".

**Browse all icons.** A button beside the search opens a dialog with all 1,544 icons in a scrolling grid, each with its name.
- The search runs over the grid with no cap.
- Choosing an icon closes the dialog and selects it.
- Escape and the close button also close it, and the scrim click closes it too.
- Focus goes to the search when the dialog opens and returns to *Browse all icons* when it closes, including in browsers where a click doesn't focus the button.
- The dialog has its own styles in `BadgeBuilder.css`, because the builder is shared by the console and the portal and each app's dialog styles are its own.

**New dependency: `lucide-static` 0.469.0** (ISC, no dependencies of its own). It's a dev dependency, pinned exactly to the same release as `lucide-react`. Only its `tags.json` is used, and the bundler copies it into the lazy `badge-icons` chunk; no images or font are bundled. Its 1,544 entries map one to one onto `lucide-react`'s icons, and a test holds that. The repo owner approved adding it.

**Bundle:** the lazy `badge-icons` chunk grows from about 104 kB to about 140 kB gzipped. It still loads only when someone searches or browses. The main bundles are unchanged.

**Tests:**
- searching by tag, and name matches ranking before tag matches;
- hyphenated names;
- an empty query returning every icon;
- the tags covering every icon;
- the dialog: all icons shown, narrowed by meaning, choosing, focus in and back, and Escape.

**Checks:**
- `npm run lint` passes.
- `vitest` passes 1593 of 1593.
- Both the console and the portal bundles build.
