title: fix(vta-config): make the config attestation view canonical JSON
body:
## Why

`AppConfig::compute_config_attestation_view` produced its bytes with `serde_json::to_vec`. Those bytes are the `configView` that `vta/attestation/config-report` returns, and the enclave's evidence binds their SHA-384.

The config contains `policy.approver_sets`, a `HashMap<String, Vec<String>>`. A `HashMap`'s iteration order is randomly seeded per map, so one configuration produced a different view and digest in every process:
- two enclaves in the same fleet with identical config attested different digests;
- one enclave attested a different digest after a restart, with nothing changed.

The task specification calls the view "a canonical, secret-free view" (`vta/attestation/config-report/0.1`). Struct order plus `HashMap` order isn't canonical.

## What

The view is now RFC 8785 canonical JSON, using `serde_json_canonicalizer`, which is already a workspace dependency. Equal configurations now give equal bytes whatever the field types: this fixes `approver_sets` and any map added later. `approver_sets` keeps its type, so no public field changes.

## Compatibility

- **Verifiers:** unaffected. Following config-report/0.1 verification step 3, a verifier base64-decodes the `configView` it is served and hashes those bytes. It never re-derives them. `vta_sdk::attestation` does exactly that.
- **Stored or pinned digests:** none. `capture_effective_config_attestation` runs at each boot (and again on an attested soft restart). The boot-log anchor and the pull endpoint both read that one captured value.
- **What an operator sees:** the view's member order changes from struct order to sorted, which JSON readers don't notice. The digest in the boot log is now stable for an unchanged config, where before it could differ on every boot.

## Tests

- New `config_attestation_view_is_the_same_bytes_for_the_same_config`: six configs with eight approver sets written in different orders must give identical view bytes and digest. It fails on the old code.
- `cargo nextest run --workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client`: 7125 passed
- `cargo nextest run -p vtc-service -p vtc-client`: 3664 passed
- Doc tests pass; clippy `-D warnings` and fmt are clean.

title: fix(vtc-mcp): vtc_status reports reachability from calls, not a flag latched at connect
body:
> **Stacked on #2504** (which is stacked on #2503). Merge order: #2503 → #2504 → this. GitHub retargets each as its base merges.

## Problem

`vtc_status` reported `connected: self.client.is_some()`, which is true for the life of the process once a session had been opened. During the 15-minute token-expiry bug (#2503) the bridge said `connected: true` while every call failed with `websocket closed by the mediator`. This is the R6.2 counterexample: a health flag must be driven by a signal that can go false again.

## Change

- New `vtc-mcp/src/health.rs`, holding a `TransportHealth` record shared by every MCP session. Every community call is passed through `self.health.observe(…)`. That's 15 call sites across `server.rs`, `signin.rs` and `workflows.rs`. Each result is classified:
  - **Reached:** `Ok`, `Http`, `NotFound`, `SignIn`, `Refused`, `Parked`. The community answered.
  - **Unreachable:** `Session`, `Transport` (HTTPS), `NoTransport`.
  - **No signal:** local refusals (unpinned URI, schema failure, signing) and future variants, since `VtcError` is `#[non_exhaustive]`.
- `vtc_status`:
  - `connected` is now `client.is_some() && health.reachable()`: true unless a transport failure is the latest signal.
  - **new** `transportHealth`: `{ lastReachedAt, lastFailureAt, lastFailure }`
  - **new** `serving`: `"stdio"`, or the `--listen` URL
- Docs: operator page §6 (what `connected` means now) and the skill (what to do on `connected: false`).

## Tests

- `health::tests` (3 new):
  - a transport failure turns `connected` false, and a refusal turns it back
  - a local refusal changes nothing
  - **`every_community_call_is_observed`**: a census over the sources. An awaited `client.<method>(…)` that isn't inside `health.observe(` fails it. Checked by unwrapping `call_operation`'s `send_task`: the test failed, naming `server.rs:564 client.send_task`.
- `cargo nextest run -p vtc-mcp`: **46 passed**. `cargo clippy -p vtc-mcp --all-targets -- -D warnings` and `cargo fmt --check` are clean.
- Live, on the launchd `--listen` bridge against first-vtc: `vtc_status` reports `serving: "http://127.0.0.1:7465/mcp"`, `connected: true` and `transportHealth.lastReachedAt` from the startup discovery call.

## Pre-merge checklist

- [x] No new HTTP clients or timeouts (R1.2)
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3): `TransportHealth` takes a `std::sync::Mutex` only after the call returns, never across an `.await`.
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect (R2.1): n/a, the state is observational.
- [x] Retries (R1.4): none added.
- [x] Loops (R1.5) and acks (R1.6): n/a.
- [x] Wire types (R3.*): `vtc_status` gains two fields; nothing removed. `connected` keeps its name with an honest meaning.
- [x] Config absence (R5.*): n/a.
- [x] **Logs/status claim only what was verified (R6.*): this PR.**
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" (R2.1): nothing persisted.
- [x] Deviations flagged: none.

title: fix(vtc-mcp): vtc_status reports reachability from calls, not a flag latched at connect (#2506)
body:
fix(vtc-mcp): vtc_status reports reachability from calls, not a flag latched at connect (#2506)

* fix(vta-sdk): reconnect a TspSession whose websocket the mediator closed

The mediator closes every websocket when the access token it was opened
with expires (close 1008, "authentication token expired"; 900 s by
default). `TspSession::request` reconnected only after a reply timeout, so
a long-lived session kept the dead socket and every later request failed
at once with "TSP websocket closed by the mediator". vtc-mcp, which holds
one session for the life of the MCP server, stopped working after a
quarter of an hour.

A request that finds the socket closed or broken now reconnects once (a
fresh authentication, so a fresh token) and keeps waiting on the same
waiter until its own deadline, or STRANDED_REPLY_GRACE if that is later.
The request went out over the TSP transport's HTTP post, so its reply is
in the inbox and the new socket's flush-on-connect delivers it; nothing
is resent.

Concurrent requests failing on the same close share one reconnect: the
session numbers its sockets, and a waiter reconnects only if the socket
it saw die is still the current one. Each opening its own would evict the
one before, losing any reply already flushed onto an evicted socket
(raw-TSP mode deletes a frame once written).

tests/e2e/tests/tsp_reconnect_on_close.rs drives both cases against a
TestMediator with a 5 s access token; both fail on the previous code with
the production error.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* feat(vtc-mcp): --listen serves every MCP host on the machine from one bridge

The mediator holds one websocket per DID. A stdio bridge is one process per
MCP host, so two assistant sessions on one agent key are two sockets for one
DID: each reconnect evicts the other, and in raw-TSP mode (flush-on-connect,
delete-on-send) a reply flushed onto the other process's socket is gone, so
the request it answers fails although the community acted on it.

`--listen <loopback addr>` serves MCP's streamable HTTP transport at /mcp
from one process holding the one community session. Each MCP session is a
clone of the bridge over the same client, guard, recorder and sign-in state;
TspSession already routes concurrent replies to their waiters, and an
elicitation goes back on the calling session's own peer. stdio stays the
default.

The endpoint speaks with the bridge's standing, so it takes the place of the
boundary stdio got from process spawn:

- loopback only, checked before binding, with no flag to widen it;
- a bearer token on every request, compared in constant time, from
  VTC_MCP_LISTEN_TOKEN or an owner-only `listen-token` file in the state
  directory, generated on first use and refused when others can read it;
- no `Origin` and a loopback `Host` (rmcp's checks, both enforced), so a
  browser page cannot reach it by DNS rebinding.

Stops on SIGINT/SIGTERM, closing every MCP session and then the community
session. Design note D7 and phase 8; operator page section 7.1.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(vtc-mcp): serve MCP up to 2025-11-25 so confirmations can ask the human

Over --listen, Claude Code speaks MCP 2026-07-28: no `initialize`, the
version and capabilities in each request's _meta. rmcp serves that
statelessly with no client capabilities, and 2026-07-28 forbids
server-to-client requests, so every confirmation (--confirm,
vtc_actions_decide) was refused as "this MCP host cannot ask you" — seen
live on auth/signing-key/enroll.

VtcMcp now supports protocol versions up to 2025-11-25. A host offering
2026-07-28 is refused with the versions the bridge serves and falls back to
`initialize`, keeping a session and its elicitation capability. Verified
against Claude Code: it probed with 2026-07-28, was refused, initialized at
2025-11-25 with form elicitation, and the enroll and revoke confirmations
both reached the human.

The cap lifts once confirmation is answered with an InputRequiredResult.
a_host_speaking_2026_07_28_is_sent_back_to_a_version_that_can_ask fails
without the cap.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(vtc-mcp): vtc_status reports reachability from calls, not a flag latched at connect

`connected` was `self.client.is_some()`: true for the life of the process
once a session had been opened, so a bridge whose mediator socket had been
closed for hours reported itself connected while every call failed (R6.2:
a health flag must be driven by a signal that can go false again).

Every community call now reports its result to a shared TransportHealth:
a session or HTTPS transport failure turns `connected` false; the next
answer from the community (a success, a refusal, a parked action) turns it
true; a local refusal (unpinned URI, schema failure) says nothing.
`vtc_status` adds `transportHealth` (lastReachedAt, lastFailureAt,
lastFailure) and `serving` (`stdio` or the --listen URL).

every_community_call_is_observed is a census over the sources: an awaited
`client.<method>(…)` that is not the argument of `health.observe(` fails it
(checked by unwrapping one call). Operator page section 6 and the skill
say what `connected: false` means.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: feat(acl): register the additive context-create capability (Appendix C.2)
body:
Registers `context-create` in the Appendix C.2 capability registry as an **additive** capability (VTI-ACL-033).

**Why.** An automated provisioner such as an agent gateway must create a child context per managed agent. Under VTI-CTX-020 it needs act authority over the parent, which a non-admin entry scoped to that parent already has. What it lacks is a gated capability for the act, short of being made an administrator, which would also let it rewrite ACL entries and re-point keys in the subtree.

**What the capability allows:**
- creating child contexts beneath a context the entry already acts in. Root creation still requires unrestricted act authority (VTI-CTX-020).
- setting the **first** identifier of a context it created, and only to a `did:key` of a key that context holds. Changing or clearing an established identifier stays an administrator's act.

It is additive because no role implies it. Granting it requires unrestricted act authority.

Implementation: OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#2302.

title: feat(vtc-mcp): --listen serves every MCP host on the machine from one bridge
body:
> **Stacked on #2503** (the `TspSession` reconnect fix): a long-running shared bridge depends on it. This PR targets that branch so its diff shows only this change; GitHub retargets it to `main` when #2503 merges.

## Problem

The mediator holds one websocket per DID. A stdio bridge is one process per MCP host, so two assistant sessions on one agent key put two sockets on one DID:

- each reconnect evicts the other socket;
- in raw-TSP mode (flush-on-connect, delete-on-send), a reply flushed onto the *other* process's socket is deleted once written, so the request it answers fails even though the community acted on it.

Until now the only workaround was a separate agent key per session, with an enrolment for each.

## Change

`vtc-mcp --listen <loopback addr>` serves MCP's streamable HTTP transport at `/mcp` from **one** process holding **one** community session (`vtc-mcp/src/listen.rs`).

- **One bridge, many sessions:** each MCP session is a clone of the bridge over the same `VtcClient`, guard, recorder and sign-in state. `TspSession` already routes concurrent replies to their waiters.
- **Approvals:** an elicitation (`--confirm`, `vtc_actions_decide`) goes back on the *calling* session's peer.
- **stdio stays the default** and is unchanged.

The endpoint speaks with the bridge's standing (for an administrator's delegation, the administrator's), so it replaces the boundary stdio got from process spawn. None of these checks can be turned off:

| Guard | How |
|---|---|
| Loopback only | `check_loopback` before binding; refuses `0.0.0.0`, LAN addresses and `[::]` |
| Bearer token | `Authorization: Bearer <token>` on every request, compared in constant time (`subtle`). From `VTC_MCP_LISTEN_TOKEN` (at least 32 chars), else an owner-only `listen-token` file in the state directory, generated on first use (256 bits) and **refused if group- or world-readable** |
| No browsers | `Origin` refused (`enforce_origin_validation`) and `Host` restricted to loopback names (rmcp's default list), against DNS rebinding |
| Clean shutdown | SIGINT/SIGTERM cancels every MCP session, then the community session closes |

Host configuration (operator page §7.1):

```json
{ "type": "http", "url": "http://127.0.0.1:7465/mcp",
  "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${VTC_MCP_LISTEN_TOKEN}" } }
```

## Also

- `key_reuse::state_dir()` is split out of `default_path()` so the token file shares the state directory. `write_owner_only` is `pub(crate)`, and its temp-file name is derived from the file name, which is unchanged for the existing note.
- Docs:
  - design note: **D7** and rollout phase 8
  - operator page: §2.1 layer 1, new §7.1, three troubleshooting rows
  - `vtc-mcp/CLAUDE.md`: a rule for the listener
  - the workspace crate-map row
- Dependencies: rmcp's `transport-streamable-http-server` feature, plus workspace `axum`, `subtle`, `tokio-util`, and `reqwest` as a dev-dependency. The only new crate in the lockfile is `sse-stream`.

## Tests

- `cargo nextest run -p vtc-mcp`: **42 passed**, 9 of them new in `listen::tests`:
  - loopback-only bind
  - token generated with mode 0600, then reused
  - group-readable token file refused
  - environment wins over the file; short token refused
  - over real HTTP:
    - missing, wrong or Basic credentials → `401` with `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer`
    - an `Origin` header with a valid token → `403`
    - **two MCP sessions on one bridge** get distinct `mcp-session-id`s and both list tools
- `cargo nextest run -p vta-mcp -p vti-mcp-common`: 40 passed (they share `rmcp`).
- `cargo clippy -p vtc-mcp --all-targets -- -D warnings` and `cargo fmt --all -- --check` are clean.
- Smoke test of the release binary: `--listen 0.0.0.0:…` refused at startup; token file created 0600; `401` without the token, `200` plus a session id with it, `403` with an `Origin`; clean exit on SIGTERM.
- **Not yet run:** a live run against a community with several real hosts attached.

## Pre-merge checklist

- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2): `reqwest` is a dev-dependency only (tests).
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3): the listener adds no locks; shared state is the bridge's existing `Arc`s.
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect (R2.1): the only local write is the token file, before anything is served.
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off (R1.4): no retries added.
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5): `axum::serve` keeps accepting past a failed connection; a bad request is answered and the server carries on.
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6): n/a.
- [x] New/changed wire types (R3.*): none; MCP over HTTP is rmcp's.
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive (R5.*): no `--listen` means stdio. With `--listen`, no token source is a startup error, an unreadable or too-open token file is a startup error, and a non-loopback address is a startup error.
- [ ] Logs/status claim only what was verified (R6.*): `vtc_status` does not yet report the serving mode, and its `connected` flag is still latched (noted on #2503). Follow-up.
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" (R2.1): the token file is written atomically (temp file plus rename).
- [x] Deviations flagged: none beyond R6 above.

title: feat(vtc-mcp): --listen serves every MCP host on the machine from one bridge (#2504)
body:
feat(vtc-mcp): --listen serves every MCP host on the machine from one bridge (#2504)

* fix(vta-sdk): reconnect a TspSession whose websocket the mediator closed

The mediator closes every websocket when the access token it was opened
with expires (close 1008, "authentication token expired"; 900 s by
default). `TspSession::request` reconnected only after a reply timeout, so
a long-lived session kept the dead socket and every later request failed
at once with "TSP websocket closed by the mediator". vtc-mcp, which holds
one session for the life of the MCP server, stopped working after a
quarter of an hour.

A request that finds the socket closed or broken now reconnects once (a
fresh authentication, so a fresh token) and keeps waiting on the same
waiter until its own deadline, or STRANDED_REPLY_GRACE if that is later.
The request went out over the TSP transport's HTTP post, so its reply is
in the inbox and the new socket's flush-on-connect delivers it; nothing
is resent.

Concurrent requests failing on the same close share one reconnect: the
session numbers its sockets, and a waiter reconnects only if the socket
it saw die is still the current one. Each opening its own would evict the
one before, losing any reply already flushed onto an evicted socket
(raw-TSP mode deletes a frame once written).

tests/e2e/tests/tsp_reconnect_on_close.rs drives both cases against a
TestMediator with a 5 s access token; both fail on the previous code with
the production error.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* feat(vtc-mcp): --listen serves every MCP host on the machine from one bridge

The mediator holds one websocket per DID. A stdio bridge is one process per
MCP host, so two assistant sessions on one agent key are two sockets for one
DID: each reconnect evicts the other, and in raw-TSP mode (flush-on-connect,
delete-on-send) a reply flushed onto the other process's socket is gone, so
the request it answers fails although the community acted on it.

`--listen <loopback addr>` serves MCP's streamable HTTP transport at /mcp
from one process holding the one community session. Each MCP session is a
clone of the bridge over the same client, guard, recorder and sign-in state;
TspSession already routes concurrent replies to their waiters, and an
elicitation goes back on the calling session's own peer. stdio stays the
default.

The endpoint speaks with the bridge's standing, so it takes the place of the
boundary stdio got from process spawn:

- loopback only, checked before binding, with no flag to widen it;
- a bearer token on every request, compared in constant time, from
  VTC_MCP_LISTEN_TOKEN or an owner-only `listen-token` file in the state
  directory, generated on first use and refused when others can read it;
- no `Origin` and a loopback `Host` (rmcp's checks, both enforced), so a
  browser page cannot reach it by DNS rebinding.

Stops on SIGINT/SIGTERM, closing every MCP session and then the community
session. Design note D7 and phase 8; operator page section 7.1.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(vtc-mcp): serve MCP up to 2025-11-25 so confirmations can ask the human

Over --listen, Claude Code speaks MCP 2026-07-28: no `initialize`, the
version and capabilities in each request's _meta. rmcp serves that
statelessly with no client capabilities, and 2026-07-28 forbids
server-to-client requests, so every confirmation (--confirm,
vtc_actions_decide) was refused as "this MCP host cannot ask you" — seen
live on auth/signing-key/enroll.

VtcMcp now supports protocol versions up to 2025-11-25. A host offering
2026-07-28 is refused with the versions the bridge serves and falls back to
`initialize`, keeping a session and its elicitation capability. Verified
against Claude Code: it probed with 2026-07-28, was refused, initialized at
2025-11-25 with form elicitation, and the enroll and revoke confirmations
both reached the human.

The cap lifts once confirmation is answered with an InputRequiredResult.
a_host_speaking_2026_07_28_is_sent_back_to_a_version_that_can_ask fails
without the cap.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: fix(vtc): badge holders and awards carry the holder's projected directory fields
body:
A badge's *Who holds it* list in the portal showed every holder as "A member" with a "?" avatar, even though their directory card shows a name and picture.

**Cause:** `projected_fields` in `trust_tasks/badge_tasks.rs` read `fields` from the top of what `directory::read::show` answers. That function answers the `vtc/directory/entries/show` payload, `{ "entry": { …, "fields" } }`, so `fields` sits one level down and the top-level read always came back empty. As a result, `vtc/badges/holders/list` never carried the `fields` its schema promises ("projected exactly as `vtc/directory/entries/show` would project them"). The same helper feeds `awards/list`, so the console's award list never got them either.

**Fix:** read `entry.fields`. The projection is unchanged and is still made for the caller, so a holder shows only what the directory would show that caller.

**Test:** the holders-list assertion in `an_award_is_an_offer_until_accepted…` now requires each holder's projected `fields`. It fails without the fix, with the response missing `fields`, and passes with it.

**Also:** the console's *Credential* settings text and the portal's inside-only regime line still said the credential is issued by "the badge's own group identity". Since #2501 the community issues it, so both now say that.

**Checks:**
- `cargo nextest run -p vtc-service badges`: 39 of 39 pass.
- `cargo clippy -p vtc-service --all-targets -D warnings` is clean, and `cargo fmt --check` passes.
- Admin UI: `npm run lint` passes, and `vitest` passes 1587 of 1587.

title: feat(resolver): resolve did:webs (VTI-LNK-052, VTI-KEY-003)
body:
## What

Turns on the resolver SDK's `did-webs` feature and raises it to `affinidi-did-resolver-cache-sdk` 0.8.47, so VTA and CLI resolvers can resolve `did:webs`. A did:webs verifies when its KERI key event log verifies (VTI-LNK-052).

## Spec

- **VTI-LNK-052:** a contact's or peer's did:webs is verified by verifying its KERI key event log. The did-webs crate does that, and also checks the published `did.json` against the verified key state.
- **VTI-KEY-001 / VTI-KEY-003:** a node's own identity stays did:webvh or did:scid:vh. Resolving another method is the MAY in VTI-KEY-003.
- **VTI-KEY-173:** no key-role identity is ever created under did:webs. This PR only adds resolution.
- **Not changed:** member DID rotation still accepts only did:key, did:webvh and did:scid. Widening that is a separate policy decision.

## Safety

- **Host policy:** since resolver SDK 0.8.46 (affinidi-tdk-rs#987), did:webs resolution follows the same host policy as did:web, did:webvh and did:scid. It fetches only from public hosts, follows no redirects, uses no proxy, and checks the address a hostname resolves to when it connects.
  - The new test `default_config_refuses_loopback_webs_did_without_connecting` goes through the construction path every VTA and CLI resolver uses. A did:webs naming loopback, a `.local` host or the cloud metadata address is refused by the host policy, and the listener sees no connection.
- **No global `serde_json` change:** 0.8.47 is built on did-webs 0.9 and keri 0.5, which no longer turn on `serde_json`'s `preserve_order` for the whole build (affinidi-tdk-rs#988, affinidi-keri-rs#14). An earlier attempt on 0.8.46 broke idempotency hashes, page cursors and the VTI-08 stack budget. #2500 made the hashes independent of that setting anyway. `cargo tree -i serde_json -e features` now shows no `preserve_order`.

## Tests

- `cargo nextest run --workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client`: 7114 passed
- `cargo nextest run -p vtc-service -p vtc-client`: 3664 passed
- doc tests pass; clippy `-D warnings` and fmt are clean

title: fix(vta-sdk): reconnect a TspSession whose websocket the mediator closed
body:
## Problem

The mediator closes every websocket when the access token it was opened with expires (close 1008, `authentication token expired`; 900 s by default). `TspSession::request` reconnected only after a **reply timeout**, so a long-lived session kept the dead socket and every later request failed immediately with `TSP websocket closed by the mediator`.

Seen in production with `vtc-mcp`, which holds one `TspSession` for the life of the MCP server: about 16 minutes after startup every `vtc_call` failed, the first with `authentication token expired (1008)` and the rest with `websocket closed by the mediator`, until the server was restarted.

## Fix (`vta-sdk/src/session.rs`)

- `pump_once` now reports a closed or broken socket as `SocketFault::Gone`, separate from a frame it couldn't read.
- `await_reply` returns a `ReplyFailure`: `TimedOut`, `SocketGone { generation }` or `Failed`.
- `request` handles `SocketGone` by reconnecting **once**. That runs a fresh authentication, so it gets a fresh token. It then keeps waiting on the same waiter until the request's own deadline, or `STRANDED_REPLY_GRACE` if that is later. The request already went out over the HTTP post, so its reply is in the inbox and the new socket's flush-on-connect delivers it. **Nothing is resent.**
- `reconnect(expected_generation)`: the session numbers its sockets (`ws_generation`, written only under the `ws` lock). A waiter reconnects only if the socket it saw die is still the current one, so concurrent requests failing on one close share a single reconnect. Without that, each would evict the last, and a reply already flushed onto an evicted socket would be lost, because raw-TSP mode deletes a frame once it is written. The reply-timeout path is unchanged (`reconnect(None)`).

## Tests

- New, `tests/e2e/tests/tsp_reconnect_on_close.rs`: hermetic, using a `TestMediator` with a 5 s access token.
  - `a_request_after_the_token_expired_reconnects_and_gets_its_reply`
  - `concurrent_requests_on_a_closed_socket_all_get_their_replies`
  - Both **fail on the previous code** with the production error: `TSP websocket closed by the mediator: authentication token expired (1008)`.
- `cargo nextest run -p vti-e2e-tests -E 'binary(/^tsp_/)'`: 112 passed, including `tsp_stranded_reply`.
- `cargo nextest run -p vta-sdk --features tsp --lib`: 460 passed.
- `cargo clippy -p vta-sdk -p vtc-mcp -p vti-e2e-tests --all-targets -- -D warnings` and `cargo fmt --all -- --check` are clean.
- Not run: the full workspace suite. Separately, `vta-sdk`'s `typed_proof_verify` target doesn't compile under `-p vta-sdk --features tsp` alone (`trust_task_proof` is configured out). That failure predates this change and reproduces without it.

## Pre-merge checklist

- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2): the reconnect is bounded by `STRANDED_REPLY_GRACE`, and the wait by the request's deadline plus at most one grace.
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3): **deviation, pre-existing and unchanged.** `reconnect` holds the socket's own `ws` lock across the bounded connect, as it already did and as its doc explains (releasing it lets a pumping request see the eviction as a failure).
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect (R2.1): the only local state is the socket and its generation, swapped after the new socket is open.
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4): one reconnect per request, and no resend.
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5): `receive_next` still returns `Err` on a dead socket for its caller to reconnect on, as documented.
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6): no change.
- [x] New/changed wire types (R3.*): none.
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive (R5.*): no config.
- [ ] Logs/status claim only what was verified (R6.*): **not addressed here.** `vtc-mcp`'s `vtc_status` reports `connected: client.is_some()`, which stays `true` over a dead socket. Follow-up.
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1): a crash mid-reconnect leaves only an unread inbox, which the next connect flushes.
- [x] Deviations flagged: R1.3 above.

title: feat(vtc): the community issues the badge credential, named (VTI-BDG-060, 064, 080)
body:
The community, not the badge group, now issues the badge credential (VTI-BDG-060, 064, 080). This follows dtgwg-vti-spec #110 and trust-tasks-tf #1063.

**Why:** a verifier outside the community knows the community and nothing about a badge group's DID. A credential issued by `did:webvh:…:note-manage` could be tied to the community only through the trust registry or the group's authority credential, and neither travels with the badge. The embedded endorsement was of the Achievement and never named the group.

**The credential** (`badges::credential`):
- Signed as the community (`community_key_id`), not with the group's key.
- `issuer` is the community's `Profile` with its DID, its `name` from the community profile, and its `url` (the public origin). The Achievement's `creator` is the same `Profile`, so wallets show "First VTC", not a DID.
- `credentialSchema` names the Open Badges 3.0 JSON Schema (`1EdTechJsonSchemaValidator2019`), so the 1EdTech validator checks it.
- **Evidence:** the `description` is `Accepted 2026-11-08T22:42:06Z`, to the second, where it used to carry nanoseconds and `+00:00`. The `urn:vtc:award:…` `id` is gone; it used an unregistered URN namespace and was optional.
- **No embedded `EndorsementCredential`:** the issuer is the creator. `ensure_endorsement`, `endorsement_document` and `Badge.endorsement` are removed. Stored badges that still carry the field read fine, because the field is simply ignored.
- **Offer:** the group's authority credential no longer rides with the offer, because there is no chain to show.
- **Guard:** `issue` refuses a group that does not back the badge.

**Public Achievement** (`/badges/<id>`): its `creator` is the community's named `Profile`, and it carries no endorsement.

**Registry** (`badges::registry`): each record is `{entity: the community's DID, authority: the community's DID, issue, Achievement id}`. On its next pass, the projector withdraws the records that named group DIDs and publishes the new ones, because the key includes the entity.

**Console:** a badge's details now show:
- the badge group's DID with copy and QR (`DidText`);
- *Issued by: The community, also the badge's creator*, with the community's DID and copy and QR.

**Already issued:** credentials issued before this change name the group. They stand until renewal (inside only) or a re-issue replaces them. Nothing revokes them.

**Docs:**
- the operator guide (*The credential*, *The trust registry*, the public-locations table);
- the design note;
- the `vtc-service/CLAUDE.md` badges flow, which now says never to sign as the group.

**Checks:**
- `cargo nextest run -p vtc-service -p vtc-client`: 3664 of 3664 pass.
- `cargo clippy -p vtc-service --all-targets -D warnings` is clean, and `cargo fmt` was run.
- Admin UI: `npm run lint` passes, and `vitest` passes 1585 of 1585, including a new details-page test for the two DIDs.

title: fix: hash canonical JSON, so digests don't depend on serde_json's map order
body:
## Why

Several digests hashed `serde_json::to_vec` output. That output is sorted only while `serde_json`'s `preserve_order` feature is off, and any dependency can turn that feature on for the whole build, because Cargo unifies features. The KERI crates did exactly that when I tried to add did:webs resolution to the VTA resolver (VTI-LNK-052). With the feature on:

- `idempotency::the_request_hash_is_stable_across_member_ordering` failed. A retry whose members came in another order was refused as a different request.
- `device::list_pages_by_limit_and_next_cursor` failed. Next-page cursors no longer matched their filters.
- `vti-rooms` `test_vectors_match_the_fixture` failed (test only).

KERI 0.5 stops turning the feature on (affinidi-keri-rs#14). Even so, VTI shouldn't depend on a feature that any dependency can flip.

## What

These digests now hash RFC 8785 canonical JSON, using `serde_json_canonicalizer`, which is already a workspace dependency:

- `vta-service`: idempotency payload hash; device, persona and vault list-cursor filter digests; collection fingerprint.
- `vtc-service`: git namespace list-cursor filter digest and role digest; vetting profiles filter digest; election ticket doc digest; admin-events change digest.

The canonical bytes match today's sorted output for these inputs (ASCII keys, compact form, integers), so stored idempotency records and open cursors stay valid across the upgrade.

The room file vectors test now compares JSON values rather than text.

Not changed: `vta-config`'s attestation view serializes a struct whose `approver_sets` field is a `HashMap`, so its key order can differ from one process to the next. That needs a digest format change and belongs in its own PR.

## Tests

- Normal build:
  - `cargo nextest run --workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client`: 7113 passed
  - `cargo nextest run -p vtc-service -p vtc-client`: 3664 passed
  - doc tests pass; clippy `-D warnings` and fmt are clean

title: fix: hash canonical JSON, so digests don't depend on serde_json's map order (#2500)
body:
fix: hash canonical JSON, so digests don't depend on serde_json's map order (#2500)

Idempotency hashes, list cursors' filter digests, the election ticket
digest, the git namespace role digest, the admin-events change digest and
the collection fingerprint all hashed `serde_json::to_vec` output. That is
sorted only while serde_json's `preserve_order` feature is off, and any
dependency can turn it on for the whole build (cargo unifies features).
With it on, the same request with its members in another order hashed
differently: a retry was refused as a different request, and a page cursor
failed against the filters it was minted for.

Each now hashes RFC 8785 canonical JSON (serde_json_canonicalizer, already a
workspace dependency). For these inputs — ASCII keys, compact, integer
numbers — the canonical bytes equal today's sorted output, so stored
idempotency records and open cursors stay valid across the upgrade.

The room file vectors test compares JSON values rather than text, since key
order is not part of the vectors.

title: spec(vtc/badges): the community issues the badge credential (VTI-BDG-060, 064, 080)
body:
The prose for the VTI spec change that makes the community the issuer of the badge credential (VTI-BDG-060, 064, 080).

**`vtc/badges/mine/accept/0.1`, *The badge credential*:**
- Signed as the community's own DID, not the badge group's.
- `issuer` is the community's `Profile`, with its `name` and, where the community has a public origin, its `url`. The Achievement's `creator` is the same `Profile`.
- `credentialSchema` names the Open Badges 3.0 JSON Schema (`1EdTechJsonSchemaValidator2019`), so OB3 validators check the credential.
- No embedded `endorsement`, because the issuer is the creator.
- Each `evidence` entry's `description` is the date its award was accepted, to the second in UTC.
- The closing note now says the issuer is the community, so the credential is enough for a verifier.

**`vtc/badges/create/0.1` and `promote/0.1`:** the registry projects the badge as one the community issues.

This changes prose only. No schema changes, so no bundle or digest changes and VTI needs no re-pin. The tasks stay at `draft`.

title: badges: the community issues the badge credential (VTI-BDG-060, 064, 080)
body:
The badge credential's issuer moves from the badge group to the community.

**Why:** a verifier outside the community knows the community by its identifier, its website and its registry entries, and knows nothing about a badge group's DID. VTI-BDG-064 let a verifier tie a group-issued credential to the community "by the community's endorsement in the credential". But that endorsement was of the Achievement and never named the group. So in practice the link needed the registry or the community's authorization credential to the group, and neither travels with the credential.

**Changes:**
- **VTI-BDG-060:** the community issues the credential, names itself in the issuer, and is the badge's creator. No endorsement is embedded, because the issuer is the creator.
- **VTI-BDG-064:** a verifier checks that the issuer is the community that created the badge.
- **VTI-BDG-080:** the registry publishes each community badge as one the community issues.
- **New rationale** for 060 and 064: the badge group keeps the owners, holders, requests and rules, and issues nothing.

VTI-BDG-063 is unchanged: retiring a badge still revokes the community's authorization credential to the group.

The Trust Task prose follows in a trust-tasks-tf PR on branch `spec/badge-issuer-community`.

title: feat(vtc): authorize another key from the console through the wallet, for an administrator whose identity lives in their VTA
body:
`cnm access authorize-key` signs the `auth/signing-key/authorize/0.1` a key
such as vtc-mcp's needs to act with an administrator's standing, but only with
a key `cnm` holds. An administrator whose identity is a persona in their VTA
had no way to sign it, so their assistant could not act for them, and a
step-up the assistant hit could not be answered from their wallet (it names
`cnm`'s key as the subject).

Console signing keys → Authorize another key builds the same document — the
named did:key, the identity, `scope: console`, an optional label, the
delegation's expiry (1 – 30 days) — usable for an hour, and has the wallet
sign it as the identity. Nothing is sent from the console: the authorization
is copied or downloaded and given to the key's holder, which enrols itself
with `auth/signing-key/enroll/0.2` (`vtc_enrol_signing_key`). The VTC's checks
are unchanged (single-use, only the named key, terms exactly the enrolment's,
not signed by a delegated key). The console refuses a non-did:key, an
out-of-range expiry, the identity itself and this browser's own key before
asking the wallet, and warns against reusing a key across communities.

vtc-mcp's `vtc_enrol_signing_key` now points at the console as well as `cnm`;
its operator page, README, skill and the console guide say how, and the
"not built yet" items for it and for the wallet step-up reader (plugin #427)
are gone.

title: fix(store): flush fjall memtables in the background so writes don't stay in memory
body:
## What and why

fjall 3.1 (3.1.12 and 3.1.13) only flushes a keyspace once that one keyspace holds 64 MiB of unflushed writes. `max_write_buffer_size` is stored but never read, and `max_journaling_size` is only checked while a flush runs. The VTA spreads its writes over ~37 keyspaces, so it never flushes. Every write it has ever made, including every overwritten version of a record, stays in memory and is replayed from the journal at startup.

On staging this OOM-killed the keyring runner VTA vta-78 461 times between Nov 4 and Nov 8. It had an 84 MB journal and under 1 MB of live data. `STORAGE_FJALL_WRITE_BUFFER` and `STORAGE_FJALL_MAX_JOURNAL` had no effect.

**Fix:** `vti_common::store::flusher` runs one background thread per `LocalStore`. It writes every keyspace with pending data to disk (`rotate_memtable`):
- when unflushed bytes reach `fjall.write_buffer` (8 MiB by default);
- after 5 minutes otherwise;
- once at startup, so a database whose journal replay refilled memory drains straight away. Existing VTAs recover on their first restart, without a storage reset.

It flushes every keyspace, not just the largest, because fjall can only delete a journal file once every keyspace has flushed past it. The store and every keyspace handle share the thread, and it is joined when the last of them drops, so reopening a directory never finds it locked.

Lowering `max_memtable_size` is not enough: fjall saves it per keyspace when the keyspace is created and reads it back on every open, so existing VTAs would keep 64 MiB.

The Nitro enclave proxy opens its own fjall database on the parent and links no workspace code, so it gets a copy of the module (`deploy/nitro/enclave-proxy/src/flusher.rs`).

Repro (20 keyspaces, ~195 MiB written, write buffer capped at 16 MiB, journal capped at 64 MiB):

| | In memory | On-disk tables | Journal |
|---|---|---|---|
| fjall alone | 208 MiB | 0 | 205 MiB |
| After sealing every keyspace | 0 MiB | 40 | 64 MiB |

`without_flusher_small_keyspaces_never_flush` pins the fjall behaviour, so it fails if a fjall upgrade fixes it upstream. The same fix for the DID hosting daemon is in affinidi/affinidi-webvh-service.

## Also in this PR

- **Flusher hardening (from review of the DID hosting copy):** stopping the flusher waits at most 5s, then logs an error and continues. A keyspace that can't be flushed is logged at `error`, with a count of consecutive failed passes. The enclave proxy's copy has the same change.
- **Test stores print fjall's own warnings and errors** (`test_fixture`). fjall explains why it poisoned a database only through `log`, and tests installed no logger, so a failing `Store(Poisoned)` test showed no cause.
- **VTA test harness fix:** `TestAppContext` owned the test's data directory, and many tests drop the context while still using the router. The directory was deleted while the store was still open. fjall's startup compaction then crashed with `ENOENT` and poisoned the store, which surfaced as random 503 / `Store(Poisoned)` failures on this branch. The directory is now deleted by the store (`Store::holding`, test-support only) once the database has closed.

## Requirements

None.

## Backport

Not labelled. A maintainer should decide which release branches need it. Staging runs vta 0.65.0 and vtc 0.20.0, and every VTA and VTC on fjall 3.1 builds memory up the same way.

## Checklist

- [x] Targets `main`
- [x] No `version =` edits in any `Cargo.toml`
- [x] Tests cover the change; `cargo fmt` and `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` are clean. Full workspace: 10,764 passed. enclave-proxy: 65 passed.
author: stormer78

title: fix(store): flush fjall memtables in the background so writes don't stay in memory (#2492)
body:
fix(store): flush fjall memtables in the background so writes don't stay in memory (#2492)

* fix(store): flush fjall memtables in the background so writes don't stay in memory

fjall 3.1 (3.1.12 and 3.1.13) only flushes a keyspace once that one
keyspace holds 64 MiB of unflushed writes. Its database-wide
max_write_buffer_size is stored but never read, and max_journaling_size
is only checked while a flush runs. The VTA spreads its writes over ~37
keyspaces, so it never flushes: every write it has ever made, including
every overwritten version of a record, stays in memory and is replayed
from the journal at startup. On staging this OOM-killed the keyring
runner VTA vta-78 461 times (84 MB journal, under 1 MB of live data).
STORAGE_FJALL_WRITE_BUFFER and STORAGE_FJALL_MAX_JOURNAL had no effect.

vti_common::store::flusher runs one background thread per LocalStore
that seals every non-empty keyspace when unflushed bytes reach
fjall.write_buffer (default 8 MiB) or after 5 minutes, and once at
startup to drain a replayed journal. Sealing every keyspace, not just
the largest, is what lets fjall delete old journal files. The thread is
shared by the store and its keyspace handles and is joined when the
last one drops, so reopening a directory never finds it locked.

Lowering max_memtable_size would not help existing VTAs: fjall persists
it per keyspace at creation and reads it back on every open.

The Nitro enclave proxy opens its own fjall database on the parent and
links no workspace code, so it gets a copy of the module.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix(store): bound the flusher's shutdown wait and escalate seal failures

Flusher::drop now waits at most 5s for its thread, then logs an error and
leaves the thread to finish, so a stalled disk cannot hang shutdown. A
keyspace that cannot be sealed is logged at error, and consecutive failing
passes are counted so a persistent failure reads as one. Failing store
startup when the thread cannot spawn is kept and documented: a store that
never flushes would grow until OOM-killed. Same change in the enclave
proxy's copy, from review of the DID hosting PR.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* test(store): print fjall's own warnings and errors from test stores

fjall reports why it poisoned a database (a failed journal write, a crashed
flush or compaction worker) only through the `log` crate. Tests install no
logger, so a test failing with Store(Poisoned) showed no cause. The test
fixture now installs a stderr logger for fjall and lsm-tree at warn and
above, which nextest prints beside a failing test.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* test(vta): delete a test app's data dir only after its store closes

TestAppContext owned the test's TempDir, and many tests drop the context
while keeping the router, so the data directory was deleted under a live
store. When fjall then compacted (it queues a compaction on open for any
keyspace with level-0 tables), the worker hit ENOENT, crashed and poisoned
the database, and the test's next write failed with Store(Poisoned) or a
503. CI showed it once fjall's own errors were printed:

  [ERROR fjall::compaction::worker] Compaction failed: Io(Os { code: 2, kind: NotFound, ... })
  [ERROR fjall::worker_pool] Worker #2 crashed: ...

The directory is now created with cleanup disabled and handed to the store
(Store::holding, test-support only), which deletes it once the database has
closed: after the store and every keyspace handle have dropped.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

title: feat(vtc-mcp): warn when an agent key is reused at a second community; say why one key per community (VTI-KEY-005, VTI-KEY-006)
body:
A community records every DID that signs in to it, enrols as an approver or
holds a delegation. Two communities that hold the same one can tell that one
person stands behind both by comparing their records, and neither can see the
reuse from its own. Only the key holder can.

- vtc-mcp keeps an owner-only local note of the communities each agent DID
  was used with ($VTC_MCP_STATE_DIR, else $XDG_STATE_HOME/vtc-mcp, else
  ~/.local/state/vtc-mcp; DIDs only). A key pointed at a second community is
  logged and reported as `keyReuseWarning` by vtc_whoami / vtc_status. It
  warns and never refuses; --no-key-reuse-check turns it off.
- docs/03-vtc/admin-access.md §3.1a and vtc-mcp.md §2.7: use a different
  approver, administrator and agent key at each community. The VTA browser
  plugin already mints one approver per community; keys carried by hand are
  the risk.
- The console's approver panels, the /admin/enrol-approver page and
  `vtc admin enrol-approver` say the same in one line.

  3. optionally `awards/offer`
  4. optionally `claims/create`, whose code is answered once, in that step's own answer
  5. `show`

title: docs(approvals): a factor or delegated key reused at two nodes correlates the subject (note on VTI-APV-016)
body:
An informative note after the rationale for VTI-APV-016.

A re-authentication factor named by a DID, and a delegated signing key, are identifiers each node records. The same one bound or delegated at two nodes correlates the subject across them, however distinct the subject's own identifiers there are (VTI-KEY-005, VTI-KEY-006). No node can detect the reuse; only the key holder can. So an agent creating such a key makes one per node, and a node that guides a subject through binding or delegating one says so.

Implemented as warnings in OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#2495.

body:
The Release PR for every package in this repo. **Merging this is the release.**

| Package | Registry | Version | Bump |
|---|---|---|---|
| `trust-tasks` | crates.io | `0.37.9` → `0.37.10` | patch |
| `trust-tasks-capability-client` | crates.io | `0.37.9` → `0.37.10` | patch |

| `trust-tasks-https` | crates.io | `0.37.9` → `0.37.10` | patch |
| `trust-tasks-proof` | crates.io | `0.37.9` → `0.37.10` | patch |
| `trust-tasks-rs` | crates.io | `0.37.9` → `0.37.10` | patch |
| `trust-tasks-tsp` | crates.io | `0.37.9` → `0.37.10` | patch |
| `@openvtc/trust-tasks` | npm | `0.28.21` → `0.28.22` | patch |
| `github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/trust-tasks-go` | Go (tag `trust-tasks-go/v0.10.21`) | `0.10.20` → `0.10.21` | patch |
| `trust_tasks` | pub.dev | `0.9.30` → `0.9.31` | patch |

What merging does, per registry (all in `publish.yml`, each keyed on "this
version is not published yet"):

- **crates.io** — `release-plz-release` tags `<crate>-v<version>`, publishes in
  dependency order and creates a GitHub Release per crate. Bump levels come from
  the commit subjects.
- **npm** — `publish-npm` publishes with OIDC provenance and tags
  `<prefix>-v<version>`.
- **Go** — `publish-go` builds, vets and tests, then pushes the tag, which *is*
  the publication. **Irreversible**: proxy.golang.org never forgets a tag.
- **pub.dev** — `tag-dart` verifies against the *published* core and pushes the
  tag; `publish-dart.yml` publishes from it.

Every bump follows the commit subjects; an undeclared API break is refused on its
pull request by that language's API compatibility check (`rs`, `ts`, `go` and
`Dart API compatibility`).

This branch is regenerated from `main` on every push, so do not commit to it —
edits are force-pushed away. See RELEASING.md.

title: feat(vtc): badge claim codes for events and the automatic badge counts (VTI-BDG-015, 025 – 027)
body:
feat(vtc): badge claim codes for events and the automatic badge counts (VTI-BDG-015, 025 – 027)

Phase 4 of member badges, from the chapter (dtgwg-vti-spec #108) and the wire
(trust-tasks-tf #1059), pinned here.

Claim codes (`vtc/badges/claims/{create,list,withdraw,redeem}/0.1`,
`badges::claims`):
- An owner (or `vtc.badges.admin`) issues a code for a community badge with a
  label, a time (at most 90 days ahead) and a claim limit. The code is 256 bits
  from the CSPRNG, answered once; the community keeps only its SHA-256 digest
  (`bcdig:`), the record (`bclaim:`, indexed by badge) and a marker per member
  who redeemed it.
- A member redeeming it is admitted as on an approved request (VTI-BDG-024):
  the claim is reserved - counted and marked under the badges lock - before the
  credential is issued, and released if the key holder fails, so a limit is
  never exceeded; then `credential::issue_with_new_award` issues the badge
  credential with a new accepted award (giver = the code's issuer) as evidence,
  offers it, and records the membership. Unknown, expired, exhausted,
  withdrawn and retired-badge codes answer `codeInvalid` alike;
  `alreadyClaimed` and `alreadyHeld` refuse a second claim.
- Withdrawing stops a code; claims made stand. Retiring a badge withdraws its
  codes. `claims/list` never answers a code.

Rule counts (VTI-BDG-015): an automatic badge's rule may read
`kudosReceived`, `ideasSelected` and `electionTickets` with `atLeast` and
`count`. `groups::check_badge_rule` admits them; `check_rule` (any other group)
refuses them. `badges::rule_counts` counts from the community's own records at
each recompute - accepted kudos awards, selected ideas by proposer entry,
tickets by the member's current DID (never whether a ballot was cast).
Accepting kudos, selecting an idea and issuing a ticket kick the dynamic
sweeper (VTI-DIR-072).

Console: *Claim codes* on a community badge's page (issue - the code shown
once - list with claims, withdraw); the rule editor offers the counts on a
badge's form only. Portal: *Have a code?* on the badges page. OpenAPI wrappers
`BadgesClaims*01`, `openapi.json` and `wire.ts` regenerated; the URIs in the
manifest and the dispatched-URI list; `claims/list` and `claims/create` pinned
in `list-limits.json`, and the vitest census learns that a claim code's
`limit` is no page size (`NOT_PAGE_SIZES`).

Pins: the four claim tasks; `vtc/badges/{create,promote}` and
`vtc/groups/{create,list,show,update}` 0.1/0.2 drafts refreshed in place for
the new `RuleCondition` members.

Tests: the claim flow (limit, double claim, withdrawal, retirement), every
declared refusal including the key holder silent and refusing (the claim given
back), an automatic badge counting accepted kudos and the badge-only rule
check; census witnesses and conformance examples; portal and console tests.
Docs: the badges operator guide (automatic badges and their counts, claim
codes, storage), the design note (phase 4 complete) and the crate guide.

title: feat(vtc/badges): claim codes and the badge rule counts (VTI-BDG-015, VTI-BDG-025 – 027)
body:
Phase 4 of VTC badges (VTI chapter: trustoverip/dtgwg-vti-spec#108).

- **`vtc/badges/claims/{create,list,withdraw,redeem}/0.1`** — claim codes for events. An owner (or `vtc.badges.admin`) issues a code: at least 128 random bits the community generates, answered once, kept only as a digest, with a label, a time (at most 90 days ahead) and a claim limit. An active member redeeming it is admitted as on an approved request (VTI-BDG-024): credential first, then an accepted award whose giver is the code's issuer. Unknown, expired, exhausted, withdrawn and retired-badge codes all answer `codeInvalid`; `alreadyClaimed` and `alreadyHeld` refuse a second claim. Withdrawing stops further claims; claims made stand. The list never answers a code.
- **`_shared/0.1/badge.schema.json`**: `ClaimId`, `ClaimSecret`, `ClaimCode`.
- **`groups/_shared/0.1` `RuleCondition`**: appends the facts `kudosReceived`, `ideasSelected`, `electionTickets` and the op `atLeast` (integer `value`). `vtc/groups/create` refuses them for any group but a badge's; `vtc/badges/create` lets an automatic badge's rule read them. `electionTickets` counts tickets the community issued — never whether a ballot was cast (VTI-VOT-001).

All additive, on drafts. Bindings regenerated in their own commit; `validate`, `check-bindings` (1340 specs agree), `build`, `build-bundles` and `check-bundles` pass locally.

title: fix(vtc): a badge group's own paths give and end the badge (VTI-BDG-013, 020, 023, 024, 063)
body:
fix(vtc): a badge group's own paths give and end the badge (VTI-BDG-013, 020, 023, 024, 063)

A badge's holding is counted by its accepted awards (VTI-BDG-022), but the
groups' own paths admitted and removed members of a badge group without ever
touching an award:

- an approved request (VTI-BDG-014 / 024) and an automatic badge's rule
  (VTI-BDG-013) admitted the member and issued the badge credential with no
  award: they did not hold the badge (not on their card, not counted) and the
  credential carried no evidence;
- an owner's `vtc/groups/members/add` admitted a member to a badge group without
  the offer VTI-BDG-020 requires;
- `vtc/groups/leave`, an opt-out, an owner's `members/remove` and the rule
  ending a membership left the awards accepted, the credential's status slot
  unrevoked and any share live (VTI-BDG-063).

Now:

- `groups::credential::issue_admitting` is the admission entry point for every
  group path (members/add, join, an approved request, the dynamic rule). For a
  badge group, `badges::credential::issue_admitting` records one accepted award
  where the member holds none - given by the approving owner, or by no one for
  a rule - and issues the credential with it as the evidence: credential first,
  the award recorded after, audited (`requestApproved` / `givenByRule`).
  `issue` stays the renewal path.
- `members/add` on a badge group is refused (`permissionDenied`, naming
  `vtc/badges/awards/offer`).
- `badges::on_group_exit` runs on every membership end outside a badge task:
  leaving or opting out closes the awards as declined (opting out is declining
  the badge, VTI-BDG-013); a removal or the rule closes them as taken back. Any
  share stops and the credential's status is revoked where it carries one;
  each change audited.
- The badge-change audit moves to `badges::audit`, shared by the tasks and the
  group paths.

Tests: an approved request gives the badge (award as the credential's
evidence), `members/add` is refused, leaving declines it and revokes the slot,
an owner's removal takes it back; an automatic badge is held by its rule once,
and opting out declines it. Docs: the badges operator guide (the group's own
paths) and the crate guide.

title: feat(vtc): badge rule facts and claim codes (VTI-BDG-015, VTI-BDG-025 – VTI-BDG-027)
body:
Phase 4 of the Community Badges chapter.

- **VTI-BDG-015**: an automatic badge's rule may also read three counts the community keeps of its own records: kudos the member accepted (`kudosReceived`), ideas they proposed that a board selected (`ideasSelected`), and elections in which the community issued them a ticket (`electionTickets`). Badge groups only; never a fact of whether a ballot was cast, which the community never knows (VTI-VOT-001). VTI-DIR-072 points here.
- **VTI-BDG-025 – 027, claim codes**, closing the chapter's open issue: an owner (or `vtc.badges.admin`) issues a 128-bit code with a label, a time and a claim limit; the community shows it once and keeps only a digest; an active member redeeming it is admitted as on an approved request (VTI-BDG-024), with an award whose giver is the issuer; unknown, expired, exhausted, withdrawn and retired-badge codes are refused alike; a member never redeems one code twice; withdrawing stops further claims; retiring the badge withdraws its codes.
- VTI-BDG-095: redeeming is a holder's act, issuing and withdrawing an owner's. The appendix's `vtc.badges.admin` covers claim codes.

The wire follows in trust-tasks-tf (`RuleCondition` facts + `atLeast`, `vtc/badges/claims/*`).

feat(vtc): badge rule facts and claim codes (VTI-BDG-015, VTI-BDG-025 – VTI-BDG-027) (#108)

An automatic badge's rule may read three counts the community keeps of its own records - kudos accepted, ideas a board selected, elections it issued the member a ticket in - badge groups only, and never whether a ballot was cast (VTI-VOT-001). Claim codes close the chapter's open issue: an owner issues a 128-bit code with a label, a time and a limit; redeeming it is the member's consent and admits them as an approved request does; bad codes are refused alike; the community keeps only a digest. VTI-DIR-072 points to VTI-BDG-015; vtc.badges.admin covers claim codes; VTI-BDG-095 places redeeming with the holder's acts and issuing with the owner's.

title: feat(vtc): badge groups published to the trust registry as issuers the community recognises (VTI-BDG-080)
body:
feat(vtc): badge groups published to the trust registry as issuers the community recognises (VTI-BDG-080)

Where the community publishes to a trust registry, each active community badge's
group is published as one TRQP authorization record under the community's
authority: `{entity: the group's DID, action: issue, resource: the badge's
Achievement id}` - the identifier every credential of the badge names - with
`context: {kind: "vtcBadgeIssuer", badgeId}`. An outside verifier asks the
registry whether the community stands behind the issuer of a badge, and the
community's status set whether the award still stands. The record never carries
the badge's name or picture, so a badge kept inside is not described to the
world (VTI-BDG-050). Kudos badges have no group and are not published.

`badges::registry`:
- `desired`: one record per active community badge whose group exists.
- `reconcile`: publish what the `breg:` mirror of accepted records lacks or
  holds differently, delete what the mirror holds and nobody wants (a retired
  badge's record goes, as VTI-BDG-080 requires); a refusal stays out of the
  mirror and is retried on the next pass.
- `verify` (every 15 minutes, where the registry can enumerate): a record the
  registry lost leaves the mirror and is published again; a marked record the
  registry holds that nobody wants is deleted. A community `issue` record
  without the marker is never touched.
- `Projector`: the one retry owner, on a one-minute tick and `kick`ed by badge
  create, promote and retire; spawned and supervised in `server.rs` only when a
  registry client and the community's DID are both configured.

The VTC's records stay the source of truth and the registry a projection, as
with capability modules and git-namespace rights. Docs: the badges operator
guide (The trust registry, storage), the design note (phase 3b complete) and
the crate guide.

Test: publication of community badges only, no name in any record, no rewrite
when nothing changed, removal on retirement, retry after a refused write, and
verify restoring a lost record, deleting a stray badge record and leaving
another `issue` record alone.

title: feat(vtc): hand a delegated key's step-up to the person's wallet (VTI-LNK-125 – VTI-LNK-131)
body:
## Why

An assistant acting for you over `vtc-mcp` signs with a key you delegated. That key can redeem an operation-bound step-up but must never make one (VTI-APV-015). Until now, every step-up-gated act it attempted could only be finished in the console.

This implements the `step-up` trigger-link flow from trustoverip/dtgwg-vti-spec#106 (VTI-LNK-125 – VTI-LNK-131). It uses the task `auth/step-up/requests/show/0.1` from trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#1056, which is pinned here.

## What

- **Community (`vtc-service`):**
  - A step-up refusal carries `details.stepUpHandoff` when the subject holds a step-up approver. It is a single-use 16-byte handle with the pending step-up's expiry.
  - The handle's row keeps the inline request and the operation exactly as received. It lives in `step_up_marks`, which is not backed up.
  - `requests/show` answers once, atomically. It returns an `approve-request/0.5` document the community signs, addressed to the subject, plus the operation.
  - Every unanswerable handle gets the same `notFound`.
  - Reading a handle is never an approval. The step-up is still recorded only from the subject's approve-response.
- **Client (`vtc-client`):** the new `step_up` module builds the link. It expires with the hand-off, and never more than 300 seconds out.
- **Bridge (`vtc-mcp`):** a refusal with a hand-off becomes a successful `stepUpRequired` result carrying the link. A workflow tool stops at that step and reports the link.
- **Docs:** the operator page gains §2.3a. The skill and both crates' CLAUDE.md files are updated.

## Not in this PR

The browser plugin's reader for the `step-up` flow is separate work. Until it ships, the operator page says to finish the act in the console.

## Checks

| Run | Result |
|---|---|
| `cargo nextest run --workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client` | 7102 passed |
| `cargo nextest run -p vtc-service -p vtc-client` | 3650 passed |
| `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` | clean |
| `cargo test --workspace --doc` | clean |
| `cargo fmt --all -- --check` | clean |

New tests:
- `vtc-service/tests/it/step_up_handoff.rs` runs the full flow: a delegated key is refused, a fresh key reads the handle, the binding is recomputed, the subject approves, and the resend succeeds. It also covers single use and the uniform `notFound`.
- Unit tests cover the link builder and the bridge's `stepUpRequired` result.

title: feat(step-up): approve a step-up from a trigger link, as the person (VTI-LNK-125 – VTI-LNK-131)
body:
## Why

A person's assistant over `vtc-mcp` acts with a key they delegated. That key can redeem a VTC step-up but never make one. Since OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#2490, the community refuses such a party with a single-use handle, and the party shows the person a `step-up` link (trustoverip/dtgwg-vti-spec#106). This PR is the wallet's reader for that link.

## What

- **Core**
  - Pins `auth/step-up/requests/show/0.1` and adds the `step-up` flow with its four reasons.
  - `vtc/step-up-handoff.ts` reads the step-up from a fresh key with the handle.
  - It checks that the request inside the reply was signed by the community, is addressed to its subject, is unexpired, and is bound to the operation returned (VTI-LNK-130).
- **Extension**
  - `step-up-flows.ts` runs in the offscreen document. It reads a step-up only for a community the wallet holds an identity at, and checks that the subject is one of them. It sends the answer, signed by the agent as the subject, to the community directly (VTI-LNK-131).
  - The background reuses `approveStepUp`'s check, approver prompt and signature.
  - The prompt shows the identity from the wallet's record. It labels the community's reason as signed by the community.
- **Entry points**
  - A paste field in the popup, accepted from extension pages only.
  - A click on a page, which `handleTriggerLink` now routes away from the sign-in window.
  - The outcome is shown as a notification, because the popup closes when the prompt opens.
- **CLAUDE.md** gains a section on the flow and what breaks it.

## Checks

| Run | Result |
|---|---|
| `npm run lint` | clean |
| `npm run build` | MV3 bundles built |
| `npm test` | every workspace green |

New tests:
- `core/tests/vtc.step-up-handoff.mjs`, 7 tests.
- `extension/tests/step-up-flows.test.mts`, 7 tests.

Two existing tests changed. The parser's unknown-flow example now uses another flow name. The task-surface census gains an entry for the read, because it goes to the VTC, not the VTA.

Not yet run live against a community.

title: feat(vtc): a holder shows a badge award outside the community — share, unshare, the verification location and the baked picture (VTI-BDG-070, 071)
body:
feat(vtc): a holder shows a badge award outside the community — share, unshare, the verification location and the baked picture (VTI-BDG-070, 071)

Serves `vtc/badges/awards/share/0.1` and `unshare/0.1` (pinned in #2487) and
answers the holder's own awards on `vtc/badges/show/0.1` (`myAwards`,
trust-tasks-tf #1057, refreshed here).

Sharing is the holder's own choice, award by award, for a badge marked
`shareableOutside`:

- `badges::share`: a 256-bit token generated for the share and derived from
  nothing (`bshare:<token>` -> award, `Award.shared` with the locations and
  `since`); a repeat share answers the same locations; `unshare` discards the
  token, revokes nothing, and a later share answers new ones.
- What is served is the holder's credential exactly as issued: each time
  `credential::issue` signs one in the outside regime it is kept at
  `bcred:<badge>:<entry>`, so a repeat award or a renewal is served at the same
  location (share item 10). A holder whose credential predates that is issued
  it again on their first share (outside the lock, as every issue is).
- `GET /badges/shared/<token>`: the credential (`application/vc+ld+json`) to a
  verifier; to a browser, a page saying what the community verifies of it
  (issued by it, in its validity period, its slot in the community's
  revocation list clear), with its own CSP. `GET .../image.png`: the badge's
  picture as a PNG with the credential baked into an `iTXt` chunk
  (`openbadgecredential`, Open Badges 3.0 baking). Unauthenticated,
  parent-root, let through the host-surface gate; neither names another
  holder or a count (VTI-BDG-071).
- A share ends with `unshare`, a take-back (`awards/revoke`), retiring the badge
  and the holder's departure (`badges::on_departure`); `share::resolve`
  re-checks the award, the token and the badge on every request, so a stopped
  share answers the same `404` as a token never issued.
- Refusals as declared: `badgesOff`, `notFound` (unknown, another's and not
  accepted alike), `notShareable` (`insideOnly` | `kudos` | `retired`),
  `publicLocationUnavailable` (no `public_url`).
- `settle_after_revoke`'s re-issue is factored out as `reissue`, which now
  re-reads each award under the badges lock before recording the credential on
  it, so it never writes back a stale award (and its share) over a newer one.

Portal: on a badge the member holds that may be shown outside, "Show it outside
the community" lists their awards, each with Share outside, then the link to
check it, the picture with the credential inside, and Stop sharing. OpenAPI
wrappers `BadgesAwards{Share,Unshare}01*`, `openapi.json` and `wire.ts`
regenerated; both URIs in the manifest and the dispatched-URI list.

`png` becomes a direct dependency (the version `image` already builds on).

Tests: three integration tests (the share flow through every ending,
re-issue on a share without a kept credential, every declared refusal), the
token, location and baking unit tests, and two portal tests. Docs: the badges
operator guide (Showing an award outside), the design note and the crate guide.

title: Let a provisioner create contexts beneath its own without administrat…
body:
…ive authority: the additive context-create capability (VTI-CTX-026 – VTI-CTX-028)

A process that mints a context for each software agent it manages sits on a host that faces the network, so it should not hold the administrative role: an administrator of a context can write access control entries for it, and a compromise of the process would then rewrite everything it created. Creating a context is the one power it needs.

VTI-CTX-020 already requires act authority covering the parent, and VTI-ACL-033 already defines an additive capability, so this adds no new mechanism. It registers one capability and states what it confers:

- VTI-CTX-026: an entry holding `context-create` may create a context beneath one its act scope covers, whatever its role, meeting the same creation requirements as any other creator.
- VTI-CTX-027: it never permits a root context or one outside the entry's act scope, confers nothing else, and writes no access control entry for the creator, so authority cannot accumulate one context at a time. Consistent with VTI-VTA-032.
- VTI-CTX-028: it may name a covered context's primary DID, only while that context has none and only to an identifier the context's own keys control; changing or clearing it stays an administrator's act. A context with no identity can be issued as nothing, so without this a creator would need an administrator to finish every context it makes.

Appendix C.2 gains the `context-create` row and the reason it is additive.

The alternative considered, a separate always-available service holding unrestricted act authority that creates contexts on callers' behalf, is recorded in the rationale and rejected: it is a new component whose only purpose is to hold the most powerful grant in the system.

This is a change proposal against the requirements. It is deliberately not a divergence-register entry, and records nothing about any implementation.

title: trust-tasks-rs-v0.37.9
body:
### Added

- **vtc/badges**: Show answers the caller's own awards (myAwards), so a holder can share one ([#1057](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1057))

* feat(vtc/badges): show answers the caller's own awards (myAwards), so a holder can share one

  vtc/badges/awards/share and unshare ([#1054](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1054)) name an award, but no read answered a holder their own accepted award identifiers for a community badge: mine/list carries badges, show only myCount. vtc/badges/show/0.1#response gains the optional myAwards - the caller's own accepted awards of the badge, newest first, each with its shared - and conformance item 4 says so. Additive, on a draft.

- **auth/step-up**: Requests/show — the subject's wallet fetches a step-up refused to a delegated producer (auth/step-up/requests/show/0.1) ([#1056](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1056))

A relying party that refuses an operation until its subject steps up carries
  the request inline in the refusal (approve-request/0.5, Inline delivery). That
  only works when the producer of the operation can gather the evidence itself.
  A process acting with a key the subject delegated to it — an assistant, an
  automation — can redeem a recorded step-up but never make one. It cannot
  forward the inline request to the subject's wallet either, because the inline
  request carries no proof.

  This adds a hand-off by reference. Beside the inline request, the relying
  party MAY carry `details.stepUpHandoff` (`$defs.Handoff`): a single-use handle
  of at least 128 bits, its expiry and this task's Type URI. The person's
  approver agent sends the handle and receives two things:

  - the relying party's own signed approve-request/0.5, addressed to the
    subject, with the same challenge and binding as the inline request;
  - the operation the step-up is bound to, exactly as received.

  The agent verifies the proof and shows the operation itself. It recomputes the
  binding where it knows the construction. It then answers with approve-response
  0.7, signed by the subject's own DID, directly to the relying party. The
  producer resends the identical operation, and the recorded step-up is redeemed.

  A handle is answered at most once, atomically. Unknown, spent, expired and
  settled handles all return `notFound`. Reading a handle is never part of an
  approval, so a party that sees the handle can spend the read but cannot
  approve.

title: feat(auth/step-up): requests/show — the subject's wallet fetches a step-up refused to a delegated producer (auth/step-up/requests/show/0.1)
body:
## Why

A step-up refusal carries its request inline (`approve-request/0.5`, *Inline delivery*). That works only when the operation's producer can gather the evidence itself.

A producer acting with a **delegated** key cannot. Examples are an AI assistant over an MCP bridge, or an automation. It can redeem a recorded step-up but never make one. It also cannot hand the inline request to the person's wallet, because the inline request carries no proof.

## What

A new task, `auth/step-up/requests/show/0.1`.

- **The hand-off.** Beside `details.stepUpRequest`, the relying party MAY carry `details.stepUpHandoff` (`$defs.Handoff`). It holds a single-use handle of at least 128 bits, an `expiresAt`, and this task's Type URI.
- **The read.** The person's approver agent sends the handle. It receives the relying party's own **signed** `approve-request/0.5`, addressed to the subject, with the same challenge and `boundTo`. It also receives the operation, exactly as received.
- **The answer.** The agent verifies the proof and shows the operation, not only the reason. It recomputes `boundTo` where it knows the construction. It answers with `approve-response/0.7`, signed by the subject's DID, directly to the relying party.
- **The redeem.** The producer resends the identical operation, and the recorded step-up is redeemed. Nothing about redeeming changes.

A handle is answered at most once, atomically. Unknown, spent, expired and settled handles all return the single code `notFound`. Reading a handle is never part of an approval.

## Checks

- `npm run validate` and `npm run build` are clean for this spec.
- All four bindings were regenerated. `npm run check-bindings` reports that all agree.
- `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --all-features --test conformance` passed 3785 tests.

## Follow-up

The VTI specification will name the trigger-link flow that carries the handle to the wallet (`/vti/flow/step-up/0.1`, in the links chapter). VTI will then implement it in the VTC, the browser plugin and `vtc-mcp`.

body:
feat(auth/step-up): requests/show — the subject's wallet fetches a step-up refused to a delegated producer (auth/step-up/requests/show/0.1) (#1056)

A relying party that refuses an operation until its subject steps up carries
the request inline in the refusal (approve-request/0.5, Inline delivery). That
only works when the producer of the operation can gather the evidence itself.
A process acting with a key the subject delegated to it — an assistant, an
automation — can redeem a recorded step-up but never make one. It cannot
forward the inline request to the subject's wallet either, because the inline
request carries no proof.

This adds a hand-off by reference. Beside the inline request, the relying
party MAY carry `details.stepUpHandoff` (`$defs.Handoff`): a single-use handle
of at least 128 bits, its expiry and this task's Type URI. The person's
approver agent sends the handle and receives two things:

- the relying party's own signed approve-request/0.5, addressed to the
  subject, with the same challenge and binding as the inline request;
- the operation the step-up is bound to, exactly as received.

The agent verifies the proof and shows the operation itself. It recomputes the
binding where it knows the construction. It then answers with approve-response
0.7, signed by the subject's own DID, directly to the relying party. The
producer resends the identical operation, and the recorded step-up is redeemed.

A handle is answered at most once, atomically. Unknown, spent, expired and
settled handles all return `notFound`. Reading a handle is never part of an
approval, so a party that sees the handle can spend the read but cannot
approve.
