title: vtc-service-v0.17.1
body:
### Added

- **vtc**: List the trusted ballot boxes, and choose one in the manifest builder ([#2370](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2370))

Pins and serves vtc/elections/ballot-boxes/list/0.1 (trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#998):
  an elections manager reads the voting services the community trusts (VTI-VOT-082), each
  with the operator and sameOperator that members are told when an election names it
  (VTI-VOT-090). The answer is read from the same live [voting] configuration create checks
  ballotBox against, so the two cannot disagree; a holder without vtc.elections.manage is
  refused with permissionDenied (VTI-VOT-080).

  - vtc-service: the handler (behind `voting`), the spine registration, a conformance
    witness, and the proof census entry (the specification recommends a proof; the
    capability check refuses an unsigned caller regardless).
  - vtc-client: `elections_ballot_boxes`.
  - cnm: `cnm elections ballot-boxes`, and the ballotBoxNotTrusted fix now points at it.
  - Console: the manifest builder's ballot-box field is a choice from the list, noting when
    the community's own operator runs the box; "Another DID…" keeps typing available, and a
    VTC that does not serve the task falls back to the typed field. A typed DID the list
    does not hold is flagged before create, since create would refuse it.

- **vtc**: Vote from the member portal through the member's wallet ([#2367](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2367))

The member portal gains an Elections page (`#/elections`,
  `#/elections/<electionId>`): the elections the roll admits the member to,
  each with its questions, schedule and disclosure (VTI-VOT-090), and buttons
  to take a ticket and to vote.

  Everything goes through the member's wallet (`window.vtaWallet.elections`,
  OpenVTC/vta-browser-plugin#404), never the portal key and never a portal
  route. The portal is the community's own code and knows who is signed in,
  and the community is never trusted to learn how anyone voted (VTI-VOT-001),
  so the ballot is filled in the wallet's own window, the member's VTA builds
  and signs the cast under a key made for that cast alone, and the wallet
  sends it to the ballot box itself after a random pause. After a vote the
  page learns only that the wallet's window closed, and whether a ticket had
  to be taken first — never whether a vote was cast. Voting with no ticket
  held takes one and stops, so ticket and cast are apart in time.

  No server change: the reads and the ticket request are the member's VTA's
  `vta/pcs/voter/{read,register}` documents, which the community already
  serves.

- **cnm**: Offline election manifest init and check ([#2365](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2365))

`cnm elections manifest init --ballot-box <DID>` writes a starting manifest
  for the community (one yes/no question, open voting by its members for a
  week from tomorrow); `cnm elections manifest check <file>` checks one as the
  community will and prints its digest. Neither opens a session: the
  community's DID comes from --vtc-did or the profile.

  check validates against the pinned vtc/elections/create/0.3 schema, then
  runs vti_voting::rules::check_new_manifest, a new shared entry point for
  everything a community checks that needs only the manifest and the clock:
  the current 0.2 shape, check_manifest's cross-field rules (VTI-VOT-010,
  VTI-VOT-060 – 064) and voting not already closed. The VTC's check_create now
  calls the same function, so the offline check and the community cannot
  drift; a 0.1-shaped manifest is refused by name at create instead of as a
  missing field. What needs the community itself (trusted ballot box,
  VTI-VOT-082; unused identifier) still waits for create.

  An invalidManifest refusal from create now suggests the offline check.

- **vtc**: Guided election manifest builder in the admin console ([#2364](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2364))

New election was a JSON textarea checked only for parsing, seeded with a
  one-question sample. A manifest has fifteen required members, four question
  shapes and rules between fields, and its digest binds every ticket and vote,
  so a mistake found after registration means cancelling and starting again.

  The console now builds it step by step (about, questions, who votes,
  schedule, counting) and ends on a review showing the manifest, a summary
  and the digest computed as the community computes it. As it goes it checks
  what create would refuse with invalidManifest: the schema's bounds, pinned
  to the vendored vtc/elections/create/0.3 bundle by a test, and the
  cross-field rules of vti_voting::rules::check_manifest (VTI-VOT-010,
  VTI-VOT-060 – 064). Create stays disabled until the review is clean; the
  community still re-checks everything.

  A previous election can seed a new one with a fresh identifier and
  schedule. The JSON view is the same value; a manifest carrying something
  the form does not edit stays there rather than being trimmed. The draft is
  kept in the tab until created or discarded.

  Also corrects the unsupportedSecrecy hint, which still said only open
  elections are served.

- **vtc**: Mark the join page's wallet code with data-oob-intent=join ([#2362](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2362))

The join page's trigger link is the sign-in page's, so a browser wallet that
  already signs in to the community signed the person straight in when they
  clicked Join, with no way to join again as a new identity. The code's link now
  carries data-oob-intent="join" on the join page only; the VTA Wallet extension
  reads it and offers a new identity beside signing in. It changes only what the
  wallet offers — the link, the request and the protocol are unchanged.

- **vtc**: Refuse a join submission from a current member at submit ([#2360](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2360))

A join request from a DID already in the community's ACL was accepted, queued
  for review, and refused only when an administrator approved it (the admit
  effect's duplicate-ACL guard). The administrator spent a review on a request
  that could never be admitted, and the applicant was never told to sign in.

  submit_inner now refuses it before anything is stored, answering
  vtc/join-requests/submit:alreadyMember — consumer-minted under SPEC.md §8.5 like
  requestAlreadyOpen, listed in the error-code census, and exported from vta-sdk
  as JOIN_REQUEST_SUBMIT_ERR_ALREADY_MEMBER. "Current" means ACL-present, as for
  invitations: a departed member may apply again.



### Fixed

- **vtc**: The Groups page speaks the console's form language ([#2376](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2376))

The Groups screens were written with bare `<label>` wrappers and four
  classes no stylesheet defines (`stack`, `inline-form`, `actions`, `kv`),
  so labels ran inline with their controls, nothing had a consistent gap,
  and every form read as a flat column. They now use the console's `Field`,
  `form-stack`, `form-actions`, `.checkbox` and `table-card` shapes, with
  short fields paired in a new `form-grid`, the lists on a group's page as
  rows with their action on the right, and the collapsible cards
  (settings, delete, where and how identities are published) with a
  styled summary.

  Two defects in the shared stylesheet surfaced on the way and are fixed
  here, so every screen gains from them: an `<input>` with no `type` (most
  of the console's) matched none of the input rules and rendered as the
  browser's default; and a `<details class="card">` ignores `display:
  flex`, so its contents had no gap. The same undefined classes in the
  Directory screen, administrators' notes and the identity cards are
  replaced too, as are `btn` / `danger` button classes elsewhere that
  named nothing (`secondary` / `destructive`).

- **vtc**: The console shows every kind of certified result ([#2375](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2375))

The certified result drew only choice questions, so a text, ranking or
  score question showed as its bare key ("q1") and nothing else. Text
  answers held back below textReleaseThreshold (VTI-VOT-065) looked like a
  missing result rather than a deliberate one.

  Each question is now headed by its text, with option labels; ranking is a
  per-place table, score an average, text the answers once released. A
  withheld text question says how many ballots release it and why it is
  held. The summary pluralises and says what the board's entries are.

- **vtc**: Say plainly what members are told about an election, and what checkpoints are for ([#2373](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2373))

The console's election page described the disclosure and the board
  checkpoints in protocol terms ("Coercion: not resisted", "Heads of the
  ballot box's board"), and the shared-operator warning overstated it: blind
  tickets keep a ballot unlinkable from the data, and the real exposure is
  matching by timing.

  Rewrite each row as what it means for a member, and the checkpoints as
  fingerprints certification checks the final board against.

- **vtc**: The portal says where a member sees their vote ([#2374](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2374))

The wallet now remembers a member's vote and shows it when its ballot
  window is opened again, with a change-vote option where the election
  allows one. The portal page still learns nothing (VTI-VOT-001), so its
  button and the note after a vote say to open the wallet from here to see
  or change the vote.

- **vtc**: The portal's election cards open, whatever the title ([#2372](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2372))

The console's manifest builder starts from `title: ""`, and the portal
  named an election `title ?? electionId`, so an untitled election's only
  link had no text and the card could not be opened. The green stage pill
  read "Take your ticket", which looked like the action but is not one.

  Name an election by its id when its title is empty, give each card an
  explicit link to the election ("Open to take your ticket", "Open to
  vote"), and label the stage "Tickets open".

- **vtc**: Show the join page to a member already signed in to the portal ([#2363](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2363))

The portal checked for a member session before it looked at ?join, so a signed-in
  member who clicked Join landed on their own pages: no code, no wallet, and so
  no way to join again as a separate identity (#2362 / vta-browser-plugin#398 were
  never reached). /members/?join now shows the join page whatever the session,
  saying who is signed in and linking to the member pages; a wallet sign-in from
  it moves the browser on to /members/.

- **admin-ui**: Passkey admin invites sign, and the wallet claim finds a late wallet ([#2359](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2359))

Minting a passkey admin invite failed in the console with "JCS cannot
  encode value of type undefined": the form sent { did: undefined }, and
  the console signs over the JCS form, which refuses an undefined member.
  A wallet invite failed the same way whenever the label was blank, and so
  did regenerating a passkey invite. Optional members are now left out.

  The tests missed it because the signed-post stand-in serialised with
  JSON.stringify, which drops undefined silently; it now canonicalises
  with the signer's JCS first, so the suite refuses what the signer does.

  The install page read the wallet's presence once, at first render, but
  the extension adds its provider as a module script that can run later,
  so a wallet invitation showed no button at all in a browser that has
  the wallet. The page now re-checks for a few seconds and on the wallet's
  lifecycle events, and says what to do when it still cannot see it.

### Added

- **vta-sdk**: Voter tasks in JSON forms that carry signed documents byte for byte ([#2371](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2371))

The typed pcs_voter_* / pcs_vote* methods round-trip through generated
  structs holding timestamps as chrono DateTimes: a manifest published with
  `.000Z` reaches the VTA as `Z`, another manifest with another digest, so
  the ticket is refused (VTI-VOT-001 depends on both sides digesting the same
  manifest). Signed reads and casts coming back are re-serialised the same way.

  Adds pcs_voter_{read,register,accept,receipt}_json and pcs_vote{,_encrypted}_json,
  schema-checked like the typed forms, and notes the hazard on the typed ones.
  pnm drops its private raw dispatch and uses them. A loopback test in
  vta-service pins both: the JSON form sends the manifest as given, the typed
  form rewrites it.

  form rewrites it.



### Fixed

- **pnm**: Carry election documents exactly as received ([#2368](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2368))

`pnm elections` asked the member's VTA through the SDK's typed
  `pcs_voter_*` / `pcs_vote*` wrappers, which round-trip the payload and the
  answer through generated structs holding timestamps as chrono `DateTime`s.
  Two things could change in that round trip:

  - the manifest sent to `voter/register` and `vote`: a manifest the
    community published as `…T00:00:00.000Z` reached the VTA as
    `…T00:00:00Z`, another manifest with another digest, so taking a ticket
    was refused ("your VTA computed another manifest digest");
  - the documents the VTA signed — the member's read, the ticket request,
    the cast — came back re-serialised, no longer necessarily the bytes
    their proofs cover.

  Every voter task now goes through `dispatch_trust_task` with the payload
  and the answer as JSON, so the manifest, the parameters and every signed
  document are carried exactly as received. The community's ticket answer
  reaches `voter/accept` without its `ext`, as that task requires.

  Found while building the same flow in OpenVTC (OpenVTC/openvtc#514).

title: vti-common-v0.53.1
body:
### Added

- **voting-service**: GET /health and /health/ready ([#2366](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2366))

The voting service served only `POST /trust-tasks`, so an operator had
  no health path, and nothing showed whether the mediator session —
  how communities register, close and cancel elections — was up.

  - `vti_common::host_session::supervise_reporting`: `supervise`, also
    reporting on a `watch` whether the identity is reachable through its
    mediator. True only while a session is served and its socket reports
    `ConnState::Connected`; false again on a socket drop, a lost session,
    or return. Driven by the transport's own state, never latched (R6.2).
    `supervise` is unchanged and delegates to it.
  - `GET /health`: always 200 while serving, with `messaging` in the body.
    For a proxy's upstream check: casts arrive over HTTPS and keep working
    while the mediator is away, so this never pulls the cast door.
  - `GET /health/ready`: 200 only while the mediator session is connected,
    503 otherwise (and always without an `[identity]`). For alerting.

title: vta-sdk-v0.77.1
body:
### Added

- **vta-sdk**: Voter tasks in JSON forms that carry signed documents byte for byte ([#2371](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2371))

The typed pcs_voter_* / pcs_vote* methods round-trip through generated
  structs holding timestamps as chrono DateTimes: a manifest published with
  `.000Z` reaches the VTA as `Z`, another manifest with another digest, so
  the ticket is refused (VTI-VOT-001 depends on both sides digesting the same
  manifest). Signed reads and casts coming back are re-serialised the same way.

  Adds pcs_voter_{read,register,accept,receipt}_json and pcs_vote{,_encrypted}_json,
  schema-checked like the typed forms, and notes the hazard on the typed ones.
  pnm drops its private raw dispatch and uses them. A loopback test in
  vta-service pins both: the JSON form sends the manifest as given, the typed
  form rewrites it.

- **vtc**: Refuse a join submission from a current member at submit ([#2360](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2360))

A join request from a DID already in the community's ACL was accepted, queued
  for review, and refused only when an administrator approved it (the admit
  effect's duplicate-ACL guard). The administrator spent a review on a request
  that could never be admitted, and the applicant was never told to sign in.

  submit_inner now refuses it before anything is stored, answering
  vtc/join-requests/submit:alreadyMember — consumer-minted under SPEC.md §8.5 like
  requestAlreadyOpen, listed in the error-code census, and exported from vta-sdk
  as JOIN_REQUEST_SUBMIT_ERR_ALREADY_MEMBER. "Current" means ACL-present, as for
  invitations: a departed member may apply again.

body:
### Added

- **voting**: TextReleaseThreshold may be as low as 1, disclosed below 10 (voting/_shared/0.3) ([#1002](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/1002))

* spec(voting): textReleaseThreshold may be as low as 1, disclosed below 10 (voting/_shared/0.3)

  VTI-VOT-065 now lets an election release text answers from a threshold of
  1: it MUST be at least 1 and SHOULD be at least 10, and below 10 the
  disclosure a member is shown before requesting a ticket MUST say so and
  that a written answer may identify its author (VTI-VOT-090). Small
  communities and surveys need written answers; the risk is disclosed rather
  than forbidden.

  voting/_shared/0.3 is 0.2 with Manifest.textReleaseThreshold minimum 1.
  Every task whose schema carries the Manifest gets a new version pinned to
  it: voting/election/register/0.3, voting/election/show/0.3,
  vta/pcs/trustee/{deal/0.4, enrol/0.3, justify/0.4, keys/0.4},
  vta/pcs/vote/0.3, vta/pcs/vote-encrypted/0.4, vta/pcs/voter/register/0.3,
  vtc/elections/create/0.4 and vtc/elections/show/0.3. The two signed reads
  that name a show version on the wire move with it: vta/pcs/trustee/read/0.3
  and vta/pcs/voter/read/0.3. Prose references in current specs follow.

What merging does, per registry (all in `publish.yml`, each keyed on "this
version is not published yet"):

- **crates.io** — `release-plz-release` tags `<crate>-v<version>`, publishes in
  dependency order and creates a GitHub Release per crate. Bump levels come from
  the commit subjects.
- **npm** — `publish-npm` publishes with OIDC provenance and tags
  `<prefix>-v<version>`.
- **Go** — `publish-go` builds, vets and tests, then pushes the tag, which *is*
  the publication. **Irreversible**: proxy.golang.org never forgets a tag.
- **pub.dev** — `tag-dart` verifies against the *published* core and pushes the
  tag; `publish-dart.yml` publishes from it.

Every bump follows the commit subjects; an undeclared API break is refused on its
pull request by that language's API compatibility check (`rs`, `ts`, `go` and
`Dart API compatibility`).

This branch is regenerated from `main` on every push, so do not commit to it —
edits are force-pushed away. See RELEASING.md.

body:
Bumps [minimatch](https://github.com/isaacs/minimatch) from 10.2.6 to 11.0.1.
Changelog

Sourced from minimatch's changelog.

change log

11.0

  • Match each path portion with Matcher from @isaacs/nonrecursive-glob-match, in place of a RegExp. Items in Minimatch.set are now strings, Matcher objects, or GLOBSTAR.
  • Remove makeRe(), Minimatch#regexp, and the MMRegExp type.
  • Remove the AST class.
  • Remove the maxExtglobRecursion option.
  • An empty path portion, such as the last one in a/b/, only matches an empty pattern portion. So a/b/ no longer matches a/b/?(x) or a/b/*(x), the same as a/b/*.
  • Add the normalize option, to normalize unicode in the pattern and in each portion of the tested path.
  • Remove the debug option and the debug() method.
  • Remove the matchOne(), slashSplit(), and levelTwoFileOptimize() methods. They are internal now.
  • Fix patterns with more than one ** and sections of different lengths between them, such as **/a/b/c/**/d/**, which failed to match some paths since 10.2.3.
  • Fix partial matching of patterns with **, which since 10.2.3 matched some paths under a dot portion that ** can not walk, and did not match some paths that end in the pattern's last portion.
  • partial matching of patterns with many ** no longer takes exponential time.
  • On Windows, a .. no longer removes the drive letter, or the host and share of a UNC path, at the start of a pattern or (at optimization level 2) a path. So C:/a/../../x no longer matches x or /x.
  • On Windows, compare the host and share of UNC paths like //host/share/... case-insensitively, the same as drive letters.
  • On Windows, long UNC paths like //?/UNC/host/share/... match //host/share/... and vice versa, the same as //?/c:/... and c:/....
  • At optimization level 2, stop splitting **/.. portions once there are braceExpandMax patterns, and do not dedupe sets of more than 1000 patterns. Before, a short pattern could take minutes to compile.
  • minimatch() keeps the 256 Minimatch objects that it used most recently, so it does not compile the same pattern again.
  • Faster to compile brace patterns that make rows that are merged, such as **/*.{png,jpg,gif}, because the Matchers for the rows that are merged are not made.

title: fix(vtc): the Groups page speaks the console's form language
body:
## What

The console's Groups screens (list, create form, a group's page) were written with bare `<label>` wrappers and four classes no stylesheet defines (`stack`, `inline-form`, `actions`, `kv`). Labels ran inline with their controls ("Name" and "Description" on one line), nothing had a consistent gap, and every form was a flat full-width column.

They now use the console's own form language: `Field`, `form-stack`, `form-actions`, `.checkbox`, `table-card`, `EmptyState`, `DidText`. Short fields pair up in a new shared `form-grid`; the lists on a group's page (requests, managers, bound rooms, what it gives) are rows with their action on the right; the collapsible cards (Settings, Delete, and the two identity cards) get a styled summary.

## Shared fixes that surfaced

- `input` with no `type` attribute (167 of them across the console) matched none of the input rules and rendered as the browser's default. The selector list now includes `input:not([type])` and `input[type="date"]`.
- `<details class="card">` ignores `display: flex`, so its contents had no gap. It is `display: block` with margins now.
- `fieldset.field` / `fieldset.form-stack` drop the browser's box; `legend.field-label` is the group's label.

## Carried through

The same undefined classes in the Directory screen, administrators' notes and the identity cards are replaced; `btn` / `danger` button classes elsewhere (invitations, recognition, elections, step-up cards) that named nothing become `secondary` / `destructive`.

The member portal (`src/members/*`) has its own stylesheet and is untouched.

## Checks

- `tsc -b --noEmit`, `npm run wire:check`: clean
- `vitest run`: 116 files, 1397 tests pass
- Rendered through the test harness and screenshotted in headless Chrome to check the layout by eye.

title: feat(codegen): superseded and retired spec versions are deprecated in every library, and withdrawn ones leave them in a quarterly batch
body:
The registry side of trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec#33 ("Superseded and Withdrawn Versions"). Every spec version ever published was generated into all four libraries forever — 1,125 versions, an 86 MB Rust tree — and none could be dropped without a breaking release.

**Deprecated.** A version is deprecated when it is `retired`, or superseded: a later version of its slug is live at an equal or higher maturity. All four generators — each implementing the rule independently, as CLAUDE.md requires — give every module a constant (`DEPRECATION` in Rust and TS, `Deprecation` in Go, `deprecation` in Dart) that is "none" or a byte-exact note (`superseded by acl/grant/0.2`, `retired; use …`, `retired`), and mark a deprecated version's root types `#[deprecated]` / `@deprecated` / `// Deprecated:` / `@Deprecated`. 427 versions are deprecated today. That is a warning for a consumer, not a break.

**Withdrawn.** A new `status: withdrawn` (meta-schema, build, lints, website). A withdrawn version is generated nowhere. `scripts/withdraw-due.mjs` (`npm run withdraw-due`) flips every version superseded or retired for 90 days, dated from git history, and adds a `supersededBy`; `.github/workflows/withdraw.yml` runs it on the first day of each quarter, regenerates the libraries and opens ONE pull request — the quarter's single breaking release for removals. Dry runs: 168 versions due on 2027-01-01, 427 on 2027-04-01.

**Verified.** `check-bindings` derives the rule a fifth time and holds all four libraries to it: no withdrawn version generated anywhere, the same deprecation note in all four. title: feat(vault)!: vault/credentials/get 0.2 returns an SD-JWT or an mdoc, not only a JSON object
body:
`vault/credentials/get/0.1` answers with `credential`, which must be a JSON object. So a maintainer holding an SD-JWT VC (a compact string) or an mdoc (CBOR) has no conforming answer. It can't return the body as stored, and turning it into an object would destroy the proof the body carries. The VTA hits this today: `get` fails for every SD-JWT credential in the vault.

**0.2** returns the body the same way `receive/0.1` accepts it:
- `credential` for a JSON object (`ldp_vc`), or `credentialBase64` (base64url, no padding) for anything else. Exactly one of the two.
- `format` is required. It is an OpenID4VC format identifier (`ldp_vc`, `dc+sd-jwt`, `mso_mdoc`, `jwt_vc_json`), so a consumer reads the body without sniffing it.
- An SD-JWT is returned with all its disclosures. Selective disclosure stays `present`'s job.
- The request is unchanged.

**Other changes:**
- 0.1 is `retired`, with `supersededBy: vault/credentials/get/0.2`.
- `fix-stale-references` moved the references to 0.1 in present, query, and `vta/witness/{accept,list}/0.2` onto 0.2.
- Rust, TS, Go and Dart bindings are regenerated. The generated response is an untagged enum, the same shape as `receive/0.1`'s payload.

Breaking (`!`): it adds a new spec version and retires 0.1.

**Checks:** `npm run validate` and `check-bindings` pass, and the trust-tasks-rs vault conformance tests pass 67/67.

title: fix(codegen)!: model an anyOf of required members as optional fields, not an untagged enum
body:
## The defect

When a payload schema says "at least one of these members" with an `anyOf` whose branches are only `{"required": [...]}` clauses, typify (0.6) turns it into an untagged enum. It emits one struct variant per branch, and each variant holds only the member its own branch requires, under the object's `deny_unknown_fields`. So a payload carrying **two** of the members matches no variant: each variant rejects the other member as unknown. The schema accepts that payload, but the generated Rust type cannot deserialize it.

For `rooms/keys/chain/0.2` this is the normal case: a member relays the rungs (`links`) together with the floor they came with (`epochFloor`). An implementation (VTI) hit it there.

## The fix

`trust-tasks-codegen` gets a new pass, `drop_anyof_of_required_members`. It works like the existing `desugar_oneof_with_compound_not`: it removes the `anyOf` only from the copy of the schema handed to typify. `generate_one` has already captured the wire schema (`SCHEMA_JSON`) before this pass runs, so `ValidatedPayload::validate_value` and the TS/Go/Dart bindings still enforce "at least one". The members become ordinary optional fields of one struct, which is the shape the other three bindings already have for these schemas.

The pass only touches that exact shape:

- every branch is exactly `{"required": [..]}`
- each named member is declared in the same node's `properties`
- the node is not beneath a `not`

It leaves alone the `anyOf`s in `acl/list`'s `dependentSchemas`, in `persona/contact/*/put`'s `oneOf` branches, and in every `not` (the `oneOf` exclusion idiom). The doc comment records why, what was tried (expanding to a `oneOf` over every non-empty subset: 2ⁿ − 1 variants), and what is lost (the compile-time statement of the constraint).

No spec text or schema changes. The specs are right; the generated Rust type was wrong.

## Affected generated types

A scan of every `specs/**/*.schema.json` for an `anyOf` of bare `required` branches, at any depth including `$defs`, found exactly these four object schemas. Regenerating changes only these four modules:

| Type | Members |
|---|---|
| `trust_tasks_rs::specs::rooms::keys::chain::v0_2::Payload` | `links` / `epochFloor` |
| `trust_tasks_rs::specs::rooms::records::curate::v0_1::Payload` | `status` / `pinned` |
| `trust_tasks_rs::specs::rooms::keys::profile::write::v0_1::Payload` | `profile` / `clear` |
| `trust_tasks_rs::specs::vtc::directory::notes::append::v0_1::Payload` | `text` / `redacts` |

`rooms/keys/profile/write/0.1` is *exactly* one, not at least one. Its schema also has `dependentSchemas: {clear: {not: {required: [profile]}}}`, which the old enum happened to encode. The struct now deserializes both members together, and the wire schema refuses that combination. A new test pins this.

## ⚠️ API break (`trust-tasks-rs`)

Each of the four `Payload` types changes from an untagged `enum` (`Variant0 { .. }`, `Variant1 { .. }`) to a `struct` with every member of the clause optional. On `chain/0.2`, `links` is a `Vec<EpochLink>` that is skipped when empty, as typify renders an optional array. Code that matched on the variants, or built them, must move to field access and `Payload::builder()`. A value with none of the members now compiles and is refused by `validate_value`, as in the other bindings. Hence the `!`.

## Tests

- **Codegen unit tests** (`drop_anyof_tests`): the pass drops the defect's own shape and recurses into `definitions`. It declines on a richer branch, on an undeclared member, on a node without `properties` (`dependentSchemas` / `oneOf` branch), and beneath a `not`.
- **`trust-tasks-rs/tests/anyof_required_members.rs`**: these tests sit behind the `rooms` / `vtc` features, with the validation tests also behind `validate`.
  - A `chain/0.2` payload with both `links` and `epochFloor` round-trips. So do a `curate` payload with both `status` and `pinned` and a `notes/append` payload with both `text` and `redacts`.
  - Each type still fails `validate_value` when none of the members is present.
  - `profile/write` with both members is refused.

## Checks run locally

- `cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen && cargo fmt --all`: the diff is the four modules above.
- TS, Go and Dart regeneration: no drift.
- `npm run check-bindings`: all agree.
- `check-enum-append-only.mjs`: OK.
- `cargo fmt --check`: OK.
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings`, with default features and with `--all-features`: OK.
- `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --no-default-features --features {acl,vault,keys} --all-targets`: OK.
- `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --features validate --all-targets`: OK.
- `cargo test --workspace --all-targets`: OK.
- `cargo doc --workspace --no-deps --all-features` with `-D warnings`: OK.
- `cargo package -p trust-tasks-rs --features validate`: OK.

title: feat(vtc/storage): vtc/storage/configs/retire 0.2 — refuse while a migration targets the config
body:
## The gap

`vtc/storage/configs/retire/0.1` refuses only `roomsAssigned` and `isDefault`. `vtc/rooms/storage/migrate/0.2` fixes a migration's `toConfig` when it is approved and **keeps it** if the room is reassigned (item 9). A migration can also sit `queued` or `paused` for a long time.

So: start moving room R onto config X, reassign R to Y, then retire X. X now has no rooms assigned, so 0.1 accepts, and X goes `draining`/`retired`. The move into X can never finish. It pauses with cause `destination` and retries forever, and no specification gives it a way out. VTI hit this and chose not to invent a fix.

## The rule (0.2)

- New task error code **`vtc/storage/configs/retire:migrationsInbound`** (`retryable: false`, `details.migrations` integer ≥ 1, detailsSchema shaped like `roomsAssigned`'s).
- **Conformance item 3:** the community MUST refuse while any migration whose `toConfig` is the config is `queued`, `running` or `paused`. `complete`/`failed` migrations don't count, and neither do migrations *off* the config (the draining step). For a retirement parked for consent, the community MUST run the check again when the parked action executes. It MUST also do the check and the state change as one step with respect to a migration starting. The Authorization text now names item 3 among the checks that re-run.
- **`retryable: false`**, as for `roomsAssigned`. The condition clears only when the migrations finish, which takes hours or days and can't be timed with `retryAfter`. A bit-for-bit retry is a document the community has already accepted (SPEC §7.2 item 11, §8.4). The remedy is a new request.
- **Converse order** (a migrate onto X approved while X's retire is parked): no new rule needed. A non-normative paragraph explains why: migrate 0.2 item 1 (`configNotActive`, re-checked at execution), retire item 2 (`roomsAssigned`) and assign's refusal of a non-active config cover it.
- **Changes from 0.1** section with a Compatibility paragraph. 0.1 stays published. A community serving 0.1 beside 0.2 SHOULD apply the same refusal to a 0.1 request. It reports with the same slug-namespaced code, which SPEC §8.5 lets a consumer emit for an invariant the version did not enumerate. A 0.1 producer that doesn't recognise the code falls back to `taskFailed`.
- Request and response schemas are unchanged from 0.1 (only `$id`). Invalid examples are carried over. Bindings for all four languages are regenerated.

## Checks run locally

`npm run build`, `npm run check-bindings`, codegen + TS/Go/Dart drift (clean after regeneration on current `main`, including #910), `test:infra`, `check-enum-append-only`, `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --features validate --all-targets`, retire conformance tests, `tsc --noEmit`, TS `npm test` + smoke, `go build/vet/gofmt/test`, `dart analyze --fatal-infos` + `dart test`.

title: feat(rooms): rooms/keys/act 0.8 — records prune and retention set
body:
## What

A new version, `rooms/keys/act/0.8`, that adds three rows' worth of types to act's closed table:

| `type` (request) | Action | Presentation inserted |
|---|---|---|
| `rooms/records/retention/set/0.1` | `admin` | yes |
| `rooms/records/prune/0.1`, `rooms/records/prune/0.2` | `admin` | yes |

Nothing else in the task changes. The request and response schemas are 0.7's (only `$id` moves, and the `type` pattern already admits `rooms/*`), and no error code is added. 0.8 is made the way 0.7 was made from 0.6: frontmatter version, a **Changes from 0.7** section (0.7's "Changes from 0.6" moves into the version history under *Status of this Document*), the two table rows, `related`, and the examples' `type`. Bindings regenerated for Rust, TypeScript, Go and Dart.

## Why

The table is closed (Recipient item 1), so a key holder on 0.7 refuses these types with `typeNotActable`. A member who holds `admin` in a room and whose keys their VTA holds can't make either request *as the member*. Their client falls back to `rooms/keys/present` and signs with its own key, so the host records the client key, not the member, as the administrator who changed the retention or pruned the room. Both tasks describe their audit trail (reason, requester, retention applied) as the only record left of what was removed, so a wrong requester there is a real problem. This came up in VTI, where `pnm` can't act as the persona for these.

**Nothing to special-case.** Both types name a room, so the member is resolved by Recipient item 2. The `private`-room same-subject binding is already inserted by Recipient item 4. The REQUIRED `reason` comes from the producer, and Recipient item 6 carries it unaltered. A prune's `dryRun` takes the same presentation, so it rides the same row.

## `rooms/epoch/prune` stays absent, and 0.8 says why

The table section now explains why `rooms/records/prune` may ride `act` and `rooms/epoch/prune` may not. Both take `admin` and both are irreversible, but they are bounded differently:

- **A records prune removes only what the room's record retention already made eligible.** That rule is stated in advance, readable by every member (`rooms/info`), set only by `admin` through `retention/set` (with a reason, kept in the audit trail), and applied by the host with nothing taken from the request. The request picks kinds and timing only, and pinned records are never removed by age. Shortening the retention and then pruning removes more, but only through a rule that was recorded and shown to every member before the prune ran.
- **It leaves the room's keys, and so its ability to read its past, intact.** It removes records from the host, not key material. Copies held by members, agents and mirrors stay readable.
- **It carries a reason and is recorded.** The `RecordPrune` mark is served to every member as `lastPrune`, and the requester is recorded where the tier discloses one. Completed through `act`, that requester is the member.

An epoch prune reaches back to whatever `beforeEpoch` the request names, against no rule set in advance, and it destroys key history. Records sealed under the pruned epochs become unopenable for every later member, every restarted device and every copy held anywhere. That still needs its own task that states its consequences.

0.7's "Deliberately absent" bullet now reads "Pruning *the key chain*…", so the two prunes can't be confused.

## Compatibility

Every type 0.7 completes, 0.8 completes on the same terms, so the table only widens. Because a type that used to be refused is now completed, the wire behaviour changes. That makes this a new version per SPEC §5.2 rather than an in-place edit: a `MINOR` increment. 0.7 remains published.

## Checks run locally

- `npm run build`: 1090 specs validated, all lints 0 non-conforming
- `npm run check-bindings`: Rust/TS/Go/Dart all agree
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`
- `node scripts/check-enum-append-only.mjs`
- `npm run check-dart-packages`, `npm run test:infra`
- `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --no-default-features --features rooms,validate --test conformance -- rooms::keys::act`: 46 passed (including `v0_8`)
- TS: `tsc --noEmit`, `npm test` (83 pass)
- Go: `go build ./...`, `go vet`, `gofmt -l`, `go test ./...`
- Dart: `dart analyze --fatal-infos` on the regenerated `act` libraries

title: chore(deps): clear RUSTSEC-2026-0387 by moving off crypto-bigint 0.5 and onto 0.7.6
body:
cargo deny fails every branch on RUSTSEC-2026-0387 (vulnerability): crypto-bigint has operations meant to be constant-time that are not. The graph carried two copies.

- crypto-bigint 0.7.5 -> 0.7.6, the patched release.
- crypto-bigint 0.5.5 has no patched release in its line. It arrived through the RustCrypto elliptic-curve 0.13 family (k256/p256/p384/p521 0.13), which reached us only through affinidi-crypto 0.2.6. affinidi-crypto 0.2.11 — semver-compatible with our requirement — has moved to the 0.14 family, so updating it (with affinidi-did-resolver-cache-sdk 0.8.43 and affinidi-did-web 0.1.6) removes the whole 0.13 line, crypto-bigint 0.5.5 with it. No advisory ignore is needed.

Lockfile only: no manifest requirement moves, so no published crate's dependency range changes. cargo deny check passes (advisories, bans, licenses, sources).

Tests for the crates that do this crypto pass locally: `trust-tasks-proof`, `trust-tasks-didcomm`, `trust-tasks-didcomm-v1`, `trust-tasks-tsp` and `trust-tasks-https` (0 failures; the ignored tests are the existing network-dependent ones).

title: feat(rooms/owner/group/remove): 0.4 — remove a private room's member from the group
body:
0.2 and 0.3 refused a `private` room with `privateRoom` and sent the owner
to 0.1, which the spec called the way to remove a member of a private room.
0.1 is superseded all the same, so once it is withdrawn no task could take

title: feat(dart): the runtime parses every SPEC §6.1 Type URI form, so third-party specs get extended codes and extends routing
body:
The Dart runtime now reads every Type URI form that SPEC §6.1 allows: the registry form, the path form under any authority (https, `did:web:…/spec/…`), and the URN form. It ports `trust-tasks-rs/src/type_uri.rs`; Go is #950 and TypeScript #951.

It also fixes a bug: `_splitVersion` in `extension.dart` couldn't read the version of a URN-form Type URI. It's replaced by the parser, and a regression test covers it.

**New, additive, from the barrel:** `TypeUri`, which has:
- `parse`/`tryParse`/`pathForm`/`urnForm`/`canonical`;
- `authority`, `isUrn`, `slug`, `major`, `minor`, `variant`;
- `bare`/`withVersion`/`isSameSpecification`.

Plus `TypeUriVariant`, `TypeUriError`, and `TypeUriFormatException` (a `FormatException`).

**Behaviour:**
- **More input accepted:**
  - `slugFromTypeUri`, `extendedCode` and `familyCode` accept any authority. Codes stay `<slug>:<local>`, as in Rust.
  - The capability client's `slugOf` and the HTTPS server's slug filter therefore now also match third-party Type URIs. Both were tested against this core, and both pass: 15/15 and 61/61.
- **Routing stays in its authority:** an `extends` chain is walked under the received authority and form. `readForVersion` routes only within the same specification, and the same slug under another authority answers `unsupportedType`.
- **Stricter, as Rust is:** `slugFromTypeUri` still throws `ArgumentError` on invalid input, but now also on a malformed version or a reserved slug that isn't on the allowlist. A test holds the allowlist to `specs/spec.meta.schema.json`.

**Tests:** format (language 3.3), `dart analyze --fatal-infos` and `dart test` (150/150) pass on stable. The SDK 3.3 floor wasn't run locally; CI covers it.

title: fix(ts): a published shared-component name never changes when a new shape appears
body:
## Problem

`ts API compatibility` fails #925, a purely additive spec change (new spec versions plus `registry/_shared/0.2`):

```
removed: SharedComponents.TrustRecord
changed: RegistryRecordPut_v0_2.TrustRecord   was: interface TrustRecord   now: interface TrustRecord_RegistryV0_1
… (18 in all)
```

The TS generator hoists every cross-file `$def` into `_shared/components.ts` and names each one from scratch on every run. A name with one shape is bare; a name with several qualifies **every** shape with its family and version. So when a new `_shared` version changes a definition, the name that already shipped bare is renamed in every module that exports it. That is a breaking npm release caused by an additive spec change.

The API check only arrived in #923, so this is the first PR to trip over it. About 20 families already have several `_shared` versions, so every future shared-schema bump would hit the same thing.

## Fix

The generator records the name it gives each component in `trust-tasks-ts/component-names.lock.json` (keyed `registry/_shared/0.1/registry.schema.json#/$defs/TrustRecord` → `TrustRecord`) and reuses it:

1. A component with a recorded name keeps it. If two shapes claim one name (an in-place additive edit split a shape), the earliest source file keeps it.
2. Any other component is named by the existing rules. The only change: a bare name that is already taken stays with its owner, and the new shape is the one that gets qualified (`TrustRecord_RegistryV0_2`). A brand-new name with several shapes still qualifies all of them.

With no lock the rules are unchanged, which is how it was seeded: regenerating `main` with this generator produces **no diff under `src/`** (830 names, 212 qualified).

The drift job in `ts.yml` now diffs the lock along with `src/`, so a regeneration that names something new must commit it. The lock sits outside `src/` and is not in the package's `files`, so it is not published.

## Checked

- `npm run build-ts-bindings` on `main`: no `src/` change; a second run is idempotent.
- `trust-tasks-ts` `npm test`: 99 passed.
- `npm run check-bindings`: all four libraries agree.
- Applied to #925's branch, then `PR_TITLE='feat(specs): …' npm run api-compat`: **ok — API compatible with @openvtc/trust-tasks@0.27.5, none removed or changed**. Old modules keep `TrustRecord`; the new 0.2 type is `TrustRecord_RegistryV0_2`, re-exported as `TrustRecord` in the 0.2/0.3 modules.

Go, Dart and Rust emit per-module types, not hoisted ones, and are unaffected. #925 will be rebased onto this once it merges.

title: spec(vta/contexts/delete): 1.1 bounds its acceptance of 1.0 by 1.0's withdrawal
body:
1.1's "A 1.1 consumer **MUST** still accept 1.0 and answer it as 1.0 specifies" reads as an obligation with no end date. It only restates SPEC §5.2 (an implementation at `M.N` MUST accept every `M.K`, `K ≤ N`), and §5.3.3 ends that obligation when the earlier version is withdrawn: a consumer MAY then refuse it with `unsupportedVersion`.

1.1 now states both halves:
- until 1.0 is withdrawn, a 1.1 consumer accepts it and answers it as 1.0 specifies;
- once 1.0 is withdrawn, a consumer MAY refuse it with `unsupportedVersion`, and a producer MUST NOT send it. Producers SHOULD send 1.1 now.

**Why in place, and why only this far.** 1.1 is `draft`, and this is a prose-only edit that touches neither the schema nor the front matter, so SPEC §5.2 has it made in place rather than as a new version. A task specification cannot relax §5.2's backward-acceptance MUST before withdrawal. Only a framework change could do that, and it would go to dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec. 1.0 was superseded on 2026-10-28, so the first withdrawal batch it is due in is 2027-04-01 (`npm run withdraw-due -- --dry --as-of 2027-04-01`).

Checks: `npm run build`, all four libraries regenerated (no drift), `check-bindings`, `check-published-schemas`, `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --features validate --test conformance` (3086 passed).

title: feat(rs): a guarded consumer for Trust Tasks of any type
body:
Fixes #969. ## The gap A consumer that opens a document of any type, routes on `type` and answers an unknown one `unsupportedType` could not be written in Rust: 1. The bindings' `unpack_trust_task::

` / `pack_trust_task::

` required `P: Payload`, so neither `TrustTask` (what `Dispatcher` takes) nor `ErrorResponse` (what it returns) could pass through. 2. `TspConsumer::{receive, consume}` (and the DIDComm consumers) needed a typed `P`, so a routing consumer lost the duplicate-execution record and the freshness bound. ## Design **Loosen the decorative bounds.** No pack/unpack function reads a `Payload` constant; the bound only refused documents. They now take any `Serialize` / `DeserializeOwned` payload, in all three bindings (TSP, DIDComm v2.1, DIDComm v1 `build_message`). The issue's reproduction compiles as written (it is a test). Loosening a bound is not a semver break, so there is no `!`. **`ErrorPayload: Payload`.** `trust-task-error` is a specification like any other (SPEC §8.1). `TYPE_URI` is the version the library **emits**, now one constant, `TRUST_TASK_ERROR_TYPE_URI` (0.6), which `trust_task_error_type_uri()` parses, so the stamp and the routing key cannot differ. check-bindings now reads that constant. The 0.1 snake_case codes still deserialize; a dispatcher routes 0.6 and later versions that extend it, and an older peer's error is read untyped. The constants follow the 0.6 front matter: recipient REQUIRED, proof RECOMMENDED. **`consume_dispatched` and a dispatched path on every consumer.** The guarded pipeline for a `TrustTask` routed by an `AsyncDispatcher`: 1. Item 3: route. `unsupportedType` / `unsupportedVersion` come from the dispatcher's own routing (now one `route` step shared with `dispatch`). Forward routes along a declared extension are pruned as `dispatch` prunes them. 2. The payload must deserialize into the registered `P`, or `malformedRequest`. 3. `consume_inbound`'s body, unchanged in substance: the item-2 schema and `SpecPolicy` come from the registration (`on_async` now records them). Freshness, the §4.8.1 cross-check, proof verification **over the document as received**, and the item-11 record all run. 4. The handler, through `dispatch`, with a context built from the resolved parties. Every refusal in 1–3 happens **before** the record is written, so an unrouteable or malformed document never burns its `id`. `consume_inbound` and `consume_dispatched` call one private `consume_core`, so the two paths cannot drift. `TspConsumer`, `DidcommConsumer` and `DidcommV1Consumer` gain `receive_dispatched` / `consume_dispatched` (plus `receive_from_dispatched` on DIDComm v2.1). These keep each consumer's own record and freshness policy. ### Rejected - **The issue's `AnyPayload` placeholder `TYPE_URI`.** It lies about the type, and anything reading the constant (`enforce_spec_policy`, `extended_code`) would act on it. - **`*_any` duplicate functions in each binding.** They are not needed once the bound is gone, and they double the surface. - **Looking spec policy up by URI inside the consumer** (`schema_index`, or the #974 `type_index`). That fails open for anything the index lacks, and it can disagree with the handler the dispatcher actually picks, especially on a forward route. The dispatcher's registration is the one source of truth for "what this consumer implements". - **Routing inside the handler after the claim.** Every unsupported or malformed arrival would then have been recorded, burning its `id`. ## Other bindings and libraries - **HTTPS:** the server already routes on `type` with its own record and freshness, so there is nothing to add. The client is request/response and typed by design. - **TypeScript, Go, Dart:** there is no dispatcher. Their consume functions take the spec policy as a value and their binding unpack is already untyped, so the caller routes and then calls the consumer's `consume`. Go documents exactly that shape. They answer `unsupportedType` with the runtime's `reject` and pack it; nothing executes, so no record is involved. This is recorded in CLAUDE.md as a deliberate difference. - The synchronous `Dispatcher` gets no guarded path; `AsyncDispatcher` is the one with a context and async handlers. ## API (all additive) - `trust_tasks_rs::consume_dispatched` and `trust_tasks_rs::TRUST_TASK_ERROR_TYPE_URI` - `impl Payload for ErrorPayload` - `receive_dispatched` / `consume_dispatched` on the three binding consumers - Looser bounds on the binding pack/unpack functions ## Tests `trust-tasks-tsp/tests/dispatched.rs` covers: - the issue's reproduction, including sealing the error and reading it back typed - a redelivery executes once - unknown type → `unsupportedType` with no record - other version → `unsupportedVersion` - malformed payload refused before the record - the freshness policy applies - the proof is verified over the received JSON, and a failure leaves no record - the future is `Send` (spawned) The DIDComm v2.1 and v1 `tests/dispatched.rs` cover record and `unsupportedType` on their paths.

title: fix: stamp issuedAt in whole seconds in every library
body:
Fixes #970.

## Cause

`TrustTask::reject_with` / `respond_with` and the dispatchers' error responses stamped `issuedAt` with `Utc::now()`, which chrono serializes at clock precision (nine fractional digits on Linux). TypeScript stamped milliseconds with `toISOString()`. Go (`SystemClock`) and Dart (`systemClock`) already wrote whole seconds.

## What SPEC says

§13.1 item 3: "A full-precision timestamp is a fingerprint". A producer **MAY** round `issuedAt` down while it stays inside the consumer's acceptance window, and the minute or hour is for a specification that states its skew. A whole second is the coarsest value that is safe without knowing the specification, and rounding down never future-dates a document (§7.2 item 13).

## Change

Every instant the framework stamps is now UTC in whole seconds, rounded down (`2026-10-28T05:14:12Z`):

| Library | Stamping sites |
|---|---|
| trust-tasks-rs | new `issued_at_now()`; `reject_with_recipient`, `respond_with`, dispatcher error responses |
| trust-tasks-https | client default `issuedAt`, the server's two fallback error documents |
| trust-tasks-capability-client | built documents, `new_attempt` |
| @openvtc/trust-tasks | new `issuedAtNow()`, default clock of `rejectWith*` / `respondWith` |
| @openvtc/trust-tasks-capability-client | built documents, `newAttempt` (inlined, so the peer range is unchanged) |
| Go, Dart | already whole seconds; now pinned by tests |

Readers are unchanged: every library still accepts any RFC 3339 precision and offset. A received document is never re-stamped, so proof verification and the item-11 digest are unaffected.

## Conformance

There is no normative conformance suite yet (SPEC §17.2), so the statement lives where the four libraries' parity tests live: identical vectors in `trust-tasks-rs/tests/issued_at_precision.rs`, `trust-tasks-ts/test/issued-at.test.ts`, `trust-tasks-go/trusttasks/issued_at_test.go` and `trust-tasks-dart/test/issued_at_test.dart`. Each checks the written form and that 0/1/3/6/9 fractional digits and an offset are all read. CLAUDE.md records the rule.

## Not in scope

The proof packages' default `created` (a Data Integrity proof member, not a framework document member) still follows each signer: TS writes milliseconds unless `.000`, Dart microseconds unless zero, Go whole seconds, and Rust uses `affinidi-data-integrity`. Callers can pass `created` explicitly. Worth a follow-up if the same fingerprint argument should apply there.

## API

Additive only: `trust_tasks_rs::issued_at_now` and `issuedAtNow` in `@openvtc/trust-tasks`. No `!`.

title: spec(vtc/install/claim/passkey): prove possession of the passkey before any authority
body:
A WebAuthn registration under the `none` attestation format, which most
platform passkeys use, signs nothing: it names the key the administrator's
DID is derived from but does not prove the installer holds it. The passkey
install now proves possession before a setup-session token is minted or any
administrator entry is written, whatever the attestation format.

- start's response adds `assertionOptions` (required): request options with
  a second fresh challenge (>=128 bits, distinct from the creation
  challenge, single-use, bound to the registration), no allowCredentials.
- finish's request adds `webauthnAssertion` (required): one
  navigator.credentials.get() assertion by the just-registered credential
  over that challenge. finish verifies it as WebAuthn §7.2 does, against
  the registered key (EdDSA/Ed25519 or ES256/P-256), before consuming the
  token, minting the setup-session token or writing an entry. Refusal:
  new declared code `possessionUnproven`, nothing consumed.
- For an invitation of an additional administrator (the community already
  has one, so vtc/admin/bootstrap answers alreadyBootstrapped), finish
  writes the entry for the derived DID, after the assertion. On a fresh
  community bootstrap writes it from the setup-session token, as before.
- Security & Privacy: possession is proven before any authority is granted.

Tightened in place: both versions are `draft` and unreleased (merged in
#976, held in Release PR #977), so SPEC §5.2's draft allowance applies and
check-published-schemas has no released copy to compare against.
vtc/admin/bootstrap/0.1 is unchanged and keeps working for its other caller,
vtc/install/claim/finish 0.3: the assertion rides in finish, not bootstrap,
because bootstrap never runs for an invited administrator.

VTI note: `vtc admin invite` will have two kinds — `--did X` uses the 0.3
wallet ceremony (token names X); no `--did` is a passkey invite, whose ACL
entry is written from the derived DID at finish (or at bootstrap on a fresh
community).

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

vtc/install/claim/finish/0.3 item 6 made the founder's approver binding wait

bootstrap answers alreadyBootstrapped, so the binding never took effect and

0.1 item 9 already writes an invited administrator's entry at finish. The

unchanged. Prose only; no schema change.

title: feat(vta/dids): method-neutral key-role family, creation and recovery, with per-method profiles
body:
## Summary

#638 scoped key roles to `did:webvh` under `vta/webvh/dids/*`. This PR moves them into a **method-neutral family** under `vta/dids/*`. The family carries every rule that is not method-specific, adds the creation and recovery paths #638 left unwritten, and puts what differs by method into **method profiles**. The normative requirements are in trustoverip/dtgwg-vti-spec#79 (VTI-KEY-*).

### Slugs

| New | Replaces | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `vta/dids/_shared/0.1` (`CONVENTIONS.md`, `key-roles.schema.json`, `method-profiles/`) | `vta/_shared/0.3` | Threat model, roles, custody and protection boundaries, recovery key, approval, authorization, compromise, overlap, audit, `keyRoles`, passkeys, error codes |
| `vta/dids/create/1.0` | *(none: the gap)* | Create a key-role identity from a key-role DID template |
| `vta/dids/update/1.0` | `vta/webvh/dids/update/2.0`, `2.1` | Non-key members and method parameters |
| `vta/dids/keys/{list,add,rotate,retire,revoke}/1.0` | `vta/webvh/dids/keys/*/1.0`, `rotate-keys/2.0` | Key-role operations |
| `vta/dids/recover/1.0` | *(new)* | A replacement VTA takes over an identity whose VTA was lost |

**Why `vta/dids`.** The custodian, and the authority being exercised, belong to the VTA. The method, by contrast, is a property of the identity, so it is a request member (`method`), not a slug segment.

**Why `keys/rotate` and not `rotate-keys`.** Every operation that changes a role set sits under `keys/`. That gives the family one review area, and `vta/dids:*` is the family error namespace.

### Creation path: a key-role DID template, used by a create task

`vta/dids/create/1.0` takes a method, a template name and variables, the method parameters, and a **recovery key**. The template must be `schemaVersion` 3. Version 3 is a new shared version, `vta/_shared/0.9/did-template.schema.json` (0.7 plus `3` and an optional `keyRoles` list of `RoleLayout`s), and is uploaded with the new `vta/did-templates/{create,get,list,update}/3.2`, which declare `extends: "3.1"`. 0.7 is untouched: editing it in place would split the shared `DidTemplate` type in TypeScript, which is a break. A v3 template:

- names **roles, never relationships**;
- has a `document` with **no key members**.

The VTA renders `verificationMethod`, the relationships and `keyRoles` itself, from the layout and the role registry. A template therefore cannot place an operational key in `assertionMethod` — which every built-in v1/v2 template effectively does today. Creation also never accepts a supplied key, key id, keyed document or history to adopt.

The shared definitions use names distinct from `vta/_shared/0.3`'s (`IdentityKeyRole`, `IdentityRoleKey`, `IdentityChangePreview`, `KeyChangeRecord`, …), so no published bare TypeScript name moves and the consumer-side generator stays equivalent.

### Method profiles (`vta/dids/_shared/0.1/method-profiles/`)

**`did:webvh` and `did:scid:vh` — eligible.**
- `update` is `updateKeys` plus `nextKeyHashes`, which always holds `[hash(routine successor), hash(recovery key)]`.
- Every entry moves the update key (`updateKeyRotates: true`) and carries the recovery hash forward.
- A recovery entry reveals the recovery key and commits a fresh one.
- The cache horizon is `ttl` vs the 24 h cap.
- Artefacts are `did.jsonl` and `did-witness.json`. The recovery proof is an `eddsa-jcs-2022` entry proof.
- Update keys are Ed25519 until the method accepts more.
- The parameter schema is `webvh-parameters.schema.json`.

**`did:webs` — ineligible as published.** The derived document puts every `k` key in both `authentication` and `assertionMethod`, and it has no room for `keyRoles` or `revoked`. The profile still states the mapping for when an extension exists:
- `update` is `k`/`kt` plus `n`/`nt`, with weights such that the recovery key alone can rotate and the routine successor alone cannot.
- Role changes are anchored by `ixn`, so they do not rotate the authority.
- `versionId` is `<sn>:<said>`.

**Ineligible by construction:** `did:key`, `did:jwk`, `did:peer`, `did:web`. Each is refused with `vta/dids:methodNotEligible` and `details.missing`.

**Adding a method** means a new profile and parameter schema. It changes no task schema: `DidMethodName` is a pattern, `methodParameters` is validated against the profile, and published artefacts and recovery requests are data.

### Security decisions (each in the conventions, tied to the §1 threat model)

1. **Separation of duty.** Each role is bound to one relationship and kept as separate material under separate custody. `capabilityInvocation` and `capabilityDelegation` are reserved, and no key may be reused across roles, identities or history.
2. **Custody.** `attestation` and `update` keys are **generated**, because a derived key is reproducible from any backup or seed. `operational` and `messaging` keys are **derived**, because they are already exposed to the service and must survive a restore. X25519 is never converted from Ed25519.
3. **Protection boundaries are defined concretely.** Plain, hardened and TEE VTAs are each **one** boundary: hardened store keys derive from the seed, and the enclave holds everything it generates. A second boundary is a second VTA, an offline token, or an HSM or KMS the VTA cannot use.
4. **Recovery key.** Every version commits a **recovery key** held outside the VTA. The VTA carries it forward unchanged and takes it only with a proof of possession over the `previewId`. A one-boundary VTA (every VTA) gets it from the operator and refuses to create an identity without one. This replaces "the committed next key in a different boundary", which no single VTA can satisfy.
5. **Compromise of the change authority.**
   - `keys/revoke role:update` with `scope: key` moves to the routine successor.
   - `scope: boundary` uses the recovery key: the VTA prepares the change and the custodian checks and signs it (`awaitingRecoveryProof`, `RecoverySigningRequest`).
   - Loss of the VTA is handled by `vta/dids/recover`.
6. **Revocation encoding.** A revoked method stays in `verificationMethod`, out of every relationship and `keyRoles`, with the W3C Controlled Identifiers **`revoked`** property set to `compromisedSince`, kept for life. A retirement removes the method. This is better than §7's interim as written: `revoked` becomes the permanent rule, it is reserved for compromise only, and generic Data Integrity verifiers already honour it.
7. **Emergency replacement and re-issue.**
   - A revocation has no overlap and is never blocked.
   - Replacements must not come from paths the compromise exposed, and are generated if the seed may be exposed.
   - An `attestation` revocation returns `followUp` with the status lists to re-sign and the artefacts to re-issue, via `vtc/credentials/reissue`.
8. **Approval.**
   - Every change starts from a VTA-computed preview, and step-up is bound to that `previewId`.
   - A quorum is required to replace the recovery commitment. Revocation is reachable with one approval.
   - Only the approver's own evidence counts. A delegated console key never does (approve-response 0.7, #983), and no node key is ever an approver.
   - The spec states how approval works; the VTI floor sets what is required.
9. **Algorithms.** No silent downgrade: a template's v3 layout mints every algorithm it lists, with no fallback. Proof sets must all verify. A recovery key committed by hash stays unpublished until it is used.
10. **`keyRoles`** is a top-level document member with the term `https://w3id.org/vti#keyRoles` (`@index`). Only the w3id registration stays open.
11. **Passkeys.** These get a new **`authenticator`** role: `authentication` only, on the holder's own identity, never on a VTA/VTC/VTN or integration, WebAuthn assertions only. They are enrolled by `vta/passkey-vms/*`, can be revoked via `keys/revoke`, and are never added or rotated.

### Lifecycle

- **Retired, with `supersededBy` pointing at the new family:** `vta/webvh/dids/keys/{list,add,retire,revoke}/1.0`, `rotate-keys/2.0`, `update/2.0` and `2.1`. `vta/_shared/0.3` carries a retirement notice.
- **`vta/webvh/dids/update/1.0` and `rotate-keys/1.0` stay live** for pre-role DIDs, with a note that a VTA must refuse them for a key-role identity. With the 2.x versions retired, trust-tasks-build's `compute_lifecycles` has no later live version to mark them superseded by. Generated `DEPRECATION`: 1.0 → `None`; 2.x → `retired; use vta/dids/...`.
- **References moved to the new family:** `keys/revoke/0.1`, `keys/export-secret/0.1`, `keys/set-exportability/0.1`, `vtc/credentials/reissue/0.1` and `rooms/owner/anchor/0.1`. These are prose, related-list and description edits only.

### Checks

- All four libraries were regenerated.
- `npm run build` and `npm run check-bindings` pass: all four agree, and every deprecation note matches.
- `check-published-schemas` passes: every released file changed only additively.
- `trust-tasks-ts-gen` equivalence passes, and TS `api-compat` reports no change or removal.
- `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --features validate --all-targets` passes, including 3116 conformance tests.
- `cargo check --workspace --all-targets` with `-D warnings` passes.
- `go build ./...` and `go vet` pass, `dart analyze` is clean, and the TS build and tests pass (126/126).

### Flagged for working-group review

1. **did:webs.** The ineligibility rule is the safe default. Making it eligible needs either (A) a did:webs extension that anchors role keys and keeps key-state keys out of every relationship (recommended), or (B) a VTI-KEY-093 amendment.
2. **did:webvh under VTA compromise.** The routine successor lives in the VTA, so a compromised VTA can drop the recovery commitment. Witness enforcement is a SHOULD. The way a witness learns which hash is the recovery hash (the second element of `nextKeyHashes`) is a profile convention, not did:webvh's.
3. **Mandatory recovery commitment at creation.** This is the safest rule, and a real deployment burden.
4. **`recover` against a VTA that is only unreachable.** That case leaves two VTAs, each believing it holds the identity. The task can only refuse on `versionConflict`.
5. **24 h verifier cache cap.** This is still the VTI proposal.

The PR title has no `!`. This is a spec change, and there is no package API break: 2.x stays generated, now deprecated.

title: feat(auth/step-up/approve-response): 0.7 — the approver's own passkey assertion is evidence on its own
body:
**Problem.** approve-response 0.5 and 0.6 require the approver's framework proof on every answer. 0.6 items 5/1a also count a console key's proof as the proof of the administrator it acts for. `auth/signing-key/enroll/0.2` item 7, however, forbids a delegated key's proof on any approve-response. The two contradict each other, and a web-console administrator, who holds only a delegated console key, has no conforming answer: VTI's console still answers at 0.4, unsigned. enroll/0.2's own reference design (step 2) told the console to answer with 0.6 passkey evidence it cannot produce.

**Decision (maintainer): a delegated console key's proof never counts as the administrator's.** Approval evidence is either the approver's own DID proof (as in 0.6) or a WebAuthn assertion by the approver's own registered passkey, over a challenge bound to the approval.

**0.7:**
- A proof by a delegated key (a console signing key, any key the RP records as acting for another identity) is `subjectMismatch` for every gate. 0.6's console-key clause is gone.
- `webauthn` evidence needs **no proof**. The RP verifies the assertion and requires the passkey to be registered to the document `issuer`, i.e. the approver. With no proof present, it also requires user verification (`userNotVerified`). A credential the RP's policy does not accept for this approver, such as a sign-in passkey once a dedicated step-up passkey exists, is refused as `credentialNotAccepted`.
- **What an unproved answer decides** (consumer 4a): only what the assertion and the RP's own state determine. The decision is `approved`, since a denial still needs the approver's proof. Subject, session and bound operation come from RP state, and the acr comes from the assertion. `grantedAcr` and `ext` are ignored. The pending step-up is taken atomically, because an unproved document's `id` is the sender's to choose and §7.2 item 11 cannot stop a second copy.
- `didSigned`, `approverSigned` and every denial still require the approver's own `assertionMethod` proof. `proofRequirement` becomes `RECOMMENDED` with these per-gate conditions.
- `assertionInvalid` `details.reason` values are lowerCamelCase, adding `userNotVerified` and `credentialNotAccepted`.

Also:
- `auth/signing-key/enroll/0.2` step 2 now answers with 0.7, unsigned, with `identityDid` as `issuer`. Its item 7 already says what 0.7 now says.
- `fix-stale-references` moved prose and description references from 0.6 to 0.7 (description-only changes to released schemas; `check-published-schemas` passes). `approve-request/0.5` no longer says the answer is always signed.

Breaking against 0.6, released as a MINOR under §5.2's draft allowance; 0.6 remains published.

title: feat(vtc/members/role/set): a community role moves with its own task
body:
Adds `vtc/members/role/set/0.1`: an administrator moves a subject's **community** role (`member`, `moderator`, `issuer`, `admin`, `custom:<name>`) with a compare-and-swap on `fromRole`.

**Why.** `acl/change-role/0.1` was the only task that moved a member's community role (member ↔ admin, re-issuing the role credential). `acl/change-role/0.2` moves only the administrative role, so its supersession of 0.1 left that operation without a task. The community role, its role credential and the community's role-change policy belong to the VTC, so they get a VTC task, and `acl/change-role` stays the generic ACL operation.

**What it covers** (the community-role half of what 0.1 did at a VTC):
- **Authority.** The administrative authority follows the role when it is exactly the authority the current community role implies (`admin` → `community-admin`, `moderator` → `moderator`, `issuer` → `credential-officer`, else none). Authority stated on its own with `acl/grant` or `acl/update` 0.2 is kept, and only the community role moves. The response returns the resulting `AclEntry` 0.2, so the outcome is visible.
- **Role credential.** A subject with a member record gets a role VAC at the new role, returned as `roleVac` and delivered best-effort.
- **Checks, in order:** the requester holds `vtc.roles.assign` (`permissionDenied`); no self-move; `notFound`; `roleNotRecognized` / `roleNotAssignable` (`application`); `stateMismatch` (with `currentRole`); the requester covers the entry; a move to the role already held is answered `changed: false`; `delegationExceedsGranter`; `lastRoleAssigner` (the last `vtc.roles.assign` holder, or the consent threshold); `deniedByPolicy`.
- **Holds** follow the VTC family: a re-authentication bound to the document's digest (approve-request/0.5 *Inline delivery*), and a parked move answered with `trust-task-next-step` → `vtc/admin/actions/show/0.3`, executed exactly once after re-checking. These are described as the model, not required (§7.3 item 13).

title: ci: the published-schemas check skips spec.meta.schema.json, which no library compiles
body:
The `published schemas change only additively` check compares every changed `.json` under `specs/`, so it also compares `specs/spec.meta.schema.json` — the front-matter schema, not a payload. #997 fails on it: `knownImplementations` items widen from a string to a string-or-object `oneOf`, which the check reads as a removed `type`/`format`/`pattern`.

That file is compiled into no library. The TS, Go and Dart generators list it in `NOT_PAYLOAD_SCHEMAS`, and `knownImplementations` is read only by the website. A meta-schema change that rejects an existing spec already fails `npm run build`, which validates every spec against it, so nothing is left unguarded.

Checked against #997 merged with this branch: the check passes; without this change it reports the same failure as CI.

title: feat(vtc/elections/ballot-boxes/list): 0.1 reads the community's trusted ballot boxes
body:
## Why

A manifest must name one of the community's trusted voting services in `ballotBox` (VTI-VOT-082). If it doesn't, `vtc/elections/create` refuses with `ballotBoxNotTrusted`. Nothing lets an administrator read that list, so today they have to ask whoever operates the host. As a result, VTI's console manifest builder (OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#2364) can only offer a free-text DID field.

## What

New task **`vtc/elections/ballot-boxes/list/0.1`**:

- **Request:** empty payload (only `ext`).
- **Response:** `{ ballotBoxes: [{ did, operator, sameOperator }] }`, at most 256 entries, in the community's own order. It is empty when the community trusts none.
- **Who:** holders of `vtc.elections.manage` only (VTI-VOT-080). Anyone else gets `permissionDenied`.
- **Conformance:**
  - The list is exactly the one `create` checks against: anything listed is accepted, and anything not listed is refused.
  - `did` is given exactly as `ballotBox` must name it, since `create` compares them verbatim.
  - `operator` and `sameOperator` are exactly what `vtc/elections/show` discloses for an election naming that ballot box (VTI-VOT-090). The administrator choosing one sees what members will be told.
- Read-only (`sideEffects: none`). The list stays host configuration; no task changes it.

## Checks

- `npm run build` / `validate`: 1159 specs valid.
- Rust, TS, Go and Dart bindings regenerated. `check-bindings`: all four agree.
- `check-published-schemas`: nothing released changed.
- `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs --features vtc --test conformance ballot_boxes`: 3 pass.

title: feat(rooms/keys/act): 0.9 completes rooms/records/put/0.4
body:
## Why

#987 published `rooms/records/put/0.4`, which lets an **open** room's record carry a file: its `FileManifest`, including the random per-file key, goes in `cleartext.file`.

Members whose keys are held by their VTA write records through `rooms/keys/act`. That covers the browser plugin and `pnm`. `rooms/keys/act/0.8`'s table is closed (Recipient item 1) and lists `rooms/records/put` only at 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3. A conforming key holder therefore refuses a 0.4 put with `typeNotActable`.

So such a member can upload an open room's blob, because `rooms/blobs/upload/begin/0.2` is in the table, but can never write the record that names it. The blob then sits unreferenced until the host collects it. Without this change, open-room files don't work for anyone whose keys a key holder holds.

## What

- New `specs/rooms/keys/act/0.9`, copied from 0.8. The `rooms/records/put` row gains `0.4`: `write`, presentation inserted, completed exactly as 0.3.
- The key holder neither mints, reads nor checks the file key:
  - the producer mints it (put 0.4 Producer item 7);
  - the host checks the record (Host item 12);
  - the key holder signs what it was handed, unaltered (Recipient item 6).
- The request and response schemas are 0.8's, and no error code is added. Because the table only widens, 0.9 declares `extends: "0.8"`, so no other spec's reference to 0.8 goes stale.
- 0.8's "Changes from 0.7" section moves into the history list as "What 0.8 changed from 0.7". The examples now name `act/0.9` and `put/0.4`.
- All four bindings are regenerated. The older `act` modules change only to carry the superseded note.

## Checks

- `npm run validate`: 1156 specs, 0 stale references; declared extensions checked.
- `npm run check-bindings`: all four agree.
- `npm run check-published-schemas`: clean.
- `cargo build --workspace --all-targets`: builds.

## Follow-on

VTI pins `rooms/records/put/0.4` and `rooms/keys/act/0.9`. Its hosts then serve 0.4 with the open-room file checks, and `pnm` and the browser plugin upload files to open rooms.

title: feat(vtc/admin/invites): create and list 0.2 — passkey invitations, with did optional
body:
vtc/admin/invites/create 0.1 required `did`, so an administrator could invite
only someone who already held a DID in a wallet; a passkey invitation — whose
administrator DID is derived from the passkey registered at
vtc/install/claim/passkey/finish 0.1 — could be issued only by the operator on
the host.

create 0.2:
- `did` is optional. Present: a wallet invitation (claimed with
  vtc/install/claim/{start,finish} 0.3). Absent: a passkey invitation.
- `did`, when present, must begin `did:`.
- Both kinds confer the same authority: an administrator entry with the
  community's full administrative authority, delegated by the inviter,
  labelled with `label`. A wallet invitation writes it now for a DID with no
  entry; a passkey invitation records it with the invitation and
  passkey/finish item 9 writes it for the derived DID.
- A passkey invitation costs what an entry-writing wallet invitation costs
  (the inviter's step-up, another administrator's consent): at its claim no
  administrator is present to authorise it, so issuing it is the grant.
- The response gains a required `kind` (`wallet` | `passkey`);
  `aclEntryCreated` is always false for a passkey invitation.

list 0.2 (with vtc/_shared/0.2/invite): each InviteSummary gains a required
`kind`; a passkey invitation's `targetDid` is absent until it is consumed, then
the derived DID.

revoke is unchanged (it takes only `jti`); its prose now links the 0.2
versions.
