title: Make a governance framework findable from the identifier document and resolve a durable identifier's log from any recorded source (VTI-KEY-052, VTI-KEY-064 to VTI-KEY-067, VTI-VTC-033, VTI-VTC-034, VTI-VTN-006, VTI-VTN-007)
body:
Hello, and thank you for taking a look. This is a **draft** and is very open to comment and revision: the shape, the wording and the open questions listed below are all up for discussion, and I would be glad to change anything that does not fit the group's direction.

**Draft.** Opened for review in context rather than for merge; three judgement items are listed under "What is open" and the text should be read with them in mind. Two commits, 210 added lines across five files, no deletions.

## What this adds

**A governance framework is findable from the identifier document, with a digest a consumer checks (commit 1).** VTI-VTC-030 to VTI-VTC-032 let a governance framework bind a community, and VTI-VTN-002 requires one of a network, but nothing said where a relying party finds it. VTI-KEY-052 gives an identifier document a place to point: a `GovernanceFramework` service whose `serviceEndpoint` is the framework's primary document as [TOIP-GOV] defines that term, with the framework's own `version` label and a `digestMultibase` over the document's bytes in the `DigestMultibase` shape [TRUST-TASKS] defines. The digest is required, and a mismatch is indeterminate rather than a failure. VTI-VTC-033 and VTI-VTN-006 require the reference of a community that has a framework and of every network; VTI-VTC-034 and VTI-VTN-007 keep "found it" apart from "it still governs" (resolving the reference shows what the framework says, never that it currently applies). Governance Considerations item 7 and a new Privacy Considerations item 16 record what the framework's host learns from the fetch and why a consumer should fetch through its usual resolution channel. Appendix F.5 records that no node type publishes the service yet (VTC-033 observed; VTN-006 open).

**A durable identifier's log resolves from any of its recorded sources, and a version behind one already verified is refused (commit 2).** VTI-KEY-162 gives `did:scid` a version floor, a check of a new source against the known ones, and a floor that survives a restart. These are not `did:scid` properties: any durable identifier's log is a hash chain that verifies wherever it is fetched from, and any source can serve a stale copy. VTI-KEY-064 to VTI-KEY-067 state the method-neutral rules of which VTI-KEY-162 is the `did:scid` instance. A log should be published at more than one independently operated source, with the set recorded in the log, which for `did:webvh` is the `watchers` parameter (VTI-KEY-064); every known source being unreachable is indeterminate, not absence (VTI-KEY-065); a version behind one already verified is refused, and the floor persists for every identity the node authorises (VTI-KEY-066); sources that fork make the outcome indeterminate, while a single answering source serving the latest known version is enough under a freshness bound, so the rule does not demand corroboration and does not penalise the publisher who provided a second source (VTI-KEY-067). Security Considerations items 24 and 25 give the reasoning. Appendix F.3 records that neither node type reads `watchers` or keeps a version floor for `did:webvh` (KEY-065 observed; KEY-066 and KEY-067 observed).

Files: `spec/04-identity-keys.md` (+131), `spec/11-vtc.md` (+27), `spec/11a-vtn.md` (+18), `spec/90-considerations.md` (+30), `spec/appendix.md` (+4).

## What is open

1. **Does VTI-KEY-066's persisted floor apply to `did:webvh`?** As written, VTI-KEY-066 carries VTI-KEY-162's "persist the latest verified version of every identity the node authorises" clause as a method-neutral MUST, so it binds `did:webvh` as well as `did:scid`, and Appendix F.3 registers that neither node type meets it. If the persisted floor should stay a `did:scid` rule, the second sentence of VTI-KEY-066 is dropped and the F.3 row narrows to the refusal of a stale version.
2. **The hash-chained-log assumption.** The rationale for VTI-KEY-064 to VTI-KEY-067 assumes the identifier's log is a hash chain that verifies independently of its source, which is true of `did:webvh` and `did:scid`. A method whose document is not a verifiable log cannot apply VTI-KEY-066 or VTI-KEY-067 and the text does not yet say what such a method does instead. Related: VTI-KEY-067 treats a stale source answering beside a current one as refused and ignored, not as tainting the resolution.
3. **The F.3 and F.5 divergence rows are observed against one implementation.** Each "observed" row states what the two node types of one implementation do today. They are self-reports and may already be out of date; they are not a measurement of any other implementation and should be read as the first entries in a register others can add to.

## How it was checked

`npm run render` builds the specification at the branch tip. Requirement identifiers were checked for collision against `origin/main`. Every [TOIP-GOV] and [TRUST-TASKS] citation points at a term the referenced document defines.

## Relation to the discussions

This is the "governance-framework reference in the DID document, with a version and a required digest" and the "currency" rows of the "What exists, and what is missing" table in dtgwg-general discussion 36 (https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-general/discussions/36), listed there as "a draft is ready and will be linked here"; and the Identity-layer rollback rule that discussion 35 (https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-general/discussions/35) leaves unrated. Neither discussion asks any community to adopt a framework; this PR only says where a framework is found and how a reference to it is checked.

**Read together with the companion Trust Tasks PR** (https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/904): the governance-framework reference shape (`GovernanceFramework` service: `serviceEndpoint`, `version`, `digestMultibase`) is shared between the two. The `understanding/offer` task's `termsRef` carries the same `{ uri, version, digestMultibase }` triple and must match the host's `GovernanceFramework` service where one is published, so a change to the shape here changes that specification too.

title: test: one set of proof vectors every library's verifier runs
body:
The fixture half of trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec#40 (ruling 5 of #31), and next step 2 of discussion #905.

**`fixtures/proof/`**: one set of signed documents plus a `manifest.json` giving each file's expected result and why, with a README.
| file | suite | expect |
|---|---|---|
| `eddsa-jcs-2022-baseline.json` | eddsa-jcs-2022 | valid (the existing interop fixture, reproduced byte for byte by every signer) |
| `ecdsa-jcs-2019-{ts,go}-{p256,p384}.json` | ecdsa-jcs-2019 | valid (the existing ECDSA fixtures, one file each) |
| `eddsa-jcs-2022-timestamp-spellings.json` | eddsa-jcs-2022 | **valid**: signed over `issuedAt: …00.000Z` and `expiresAt: …+00:00` |
| `…-timestamp-spellings-normalized.json` | eddsa-jcs-2022 | **invalid**: both rewritten to `…Z`, original proof kept |

The timestamp pair is the case SPEC §4.7 *What a consumer verifies* is about. A verifier that re-serializes a typed parse refuses the first. One that accepts the second is not checking the bytes it received.

**Tests**: one per library, each running every manifest entry:
- `trust-tasks-proof/tests/shared_vectors.rs` (`verify_raw`)
- `trust-tasks-ts-proof/test/proof.test.ts`
- `trust-tasks-dart-proof/test/shared_vectors_test.dart`
- `trust-tasks-go/proof/proof_test.go` (`TestSharedProofVectors`)

All four pass both timestamp cases. Each test lists the suites it implements, so an unsupported suite fails rather than being skipped silently. `trust-tasks-proof` implements only the eddsa suites, so it names `ecdsa-jcs-2019` as not implemented.

The new fixture was signed with the existing seed-`[7; 32]` key through `trust-tasks-go/proof`'s `Signer`, with `proofPurpose: authentication`. The per-package fixture copies are left in place for the byte-for-byte reproduction tests that already use them.

Part of trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec#40.

title: feat(ts, go)!: trust-task-error/0.6 and the unsupportedExtension and indeterminate standard codes
body:
Registry and library half of trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec#42 (ruling 7 of #31). The framework text (SPEC §8.3, `indeterminate`) landed in trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec#50. This also publishes the `trust-task-error/0.6` that framework 0.7.0's changelog listed as owed for `unsupportedExtension`.

**Spec**
- `specs/trust-task-error/0.6`: `unsupportedExtension` and `indeterminate` **appended** to the standard-code enum. It declares `extends: "0.5"`, which the build checks against the schema, so the ~130 existing references to `trust-task-error/0.5` in specs stay current and no other spec changes.

**Libraries** (all four move together; `check-bindings` compares the error URIs)
| | codes | error URI |
|---|---|---|
| Rust | `StandardCode::UnsupportedExtension`, `::Indeterminate` (hand-written; `indeterminate` retryable by default) | `trust_task_error_type_uri()` → 0.6 |
| TypeScript | `STANDARD_CODES` += both | `TRUST_TASK_ERROR_TYPE_URI` → 0.6 |
| Go | `CodeUnsupportedExtension`, `CodeIndeterminate` | `TrustTaskErrorTypeURI` → 0.6 |
| Dart | `StandardCode.unsupportedExtension`, `.indeterminate` | `trustTaskErrorTypeUri` → 0.6 |

**HTTPS binding.** The status table maps `unsupportedExtension` to `422` and `indeterminate` to `503` (it is retryable), in `bindings/https/0.3`, `trust-tasks-https` and `trust_tasks_https`. Before this, both fell through to `500`. The Dart package spells the codes out as strings so it still builds against a published core that predates them.

**Why `feat(ts)!`.** `StandardCode` is a closed union in `@openvtc/trust-tasks`, so an exhaustive `switch` over it stops compiling. `codes.ts` documents that the package took a MINOR the last time a code was added. In Rust the type is `#[non_exhaustive]`, and in Go and Dart it is an open string type, so the change is additive there. The `!` also names `go`: the Go API check counts the changed value of the exported `TrustTaskErrorTypeURI` constant as a break, which it is for a consumer that compared against it. Rust and Dart change the same value through a function and a top-level constant their checks do not treat as breaking.

Locally: `npm run build`, `npm run check-bindings`, `npm test` (trust-tasks-ts), `go test ./trusttasks/`, `dart test` (core and https), and `cargo test` for `error`, `error_flow` and `trust-tasks-https` `status` all pass. Count assertions in the Go and Dart tests moved from 14 to 16.

Part of trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec#42.

**Follow-up commit.** The TS, Go and Dart generators now leave `trust-task-error` out of their extends indexes, as `trust-tasks-codegen` does. It has no registry bundle, so the consumer-side generators cannot index it, and error documents are never routed by `extends`. The 0.6 module keeps its `EXTENDS` constant. 0.6 also gains the four Security & Privacy sub-headings the strict build requires.

body:
feat(ts, go)!: trust-task-error/0.6 and the unsupportedExtension and indeterminate standard codes (#961)

* feat(ts)!: trust-task-error/0.6 and the unsupportedExtension and indeterminate standard codes

Framework 0.7.0 added unsupportedExtension to the standard codes, and the
indeterminate ruling (SPEC §8.3) adds indeterminate: the recipient could
not decide because something it needed and does not control could not
be obtained or checked, which is neither a refusal nor a failed
verification. Both live in the closed code list of the trust-task-error
payload schema, so they need a new version.

- specs/trust-task-error/0.6: both codes appended to the enum, and
  extends: "0.5", which the build checks. References to 0.5 across the
  registry therefore stay current, and no other spec changes.
- All four libraries recognize both codes and emit 0.6:
  trust_task_error_type_uri(), TRUST_TASK_ERROR_TYPE_URI,
  TrustTaskErrorTypeURI and trustTaskErrorTypeUri move together.
  Rust's StandardCode is hand-written (trust-task-error is in
  SKIP_SLUGS) and gains UnsupportedExtension and Indeterminate, with
  indeterminate retryable by default as §8.3 gives it.
- The HTTPS binding's status table maps unsupportedExtension to 422 and
  indeterminate to 503, in the binding prose, trust-tasks-https and
  trust_tasks_https. The Dart package spells the new codes out so it
  still builds against a core that predates them.

Breaking for @openvtc/trust-tasks only: StandardCode is a closed union
there, so an exhaustive switch over it stops compiling. Rust's
StandardCode is #[non_exhaustive] and Go's and Dart's are open string
types, so the change is additive for them.

Part of trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec#42.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* fix: keep trust-task-error out of the extends indexes, and give 0.6 its Security & Privacy sections

The TS, Go and Dart generators put trust-task-error/0.6 -> 0.5 in their
extends index, while trust-tasks-codegen skips the slug and the
consumer-side generators cannot index it (it has no registry bundle), so
the equivalence checks found the prebuilt and generated indexes
different. The three generators now leave trust-task-error out, as the
Rust one does: an error document is read by the runtime's own path,

title: spec(policy): a consent decision carries its quorum and self-approval rule
body:
Registry half of trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec#39 (ruling 4 of #31). The framework rule (SPEC §6.6 rule 5, no governance defaults) landed in trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec#48.

**The defect.** `policy/_shared/0.3` defaults `requireConsent.minApprovals` to `1` and `requireConsent.excludeRequester` to `false`. JSON Schema `default` is only an annotation, but code generators and form builders apply it. A decision that left either out therefore meant a quorum of one, or a requester approving itself, and nothing on the wire showed that nobody had chosen it.

**The change**
| | |
|---|---|
| `policy/_shared/0.4` | both members **required**, no defaults. `task-consent/request/0.1` already requires both, so the two now agree. |
| `policy/evaluate/0.4` | 0.3 re-pinned to `_shared/0.4`, and nothing else. It gains the four Security & Privacy sub-headings a new version must carry. |
| `policy/get/0.1`, `policy/active/0.1` | unchanged, still on `_shared/0.3`: they use only `PolicyModule`, which did not change. |
| task-consent prose | stale `policy/evaluate/0.3` mentions moved (`npm run fix-stale-references`). |

`0.3` is released, so this is a new version, not an in-place edit; the published-schemas check would refuse that. `policy/evaluate/0.1`–`0.3` are now superseded by `0.4` and go through the normal deprecate-then-withdraw lifecycle. No hand-written code uses them.

All four libraries regenerated. The TypeScript change is additive: a new `PolicyDecision_PolicyV0_4`, and the unchanged `PolicyInput` keeps its existing name.

title: vtc-service-v0.14.0
body:
### Added

- **vtc**: Publish a member's dates as the registry record's validity window (registry/record/put/0.3) ([#2287](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2287))

The trust registry now answers recognition against a record's validity
  window (`validFrom` inclusive, `validUntil` exclusive), so a member's
  recognition holds for the period they belong rather than whenever the record
  happens to exist. The registry sync writes membership records with
  `registry/record/put/0.3` and reads them with `registry/record/query/0.3`,
  the lowerCamelCase versions whose records carry the window: `validFrom` is
  when the member joined and `validUntil` when they left.

  - A registry that predates 0.3 answers `unsupportedVersion`. The client then
    sends the 0.1 record, and remembers, so later calls skip the 0.3 attempt.
    Only `unsupportedVersion` moves to 0.1; any other answer stands.
  - The dates are also kept in the record's context (`activeFrom`, `activeTo`)
    for one release, so 0.1 readers still see them and the 0.1 fallback loses
    nothing. Removing that copy must remove the write fallback with it.
  - `validUntil` is left off when it is not after `validFrom`. The registry
    refuses such a window, which would park the sync job, and the record is a
    departed member's, which already answers `recognized: false`.
  - Reading accepts either spelling and takes the dates from the window when
    the record has one, otherwise from its context.

  Other registry tasks (record delete, git-namespace records, recognition and
  the health probe) are still sent at 0.1.

- **vtc**: Serve the current vtc/auth, list, manifest and resend versions only ([#2298](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2298))

The VTC stops serving superseded Trust Task versions in the vtc/auth,
  join-requests, members, endorsements, endorsement-types and vetting
  families, and every in-repo sender (admin console, member portal,
  vtc-client, cnm-cli) moves to the current version:

  - vtc/auth/admin-session 0.1 -> 0.2: `expiresAt` is an RFC 3339
    date-time, not Unix seconds.
  - vtc/auth/recognise/challenge 0.1 -> 0.2: `expiresAt` RFC 3339.
  - vtc/auth/recognise 0.2 -> 0.3: `data.accessExpiresAt` RFC 3339.
  - vtc/{members,join-requests,endorsements,endorsement-types}/list
    0.1 -> 0.2: `nextCursor` is absent on the last page, never `null`.
    Fixed at the cause: `vti_common::pagination::Paginated` now omits a
    `None` cursor (no list schema requires the member, so 0.1 lists
    still conform).
  - vtc/join-requests/manifest: 0.3 no longer served (0.4 only); the
    0.2/0.3 generated vocabulary types (VettingRequirements,
    CommunityBranding, RequestedAttribute, Criterion) are replaced by
    0.4's throughout, including vta_sdk::openapi wrappers
    (JoinManifest04*), vtc-client and cnm-cli.
  - vtc/vetting/vetters/resend 0.1 no longer served (0.2 only);
    VETTING_VETTER_RESEND_TYPE now names 0.2 and the *_0_2_* constants
    are removed. A non-administrator naming `memberDid` is refused
    permissionDenied (0.2 Conformance item 2).

  vtc/install/claim/{start,finish} 0.2 is deliberately left served: 0.3
  is a different ceremony (claim under a DID the founder already holds,
  with a step-up approver), and its own specification says "a passkey
  install keeps using 0.2". Retiring 0.2 would remove passkey install.

  admin-ui openapi.json and wire.ts regenerated.

- **rooms**: Room hosts serve only the current create, records/get, epoch/prune and blobs versions ([#2297](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2297))

Room hosts (vtc-service, room-host) stop serving rooms/create/0.1,
  rooms/records/get/0.1, rooms/epoch/prune/0.1, rooms/blobs/get/0.1 and
  rooms/blobs/upload/{begin,chunk,commit,abort}/0.1, and every sender in the
  workspace moves to the current version (trust-tasks-tf#921).

  A proxied upload's chunk, commit and abort are now always signed by the
  single-use uploadKey the begin names, never by the member
  (rooms/blobs/upload/begin/0.2 items 3, 14-15).

  rooms/records/put 0.1/0.2 and rooms/epoch/chain 0.1 stay served: rooms/keys/act
  0.6, the newest act VTI serves, completes no later version of either, so
  removing them would break every member write and chain read made through a
  VTA. Direct senders move to put 0.3 and chain 0.2 now.

- **persona**: Serve only the current attribute/profile/world/contact task versions ([#2296](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2296))

* feat(persona)!: serve only the current persona attribute/profile/world/contact versions

  attribute/put, attribute/promote, profile/put, profile/compose,
  local/profile/put, world/put and contact/lists/put move 1.0 -> 1.1;
  contact/put 1.0 and 1.1 -> 1.2; contact/get and contact/list 1.0 -> 1.1.
  The old versions are no longer served. On the wire the create-or-replace
  responses rename created -> wasCreated; contact get/list answer the
  holder's annotations.

- **rooms**: Serve and send only the current rooms/keys and rooms/owner/group versions ([#2295](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2295))

The VTA stops serving the superseded member-key-holder and owner-group versions,
  and every sender (vta-sdk, vta-cli-common/pnm, the VTC as a community's owner)
  sends the current one with no fallback:

  - rooms/keys/open 0.1 -> 0.2, file-key 0.1 -> 0.2, seal 0.1 -> 0.2,
    key-package 0.1 -> 0.2, list 0.1 -> 0.2, chain 0.1 -> 0.2,
    backfill 0.1 -> 0.2 (fetching with rooms/epoch/chain/0.2 only)
  - rooms/owner/group/add 0.1, 0.2 -> 0.3; remove 0.2 -> 0.3; renew 0.1 -> 0.2

  rooms/owner/group/remove/0.1 is kept, served and sent: 0.3 refuses a private
  room (privateRoom) and names 0.1 as that tier's removal, so withdrawing 0.1
  would leave no way to remove a member of a private room.



### Chore

- **deps**: Trust-tasks-rs 0.35 (affinidi-messaging-sdk 0.41, affinidi-tdk 0.33, mediator 0.46) ([#2300](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2300))

* chore(deps)!: trust-tasks-rs 0.35 (affinidi-messaging-sdk 0.41, affinidi-tdk 0.33, mediator 0.46)

  trust-tasks-rs, -proof, -https, -didcomm, -tsp and -capability-client
  0.34 -> 0.35 (0.35.3), in lockstep with affinidi-messaging-sdk 0.41,
  affinidi-tdk 0.33 (affinidi-tdk-rs #975) and the mediator crates 0.46,
  which are built on them. One trust-tasks-rs in the graph.

  0.35 brings the lowerCamelCase registry/* versions with record validity
  windows (trust-tasks-tf #925), which the VTC's registry client needs
  ([#2287](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2287)), and marks every superseded spec version deprecated
  (trust-tasks-tf #921). VTI still names many superseded versions while it
  moves to the current ones, so `deprecated` is allowed for the workspace
  (and in room-host, vti-rooms, vti-voting and vti-witness, which do not
  inherit its lints), with a note to remove it when that move is done and
  before those versions are withdrawn.

  0.35's Type URI parser accepts any scheme but `http`, case-insensitively,
  for third-party registries (trust-tasks-tf #922, #934), and keeps the
  authority as written. `HTTPS://trusttasks.org/...` now parses, as a
  lookalike authority rather than an unparseable string; the proof-purpose
  classifier still gives it Authentication, never the attestation purpose.
  The classifier test moves it to the lookalike list.

title: feat(registry): declare carried protocols in front matter
body:
Registry half of trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec#43. The framework text (SPEC §9.4 Carried Protocols, §7.3 item 23) landed in trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec#51.

- **`specs/spec.meta.schema.json`**: a `carries` object with `protocol`, `version`, `reference` (URI) and `operation`, all required.
- **Build** (`scripts/build-registry.mjs`): records `carries` in `registry.json`, and checks §9.4 rule 1 across the tree:
  - a slug carries one operation in every live version;
  - no two slugs carry the same operation of the same protocol version.
  It prints `Carried protocols: 2 version(s) carry an operation of TRQP 2.0`.
- **Site**: the spec page shows a *Carries* row linking the protocol.
- **`registry/authorization/0.2`, `registry/recognition/0.2`** declare `carries: TRQP 2.0 / authorization|recognition`. Their *TRQP field names* sections, which already hold the field mapping §9.4 rule 2 asks for, now say what they carry and give the party mapping. Front matter and prose only; no schema change.
- **`CONTRIBUTING-SPECS.md`**: *Carrying another protocol*.
- **`SPEC.md`**: regenerated from canonical `main` for the §9.4 anchor. This is the same regeneration as #958, so whichever merges second has no SPEC.md diff left.

No generated library changes: `carries` is registry metadata and reaches no generated type.

title: feat(vtc): open the community in Keyring from the landing page on phones
body:
The landing page shows the community DID as a QR code for Keyring to scan, but a phone cannot scan its own screen. There, the page only said to copy the DID into Keyring by hand.

On a touch device the pass card now shows **Open in Keyring**, a link to the same bare DID the code carries (`<a href="did:webvh:…">`). A DID is already a URI with scheme `did`, and Keyring routes a tap on it exactly as it routes a scan, so a community's DID opens its join flow. Nothing changes on the wire or in the daemon.

## Why this works (checked in Keyring)

Checked against berkmancenter/keyring-wallet @ f89d6f7, with keyring-bifold pinned at 308fcc8c:

- **iOS registers `did`**: a `CFBundleURLSchemes` entry in `app/ios/AriesBifold/Info.plist`.
- **Android registers `did`**: an intent filter with `VIEW` + `DEFAULT` + `BROWSABLE` in `AndroidManifest.xml`, so a browser hands the tap to the app.
- **Same routing as a scan**: `TabStack.handleDeepLink` → `keyringAgentLinkKind` (a bare `did:webvh:` is `'did'`) → `openKeyringLink` → `routeBareDid`, which classifies a community DID and opens `VtiJoin`.
- **Parsing**: `bareDid` matches `/^did:[a-z0-9]+:[^\s?#/]+/`, so the URI having no `//` doesn't matter.
- **Cold and warm start**: `useDeepLinks` reads `getInitialURL()` and the `url` listener, and holds the link until the wallet is unlocked.

## Changes

- `vtc-service/website-default/index.html`: the button, hidden until the QR code has loaded, and a touch caption that points to it.
- `vtc-service/website-default/site.js`: `showDidQr()` takes the profile's `communityDid` (the QR code's own source) and sets it as the button's href. It never takes the `/health` fallback text.
- `vtc-service/website-default/site.css`: the button appears only under the existing `(hover: none) and (pointer: coarse)` query, so desktop is unchanged. `.btn` sets a display, so the rule matches `:not([hidden])`.
- `docs/03-vtc/website-and-admin.md`: describes the button, what happens without a wallet, and the same link for operator sites.

## Spec

This is not a VTI trigger link, so VTI-LNK-013 (no trigger links under a custom scheme) does not apply, and nothing goes in the divergence register. A trigger-link flow for adding a community would give universal-link routing and a no-wallet fallback page (VTI-LNK-091), but only `sign-in/0.1` and `vta-claim/0.1` are registered, and both need a live request. That would start as a dtgwg-vti-spec proposal.

## Testing

- `node --check` on `site.js`. No Rust code changed, and no test refers to the old caption.
- Not yet tried on a device. To do on iOS Safari and Android Chrome against a deployed VTC:
  - [ ] Desktop: the button is hidden and the page is otherwise unchanged.
  - [ ] Phone, with Keyring killed and with it in the background: a tap shows "reading code", then the community's join screen.
  - [ ] Phone, Keyring never set up: Keyring only starts listening for links after onboarding. A tap that opens Keyring for the first time should still land on the join screen after setup. A tap while Keyring is already open on a setup screen is probably lost, which would be a Keyring fix.
  - [ ] Phone, Keyring not installed: iOS reports an invalid address and Android does nothing. The Copy button stays beside the link.

- website-default/site.css: the button appears only under the existing
  `(hover: none) and (pointer: coarse)` query, so desktop still shows
  "Scan with Keyring". `.btn` sets a display, so the rule matches
  `:not([hidden])` rather than relying on the attribute.
- docs/03-vtc/website-and-admin.md: the button, what happens without a
  wallet installed (nothing on Android, an invalid-address error on
  iOS; Copy stays beside it), and the same link for operator sites.

This is not a VTI trigger link, so VTI-LNK-013 (no trigger links under
a custom scheme) does not apply. A trigger-link flow for adding a
community would give universal-link routing and a no-wallet fallback
page (VTI-LNK-091), but the specification registers none yet.

Signed-off-by: Geoff Turk <geoff@ic3.dev>

* feat(vtc): label the phone link Join in Keyring and set it only for a DID

The link opens Keyring's join flow, not sign-in, so the button says Join
and the caption points members to Member sign-in. The href is set, and the
button shown, only for a value of the form did:<method>:..., so the page
never puts another scheme behind a button that says it opens a wallet.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* feat(vtc): lead with Join in Keyring on phones, and link the offer card

Review of the first commit raised four points.

- The button showed only once the QR image loaded, so a failed SVG hid
  it too. It now shows as soon as the profile names the DID
  (website-default/site.js, `showDidQr`).
- `(hover: none) and (pointer: coarse)` hid it on an iPad with a
  trackpad or keyboard. The button now shows on any coarse pointer
  (`any-pointer: coarse`) or when `navigator.maxTouchPoints > 1`, which
  catches iPadOS presenting itself as a Mac. A touchscreen laptop shows
  it too, harmlessly.
- On a phone the code only helps another device. Where touch is the
  only input, the button now comes first and the code and its caption
  start folded in a `<details>`, "Show the code for another device".
  Elsewhere the fold is open and its summary hidden, so desktop looks
  as before. The caption that sat under the code moves under the
  button, as a note shown with it: "New here? Join in Keyring, or copy
  the DID. Already a member? Use Member sign-in above."
- The admin console's invitation offer card gains "Open in wallet", an
  `<a href>` to the same `openid-credential-offer://` link its code
  carries, for an invitee whose wallet is on the device showing it
  (admin-ui/src/plugins/invitations.tsx).

The label, the note's wording and the `did:<method>:…` check on the
link come from the previous commit and are kept. The check now also
gates showing the button, which no longer waits for the image.

docs/03-vtc/website-and-admin.md describes the touch detection and the
fold.

Signed-off-by: Geoff Turk <geoff@ic3.dev>

* fix(vtc): drop Open in wallet from the offer card; the fold says Hide when open

The previous commit gave the admin console's invitation offer card an
"Open in wallet" link. The console runs on the administrator's device,
and the offer redeems only with a key of the invited DID, so the link
opened the administrator's own wallet with an offer it cannot redeem.
The same-device path for an invitee is the one that already existed:
copy the offer link, send it, and the invitee taps it. The link is
removed and the card reads as before.

On the landing page, the fold's summary said "Show the code for
another device" while the code was showing. It now says "Hide the
code" when open (two spans, one shown per `details[open]` state).

docs: follow the framework's rulings on proofs, decisions, holds, repeats and defaults (#958) SPEC.md is regenerated from canonical dtgwg-trust-tasks-spec at bdf2cdd, which adds: verifying a proof over the document as received (§4.7), a hold is a next step (§8.6), a decision is an outcome and not a failure (§8), a request for a state that already holds (§7.2), no governance defaults in shared schema components (§6.6), the time-limit classification (§7.2), the indeterminate standard code (§8.3), and Carried Protocols (§9.4) with the carries front matter (§7.3 item 23). No existing section number moves. The current TSP (0.1), DIDComm (0.2) and HTTPS (0.3) bindings each told the consumer to deserialise the document as TrustTask

before the pipeline runs, which invites verifying a re-serialisation. Each step now says to keep the received object and verify the proof over it. CONTRIBUTING-SPECS gains "Decisions, holds and repeated requests" and a no-governance-defaults rule for shared components, so spec authors meet the rulings when they design a schema. title: feat(spec): carried protocols and protocol families
body:
The canonical-text half of #43.

**Transport Bindings** gains a last subsection, *Carried Protocols*. It goes last so no section number moves; the registry links to sections by number.
- A **carried protocol** is defined outside the framework and uses Trust Task documents as its interface, the way it might use an HTTP API. Its **protocol family** is the set of specs that carry it. A transport binding carries Trust Task documents; a protocol family is carried *by* them.
- Seven rules for a spec declaring `carries`:
  1. one spec per operation;
  2. a member mapping, and no new meaning;
  3. every answer is an outcome, in the success response;
  4. versions move together (`extends` when additive);
  5. parties are mapped;
  6. no departures, with extra behaviour in a separate spec, composable by a ceremony;
  7. conformance to the protocol stays with the protocol.
- Non-normative: why one spec per operation and not a generic `{ protocol, operation, body }` tunnel.
- A family **MAY** be published under the protocol owner's own authority, and **SHOULD** be published or endorsed by the owner where the owner takes part.

**Specification Requirements** gains item 23, the `carries` front matter:
```yaml
carries:
  protocol: TRQP
  version: "2.0"
  reference: https://trustoverip.github.io/tswg-trust-registry-protocol/
  operation: authorization
```

**Terms:** *carried protocol*, *protocol family*.

The registry half (the `carries` field in `spec.meta.schema.json`, build validation, site display, and declarations on `registry/*`) follows in dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf.

Part of #43.

title: feat(spec): carried protocols and protocol families (#51)
body:
feat(spec): carried protocols and protocol families (#51)

Trust Task specifications already carry protocols defined elsewhere
(the registry's registry/* family carries ToIP TRQP 2.0) and more are
proposed (IEEE 7012 MyTerms), but the framework said nothing about how
such a specification relates to the protocol it carries, so each one
decided afresh, and one draft departed from its protocol in five places.

Transport Bindings gains Carried Protocols, placed last so no section
number moves. A carried protocol uses Trust Task documents as its
interface the way it might use an HTTP API; its protocol family is one
specification per operation. A specification that declares carries maps
each field, adds no meaning, reports every answer as an outcome, names
the protocol version and moves with it, maps the parties, makes no
departure (extra behaviour is a separate specification), and leaves the
protocol's own conformance to the protocol. A non-normative paragraph
says why the family is per operation and not one generic tunnel, and a
family may be published under the protocol owner's authority.

Specification Requirements gains item 23, the carries front matter:
protocol, version, reference and operation. Two terms are defined:
carried protocol and protocol family.

Closes the canonical-text item of #43.

title: feat(spec): a standard indeterminate error code
body:
Ruling 7 of #31, option (c), tracked in #42.

**Standard Error Codes** gains:

| Code | Meaning | Default `retryable` |
|---|---|---|
| `indeterminate` | Could not decide: something the recipient needs and does not control could not be obtained or checked (a schema, a `verificationMethod`'s material, a status list, a referenced document whose digest no longer matches). Neither a refusal nor a verdict on the document. | `true` |

and a paragraph, *`indeterminate` is a result of its own*:
- `proofInvalid` = verification ran and failed; `unavailable` = the recipient's own capacity or dependency; `indeterminate` = a reference someone else publishes could not be obtained or checked.
- `details` **SHOULD** name the kind of reference, within the `message` restraint rules. **MUST NOT** substitute `proofInvalid` or `permissionDenied`.
- A party retaining the error **MUST NOT** read it as refusal or failed verification.
- A consumer whose policy proceeds anyway **MUST NOT** record the determination as verified (from the discussion on dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#905).

**Release.** Like `unsupportedExtension` in 0.7.0, this is an additive change to the closed list of standard codes, so the registry publishes a new `trust-task-error` version. `trust-task-error/0.6` is already owed for `unsupportedExtension`, so one version carries both. The four libraries move to it: additive in Rust, Go and Dart, breaking in TypeScript, whose `StandardCode` is a closed union.

Part of #42.

title: feat(spec): a standard indeterminate error code (#50)
body:
feat(spec): a standard indeterminate error code (#50)

A consumer that could not obtain or check something it needed and does
not control (the schema behind a type, the material behind a
verificationMethod, a status list, a referenced document whose digest no
longer matches) had no wire form for that outcome. unavailable means
the recipient's own capacity, and proofInvalid means verification ran
and failed; neither says "could not determine".

Standard Error Codes gains indeterminate, retryable by default, and a
paragraph separating it from proofInvalid and unavailable. details
should name the kind of reference that could not be obtained; a party
retaining the error must not read it as a refusal or a failed
verification; and a consumer whose policy proceeds anyway must not
record the determination as verified.

This is an additive change to the closed list of standard codes, so the
registry publishes a new trust-task-error version carrying it.

Closes the canonical-text item of #42 (ruling 7 of #31).

title: fix(spec): say which time limits are protocol windows, advertised, or policy
body:
Ruling 6 of #31, in the narrowed form its author asked for: classify the limits and fix no number.

Consumer Requirements gains *Which time limits belong to the protocol*:

| Kind | Owner | Examples | Rule |
|---|---|---|---|
| Acceptance windows | protocol | skew tolerance, `expiresAt`, item 13, max age over `issuedAt` | framework fixes how they apply; **no default values**; 60 s of skew stays "typical" |
| Advertised windows | the consumer | `acceptanceWindow` in `trust-task-discovery` | **MUST NOT** be wider than what is enforced; binds no one |
| Lifetimes set by policy | community | authorization, delegation, consent, credential, session, payload deadline, ceremony window | evaluated under items 10 and 12; never substituted for an acceptance window, or the reverse |

The "no wider than enforced" rule already exists in `trust-task-discovery/0.3`; the framework now states it too. The Rust library's 5 minutes / 60 seconds remains a library default.

Closes #41.

title: fix(spec): say which time limits are protocol windows, advertised, or policy (#49)
body:
fix(spec): say which time limits are protocol windows, advertised, or policy (#49)

The framework requires a consumer to refuse a document outside its
acceptance window and names a typical skew, but did not say which time
limits are the protocol's, which a consumer advertises, and which a
community's policy sets, so implementations picked their own maximum age
and a fixed default was requested.

Consumer Requirements now classifies them. Acceptance windows are the
protocol's: the framework fixes how they apply and no values; there is no
default maximum age and sixty seconds of skew stays typical, not
required. An advertised window must not be wider than the one enforced.
Lifetimes of authorizations, delegations, consents, credentials and
payload deadlines are policy, evaluated under items 10 and 12, and are
not substituted for acceptance windows or the reverse.

Closes #41 (ruling 6 of #31).

title: fix(spec): a shared schema component supplies no governance default
body:
Ruling 4 of #31, tracked in #39.

**Shared Schema Components** gains rule 5, *No governance defaults*:
- A shared component **MUST NOT** supply a `default` for a governance value: a threshold or quorum, a TTL or validity period, a role, an evaluation order, or any other value a community's policy chooses.
- Such a member is **required** wherever the definition is used. An omission fails payload validation (`malformedRequest`).
- Why it matters on the wire: JSON Schema `default` is only an annotation, but code generators and form builders apply it.
- A *spec's own* schema **SHOULD NOT** supply one either, and **MUST** state it in prose where it does.

**Registry consequence.** `policy/_shared/0.3` gives `minApprovals` `"default": 1`, so it does not conform to this rule. It is released, and the registry's CI allows only additive changes to a released schema, so the fix is `policy/_shared/0.4` with every referencing spec re-pinned. That work is the registry half of #39 and follows in dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf.

Part of #39.

title: fix(spec): a request for a state that already holds
body:
Ruling 3 of #31.

Consumer Requirements, after **Relationship to idempotency**, gains *A target already in the requested state*. Item 11 covers the *same document* twice; this covers a *different* document asking for an outcome that already holds. A spec **SHOULD** follow one rule, and say which kind each operation is:

| Kind | Examples | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| Setting a state | revoke, deactivate, disable, enable, set | success; **MAY** report whether anything changed |
| Creating something | register, grant, create, issue | a task-specific error code: the request names a new thing |
| Missing target | any | a task-specific error code, **MAY** be the same as "exists but you may not see it" |

This confirms what the registry already does: `keys/revoke/0.1` and `vtc/invitations/revoke/0.1` (idempotent success), `git-trust/grant/0.1` and `device/register` (duplicate create is an error), `vtc/relationships/revoke/0.1` (one code for absent or not yours). The `CONTRIBUTING-SPECS.md` guidance on #38 follows in the registry repo.

Closes #38.

title: fix(spec): a request for a state that already holds (#47)
body:
fix(spec): a request for a state that already holds (#47)

Relationship to idempotency left the semantics of the underlying
operation to each specification and recorded no rule they follow, so a
revoke of something already revoked, a grant of something already
granted and a registration of something already registered were each
decided afresh.

A specification should now follow one rule and say which kind each
operation is: setting an existing target to a state it already has
succeeds and may report whether anything changed; creating a thing that
already exists is refused with a task-specific code; a missing target is
refused, optionally with the same code as one the requester may not see.
The rule confirms what the registry's revoke, grant and register
specifications already do.

Closes #38 (ruling 3 of #31).

body:
Ruling 2 of #31.

**Error Responses** gains *A decision is not a failure*:
- For a task that exists to produce a decision (admit or refuse a join, accept, counter or reject an agreement, answer an authorization query), every decision, negative ones included, is the task's **outcome** and goes in the success response.
- "Failure" in the existing rule means the task was **not performed**: it did not validate, the requester may not invoke it (`permissionDenied`), or the recipient could not complete it.
- `permissionDenied` = "you may not ask". A refusal in the success response = "you asked, and the answer is no". This is the line §7.2 item 10 already draws.
- A spec **SHOULD** define every decision in its success schema and **SHOULD NOT** declare an extended error code for one.

**Why SHOULD and not MUST for spec authors.** Several published registry specs declare codes that may be decisions, for example `auth/step-up/approve-request:userDeclined`, `vtc/relationships/request:declined` and `witness/session:refused`. A MUST would make them non-conforming in place. The registry review is a checklist item on #37: each one either moves the decision into its success response in its next version, or records why the code is a refusal to run.

Closes #37.

title: fix(spec): a decision a task produces is its outcome, not a failure (#46)
body:
fix(spec): a decision a task produces is its outcome, not a failure (#46)

Error Responses forbade reporting failure as a #response without saying
whether a negative decision the task exists to produce is a failure. A
denied join request went out as a success carrying the decision in one
implementation and as an error in another, and a draft agreement family
carried counter and refuse as error codes.

A decision, negative ones included, is the task's outcome and is
reported in the success response. Failure means the task was not
performed. permissionDenied says the requester may not ask; a refusal in
the success response says it asked and the answer is no. A specification
should define every decision in its success schema and should not
declare an error code for one. The spec-author rule is a SHOULD so the
registry specs that declare such codes today are not made non-conforming
in place; they move in their next versions.

title: fix(spec): a hold for approval, consent or step-up is a next step
body:
Ruling 1 of #31.

**Reserved Response-Type Slugs** gains *A hold is a next step*:
- A task held for an approval, a consent decision, a step-up or any other act not yet performed is **blocked**, whoever has to act. A consumer **MUST** answer with `trust-task-next-step` and **MUST NOT** answer with `taskFailed`, `permissionDenied` or another error whose code or `details` says the task is held.
- What `expects` names:
  - **the producer can act** (a step-up it can complete): the task that performs the act;
  - **a third party must act** (an approver elsewhere, an administrator, a quorum): a task by which the producer learns the outcome or resumes; failing that, the originating Type URI with `continuation: resubmit`, answered with the outcome once known or another next step.
- A hold that ends because the act is **declined** is a refusal (`permissionDenied`), not another next step. A hold the consumer **abandons** leaves nothing pending, and a resubmission is a new request.

No schema change: `trust-task-next-step/0.1` already carries `expects` and `continuation`.

Closes #36.

title: fix(spec): a hold for approval, consent or step-up is a next step (#45)
body:
fix(spec): a hold for approval, consent or step-up is a next step (#45)

Reserved Response-Type Slugs said a blocked task is a next step, not an
error, but not whether a task held for an approval, a consent decision or
a step-up is blocked in that sense, or what expects names when someone
other than the producer has to act. Implementations answered such holds
with taskFailed and a reason, which closes the exchange.

A held task is blocked whoever has to act, and a consumer must answer it
with a next step, never an error whose code or details says it is held.
expects names the task that performs the act when the producer can, a
task to learn the outcome or resume when a third party has to act, and
otherwise the originating type with continuation resubmit. A declined act
is a refusal and is answered permissionDenied.

Closes #36 (ruling 1 of #31).

title: fix(spec): verify a proof over the document as received
body:
Ruling 5 of #31, tracked in #40.

**Proof** gains a paragraph, *What a consumer verifies*:
- A consumer **MUST** verify a `proof` over the JSON object as received, with only the top-level `proof` removed, canonicalized as the cryptosuite requires.
- It **MUST NOT** verify a re-serialization of a typed representation. A typed parse can rewrite `.000Z` / `+00:00` / `z`, drop a `null` on an optional member, or drop an unmodelled member, and a correctly signed document is then refused as `proofInvalid`.
- Proof options come from the `proof` member as received.
- The typed document a consumer acts on is parsed from that same object, so what it acts on is what it verified.
- A document read as an earlier version under a declared extension is still verified as received, never as the pruned copy.

**What a Transport Binding Specifies** gains *Order of deserialization and verification*: a binding that describes deserializing the carried document must keep the received object for verification.

This writes down what the registry's four libraries and VTI already do. The registry-side items of #40 (TSP binding 0.1 step 3, the other bindings, a shared fixture set) follow in the registry repository.

Part of #40.

title: vtc-client-v0.29.0
body:
### Added

- **vtc**: Serve the current vtc/auth, list, manifest and resend versions only ([#2298](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2298))

The VTC stops serving superseded Trust Task versions in the vtc/auth,
  join-requests, members, endorsements, endorsement-types and vetting
  families, and every in-repo sender (admin console, member portal,
  vtc-client, cnm-cli) moves to the current version:

  - vtc/auth/admin-session 0.1 -> 0.2: `expiresAt` is an RFC 3339
    date-time, not Unix seconds.
  - vtc/auth/recognise/challenge 0.1 -> 0.2: `expiresAt` RFC 3339.
  - vtc/auth/recognise 0.2 -> 0.3: `data.accessExpiresAt` RFC 3339.
  - vtc/{members,join-requests,endorsements,endorsement-types}/list
    0.1 -> 0.2: `nextCursor` is absent on the last page, never `null`.
    Fixed at the cause: `vti_common::pagination::Paginated` now omits a
    `None` cursor (no list schema requires the member, so 0.1 lists
    still conform).
  - vtc/join-requests/manifest: 0.3 no longer served (0.4 only); the
    0.2/0.3 generated vocabulary types (VettingRequirements,
    CommunityBranding, RequestedAttribute, Criterion) are replaced by
    0.4's throughout, including vta_sdk::openapi wrappers
    (JoinManifest04*), vtc-client and cnm-cli.
  - vtc/vetting/vetters/resend 0.1 no longer served (0.2 only);
    VETTING_VETTER_RESEND_TYPE now names 0.2 and the *_0_2_* constants
    are removed. A non-administrator naming `memberDid` is refused
    permissionDenied (0.2 Conformance item 2).

  vtc/install/claim/{start,finish} 0.2 is deliberately left served: 0.3
  is a different ceremony (claim under a DID the founder already holds,
  with a step-up approver), and its own specification says "a passkey
  install keeps using 0.2". Retiring 0.2 would remove passkey install.

  admin-ui openapi.json and wire.ts regenerated.

- **rooms**: Room hosts serve only the current create, records/get, epoch/prune and blobs versions ([#2297](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2297))

Room hosts (vtc-service, room-host) stop serving rooms/create/0.1,
  rooms/records/get/0.1, rooms/epoch/prune/0.1, rooms/blobs/get/0.1 and
  rooms/blobs/upload/{begin,chunk,commit,abort}/0.1, and every sender in the
  workspace moves to the current version (trust-tasks-tf#921).

  A proxied upload's chunk, commit and abort are now always signed by the
  single-use uploadKey the begin names, never by the member
  (rooms/blobs/upload/begin/0.2 items 3, 14-15).

  rooms/records/put 0.1/0.2 and rooms/epoch/chain 0.1 stay served: rooms/keys/act
  0.6, the newest act VTI serves, completes no later version of either, so
  removing them would break every member write and chain read made through a
  VTA. Direct senders move to put 0.3 and chain 0.2 now.

- **rooms**: Serve and send only the current rooms/keys and rooms/owner/group versions ([#2295](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2295))

The VTA stops serving the superseded member-key-holder and owner-group versions,
  and every sender (vta-sdk, vta-cli-common/pnm, the VTC as a community's owner)
  sends the current one with no fallback:

  - rooms/keys/open 0.1 -> 0.2, file-key 0.1 -> 0.2, seal 0.1 -> 0.2,
    key-package 0.1 -> 0.2, list 0.1 -> 0.2, chain 0.1 -> 0.2,
    backfill 0.1 -> 0.2 (fetching with rooms/epoch/chain/0.2 only)
  - rooms/owner/group/add 0.1, 0.2 -> 0.3; remove 0.2 -> 0.3; renew 0.1 -> 0.2

  rooms/owner/group/remove/0.1 is kept, served and sent: 0.3 refuses a private
  room (privateRoom) and names 0.1 as that tier's removal, so withdrawing 0.1
  would leave no way to remove a member of a private room.



### Chore

- **deps**: Trust-tasks-rs 0.35 (affinidi-messaging-sdk 0.41, affinidi-tdk 0.33, mediator 0.46) ([#2300](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2300))

* chore(deps)!: trust-tasks-rs 0.35 (affinidi-messaging-sdk 0.41, affinidi-tdk 0.33, mediator 0.46)

  trust-tasks-rs, -proof, -https, -didcomm, -tsp and -capability-client
  0.34 -> 0.35 (0.35.3), in lockstep with affinidi-messaging-sdk 0.41,
  affinidi-tdk 0.33 (affinidi-tdk-rs #975) and the mediator crates 0.46,
  which are built on them. One trust-tasks-rs in the graph.

  0.35 brings the lowerCamelCase registry/* versions with record validity
  windows (trust-tasks-tf #925), which the VTC's registry client needs
  ([#2287](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2287)), and marks every superseded spec version deprecated
  (trust-tasks-tf #921). VTI still names many superseded versions while it
  moves to the current ones, so `deprecated` is allowed for the workspace
  (and in room-host, vti-rooms, vti-voting and vti-witness, which do not
  inherit its lints), with a note to remove it when that move is done and
  before those versions are withdrawn.

  0.35's Type URI parser accepts any scheme but `http`, case-insensitively,
  for third-party registries (trust-tasks-tf #922, #934), and keeps the
  authority as written. `HTTPS://trusttasks.org/...` now parses, as a
  lookalike authority rather than an unparseable string; the proof-purpose
  classifier still gives it Authentication, never the attestation purpose.
  The classifier test moves it to the lookalike list.

## `vta-sdk`

## [0.74.0](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/compare/vta-sdk-v0.73.0...vta-sdk-v0.74.0) — 2026-10-27 ### Added - **vtc**: Serve the current vtc/auth, list, manifest and resend versions only ([#2298](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2298)) The VTC stops serving superseded Trust Task versions in the vtc/auth, join-requests, members, endorsements, endorsement-types and vetting families, and every in-repo sender (admin console, member portal, vtc-client, cnm-cli) moves to the current version: - vtc/auth/admin-session 0.1 -> 0.2: `expiresAt` is an RFC 3339 date-time, not Unix seconds. - vtc/auth/recognise/challenge 0.1 -> 0.2: `expiresAt` RFC 3339. - vtc/auth/recognise 0.2 -> 0.3: `data.accessExpiresAt` RFC 3339. - vtc/{members,join-requests,endorsements,endorsement-types}/list 0.1 -> 0.2: `nextCursor` is absent on the last page, never `null`. Fixed at the cause: `vti_common::pagination::Paginated` now omits a `None` cursor (no list schema requires the member, so 0.1 lists still conform). - vtc/join-requests/manifest: 0.3 no longer served (0.4 only); the 0.2/0.3 generated vocabulary types (VettingRequirements, CommunityBranding, RequestedAttribute, Criterion) are replaced by 0.4's throughout, including vta_sdk::openapi wrappers (JoinManifest04*), vtc-client and cnm-cli. - vtc/vetting/vetters/resend 0.1 no longer served (0.2 only); VETTING_VETTER_RESEND_TYPE now names 0.2 and the *_0_2_* constants are removed. A non-administrator naming `memberDid` is refused permissionDenied (0.2 Conformance item 2). vtc/install/claim/{start,finish} 0.2 is deliberately left served: 0.3 is a different ceremony (claim under a DID the founder already holds, with a step-up approver), and its own specification says "a passkey install keeps using 0.2". Retiring 0.2 would remove passkey install. admin-ui openapi.json and wire.ts regenerated. - **rooms**: Room hosts serve only the current create, records/get, epoch/prune and blobs versions ([#2297](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2297)) Room hosts (vtc-service, room-host) stop serving rooms/create/0.1, rooms/records/get/0.1, rooms/epoch/prune/0.1, rooms/blobs/get/0.1 and rooms/blobs/upload/{begin,chunk,commit,abort}/0.1, and every sender in the workspace moves to the current version (trust-tasks-tf#921). A proxied upload's chunk, commit and abort are now always signed by the single-use uploadKey the begin names, never by the member (rooms/blobs/upload/begin/0.2 items 3, 14-15). rooms/records/put 0.1/0.2 and rooms/epoch/chain 0.1 stay served: rooms/keys/act 0.6, the newest act VTI serves, completes no later version of either, so removing them would break every member write and chain read made through a VTA. Direct senders move to put 0.3 and chain 0.2 now. - **persona**: Serve only the current attribute/profile/world/contact task versions ([#2296](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2296)) * feat(persona)!: serve only the current persona attribute/profile/world/contact versions attribute/put, attribute/promote, profile/put, profile/compose, local/profile/put, world/put and contact/lists/put move 1.0 -> 1.1; contact/put 1.0 and 1.1 -> 1.2; contact/get and contact/list 1.0 -> 1.1. The old versions are no longer served. On the wire the create-or-replace responses rename created -> wasCreated; contact get/list answer the holder's annotations. - **rooms**: Serve and send only the current rooms/keys and rooms/owner/group versions ([#2295](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2295)) The VTA stops serving the superseded member-key-holder and owner-group versions, and every sender (vta-sdk, vta-cli-common/pnm, the VTC as a community's owner) sends the current one with no fallback: - rooms/keys/open 0.1 -> 0.2, file-key 0.1 -> 0.2, seal 0.1 -> 0.2, key-package 0.1 -> 0.2, list 0.1 -> 0.2, chain 0.1 -> 0.2, backfill 0.1 -> 0.2 (fetching with rooms/epoch/chain/0.2 only) - rooms/owner/group/add 0.1, 0.2 -> 0.3; remove 0.2 -> 0.3; renew 0.1 -> 0.2 rooms/owner/group/remove/0.1 is kept, served and sent: 0.3 refuses a private room (privateRoom) and names 0.1 as that tier's removal, so withdrawing 0.1 would leave no way to remove a member of a private room. ### Chore - **deps**: Trust-tasks-rs 0.35 (affinidi-messaging-sdk 0.41, affinidi-tdk 0.33, mediator 0.46) ([#2300](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2300)) * chore(deps)!: trust-tasks-rs 0.35 (affinidi-messaging-sdk 0.41, affinidi-tdk 0.33, mediator 0.46) trust-tasks-rs, -proof, -https, -didcomm, -tsp and -capability-client 0.34 -> 0.35 (0.35.3), in lockstep with affinidi-messaging-sdk 0.41, affinidi-tdk 0.33 (affinidi-tdk-rs #975) and the mediator crates 0.46, which are built on them. One trust-tasks-rs in the graph. 0.35 brings the lowerCamelCase registry/* versions with record validity windows (trust-tasks-tf #925), which the VTC's registry client needs ([#2287](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/2287)), and marks every superseded spec version deprecated (trust-tasks-tf #921). VTI still names many superseded versions while it moves to the current ones, so `deprecated` is allowed for the workspace (and in room-host, vti-rooms, vti-voting and vti-witness, which do not inherit its lints), with a note to remove it when that move is done and before those versions are withdrawn. 0.35's Type URI parser accepts any scheme but `http`, case-insensitively, for third-party registries (trust-tasks-tf #922, #934), and keeps the authority as written. `HTTPS://trusttasks.org/...` now parses, as a lookalike authority rather than an unparseable string; the proof-purpose classifier still gives it Authentication, never the attestation purpose. The classifier test moves it to the lookalike list.

title: ci(release): a package with no CHANGELOG.md gets one started instead of failing the Release PR
body:
Follow-up to #956. `release-bump-{ts,go,dart}.sh` read `<pkg>/CHANGELOG.md` to prepend each release's section, so a package first published by hand without one crashes the Release PR job with ENOENT, and that one job stops the release of **every** package (as `trust-tasks-ts-gen` did after #954).

Each script now creates the file with a `# Changelog — \`<package>\`` title when it is missing and emits a `::warning::` asking for the versioning preamble in the Release PR. The existing insertion logic already handles a file with no `## ` heading (it appends).

Checked: `bash -n` on all three; simulated the create-then-prepend path on a scratch file.

title: trust-tasks-v0.35.4
body:
### Added

- The prebuilt specification modules are deprecated in all four libraries; generate the tasks you use ([#954](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/954))

Milestone 5 of docs/design/consumer-side-generation.md. Every prebuilt module
  outside the framework's own specifications (trust-task-*, trust-ceremony-*,
  _framework/) is deprecated, so that an application is told to pin the tasks it
  uses with the trust-tasks CLI and generate them instead. Nothing is removed:
  the withdrawal batch that removes them is chosen later, at least 90 days after
  this ships.

  Each library marks the prebuilt entry point where its toolchain reports a
  deprecation, never the module body, which is also what the consumer-side
  generators emit:

  - Rust: #[deprecated] on each gated family module in trust-tasks-rs's
    specs/mod.rs (trust-tasks-codegen). It reaches every path and item under the
    module; framework modules and trust-tasks-build's output are unmarked.
  - TypeScript: the root index re-exports each module as
    `import * as _X …; /** @deprecated … */ export import X = _X;`, because
    TypeScript ignores @deprecated on `export * as`. API compatibility against
    0.27.8: nothing removed or changed. A deep import of a module file is not
    marked; TypeScript has no module-level deprecation.
  - Go: a `Deprecated:` paragraph in each prebuilt package's doc, which gopls and
    staticcheck (SA1019) report on import.
  - Dart: @Deprecated on each prebuilt library's `library` directive, which the
    analyzer reports on import from another package. This package's own tests
    use them, so analysis_options ignores the same-package diagnostic SDKs
    before 3.4 report.

  The TS, Go and Dart equivalence tests mask exactly the mark; every consumer
  generator is still held to the prebuilt tree as before. Hand-written Rust that
  uses prebuilt modules on purpose — the acl-specimen test modules, the
  integration tests and the examples — carries #[allow(deprecated)]; none of the
  runtime does.

  GETTING-STARTED, the four library READMEs, the design doc and CLAUDE.md say
  so, and point at each language's generator.



### Documentation

- GETTING-STARTED pins and generates the task it uses, in all four languages ([#955](https://github.com/trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf/pull/955))

The walkthroughs taught the prebuilt specification modules, which #954
  deprecated. They now start where an application does: `trust-tasks add
  acl/grant/0.2`, then each language's generator.

  - §1 is "pin the tasks you use, then one dependency line": the CLI, the
    facade with `default-features = false` plus a build.rs that generates
    through it (`runtime_path("::trust_tasks")`), and `trust-tasks generate
    --lang ts|go|dart` for the others. The facade line said version "0.1"; it is
    0.35. The advice to trim the 26 per-family features is gone with them.
  - §2's Rust is still extracted verbatim from a runnable example, now an
    application of its own, examples/getting-started (trust-tasks.lock pinning
    acl/grant/0.2, its vendored bundle, a build.rs), instead of an example of
    the facade crate, which cannot have a build script per example. The only
    code change is the `use` line: `tasks::acl::grant::v0_2`, generated, for
    `trust_tasks::specs::acl::grant::v0_2`. It runs end to end
    (`cargo run -p trust-tasks-example-getting-started`), and
    getting_started_snippets follows it.
  - §3–3b (TypeScript, Go, Dart) import the runtime and the generated module
    instead of the package's prebuilt one, and move from acl/grant 0.1, which is
    superseded, to 0.2, as the Rust uses. Every name in them was checked against
    generated 0.2 code and the consumer example apps.

  The facade's README and crate docs point at the new example, and lose the
  dev-dependencies only the old one needed.

  _framework/) is deprecated, so that an application is told to pin the tasks it
  uses with the trust-tasks CLI and generate them instead. Nothing is removed:
  the withdrawal batch that removes them is chosen later, at least 90 days after
  this ships.

  Each library marks the prebuilt entry point where its toolchain reports a
  deprecation, never the module body, which is also what the consumer-side
  generators emit:

  - Rust: #[deprecated] on each gated family module in trust-tasks-rs's
    specs/mod.rs (trust-tasks-codegen). It reaches every path and item under the
    module; framework modules and trust-tasks-build's output are unmarked.
  - TypeScript: the root index re-exports each module as
    `import * as _X …; /** @deprecated … */ export import X = _X;`, because
    TypeScript ignores @deprecated on `export * as`. API compatibility against
    0.27.8: nothing removed or changed. A deep import of a module file is not
    marked; TypeScript has no module-level deprecation.
  - Go: a `Deprecated:` paragraph in each prebuilt package's doc, which gopls and
    staticcheck (SA1019) report on import.
  - Dart: @Deprecated on each prebuilt library's `library` directive, which the
    analyzer reports on import from another package. This package's own tests
    use them, so analysis_options ignores the same-package diagnostic SDKs
    before 3.4 report.

  The TS, Go and Dart equivalence tests mask exactly the mark; every consumer
  generator is still held to the prebuilt tree as before. Hand-written Rust that
  uses prebuilt modules on purpose — the acl-specimen test modules, the
  integration tests and the examples — carries #[allow(deprecated)]; none of the
  runtime does.

  GETTING-STARTED, the four library READMEs, the design doc and CLAUDE.md say
  so, and point at each language's generator.

title: feat(vtc): publish a member's dates as the registry record's validity window (registry/record/put/0.3)
body:
> **Draft: blocked on trust-tasks 0.35.** `trust_task_manifest::every_bound_canonical_task_exists_in_the_registry` fails on `registry/record/put/0.3` and `registry/record/query/0.3`, because this workspace is on trust-tasks-rs 0.34 and those versions first ship in **0.35.1**. That test is right to fail, and its message says raising the exception count is the wrong fix. This turns green once the workspace moves to trust-tasks 0.35, which waits on `affinidi-messaging-sdk` releasing on 0.35. Opened now so the change is visible and stays current.

## What and why

The trust registry now judges every recognition and authorization query against the record's **validity window** (`validFrom` inclusive, `validUntil` exclusive) as of `context.time`. That shipped in affinidi/affinidi-trust-registry-rs#168, with the spec in trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#925. Until now the VTC carried a member's dates only inside the record's opaque `context`, so the registry answered `recognized` regardless of when the member belonged.

The registry sync now writes membership records with `registry/record/put/0.3` and reads them with `registry/record/query/0.3`. `validFrom` is when the member joined (`active_from`) and `validUntil` when they left (`active_to`).

| Situation | What the VTC sends |
|---|---|
| registry answers 0.3 | `put/0.3`: lowerCamelCase record with `validFrom` / `validUntil`, dates also in `context` |
| registry answers `unsupportedVersion` (predates 0.3) | `put/0.1` record (dates in `context`), remembered for later calls |
| any other rejection | the rejection stands; no fallback |
| `active_to` not after `active_from` | `validUntil` left off (the registry refuses such a window, which would park the job; the record is a departed member's, already `recognized: false`) |

**Reads** accept either spelling and take the dates from the window when present, otherwise from `context`.

**Transition (R3.4/R3.6):** `activeFrom` / `activeTo` stay in `context` for one release, so 0.1 readers still see them and the 0.1 fallback loses nothing. Removing that copy must remove the write fallback with it; the code says so at `round_trip_versioned`.

**Not changed:** record delete, git-namespace records, recognition queries and the health probe are still sent at 0.1. The plain REST arm is unchanged.

## Spec

- **VTI-REG-001:** no new personal data. The dates were already published in `context`; they now also sit in the record's own window.
- **VTI-REG-011:** answers already carry their evaluation time; the window makes it meaningful.

## Tests

- `registry::messaging` unit tests: 22 pass. New ones cover:
  - the 0.3 record carries the window and stays lowerCamelCase;
  - an end not after the start is not sent;
  - a 0.3 record reads back with its window;
  - the window wins over the context dates.
- `registry_didcomm` integration tests (in-process mediator): 9 pass. The write and read tests now expect 0.3. New: `a_registry_without_put_0_3_gets_the_0_1_record` (fallback on `unsupportedVersion`, and the next write goes straight to 0.1).
- Fails until trust-tasks 0.35: the census test named above.

## Pre-merge checklist

- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2): no new clients; same reply window
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3): the version memory is an `AtomicBool`
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1): the sync job is unchanged; a put replaces the record, so a resend is idempotent
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4): one re-send, only on `unsupportedVersion`, of an idempotent put
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5): n/a
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6): n/a
- [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, deny_unknown_fields where security-relevant, schema registered, all consumers (incl. JS) updated (R3.*): camelCase from the registered specs (`put/0.3`, `query/0.3`); 0.1 readers kept working via the `context` copy
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive; fail-closed if enforcement can't start (R5.*): a record missing `recognized` still reads as departed (R3.3)
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified; background-job failures are surfaced (R6.*): the downgrade to 0.1 is logged (`warn`) with the registry and task
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1)
- [x] Deviations from this guide flagged explicitly with rule numbers

Follow-up to #2300, which merged before this commit reached it.

`trust-tasks-rs` 0.35 with every spec needs ~14 GB to compile (13 GB on 0.34), and the macOS runner has 7 GB. ## What and why

The lockstep move to `trust-tasks-rs` 0.35, the release #2287 needs: its census test refuses `registry/record/put/0.3` and `query/0.3` until VTI is on 0.35.

- `trust-tasks-rs`, `-proof`, `-https`, `-didcomm`, `-tsp` and `-capability-client` 0.34 → 0.35 (0.35.3), with `affinidi-messaging-sdk` 0.41, `affinidi-tdk` 0.33 (affinidi/affinidi-tdk-rs#975) and the mediator crates 0.46 (`mediator-admin`, `mediator-tui`, `test-mediator`), which are built on them. - 0.35 marks every superseded spec version deprecated (trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#921). VTI still names many of them (1,869 uses across 13 crates) while it moves to the current versions, so `deprecated` is allowed in `[workspace.lints.rust]` and, with a pointer to it, in `room-host`, `vti-rooms`, `vti-voting` and `vti-witness`, which do not inherit the workspace lints. The note says to remove it once that move is done, before those versions are withdrawn (about 90 days after they were superseded). Removing it then lists whatever is left.
- 0.35's Type URI parser accepts any scheme but `http`, case-insensitively, so third-party registries can be named (trustoverip/dtgwg-trust-tasks-tf#922, #934), and it keeps the authority as written. `HTTPS://trusttasks.org/…` therefore parses now, as a lookalike authority rather than an unparseable string. `purpose_for_document_type` grants the attestation purpose only to the canonical `https://trusttasks.org` authority, so it still gets `Authentication`, like `https://TrustTasks.org/…` already does. `vta-sdk/tests/proof_purpose_classifier.rs` moves the case to that list.

- **CI memory.** `trust-tasks-rs` with every spec peaks at ~14 GB to compile on 0.35.3 (13 GB on 0.34.1; 14.9 GB for a release build), and the ubuntu-latest runner has 16 GB. The first run of this PR had Clippy, every Test job and both Docker images killed mid-compile. A new `.github/actions/add-swap` adds 16 GB of swap on `/mnt`; `rust-cache` calls it, so every compile job in `ci.yml` gets it, and the mobile, semver-report, release-bump-guard and Docker jobs call it directly. The macOS iOS legs page on their 7 GB anyway (46 and 60+ minutes against 31-34 on main), so the mobile limit is 90 minutes for now. Both note that they go when VTI compiles only the spec versions it uses (`trust-tasks-build`), which is the lasting fix.

**Later:** SDK 0.43 speaks the `messaging/*` 0.2 tasks and mediator 0.47 serves them (affinidi/affinidi-tdk-rs#977, affinidi/affinidi-messaging-mediator#40, #42). VTI takes both together once mediator 0.47 is released.

## Requirements

None.

none

- [x] No `version =` edits in any `Cargo.toml` (dependency requirements only)
- [x] Tests cover the change; `cargo fmt` and `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` are clean (workspace, and `-p vtc-service --features vetting-pcs,voting`)

`cargo test --workspace --no-fail-fast`: 10,242 passed, 0 failed, including `every_bound_canonical_task_exists_in_the_registry`.

### Pre-merge checklist (vti-stack-development-guide §9)

- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2): none added
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3): none added
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1): no code path changed
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4): none added
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5): untouched
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6): untouched

title: docs: GETTING-STARTED pins and generates the task it uses, in all four languages
body:
Follow-up to #954. GETTING-STARTED taught the prebuilt modules that #954 deprecated. It now starts where an application does: `trust-tasks add acl/grant/0.2`, then each language's generator.

**§1, "Pin the tasks you use, then one dependency line":**
- The CLI, then the facade with `default-features = false`, plus a `build.rs` that generates through it (`runtime_path("::trust_tasks")`).
- `trust-tasks generate --lang ts|go|dart` for the other three.
- The facade line said `version = "0.1"`; it's now 0.35.
- The advice about trimming the 26 per-family features is gone, along with the modules it referred to.

**§2, Rust:** still extracted verbatim from a runnable example, and `getting_started_snippets` still enforces it.
- The example is now an application of its own, `examples/getting-started`: `trust-tasks.lock` pinning `acl/grant/0.2`, its vendored bundle, and a `build.rs`. A facade-crate example can't have its own build script.
- The only code change is the `use` line: generated `tasks::acl::grant::v0_2` replaces `trust_tasks::specs::acl::grant::v0_2`.
- `cargo run -p trust-tasks-example-getting-started` runs the signed round trip end to end.

**§3–3b, TypeScript, Go and Dart:**
- They import the runtime and the generated module.
- They move from `acl/grant` 0.1, which is superseded, to 0.2, as the Rust uses.
- Every name was checked against generated 0.2 code and the consumer example apps. Go has no `declareExtends`: it passes `tasks.ExtendsOf` to `ReadForSpecWith` where needed.

**Also:**
- The facade's README and crate docs point at the new example.
- The facade drops the dev-dependencies only the old example used.
- The new crate is `publish = false` and excluded from `cargo package`.

**Checked:** `cargo clippy -D warnings` passes on the new crate and the facade, with default and all features. `getting_started_snippets` passes, and the example runs.

title: feat: the prebuilt specification modules are deprecated in all four libraries; generate the tasks you use
body:
Milestone 5 of `docs/design/consumer-side-generation.md`, deprecated now as decided. Every prebuilt specification module outside the framework's own (`trust-task-*`, `trust-ceremony-*`, `_framework/`) is marked deprecated, pointing at the CLI and each language's generator.

**Nothing is removed.** The withdrawal batch that removes them is chosen later, and is at least 90 days after this releases (earliest 1 Apr 2027).

**Where each library marks it.** Only on the prebuilt entry point, never the module body, which is also what the consumer-side generators emit:

| Library | Mark | Reported by |
|---|---|---|
| Rust | `#[deprecated]` on the 34 gated family modules in `trust-tasks-rs/src/specs/mod.rs` (trust-tasks-codegen). It reaches every path and item underneath. | rustc. A build with `-D warnings` fails until the code migrates or allows it. |
| TypeScript | 1,257 root re-exports, spelled `import * as _X …; /** @deprecated … */ export import X = _X;`. TypeScript ignores `@deprecated` on `export * as`. | Editors and `no-deprecated` lint. Deep imports of a module file aren't marked: TypeScript has no module-level deprecation. |
| Go | A `Deprecated:` paragraph in each prebuilt package doc | gopls and staticcheck SA1019 |
| Dart | `@Deprecated` on each prebuilt `library` directive | Analyzer `deprecated_member_use`, on import from another package |

**Checked:**
- **Rust:**
  - Workspace `cargo clippy --all-targets -D warnings` is clean with all features and with default features.
  - The single-family (`vault`) build and tests pass.
  - The consumer example app runs, and its generated tasks are unmarked.
  - The `getting_started_snippets` test passes.
  - Codegen is drift-free.
  - Our own uses are all test modules, integration tests and examples. Each now carries `#[allow(deprecated)]`. No runtime code uses a deprecated family.
- **TypeScript:**
  - `tsc`, 123 tests and smoke pass.
  - API compatibility against 0.27.8 passes: 61 added, nothing removed or changed.
  - Every one of the 1,257 marks is in `dist/index.d.ts`.
- **Go:** `vet` and tests pass. The equivalence test (1,127 packages) passes with the new doc masked.
- **Dart:**
  - Analyze with `--fatal-infos` and 150 tests pass.
  - `analysis_options` ignores the same-package diagnostic that SDK 3.3 reports for the package's own tests.
  - Equivalence is unchanged: 1,106 identical plus the 14 known reorderings.
- **Cross-language:** `check-bindings` passes, with all four agreeing. Each equivalence test masks exactly the mark.

**Docs:** GETTING-STARTED, the four library READMEs, the design doc ("Milestone 5") and CLAUDE.md.

**Follow-up:** GETTING-STARTED's walkthroughs (§2–3b) still use the prebuilt modules; the notice at the top says so. I'd rewrite them onto generated code in a separate PR.

**Downstream:** the ~25 crates on crates.io that depend on `trust-tasks-rs`, mostly VTA, VTC, did-hosting, trust-registry and openvtc, get deprecation warnings when they take this release. Builds with `-D warnings` fail until they migrate or add `#[allow(deprecated)]`. The mediator already generates its own types (its #40).
